notes: Wild fennel (fronda di finocchietto) is the leafy fronds, not the seeds. In Australia, you may find it frozen in the Asian or Italian section; if not, a small amount of fresh dill mixed with a pinch of ground fennel seed is an acceptable substitute, though the taste won't be quite the same.
The pasta can be made up to 2 hours ahead and kept covered on the bench. You can also freeze it on a tray, then bag it; cook from frozen, adding 1–2 minutes to the cooking time.
If fresh sardines are hard to find, use tinned sardines in oil (drain well and add them to the sauce at the end, just to warm through, so they don't fall apart).
Food safety: Raw and lightly cooked foods aren't recommended for pregnant women, young children, older people or anyone with a weakened immune system.

steps.text: Make the pasta: pile the flour on a clean bench, make a well in the centre and crack the eggs into it. With a fork, beat the eggs lightly, then gradually incorporate the flour, mixing with your fingers until a shaggy dough forms. Knead for 10 minutes until smooth and elastic. Wrap in plastic wrap and rest for 30 minutes.
While the dough rests, steep the saffron in the warm water until the colour is deep gold, about 5 minutes.
In a small frying pan over medium heat, lightly toast the pine nuts, shaking often, until fragrant, about 3 minutes. Set aside.

Heat the olive oil in a large frying pan over medium heat. Add the sliced onion and cook gently, stirring, until soft and golden, about 8 minutes. Add the chopped garlic and cook for another minute until fragrant.

Add the fresh sardines (or break them into large pieces if very large) to the pan and cook gently, stirring carefully, until the flesh is opaque and beginning to flake, about 5 minutes. Pour in the saffron water and add the chopped wild fennel. Stir gently and simmer for 5 minutes. Season with salt and black pepper. Turn off the heat.
Bring a large pot of salted water to a boil until it is at a rolling, bubbling boil.

Roll out the pasta dough thinly (about 2 mm) on a floured bench. If you have a pasta machine, use it. Cut into long, irregular ribbons or shapes, traditional pasta ca' le sardine is not uniform; think rustic and handmade.
Cook the pasta in the boiling water, stirring gently, until al dente, about 4–5 minutes for fresh pasta. (Test a piece; it should have a slight bite.)
Reserve 200 ml of the pasta cooking water, then drain the pasta.

Gently reheat the sardine sauce over medium-low heat. Add the cooked pasta to the sauce and toss carefully, adding pasta water a little at a time to loosen the sauce and help it coat the pasta. The pasta should look silky, not dry or soupy.
Divide among bowls, scatter the toasted pine nuts over the top, and serve at once.

notes: The key is steam. Wrap that lid in a towel, no shortcuts. If your kitchen is very cold, you may need another 5 minutes.
Listen for the gentle crackling around 15 minutes in. That's how you know it's working.
If the tahdig is too dark or burns, it happens. Serve it anyway, bitter tahdig with yoghurt is still tahdig.

steps.text: Rinse the basmati rice under cold water until the water runs mostly clear. This removes excess starch. Soak in cold water for 30 minutes, then drain.

Bring a large pot of salted water (like the sea) to a boil. Add the drained rice and cook uncovered for about 8 minutes, until the grains are just starting to soften on the outside but still firm in the centre. The rice should be only half-cooked.
Drain the rice well through a fine sieve, shaking gently to remove excess water.
Melt the butter in the same pot over medium heat. Add the drained rice, stirring gently to coat with butter. Spread it in an even layer. Make a well in the centre with the back of a spoon.

Wrap the lid tightly in a clean kitchen towel so the steam stays trapped, then place it firmly on the pot. Reduce the heat to medium-low and cook for 30 minutes. You want to hear a gentle crackling sound after about 15 minutes, that's the tahdig forming.

Remove from heat. Let it rest for 5 minutes with the lid still on. Carefully run a thin knife around the edges of the pot, then place a large serving platter upside-down over the pot and flip everything out in one confident motion. The rice will mound on the platter with the golden tahdig crust on top.
Serve the tahdig hot with cold Greek yoghurt on the side. Break off pieces of the crispy rice and eat it together with a spoonful of yoghurt. This is the prize.

notes: Cook the shrimp in batches to avoid crowding the pan, this ensures even cooking and a proper sear.
Stone-ground grits take longer than instant grits and have better flavour. Don't skip the low-and-slow cooking.
Food safety:

steps.text: Bring the chicken stock to a boil in a saucepan. Slowly whisk in the grits, stirring constantly to avoid lumps. Once combined, reduce the heat to low and cook, stirring often, for 25 to 30 minutes until the grits are creamy and tender and pull away from the sides of the pan.
While the grits cook, fry the bacon in a large cast-iron frying pan over medium heat until crispy, about 8 minutes. Remove to a plate, leaving about 1 tbsp of bacon fat in the pan.
Add the butter to the frying pan with the bacon fat. Once foaming, add the garlic and cook, stirring, for about 1 minute until fragrant.

Season the shrimp well with salt and pepper. Add half to the frying pan in a single layer and cook without stirring for 2 minutes until the underside is pink. Stir and cook for a further 2 to 3 minutes until fully opaque throughout with no translucency. Transfer to a plate and repeat with the remaining shrimp.
Once the grits are creamy, stir in the cream, lemon zest, and cooked bacon. Season to taste with salt, pepper, and lemon juice.

Return all the shrimp to the frying pan and warm through over medium heat for about 1 minute. Top with spring onions and a drizzle of hot sauce if you like. Serve the shrimp alongside the creamy grits.

notes: Make it ahead: prep the vegetables and pat the chicken dry the night before, then assemble and roast when you get home.
Swap in whatever root veg you have, parsnips, sweet potato or beets all work. Keep the total weight around 900 g.
Leftovers reheat brilliantly at 180°C for 15 minutes, or shred the chicken and toss with the vegetables for a next-day grain bowl.
Food safety:
If fresh crawfish isn't available, frozen works just fine, thaw it first.
The roux is everything: low and slow, stirring often. Once it's dark brown, you've got the soul of the dish.
Make this ahead: the étouffée keeps for 3 days in the fridge and tastes even better reheated.
Cook chicken until it reaches 75°C in the thickest part and the juices run clear.

steps.text: Melt butter in a heavy-based pot over medium heat. Add flour and stir constantly, scraping the bottom, for 12 to 15 minutes until the roux is dark brown and nutty-smelling. This is the foundation, don't rush it or let it burn.
Add the chopped onion, celery and capsicum to the roux. Stir well and cook until soft, about 8 minutes. Add the garlic and cook for another minute.
Stir in the cayenne, paprika, oregano and thyme. Cook for 1 minute until fragrant.
Pour in the chicken stock, stirring to combine. Bring to a simmer and cook for 5 minutes to let the flavours blend.
Add the crawfish and stir gently. Simmer for 8 to 10 minutes until the crawfish is heated through. Season to taste with salt and pepper.
Serve over steamed rice, garnished with spring onion and fresh parsley.

notes: Żur (sour rye starter) can be found in Polish or Eastern European grocery shops, or made at home by fermenting rye flour in water for 24 hours. It keeps in the fridge for weeks.
Make this a day ahead if you can, the flavours deepen overnight. Reheat gently on the stove, adding a splash of water if needed.
Good kielbasa makes this soup. Don't skip it or use thin sausages; you need that smoky, meaty backbone.
Cook mince and sausages until they reach 75°C in the centre, with no pink left.
Make it a day ahead: the flavours deepen as it sits. Reheat gently on the stove top.
Serve with rice and peas, or plain white rice to soak up the curry.
Can't find goat? Lamb shoulder works, though it cooks faster, check it at 60 minutes.

steps.text: Heat the oil in a large, heavy pot over medium-high heat. Working in batches, brown the goat meat on all sides, about 3–4 minutes per batch. Remove and set aside.
In the same pot, add the onions and cook, stirring, until soft and golden, about 5 minutes. Add the garlic and ginger, and cook for another minute until fragrant.
Stir in the curry powder, cumin and turmeric, and cook for 2 minutes, stirring constantly, until the spices are dark and fragrant.

Return the goat to the pot. Add the water and crushed tomatoes, scraping up any browned bits from the bottom. Stir in the salt, pepper and thyme. Bring to a gentle simmer until the liquid is bubbling lightly.
Cover with a lid and simmer gently for 45 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the meat is beginning to soften.
Add the potato chunks and the white parts of the spring onions. Simmer, covered, for a further 30–35 minutes until the meat is fall-apart tender and the potatoes are soft. Taste and adjust seasoning.
Stir in the green parts of the spring onions just before serving. Serve hot in a deep bowl with the broth.

notes: Marinade the paneer for at least 10 minutes, but up to 2 hours in the fridge makes it taste even better.
Use a good non-stick pan or oil-brushed stainless steel so the paneer doesn't stick. Don't move the pieces around too much, let them get a nice golden crust.
If you have wooden skewers, soak them in water for 30 minutes before threading.

steps.text: Mix yoghurt, ginger-garlic paste, ground coriander, ground cumin, garam masala, cayenne, kashmiri chilli powder, lemon juice and salt in a bowl. Add paneer cubes and stir gently to coat. Set aside for at least 10 minutes (or up to 2 hours in the fridge).
Heat oil in a large frying pan or frying pan over medium-high heat until it shimmers.

Thread paneer, onion and capsicum onto skewers, alternating pieces (or cook them separate in the pan if you don't have skewers). Working in batches, cook until the paneer is golden on all sides and the vegetables are softened and charred, about 8–10 minutes.
Transfer to a serving plate, scatter with fresh coriander and serve hot with lemon wedges and roti or rice.

notes: Keeps in an airtight container in the fridge for 3 days.
Make ahead: prepare and slice the day before; store in an airtight container and eat chilled or bring to room temperature.
For extra fillings, try adding finely chopped mushroom or zucchini, just squeeze out excess moisture first.

steps.text: Blanch the spinach in salted boiling water for 1 minute, then drain and squeeze dry. Mix with the grated carrot and chopped spring onion in a small bowl.
Crack the eggs into a large bowl, add soy sauce, sesame oil and a pinch of salt, then whisk until well combined. Stir the vegetable mixture into the egg.

Heat 1 tbsp neutral oil in a large non-stick frying pan over medium heat. When hot, pour in half the egg mixture and tilt the pan to spread it into a thin, even layer, about 3 mm thick. Cook for 2–3 minutes until the bottom is set but the top is still slightly wet.
Starting from one long edge, roll the omelette tightly towards the opposite edge, using a spatula to help fold as you go. Slide onto a plate and set aside to cool slightly.
Repeat with the remaining 1 tbsp oil and egg mixture to make a second roll.
Once both rolls have cooled to room temperature, wrap them tightly in cling film and refrigerate for at least 30 minutes, this makes them easier to slice.
Unwrap and slice each roll into 1.5 cm thick rounds. Serve chilled or at room temperature.

notes: Freeze the cooked mince mixture in portions for an even quicker future dinner, just thaw and warm through.
Swap flour tortillas for corn ones, or lettuce leaves if you're out of bread.
Greek yoghurt works just as well as sour cream here.
Food safety: Cook mince and sausages until no pink remains and the centre reaches 75°C.

steps.text: Heat the oil in a large frying pan over medium-high heat. Add the onion and cook, stirring occasionally, until softened, about 3 minutes.
Add the beef mince and cook, breaking it up with a spoon as it browns, until cooked through (no pink remaining), about 5 minutes. Drain off any excess fat if needed.
Stir in the taco seasoning, frozen corn and frozen capsicum until the seasoning is fragrant. Add the water and bring to a simmer until the sauce has thickened and the vegetables are tender.
Cook, stirring occasionally, for 5 minutes or until the vegetables are heated through and the sauce has reduced slightly. Season with salt and pepper to taste.
Warm the tortillas in a dry frying pan for 30 seconds each side, or wrap in foil and heat in a 160°C oven for 5 minutes.
Set out the warm tortillas, spiced beef mixture and all the toppings. Let everyone build their own tacos.

notes: Make the pastry up to 2 days ahead and store in the fridge; the filling can also be made a day early and reheated gently before assembling.
If you can't find mixed mushrooms, use whatever is available, button mushrooms alone work just fine, though you'll lose some of that forest-floor flavour.
Food safety: Raw and lightly cooked foods aren't recommended for pregnant women, young children, older people or anyone with a weakened immune system.
Make it ahead: tabbouleh keeps in the fridge for up to 2 days in an airtight container. The flavours actually get better the next day.
Swap the fresh mint for dried mint if that's all you have, use about a third of the amount.
Serve with cos lettuce leaves or pita bread for scooping.
Make ahead: prepare the dalo and taro leaves the day before, stored in separate airtight containers in the fridge.
Swap the white fish for any firm fish, use what's fresh. Trevally, snapper or bream all work beautifully.
Use coconut cream mixed with a little water if you can't find coconut milk, or stir in 2 tbsp grated fresh coconut at the end for deeper flavour.
Food safety: Cook fish until it is opaque and flakes easily (63°C in the thickest part), and prawns until pink and opaque all the way through.

steps.text: Heat the oil in a large pot over medium heat. Add the onion and garlic, and cook gently until soft and fragrant, about 3 minutes.
Add the dalo chunks and cook for 5 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the edges start to soften.
Pour in the coconut milk and bring to a simmer until it is gently bubbling. Add the salt and stir well.
Add the fish chunks and taro leaves, folding them gently into the coconut milk. Simmer for 15 to 20 minutes, until the fish is cooked through and the dalo is tender.
Taste and adjust the salt and pepper. Serve hot in bowls with the creamy sauce spooned over.

notes: If you can't find fresh lemon myrtle leaves, dried lemon myrtle powder works well, use about 1 tsp mixed with a little salt and pepper to season the cavity and skin.
The pan juices make a simple sauce: deglaze the hot tray with a splash of water or stock, scraping up the browned bits, and drizzle over the carved chicken.
Food safety:
Gudeg keeps well in the fridge for up to 3 days and tastes even better the next day as the flavours deepen. Reheat gently on the stove.
Serve with steamed rice and a simple fried chicken or hard-boiled eggs on the side, Yogyakarta style.

steps.text: Heat a large, heavy-based pot or dutch oven over medium heat. Add the sliced shallots, garlic, and ginger, stirring constantly until they release their fragrance and soften, about 3 minutes.
Stir in the ground turmeric and coriander, stirring for 1 minute more until the spices coat the aromatics.
Add the jackfruit chunks, stirring well to combine with the spice paste, about 2 minutes.
Pour in the coconut milk and water. Add the bay leaves, makrut lime leaves, and red chillies. Bring to a simmer until gently bubbling and fragrant.

Reduce the heat to low and simmer gently, uncovered, for 75–90 minutes, stirring occasionally. The jackfruit will soften, fray at the edges, and turn golden as it absorbs the coconut and spices. The sauce will thicken and deepen in colour.
Taste and adjust the salt. The gudeg is ready when the jackfruit is very tender and almost dissolving, and the sauce is rich and silky.

notes: The marinade works best overnight. Plan ahead or marinate for at least 4 hours.
Leftover carne asada is great in tacos, quesadillas or over rice the next day.
Food safety:
This freezes beautifully, make a double batch and freeze half. Thaw overnight and reheat gently.
Any root vegetables work here: turnip instead of swede, celeriac, or even a bit of cabbage. Swap parsnip for more carrot if that's what you've got.
If you can't find a ham bone, a ham hock works just as well, or use chicken stock and add a splash of ham or bacon for flavour.
Marinate overnight if you have the time, it'll be even more tender.
Cook over charcoal if you can. It makes all the difference, mate.
Pink lamb is the way. It's not overcooked until it's grey.
Food safety: Braised beef and lamb cook well past 75°C on the way to tender, so they are safe once soft.

steps.text: Combine olive oil, lemon juice, garlic, oregano, salt and pepper in a bowl. Add lamb and stir until coated. Cover and marinate in the fridge for at least 2 hours, or overnight.
Thread lamb onto skewers, alternating with onion and capsicum pieces. If using wooden skewers, soak them in water first.
Heat your grill or chargrill to high until very hot, or get your coals hot and glowing, covered in a light grey ash.
Lay skewers on the grill and cook for 20–25 minutes, turning every 2–3 minutes to char evenly on all sides. The lamb is ready when it's charred outside and pink inside.
Rest for 2 minutes, then serve with lemon wedges and extra oregano.

notes: Make the broth the night before and chill it; the fat will solidify on top and you can lift it off. This also lets the flavours develop further overnight.
If chicken bones are hard to find, ask the butcher, they'll usually give them to you cheap or free. Chicken feet add real gelatin and depth to the broth.
You can poach a whole chicken breast in the simmering broth for the last 20 minutes, then shred it to serve. Or buy a rotisserie chicken and shred that instead.
Cook chicken until it reaches 75°C in the thickest part and the juices run clear.
Food safety:

steps.text: Heat a heavy-based pot or wok over medium-high heat. Place the unpeeled ginger and onion directly on the heat and char them, turning occasionally, until blackened all over, about 8–10 minutes. This gives the broth a subtle, sweet depth. Scrape away the worst of the char if you like, but don't wash it off.

Blanch the chicken bones and pieces: bring a large pot of water to the boil, add the chicken, and simmer for 2 minutes. Drain and rinse the bones under cold water, then scrape away any scum. This keeps your broth clear and clean.

In a clean pot, add 2 litres of water and bring to the boil. Add the blanched chicken bones, charred ginger and onion, star anise, cinnamon stick, garlic, coriander seeds and peppercorns. Bring back to the boil, then reduce the heat to low and simmer, uncovered, for at least 3 hours. The longer you go, the better, Mum simmers hers overnight. Skim off any foam that rises in the first 20 minutes.
About 30 minutes before you want to eat, taste the broth and adjust with fish sauce and salt. Strain the broth through a fine sieve, discarding the solids.
Cook the rice noodles according to packet directions, usually a few minutes in boiling water, until soft and tender but still slightly springy, then drain.

To serve, place a nest of noodles in each bowl. Ladle the hot broth over the noodles, then top with shredded cooked chicken. Scatter with fresh herbs, spring onion and chilli. Serve with lime wedges and extra fish sauce on the side so people can adjust the seasoning.

If you're making this ahead, simmer the broth the night before and refrigerate it. The next day, skim off any fat that has solidified on top, then gently reheat until steaming and bubbling lightly before serving.

Make the filling: heat the 2 tbsp ghee in a pan over medium heat. Add the dates and cardamom, stirring often, until the dates soften into a paste, about 5 minutes. Season with salt and set aside to cool.

Make the dough: in a bowl, cream the softened ghee with the sugar until pale, about 2 minutes. Add the flour, cardamom, cinnamon if using, salt and milk. Mix gently with your hands until the dough comes together, it should be soft but not sticky. If too dry, add a touch more milk.
Roll: working with about 1 tbsp of dough at a time, gently roll each piece into a ball. Flatten between your palms into a disc about 6 cm across and ½ cm thick.
Stuff: place a teaspoon of date filling in the centre of each disc. Fold the edges up and gently seal, then flatten again into a thick oval or disc shape.
Mark: using a fork or the tip of a knife, press a gentle pattern into the top of each cookie, traditional kleicha have a decorative crosshatch or lattice. Do this gently so you don't break through.

Heat the oven to 180°C, then bake: place the cookies on a lined baking tray, leaving a little space between each. Bake for 15–20 minutes, until the edges are golden brown but the centres still feel soft to the touch. They will firm up as they cool.
Cool: let them rest on the tray for 5 minutes, then transfer to a wire rack. They'll crisp up at the edges while staying tender inside.

notes: Make ahead: prepare the filling and dough the day before, keep both covered in the fridge. Assemble and bake fresh when you're ready.
Freeze: uncooked empanadas freeze well for up to a month. Bake straight from frozen, adding 5–7 minutes to the cooking time.

Food safety: Cook mince and sausages until no pink remains and the centre reaches 75°C. Raw and lightly cooked foods aren't recommended for pregnant women, young children, older people or anyone with a weakened immune system.
Use only the freshest, sashimi-grade ahi from a reliable fishmonger. Serve immediately after assembly.
Make the rice ahead and chill it completely before building the bowls.
Swap cucumber for daikon radish if you want a bit of crunch and bite.

The fish here is eaten raw or only cured in citrus. Buy sashimi-grade fish from a fishmonger, keep it cold and eat it the same day; skip it for anyone pregnant, very young, elderly or with low immunity.

Food safety: The seafood here is served raw or cured, so buy sashimi-grade, keep it cold and eat it the day it is made; for anyone who should avoid raw fish, cook it until opaque. Raw and lightly cooked foods aren't recommended for pregnant women, young children, older people or anyone with a weakened immune system.

steps.text: In a bowl, whisk together soy sauce, sesame oil, ginger and rice vinegar.
Add the ahi cubes and gently toss to coat. Let sit in the fridge for 5 minutes, until the surface of the fish is lightly coated in the marinade.
Divide the chilled rice between two bowls.
Top each bowl with marinated ahi and its liquid, then layer the cucumber slices and spring onions.
Sprinkle with sesame seeds and serve immediately with lime wedges on the side.

notes: The key is bringing the fish to room temperature first, it cooks through more evenly. If your perch is larger (750 g), add 2–3 minutes to the steaming time.
If you can't find perch, use any firm white fish whole, about 500 g: bream, snapper, or barramundi work well.
Sashimi-grade fish is not needed here; a regular market-fresh white fish is perfect.

steps.text: Remove the perch from the fridge 15 minutes before cooking to bring it to room temperature. This allows the heat to penetrate evenly. Pat dry with paper towel inside and out.

Fill a wok or large pot with water to a depth of about 5 cm and bring to a rolling boil. Set a bamboo steamer rack or metal steaming stand inside, or use a plate on chopsticks to elevate the fish above the water.
Place the perch on a heatproof plate that fits inside your steamer. Season lightly with salt inside the cavity and on the skin.

Carefully transfer the plate to the steamer. Cover with a lid and steam over high heat for 10–12 minutes, until the eye of the fish turns white and cloudy and the flesh is opaque when you gently press it at the thickest part near the backbone.
While the fish steams, warm the neutral oil in a small pan until just smoking, about 2 minutes on medium-high heat.
Remove the fish from the steamer and transfer to a serving plate. Scatter the ginger matchsticks and spring onion lengths over the top.
Pour the light soy sauce over the fish, then immediately pour the hot oil over the ginger and spring onion. The oil will sizzle and release their aromatics. Serve at once.

notes: Serve hot for a traditional bowl, or chill it and serve cold on a warm day.
The balance of tamarind and sugar is personal, start with less sugar and add to taste as you simmer.
This tastes better the next day, make it ahead and reheat gently.
If pearl onions are hard to find, use small shallots or just brown onion cut into chunks; the cooking time stays the same.
Serve with crusty bread, rice, or soft polenta to soak up the incredible sauce.
Food safety: Braised beef and lamb cook well past 75°C on the way to tender, so they are safe once soft.
Slice the steak against the grain, it'll be more tender. If it's too thick, pop it in the freezer for 15 minutes first to make it easier to slice.
Any supermarket steak works: the thinner you slice it, the less time it needs. Rib eye stays juicy, sirloin is leaner.
Make the marinade ahead and marinate the beef for up to 2 hours if you want deeper flavour, just let it come to room temperature before cooking.
Food safety: Steaks and roasting cuts of beef or lamb can be served pink: about 60°C in the centre is medium-rare, 70°C is well done.
This soup freezes beautifully and tastes even better the next day. Make a double batch on Sunday and freeze in portions for busy weeknights.
If you can't find egusi, you can substitute with equal parts ground almonds and sesame seeds, though the texture won't be quite the same.
Food safety: Steaks and roasting cuts of beef or lamb can be served pink: about 60°C in the centre is medium-rare, 70°C is well done.
Food safety:
Food safety: Cook chicken and other poultry until the juices run clear and the thickest part reaches 75°C.
Larb is best served warm or at room temperature. If you can't find toasted rice powder at the markets, toast and grind white rice yourself, it only takes five minutes.
The heat is important: adjust the chillies to your taste, but the dish should have a good kick. Nok doesn't hold back.
Food safety: Cook mince and sausages until no pink remains and the centre reaches 75°C.
Make the filling the day before and refrigerate; assemble and bake just before serving.
Works just as well in the slow cooker: combine all filling ingredients, cook on low for 6–8 hours, then proceed from step 4.
Food safety:
This stew improves the next day when the flavours have had time to meld. Cool quickly and refrigerate for up to 3 days, or freeze for up to 3 months.
If you don't have wine, use an extra 250 ml beef stock instead.
For camp oven: brown the meat and veg in a big Dutch oven, then pop it straight into the coals for 3 to 4 hours.

Food safety: Braised beef and lamb cook well past 75°C on the way to tender, so they are safe once soft. Raw and lightly cooked foods aren't recommended for pregnant women, young children, older people or anyone with a weakened immune system.
Make the carnitas up to 2 days ahead; reheat gently in a low oven or on the stove with a splash of water.
The reserved pork cooking liquid is liquid gold, use it to warm the carnitas or sip as a broth.
No corn tortillas? Flour tortillas work fine, but corn is the real deal.
Food safety: Cook fresh pork to at least 70°C in the thickest part.

steps.text: Heat the olive oil in a large baking dish or shallow ovenproof pan over medium heat. Add the onion and cook gently, stirring, until softened and translucent, about 5 minutes.
Add the garlic and cook, stirring, for 1 minute until fragrant.
Add the crushed tomatoes, drained beans, oregano, bay leaves, and chilli flakes. Stir well to combine. Season with salt and pepper to taste.
Add 120 ml of water to loosen the sauce slightly, the beans should be mostly submerged in tomato liquid.

Transfer the dish to a 180°C oven (or continue cooking in the pan if it's heatproof). Bake uncovered for 45–50 minutes, until the sauce has thickened and reduced slightly and the flavours have melded. Stir once halfway through.
Taste and adjust seasoning if needed. The beans should be tender and the sauce should coat them richly. Serve warm or at room temperature.

notes: Make the curry paste up to a day ahead and keep it covered in the fridge. Fresh fish is best for this curry, ask your fishmonger what looks good on the day.
Use whatever white fish is fresh and local: snapper, flathead or barramundi all work well.
Food safety: Cook fish until it is opaque and flakes easily (63°C in the thickest part), and prawns until pink and opaque all the way through.
Make a bigger batch and cool the broth quickly; it freezes well for up to 3 months.
If you can't find good pork bones, use a ham hock or extra corned beef – the broth won't be quite as rich but it'll still be aroha kai.
Fresh watercress is key. If you can't get it, try silverbeet (spinach) or spring greens – add them the same way, just wilted.
Food safety: Braised beef and lamb cook well past 75°C on the way to tender, so they are safe once soft.
Yassa is even better the next day. Cool quickly, cover and refrigerate for up to 3 days, or freeze for up to 3 months. Reheat gently on the stove.
Use thighs and drumsticks rather than breast, they stay moist and the skin crisps beautifully in the pan.
Food safety:
The dough can be made up to 8 hours ahead and kept covered at room temperature. If it dries out, spritz lightly with water.
The filling can be made several hours ahead and refrigerated. Assemble the dumplings no more than 1 hour before steaming.
If you don't have a bamboo steamer, use a metal steamer rack or even a heatproof plate set on chopsticks above the simmering water, the key is gentle, steady steam.
Food safety: Cook mince and sausages until no pink remains and the centre reaches 75°C.

steps.text: Make the dough: mix the hot water into the flour and salt with chopsticks or a fork until a shaggy dough forms. Once cool enough to handle, knead for 8–10 minutes until smooth and elastic. The dough should feel soft and slightly sticky, this high hydration gives you that tender wrapper. Cover and rest for at least 30 minutes.

Make the filling: mix the pork, gelatine, spring onion, soy sauce, sesame oil, shaoxing wine, ginger and sugar in a bowl. Stir until just combined, don't overwork it or it will become dense. Taste and adjust seasoning if needed.

Divide the dough into 16 equal pieces. Roll each into a ball, then use a small rolling pin or your fingers to flatten into a thin disc about 10 cm across, slightly thicker at the edges than the centre.

Place about 1 tbsp of filling in the centre of each wrapper. Bring the edges up and gather at the top, pleating as you go, then twist gently to seal. The dumpling should look like a little purse. Place seam-side up on a small square of baking paper (this stops it sticking to the steamer).
Set up a steamer: bring water to a boil in a wok or large pot, and place a bamboo steamer basket or metal steamer rack above it, making sure the water doesn't touch the base of the basket.

Working in batches, carefully place 4–6 dumplings seam-side up in the steamer, still on their paper squares. Steam over simmering water for 10–12 minutes, until the wrappers are translucent and cooked through. You'll see a slight sheen on them when they're ready.

Transfer the cooked dumplings to a serving platter. Warm the chicken stock gently with the ginger slices and spring onion if using, then ladle into small bowls or a shallow serving dish. Serve the dumplings alongside, with black vinegar and extra stock for dipping.

notes: Make the dosa batter 1 to 2 days ahead and keep it in the fridge. It ferments and becomes more flavourful. Use it straight from the fridge, don't bring it to room temperature.
If the batter is too thick, thin it with a splash of water. It should pour easily but still coat the pan.
The potato can be boiled and diced an hour ahead.
This keeps well in the fridge for 2 days and freezes beautifully for up to 3 months. Reheat gently on the stove.
Ayesha's tip: Don't rush the tomato-breaking-down stage. That's where the flavour sits. If you like more heat, add a pinch of dried chilli flakes with the ground spices or more green chilli.
Food safety:
Use the freshest sashimi-grade tuna available. If you're unsure about the source, ask your fishmonger.
Coconut vinegar adds a more authentic Visayan flavour, but white vinegar works well too.
Eat the same day you make it – the acid cures the fish but doesn't preserve it like cooking does.

The fish here is eaten raw or only cured in citrus. Buy sashimi-grade fish from a fishmonger, keep it cold and eat it the same day; skip it for anyone pregnant, very young, elderly or with low immunity.

Food safety: The seafood here is served raw or cured, so buy sashimi-grade, keep it cold and eat it the day it is made; for anyone who should avoid raw fish, cook it until opaque. Raw and lightly cooked foods aren't recommended for pregnant women, young children, older people or anyone with a weakened immune system.
The laksa paste can be made the day before and kept in an airtight container in the fridge.
Use the freshest mackerel you can find, the quality makes all the difference. If fresh mackerel is hard to find, try Spanish mackerel or another firm white fish.
The broth can be made ahead and reheated gently; cook the noodles fresh just before serving.
Food safety: Raw and lightly cooked foods aren't recommended for pregnant women, young children, older people or anyone with a weakened immune system.

steps.text: Soak the dried chillies in hot water for 10 minutes until soft. Drain and roughly chop.
Pound the softened chillies, garlic, galangal, ginger, shrimp paste and 2 tbsp tamarind paste together in a mortar until you have a rough paste (or blend in a food processor).
Heat the 2 tbsp oil in a large pot over medium heat. Add the laksa paste and fry, stirring, for about 3 minutes until fragrant and darker in colour.
Pour in the fish stock and bring to a gentle simmer. Add the halved mackerel and cook for 8 to 10 minutes until the fish is cooked through, the flesh should flake easily.

Stir in the coconut milk and the extra 2 tbsp tamarind paste. Taste and season with salt and palm sugar if you like a bit of sweetness. Simmer for another 2 minutes. The broth should be spicy, sour and rich.
While the soup cooks, blanch the fresh rice noodles in a large pot of boiling water for 1 to 2 minutes until just tender. Divide among serving bowls.
Carefully remove the mackerel pieces from the soup and divide among the bowls. Ladle the hot broth over the noodles.
Top each bowl with cucumber, pineapple, a hard-boiled egg half, fresh herbs and fried shallots. Serve hot.

notes: Make this the day before and reheat gently, the flavour deepens overnight.
Freeze the sauce in portions for up to three months.
Serve over fresh pasta, pappardelle, or rigatoni, with a scatter of fresh basil and parmesan.
Cook pork until it reaches at least 70°C in the thickest part (75°C for mince and sausages).
Food safety:
Borscht keeps well in the fridge for up to 4 days, and the flavour deepens each day. Reheat gently on the stove.
For a vegetarian version, skip the beef and use vegetable stock instead; the soup will need only 45 minutes on the stove after the vegetables go in.
Some cooks add 200 g cooked kidney beans with the potatoes for a heartier soup.
Food safety: Braised beef and lamb cook well past 75°C on the way to tender, so they are safe once soft.
Bredie improves overnight as the spices deepen. Make it the day before and gently reheat it.
If you can't find dried apricots, use dried peaches or a combination of apricots and raisins.
Traditionally made with mutton; lamb shoulder works beautifully and cooks a little faster.
Food safety: Braised beef and lamb cook well past 75°C on the way to tender, so they are safe once soft.

steps.text: Heat the oil in a large, heavy pot over medium-high heat. Working in batches, brown the lamb on all sides, about 3–4 minutes per batch. Set aside.
In the same pot, cook the onions over medium heat, stirring, until soft and golden, about 8 minutes. Add the garlic and cook for 1 minute more.
Add the turmeric, cinnamon, coriander and black pepper. Stir through the onions, cooking gently for 1 minute until fragrant.

Return the lamb to the pot. Pour in the stock and add the bay leaves. Stir in the golden syrup and apricots. Bring to a simmer, then reduce the heat to low, cover, and cook gently for 1 hour, or until the lamb is very tender.
Stir in the lemon juice, taste, and adjust the salt and spices if needed. The stew should be balanced, warm spice, a touch of sweetness from the apricots, and a hint of brightness from the lemon.
Serve hot, spooned over plain boiled rice.

notes: Make the potato mixture just before frying, it will start to weep if left to sit. If you must wait, drain and squeeze it again before cooking.
The crème fraîche topping can be made up to a day ahead and kept refrigerated.

steps.text: Squeeze the grated potato and onion firmly in a clean tea towel to remove as much moisture as possible, this is essential for crispy pancakes.
In a bowl, whisk the eggs, then stir in the drained potato and onion, flour, salt and pepper until combined.

Heat about 5 mm of oil in a large frying pan over medium-high heat. When the oil is shimmering, carefully spoon the mixture into the pan in loose mounds (about 6 cm across) and flatten them gently with the back of a spatula.

Fry for 4 to 5 minutes until the underside is golden and crisp. Flip and cook the other side for another 3 to 4 minutes until golden. Work in batches and keep cooked pancakes warm on a plate lined with paper towel.
While the pancakes cook, fold the dill into the crème fraîche and season lightly with salt and pepper.
Serve the warm pancakes topped with a spoonful of dill crème fraîche and a few pieces of smoked salmon. Finish with a squeeze of lemon if you like.

notes: This adobo tastes even better the next day, anak. Keep it in the fridge and warm it gently before serving.
If you don't have calamansi, use fresh lime juice or good white vinegar, both work beautifully.
Corazon always serves this with plain steamed white rice and a simple green vegetable.
Food safety: Cook chicken and other poultry until the juices run clear and the thickest part reaches 75°C.

steps.text: Heat the oil in a large heavy pot or deep pan over medium-high heat. Working in batches, brown the chicken pieces all over, about 5 minutes per batch. Set aside.
In the same pot, add the crushed garlic and peppercorns. Stir constantly for about 1 minute until fragrant.
Pour in the vinegar and soy sauce, stirring well to combine. Return the chicken to the pot and add the bay leaves and water. Bring to a simmer until the liquid is gently bubbling.
Reduce heat to low, cover, and braise gently for 40–45 minutes, turning the chicken halfway through, until the chicken is very tender and cooked through (the juices should run clear when pierced).
Taste and adjust salt as needed. The sauce should be rich and deeply flavoured.
Serve hot with steamed rice, anak.
Score the flesh of each eggplant half with shallow cuts in a crosshatch pattern, being careful not to pierce the skin.
Brush the eggplant flesh generously with oil. Season lightly with salt.
Heat a grill pan or barbecue to medium-high. Grill the eggplants flesh-side down for 6 to 8 minutes, until soft and charred. Turn skin-side down and grill for another 1 to 2 minutes.
While the eggplants cook, whisk together the miso, sugar, mirin, and dashi powder in a small bowl until smooth.
Transfer the grilled eggplants to a serving plate, flesh-side up. Spread the miso glaze generously over the hot flesh, it will warm and soften.
Scatter sesame seeds over the top and serve at once.

notes: Cold, leftover rice works best, warm rice gets mushy. Spread it on a tray and refrigerate for at least 2 hours.
The key to those crispy golden bits (cơm cháy) is letting the rice sit untouched on the hot pan for 30 seconds at a time before stirring.
For extra flavour, add a splash of soy sauce or a drizzle of chilli oil after cooking.

Food safety: Cook fish until it is opaque and flakes easily (63°C in the thickest part), and prawns until pink and opaque all the way through. Cool any leftover rice quickly and refrigerate it within an hour; reheat it until steaming hot.
Nduja keeps well in the fridge for weeks once opened. Wrap it tightly or keep it in an airtight container.
If you can't find nduja at your local deli, check the Italian section at a good supermarket or order it online, it's worth the hunt.

steps.text: Bring a large pot of salted water to the boil and cook the spaghetti until just al dente, about 9–10 minutes. Reserve 200 ml of pasta water, then drain.

While the pasta cooks, place the nduja and garlic in a large frying pan over medium-low heat. Stir gently for 2–3 minutes until the nduja starts to break down and release its oils, don't let it brown.
Add the crushed tomatoes to the pan and stir well to combine with the nduja and garlic. Simmer for 4–5 minutes until the sauce thickens slightly.
Pour in the cream and stir through. Season with salt and black pepper to taste. Add a splash of pasta water if the sauce is too thick, it should coat the pasta loosely.
Add the cooked spaghetti to the pan and toss gently to coat every strand. Add a little more pasta water if needed to loosen the sauce.
Divide among four bowls and finish with a generous handful of grated parmesan and a basil leaf, if you like.

notes: Make a big batch of sambal matah and keep it in the fridge for up to three days, it's brilliant on rice, eggs, or any leftover protein.
If you can't find fresh lime, use lemon or bottled lime juice, but fresh is so much better.
Tempeh keeps in the fridge for ages; fry it whenever you need a quick, protein-packed lunch.

steps.text: Make the sambal matah first: combine the shallots, chillies and garlic in a bowl. Add the lime juice and neutral oil, then taste and add salt. Set aside while you fry the tempeh.
Heat about 1 cm of neutral oil in a frying pan over medium-high heat until it shimmers. Test with a piece of tempeh, it should sizzle immediately.
Working in batches so you don't crowd the pan, fry the tempeh slices until golden and crispy on both sides, about 3–4 minutes total. Drain on paper towel and sprinkle with salt while still hot.
Arrange the hot fried tempeh on a plate and spoon the sambal matah over the top. Eat straight away, the contrast between the crispy, hot tempeh and the cool, bright sambal is the whole point.

notes: The key is drying the tofu well before frying, squeeze it gently between clean cloths to release as much water as you can.
Atsuage is best eaten straight away, while the outside is still crackling and the inside soft.

steps.text: Pat the tofu slices dry with paper towels. Blot both sides well, this is important for crispy frying.

Heat about 3 cm of oil in a small, deep pan to 160°C. The tofu will sink and then float as it cooks; if you don't have a thermometer, test with a wooden chopstick, bubbles should form steadily around it.
Carefully lower the tofu into the hot oil. Fry for 4 minutes until the surface is golden and crispy, then gently turn it over and fry for another 4 minutes until both sides are golden.
Warm the dashi in a small saucepan. Stir in the soy sauce and mirin.
Transfer the hot tofu to a bowl. Pour the hot dashi over it. Top with the grated daikon and spring onion. Eat while it's still steaming.

notes: Salt cod must be soaked for 24 hours before cooking. Start the night before.
Choricero peppers are essential, they give the sauce its deep colour and flavour. Find them in Spanish delis or good supermarkets; regular dried peppers work but won't taste the same.
This dish is best made in a heavy earthenware cazuela, but any heavy-bottomed pan works fine.

steps.text: Soak the salt cod in cold water for 24 hours, changing the water every 6–8 hours. This draws out the salt. After soaking, drain and place in a large pot with 1 litre of fresh cold water. Bring slowly to a gentle simmer, do not boil. Simmer for 8–10 minutes until the flesh is tender and flakes easily. Remove from heat, drain gently, and set aside on a warm plate. Keep the cooking broth.

While the cod simmers, prepare the sauce. Toast the dried choricero peppers briefly in a dry pan over medium heat, about 30 seconds each side, until fragrant. Soak them in 200 ml of warm water for 10 minutes to soften, then drain. Scrape the flesh from the skin with a spoon and discard the skins and seeds. You should have a dark red paste.

Heat the olive oil in a heavy pan over medium heat. Add the chopped onion and cook gently, stirring occasionally, for about 8 minutes until soft and golden. Add the sliced garlic and cook for 1 minute more until fragrant.

Stir in the paprika and cook for 30 seconds. Add the pepper paste you made, the tinned tomatoes, and 2 tablespoons of water. Stir well to combine. Simmer gently for 15 minutes, stirring often, until the sauce darkens and thickens slightly. Season with salt and black pepper to taste.

Carefully place the warm salt cod fillets into the sauce. Pour about 100 ml of the reserved cooking broth around (not over) the cod. Simmer very gently for 5 minutes, the cod will break apart if you're rough with it. The sauce should be rich, dark, and coat the fish.
Serve in deep earthenware bowls with the sauce spooned around the fish. Eat with good bread and a glass of txakoli or dry white wine.

notes: Make the quenelle mixture up to 2 hours ahead and chill. The sauce can be made while the quenelles poach.
If pike isn't available, perch, barramundi or any firm white fish works well, this is a weeknight dinner, not a pilgrimage.
Food safety: Cook fish until it is opaque and flakes easily (63°C in the thickest part), and prawns until pink and opaque all the way through.

steps.text: Pulse the fish fillet in a food processor until very finely minced. Add the softened butter and pulse until you have a pale, creamy paste. Work in the eggs one at a time, then fold in the cream by hand. Season with salt, white pepper and nutmeg. Taste a tiny spoonful by poaching it briefly in a small pan of water to check the seasoning. Chill for 10 minutes.

Bring the stock to a gentle simmer in a large, wide pan. Using two warm wet spoons, shape the pike mixture into quenelle shapes (or simply oval dumplings, don't fuss). Gently slide them into the simmering stock. They'll sink, then float to the surface when cooked through, about 4 minutes. Poach in two batches if needed so they're not crowded. Lift them out with a slotted spoon and keep warm on a plate.

For the sauce: melt the butter in a small pan over medium heat. Whisk in the flour to make a smooth roux and cook, stirring, for 2 minutes. Gradually whisk in the stock, then the cream, stirring until smooth. Simmer for 3 minutes. Stir in the cooked prawn and sherry, season with salt, white pepper and a pinch of cayenne. Taste and adjust.
Arrange the quenelles in a warmed shallow dish or on individual plates. Pour the Nantua sauce over and serve at once.

notes: Leftovers keep in the fridge for 3 days. Reheat gently on the stove, adding a splash of water if it's thickened too much.
Use rotisserie chicken, or shredded leftover roast chicken. If you don't have cooked chicken, add 300 g raw chicken breast to the pot with the stock and cook for 12 minutes before adding lentils.
Swap red lentils for brown lentils if you prefer a firmer texture; they'll need the full 25 minutes to cook.
Cook chicken until it reaches 75°C in the thickest part and the juices run clear.
Make the sauce while the pork cooks: mix mirin, soy sauce and water in a small bowl and you're ready to go.
No fresh pork cutlets? Thin chicken breast works just as well, pound it to 5 mm and it'll cook in the same time.
Leftover rice from lunch? This dish is your friend. Just make sure it's still warm when you serve.

Food safety: Cook fresh pork to at least 70°C in the thickest part. Raw and lightly cooked foods aren't recommended for pregnant women, young children, older people or anyone with a weakened immune system. Cool any leftover rice quickly and refrigerate it within an hour; reheat it until steaming hot.

steps.text: Set up your crumbing station: put the flour in one shallow bowl, beaten egg in another, and panko in a third. Season the pork with salt and pepper, then coat in flour, shaking off excess. Dip in beaten egg, then press into panko until fully coated.

Heat 3 tbsp oil in a large frying pan over medium-high heat. When it's hot and shimmering, carefully lay the pork cutlets in and cook until golden and crisp, 3 to 4 minutes on each side. The pork is done when it reaches 63°C in the thickest part. Transfer to a plate.
In the same pan, reduce heat to medium and add the sliced onion. Cook, stirring, until soft and golden, about 4 minutes. Add the mirin, soy sauce and water, and bring to a simmer.
Slice each pork cutlet into strips. Return the pork to the pan, nestled among the onions, and simmer for 2 minutes to warm through and coat with sauce.

Push the pork and onions to the sides of the pan. Pour the beaten eggs into the sauce, and without stirring, let them cook for 1 to 2 minutes until just set but still slightly glossy on top, you want the eggs to stay soft.
Divide the warm rice between two bowls. Carefully slide the pork, onions and egg over the rice, spoon the sauce over top, and scatter spring onions and nori strips if using. Serve immediately.

notes: Make the braised pork up to 2 days ahead. It keeps in the fridge in its sauce and tastes even better reheated.
The eggs are best cooked just before serving, but you can boil them ahead and reheat gently in hot water.

Food safety: Cook fresh pork to at least 70°C in the thickest part. Raw and lightly cooked foods aren't recommended for pregnant women, young children, older people or anyone with a weakened immune system.
The filling must cool completely before adding the pastry, or it'll go soggy. Make it the day before if you like.
You can freeze the uncooked pie for up to a month. Bake straight from frozen, adding 10–15 minutes to the cooking time.
Swaps: button mushrooms work fine if you can't get swiss browns, or use a mix. Crème fraîche instead of cream if that's what you've got.
Cook chicken until it reaches 75°C in the thickest part and the juices run clear.
Food safety: Raw and lightly cooked foods aren't recommended for pregnant women, young children, older people or anyone with a weakened immune system.

steps.text: Make the pastry: rub the butter into the flour and salt until it looks like breadcrumbs. Mix the egg yolk with cold water, pour it in, and bring it together into a dough with your hands. Wrap in cling film and chill while you make the filling.
Melt the butter in a large heavy-bottomed pan over medium-high heat. Season the chicken with salt and pepper, then brown it in batches, about 3 minutes each side, don't crowd the pan. Set aside.
In the same pan, add the onion and cook until soft, about 5 minutes. Add the garlic and mushrooms, stir, and cook until the mushrooms release their liquid and it evaporates, about 8 minutes.

Sprinkle the flour over the veg, stir well, and cook for 1 minute. Pour in the stock and cream, add the mustard, and stir to combine. Return the chicken to the pan, bring to a simmer, and cook gently for 10 minutes. Taste and adjust the seasoning. Let it cool completely, this is important or the pastry will be soggy.

Preheat the oven to 200°C. Pour the cooled filling into a 1.5 litre pie dish. Roll out the pastry on a floured bench to about 5 mm thick and about 2 cm larger than the dish. Lay it over the filling, press the edges down, and trim with a knife. Brush with beaten egg.
Bake for 25–30 minutes until the pastry is golden brown and the filling bubbles at the edges. Rest for 5 minutes before serving.

notes: Use well-aged kimchi for the deepest flavour; old kimchi that's been fermenting for months is better than fresh.
Don't skip the skimming step, it keeps the braise clean and clear.
Leftover kimchi-jjim reheats gently on the stove with a splash of water.
Food safety: Cook fresh pork to at least 70°C in the thickest part.
Make it the day before and reheat gently, the flavours deepen. Store in an airtight container in the fridge for up to 4 days.
Serve with couscous or warm flatbread to soak up the sauce.
If you can't find saffron, add a pinch of turmeric instead for warmth and colour.
Food safety: Braised beef and lamb cook well past 75°C on the way to tender, so they are safe once soft.

steps.text: Heat the olive oil in a large heavy pot or tagine over medium-high heat. Season the lamb pieces with salt and pepper, then brown them in batches, 3–4 minutes per side. Set aside.
In the same pot, cook the onion until soft, about 5 minutes. Add the chopped fresh garlic and fresh ginger, and stir for 1 minute until fragrant.
Add the ground ginger, cinnamon, and cumin, stirring constantly for 30 seconds until fragrant, to toast the spices.
Return the lamb to the pot and stir well to coat. Pour in the chicken stock and bring to a simmer. Cover and cook gently on low heat for 60 minutes, stirring occasionally.
Add the saffron threads and prunes, and stir. Simmer, covered, for another 20–30 minutes until the lamb is very tender and the sauce has thickened slightly.
Taste and adjust seasoning with salt and pepper. Serve hot, scattered with fresh coriander if you like.

notes: Make the sambal ahead and reheat it just before frying the ikan bilis, the anchovies need to go in hot to stay crispy.
If the ikan bilis are very small, you don't need to clean them; just rinse and fry whole.
For less heat, remove some of the chilli seeds before pounding.
Dough can be made ahead and refrigerated for up to 24 hours. Bring to room temperature before rolling.
Cooked varenyky freeze well for up to 1 month. Reheat by boiling briefly in salted water until they float again, or pan-fry with the caramelised onions.
The filling is traditional, but varenyky are also delicious filled with fried cabbage and mushrooms, or with cherries and sugar for dessert.
Food safety: Raw and lightly cooked foods aren't recommended for pregnant women, young children, older people or anyone with a weakened immune system.
Light soup keeps in the fridge for up to 3 days and freezes well for a month. Just reheat gently on the stove.
If you can't find groundnut paste, smooth peanut butter works just fine.
Food safety:
Make the filling up to 2 hours ahead and chill. Roll the börek just before frying.
If yufka dries out, cover unused sheets with a damp tea towel.
Leftover börek can be reheated in a 180°C oven for 5 minutes to crisp up again.
Cook mince and sausages until they reach 75°C in the centre, with no pink left.
Food safety:

steps.text: Heat 1 tbsp neutral oil in a large pan over medium-high heat. Add the chopped onion and cook, stirring, until softened and golden, about 4 minutes.
Add the beef mince and cook, stirring to break it up, until browned through, about 6 minutes. Drain off any excess fat.
Stir in the cumin, black pepper, salt and parsley. Remove from heat and let cool for 5 minutes.
Fold in the crumbled cheese and stir to combine. Taste and adjust seasoning. Let the filling cool completely.
Lay one sheet of yufka on a clean work surface. Place 3 tbsp of filling along one long edge, leaving a 2 cm border.

Fold the sides in by about 2 cm on each end, then roll tightly away from you, keeping it as firm as you can. The roll should be about 10 cm long and shaped like a tight cylinder. Repeat with remaining yufka and filling.
Heat neutral oil in a large, deep frying pan to 180°C (or until a small piece of yufka sizzles immediately when dropped in).
Carefully place 2 or 3 börek at a time into the hot oil, don't crowd the pan. Fry until deep golden brown all over, about 3 minutes, turning once halfway through.
Transfer to a paper towel to drain. Serve hot.
Drain the soaked chickpeas well and grind them with the ginger and green chillies in a food processor until smooth, adding a little water if needed. The batter should be fine and creamy.

Transfer to a bowl and stir in the salt and citric acid. Cover loosely with a kitchen towel or cling film and leave to ferment at room temperature for 8 to 12 hours, or overnight. The batter will become slightly fluffy and airy.

Set up a steamer: fill a large pot with water and bring to a simmer. Oil a round cake tin or two loaf tins, or a microwave-safe dish if you prefer. Place them in a steamer basket or on a trivet inside the pot so they sit above the water.
Add the bicarbonate of soda to the fermented batter and stir gently but thoroughly, this will make it light and spongy. Do this just before steaming, as it loses its effect if left to sit.
Carefully pour the batter into the prepared tin(s). Cover with foil or a lid and steam for 15 to 20 minutes, until a skewer inserted into the centre comes out clean and the top feels springy.

While the dhokla steams, make the tadka: heat the oil in a small pan over medium heat until hot. Add the mustard seeds and let them crackle and pop for 30 seconds, then add the curry leaves and asafoetida. Stir for another 10 seconds until fragrant.

Remove the dhokla from the steamer and carefully run a knife around the edges to loosen it. Turn it out onto a serving plate or board. Immediately pour the hot tadka over the top, letting the oil and seeds soak in.
Leave to cool for a few minutes, then cut into squares or wedges and serve warm with chutney if you like. Leftover dhokla can be wrapped and kept in the fridge for 3 to 4 days.

notes: The laksa paste is the backbone, a good quality one saves time. If you can't find tamarind paste, soak a ball of tamarind pulp in hot water for 10 minutes, then strain.
Make the broth first and it'll wait for you while you fry the tofu and fish cakes. The noodles should be cooked fresh just before serving.
Some people add prawns to this laksa. If you'd like them, toss in 200 g of cooked prawns if that's how you like it.
Makes a generous batch. Keeps in the fridge for up to 4 days or freezes well for a month.
If you can't find guajillo or ancho chillies, use 3–4 dried red chillies of any kind, the technique is what matters.
If you prefer a thinner soup, add more stock or water before blending.
Make the crispy onion topping ahead and store in an airtight container, it keeps for 3 days and turns any soup into something special.
Cook chicken until it reaches 75°C in the thickest part and the juices run clear.
The galette batter can be made up to 4 hours ahead and kept covered in the fridge. Bring to room temperature for 10 minutes before cooking.
Clean mussels well under cold running water, pulling away any beard. Discard any that are open and won't close when tapped.

Food safety: Cook fish until it is opaque and flakes easily (63°C in the thickest part), and prawns until pink and opaque all the way through. Throw away any mussels or clams whose shells stay closed after cooking. Raw and lightly cooked foods aren't recommended for pregnant women, young children, older people or anyone with a weakened immune system.
Swap the corned beef for tinned tuna or cooked chicken if that's what you've got.
Serve over rice or with fresh bread to soak up the sauce.
Any leftover veg works here, carrots, green beans, capsicum, whatever's in the crisper.
The dough can be made up to 4 hours ahead, wrapped and refrigerated. Let it come to room temperature before stretching.
The broth keeps for 3 days in the fridge and tastes even better the next day.
If you're nervous about pulling noodles, you can roll the final dough thin and cut it into thick strands instead, it won't be quite the same, but it'll still be good.
Food safety: Braised beef and lamb cook well past 75°C on the way to tender, so they are safe once soft.

steps.text: Make the dough: mix flour and salt in a bowl. Add warm water gradually, stirring with your fingers until a shaggy dough forms. Knead on a bench for 8–10 minutes until smooth and elastic. Cover and rest for 20 minutes.
While the dough rests, make the broth: heat oil in a large pot over medium-high heat. Add beef pieces in batches and brown on all sides, about 6 minutes total. Remove and set aside.
In the same pot, add onion, garlic, and ginger. Stir until fragrant, about 2 minutes. Add doubanjiang and stir constantly for 1 minute until it darkens slightly.

Return beef to the pot. Add sichuan pepper, cloves, star anise, bay leaf, and dried chillies. Stir to coat, then pour in stock. Bring to a simmer, then reduce heat to low. Cover and cook for 45 minutes until beef is very tender.
Season the broth with soy sauce and salt to taste. Keep warm on a low heat.
Divide the rested dough into two equal pieces. Oil your hands and the bench. Take one piece and stretch it gently into a rough rectangle about 20 cm long.

Fold the rectangle in half, then in half again (folding into quarters), and roll it loosely into a log. Repeat this process two more times, resting 5 minutes between each fold. This builds layers and develops the stretch.

Bring a large pot of salted water to a boil. Take your final dough log and, holding each end, gently stretch it by pulling away from your body and up over your arm, then back down, this distributes the gluten evenly. Stretch and fold, stretch and fold, until the noodle is about 50 cm long and very thin.
Pull the stretched noodle away from your arm and, using one fluid motion, lay it down into the boiling water. It will curl and coil, this is perfect. Repeat with the second piece of dough.
The noodles will rise to the surface within 2–3 minutes. Let them cook for another 1–2 minutes until they're just tender, then use a strainer to carefully lift them into serving bowls.
Pour hot broth into each bowl with the noodles. Top generously with coriander, spring onion, a drizzle of chilli oil, and white pepper.

notes: The ragù freezes beautifully for up to three months. Make a double batch when you have time.
Fresh tagliatelle is essential here. If you can't find it, use dried pappardelle, cook it to packet instructions instead.
Food safety: Cook mince and sausages until no pink remains and the centre reaches 75°C.

steps.text: Heat the olive oil in a large, heavy-based pot over medium heat. Add the pancetta and cook, stirring, until the fat renders, about 4 minutes.
Add the onion, carrot and celery. Cook, stirring often, until soft and golden, about 8 minutes. This is your soffritto, don't rush it.

Increase the heat to medium-high. Add the beef and pork mince, breaking it up with a wooden spoon. Cook, stirring often, until the meat is no longer pink, about 10 minutes. Season with salt and pepper.
Pour in the white wine and scrape the bottom of the pot to lift the browned bits. Let the wine reduce until nearly evaporated, about 5 minutes.
Stir in the tomato paste and cook for 1 minute. Add the crushed tomatoes and stir well.
Reduce the heat to low. The ragù should barely simmer, just occasional lazy bubbles. Cook uncovered for 2 hours, stirring every 15 minutes or so. The sauce will thicken and darken.
Pour in the milk and stir well. Continue to simmer on low heat for another 1 hour, stirring occasionally. The sauce will be rich, thick and deep brown. Taste and adjust the salt and pepper.
About 30 minutes before serving, bring a large pot of salted water to a boil. Cook the tagliatelle for 2 to 3 minutes, or until tender. Fresh pasta cooks fast.
Drain the pasta, reserving a cup of pasta water. Toss the tagliatelle with the ragù in the pot, adding a splash of pasta water if needed to loosen it. Serve with freshly grated Parmesan.

notes: This curry tastes even better the next day. Reheat gently on the stove or in the microwave until warm through.
Use any firm white fish you like, snapper, barramundi, bream or cod all work well. Avoid delicate fish that will fall apart.
Serve with steamed rice, appam, or flatbread to soak up the coconut broth.
Food safety:

steps.text: Heat the oil in a large pan over medium-high heat. When it shimmers, add the cumin and coriander seeds and toast, stirring constantly, until they release their fragrance and darken slightly, about 2 minutes. Watch them closely so they don't burn.
Add the curry leaves, then the onion. Cook, stirring often, until the onion is soft and golden, about 8 minutes.
Stir in the garlic, ginger and green chilli. Cook for another minute until fragrant.
Add the tomatoes and cook, stirring occasionally, until they break down and the raw edge is gone, about 5 minutes.
Pour in the coconut milk and stir well. Bring to a gentle simmer, then carefully place the fish pieces into the curry. Season with salt and cook until the fish is opaque and flakes easily.
Simmer gently, uncovered, for 8–10 minutes, until the fish is cooked through and flakes easily. Do not stir aggressively or the fish will break apart; you can gently turn the pieces once if needed.
Taste and adjust salt if needed. Serve hot, scattered with fresh coriander if you like, alongside steamed rice.

notes: Pilau tastes even better the next day. Reheat gently with a splash of water.
If beef chuck is hard to find, use beef shin or any tough cut that braises well.
Food safety: Braised beef and lamb cook well past 75°C on the way to tender, so they are safe once soft.
If you can't find fresh holy basil, Thai basil works fine, use the same amount. Regular basil will change the flavour but won't ruin it.
Prep everything before you start cooking: mince the garlic, slice the chillies, tear the basil, measure the sauce. Once the wok hits temperature, there's no time to stop.
Food safety: Cook mince and sausages until no pink remains and the centre reaches 75°C.

steps.text: Heat your wok on high heat until it's smoking hot, about 2 minutes.
Add the oil, then immediately add the minced garlic and sliced chillies. Stir constantly for 30 seconds until fragrant.
Add the pork mince and break it up with the spatula. Stir-fry, without stirring constantly, for 2–3 minutes until cooked through and starting to caramelize. You want colour on it.
Add the fish sauce and palm sugar. Toss well for 30 seconds to combine.
Pull the wok off the heat. Add the fresh holy basil leaves and fold through gently until just wilted and fragrant, don't let them brown.
Transfer the rice to a bowl or plate. Top with the pad grapow moo. Garnish with fried garlic and a fried egg if you want the real street-stall experience.

notes: Make the filling while the onion cooks, so everything comes together quickly.
Keep your hands wet when rolling, it stops the meat from sticking and makes shaping easier.
These freeze well raw; just add a couple of extra minutes to the cooking time straight from the freezer.
Food safety: Cook mince and sausages until no pink remains and the centre reaches 75°C.
Tastes just as good at room temperature, perfect for setting out on the table while you cook other things.
You can add a pinch of smoked paprika or cumin if you want a little more flavour, but honestly, the simplicity is the point.

steps.text: Heat the olive oil in a large frying pan over medium heat. Add the sliced garlic and cook, stirring gently, for about 1 minute until fragrant but not coloured.
Add the drained chickpeas and stir to coat with the oil. Cook for 2 minutes, then add the chopped spinach in batches, stirring as it wilts into the pan, this will take about 4–5 minutes in total.
Once all the spinach is wilted and the chickpeas are heated through, season with salt and black pepper to taste. Serve hot or at room temperature with a lemon wedge on the side if you like.

notes: If you can't find fresh crab, use 400 g tinned crab or frozen crab meat, thawed.
The noodle batter can be made up to 2 hours ahead and refrigerated; let it come to room temperature before using.
A bánh canh press makes thick, even noodles, but a large-holed colander works just as well.
Food safety: Cook fish until it is opaque and flakes easily (63°C in the thickest part), and prawns until pink and opaque all the way through.

steps.text: Make the noodle dough: Pour 100 ml boiling water over the tapioca starch in a bowl and stir well. Let it cool for 2 minutes. Add the salt, then gradually add cold water while stirring until the mixture is smooth and has the texture of thick pancake batter, it should be glossy and slightly translucent. Let it rest for 10 minutes.

Bring a large pot of water (at least 2 litres) to a rolling boil. Working in batches, push the noodle batter through a large-holed colander or bánh canh press directly into the boiling water. The noodles should be thick and rope-like, about the width of a finger. Stir gently to prevent sticking. Boil for 3-4 minutes until they float and are tender but still chewy. Remove with a slotted spoon and set aside.
For the broth, heat the chicken stock and water in a large pot over medium heat. Add the crushed garlic and simmer for 3 minutes until fragrant.
Stir in the fish sauce, sugar and crab meat. Simmer for 5 minutes to warm through and let the crab flavour infuse. Taste and adjust with salt and white pepper.
Divide the cooked noodles among four bowls. Pour the hot crab broth over each serving.
Top each bowl with fresh coriander, spring onion, fried garlic and sliced chilli if using. Serve with a lime wedge on the side.

notes: Food safety: Cook chicken and other poultry until the juices run clear and the thickest part reaches 75°C. Raw and lightly cooked foods aren't recommended for pregnant women, young children, older people or anyone with a weakened immune system.
Use bone-in chicken thighs if you prefer, they stay juicier. Cut around the bone and into cubes.
Presoaking wooden skewers for 30 minutes prevents burning, but metal skewers work best and cook faster.
Food safety: Cook chicken and other poultry until the juices run clear and the thickest part reaches 75°C.

steps.text: Thread the chicken cubes onto two metal skewers, leaving a small gap between each piece so they cook evenly until cooked through and golden. Pat dry with paper towel.
Heat the neutral oil in a frying pan over medium-high heat until shimmering, about 1 minute.
Place the skewers in the pan and cook without moving them for 4 minutes, until the bottom is golden and slightly charred.
Turn the skewers and cook for another 4 minutes until golden on the second side.
Turn once more and cook for 2–3 minutes, turning as needed, until the chicken is cooked through (no pink inside). The outside should be blistered and charred in patches.
Transfer to a plate, season generously with salt, and serve immediately with lemon wedges to squeeze over.

notes: The chickpea curry can be made ahead and reheated gently; make the bread fresh just before serving for the best texture.
If your kitchen scales aren't handy, the bread dough works with about 2 cups flour, 1 tsp baking powder, 1 tsp salt, 1 tbsp oil, and ¾ cup warm water.
Doubles are best eaten fresh and hot, the contrast between the warm spiced chickpea and crispy-soft bread is half the magic.
The syrup can be made an hour ahead and kept warm in a low oven or over a very low heat. It must be hot when you dip the koeksisters.
Make sure your oil is at the right temperature, if it's not hot enough, the koeksisters will be greasy instead of crisp.
Store cooled koeksisters in an airtight container for up to 2 days, though they're best fresh and warm.
Food safety: Raw and lightly cooked foods aren't recommended for pregnant women, young children, older people or anyone with a weakened immune system.

steps.text: Make the syrup first so it's ready when you need it. In a small saucepan, combine the sugar, water, ground ginger and cinnamon stick. Bring to the boil, stirring until the sugar dissolves, then reduce the heat and simmer for 5 minutes. Remove from the heat, stir in the lemon juice, and set aside. The syrup must stay hot.
Sift the flour, baking powder and salt into a bowl. Rub in the cold butter with your fingertips until the mixture resembles breadcrumbs. Do this gently, you want the dough light, not worked.

In a small jug, whisk the egg and milk together. Make a well in the centre of the dry ingredients and pour in the egg mixture. Mix gently with a fork until a soft dough forms. Do not knead. If it's too dry, add a few drops more milk.
Turn the dough out onto a lightly floured surface and shape into a ball. Wrap in cling film and rest for 10 minutes.
Roll the dough out thinly, about 3 mm thick. Using a sharp knife, cut into strips about 2 cm wide and 12 cm long.
Take each strip and plait (braid) it gently, pinching the ends to seal. The plaits should be loose and airy.
Heat the oil in a deep frying pan to 180°C (a cube of bread should brown in 30 seconds). Working in batches so you don't crowd the pan, carefully lower the plaited strips into the hot oil.
Fry for about 1 minute on each side until deep golden. They should be crisp and light. Remove with a slotted spoon.
Immediately dip each hot koeksister into the hot syrup, turning to coat all over. The syrup will cling and caramelize on the outside. Place on a rack or paper towel to cool and set.
Serve warm or at room temperature.
Drain the soaked salt cod and check for any remaining small bones. Flake the cod roughly into bite-sized pieces by hand, don't cut it; the irregular shreds are essential to esqueixada.
In a large bowl, combine the flaked salt cod, fresh tomatoes, red onion and olives. If using tinned tomatoes, drain well and add them too.
Dress with the olive oil and red wine vinegar, tossing gently to combine. Taste and adjust seasoning with salt (go easy, the cod is already salty) and a good grind of black pepper.
Let the salad rest at room temperature for 15 minutes, until the tomato juices have mingled with the dressing and the flavours meld, then scatter with parsley if you like and serve.

notes: The pickled beetroot can be made a day ahead and keeps in the fridge for up to a week.
If you can't find waxy potatoes, use any small firm potatoes and cut them in half.
Frikadeller freeze well uncooked; shape and refrigerate on a tray for 30 minutes, then freeze in a bag for up to three months.

Food safety: Cook mince and sausages until no pink remains and the centre reaches 75°C. Raw and lightly cooked foods aren't recommended for pregnant women, young children, older people or anyone with a weakened immune system.

steps.text: Start the pickled beetroot: layer the beetroot in a bowl. In a small saucepan, heat the vinegar, water, sugar, salt, pepper and bay leaf over medium heat, stirring until the sugar dissolves. Pour over the beetroot and let it cool while you cook the rest.

For the caramelised onions, melt the butter in a large frying pan over medium-low heat. Add the sliced onions and salt, stirring often. Cook for 20 to 25 minutes, until very soft and golden; set aside.
Meanwhile, start the potatoes: cut them into even-sized pieces and place in a pot of cold salted water. Bring to a boil and cook for 12 to 15 minutes, until tender.

While the potatoes cook, make the meatballs. Mix the pork, beef, grated onion, milk, breadcrumbs, egg, salt and pepper gently with your hands until just combined, don't overwork. Shape into 12 to 16 balls about the size of a golf ball.
Heat butter or oil in a large frying pan over medium heat. Working in batches if needed, cook the meatballs, turning gently, for 8 to 10 minutes total, until golden and cooked through.
Drain the potatoes and return them to the pot. Add the butter and a pinch of salt, and toss gently to coat.
Divide the potatoes among serving plates. Top with the meatballs and caramelised onions, then serve with the pickled beetroot on the side. Scatter with fresh dill if you like.

notes: Make ahead: Mix the dough and shape the arepas up to 2 hours before cooking, then refrigerate, bring to room temperature before cooking.
Swap: If you can't find queso de mano, fresh mozzarella or even mild cheddar works, though it won't be quite the same.
You can cook arepas on a griddle, heavy-bottomed frying pan, or a cast-iron frying pan, whatever you have. The sound and smell tell you more than the time does.

steps.text: Mix the corn flour, warm water and salt in a bowl, stirring until you have a soft, moist dough. Let it rest for 2–3 minutes.
Wet your hands. Divide the dough into 2 balls and gently flatten each into a thick disc about 8 cm across and 1 cm thick.
Heat a griddle or heavy frying pan over medium heat. Once hot, place the arepas on the griddle.
Cook for 6–7 minutes until the bottom is golden and crusty, then flip and cook the other side for another 6–7 minutes until both sides are golden and the arepa sounds hollow when tapped.
Using a thin knife, carefully cut a pocket into the side of each warm arepa without splitting it open completely.
Stuff each arepa with the cheese strips while the arepa is still warm, the residual heat will melt the cheese slightly. Serve immediately.
Rinse the lentils and place in a saucepan with 500 ml water. Bring to the boil, then simmer for 12 minutes until just soft but not falling apart. Drain well and let cool slightly.

In a large bowl, combine the warm lentils with the bulgur, diced onion, garlic, tomato paste, cumin, Aleppo pepper, cinnamon and parsley. Mix gently but thoroughly until it just comes together. Season with salt and pepper. Let sit for 10 minutes so the bulgur absorbs moisture.
With damp hands, shape the mixture into oval meatballs about 4 cm long. Place on a plate.
Heat a thin layer of oil in a large frying pan over medium-high heat. Once shimmering, carefully add the köfte in batches, don't crowd the pan.
Fry for 3 to 4 minutes on each side until golden and crispy all over. Transfer to a plate lined with paper towel.
Serve warm with lemon wedges and yoghurt on the side.
Heat the sesame oil in a large shallow pot or braising pan over medium heat.
Add the shiitake mushrooms, cut side down, and let them sit undisturbed for 2 minutes until they begin to brown.
Turn the mushrooms and cook for another 2 minutes, then pour in the soy sauce, sugar, and water.
Bring to a gentle simmer, then lower the heat and braise, uncovered, for about 15 minutes, until the mushrooms are tender and the liquid has reduced by half.
Taste and adjust the soy sauce or water as needed, the braise should taste rich but not overly salty, with a glossy, slightly thickened sauce and tender mushrooms.
Scatter the spring onions over the top and cook for 1 minute, then transfer to a serving bowl.
Finish with the toasted sesame seeds and a pinch of black pepper. Serve warm or at room temperature.

notes: Cook the rice in advance and cool quickly; reheat gently before serving if you like. You can marinate the tofu overnight.
Fried shallots keep in an airtight container for a week.
The marinade ingredients are flexible, add a pinch of chilli flakes or a splash of rice vinegar if you like.
