The cucumber salad can be made up to 2 hours ahead and kept in the fridge. Drain before serving.
Use the best-quality pâté and bacon you can find, this sandwich lives or dies by those two things.
Cook chicken until it reaches 75°C in the thickest part and the juices run clear.
Cook pork until it reaches at least 70°C in the thickest part (75°C for mince and sausages).

steps.text: Make the cucumber salad: toss the sliced cucumber with the vinegar, sugar, salt and pepper. Set aside for at least 10 minutes so the cucumbers soften and flavour the brine.
While the cucumber sits, cook the bacon in a frying pan over medium-high heat until crispy, about 5–6 minutes. Transfer to a plate lined with paper towel.
Lightly toast the rye bread until just crisp at the edges if you like it warm, or leave it as is.
Spread each slice generously with pâté.
Top each slice with 2 rashers of bacon, then a spoonful of the cucumber salad (drain off excess liquid first). Sprinkle with fresh dill if you have it, and a pinch of flaky salt.
Serve straight away while the bacon is still warm.

notes: The soup thickens considerably as it cools. Reheat gently with a little water if needed.
Make it a day ahead, the flavour improves overnight. Store in the fridge for up to 4 days.
This stew tastes better the next day. Make it ahead and reheat gently on the stove.
Dried limes (omani limes) are available at Middle Eastern grocers; if you can't find them, preserved lemon works but use less, the flavour is more intense.

Food safety: Braised beef and lamb cook well past 75°C on the way to tender, so they are safe once soft. If using dried kidney beans, soak them, then boil them hard for at least 10 minutes before simmering, to destroy a natural toxin.
Leftovers keep, covered, in the fridge for three days and taste even better reheated gently on the stove.
If you can find saucisson de Lyon or a good Lyonnaise sausage, use it; otherwise a quality pork sausage works fine.
Food safety: Cook mince and sausages until no pink remains and the centre reaches 75°C.

steps.text: Heat the olive oil in a large, heavy-based pot or braising dish over medium heat. Add the diced onion and cook, stirring, until soft and golden, about 5 minutes.
Add the chopped garlic and carrot rounds, and cook for another 2 minutes until fragrant.
Stir in the lentils, tinned tomatoes, chicken stock, bay leaf and thyme. Bring to a simmer until gently bubbling, then nestle the whole sausages into the lentil mixture.

Cover and braise over a low heat for 35–40 minutes, until the lentils are tender and the sausages are cooked through. The sausages should be opaque and firm inside (check by piercing with a knife; juices should run clear).
Remove the bay leaf and thyme sprig. Taste and season with salt and black pepper. Serve the sausages on a bed of lentils, spooning the braising liquid over the top.

Make the filling: combine feta, parsley, dill, spring onion, half the beaten egg, salt and pepper in a bowl. Mix gently, you want the cheese to hold together, not become mushy. Taste and adjust seasoning.
Set up your workspace: lay one sheet of yufka on a clean bench, long edge closest to you. If the yufka is very large, cut it in half lengthwise to make two strips.

Spoon about 2 tbsp filling along the bottom edge, leaving 2 cm on each side. Fold the sides in over the filling, then roll tightly away from you until you have a long, thin, cigarette-shaped roll. Press gently to seal. The seam should be on the bottom.
Brush the outside lightly with remaining beaten egg to help it seal and get golden. Repeat with remaining yufka and filling.
Heat the oil in a deep heavy-bottomed pan or Dutch oven to 170–180°C. If you don't have a thermometer, test with a small piece of pastry, it should sizzle immediately and brown in about 30 seconds.
Working in batches of 3 or 4, fry the börek seam-side down first until they're golden and crispy, about 2 minutes. Turn carefully and fry the other side until evenly golden, another 1–2 minutes.
Remove with a slotted spoon and drain on paper towel. Keep warm while you fry the rest.
Serve hot, while they're still crispy, with lemon wedges and yoghurt for dipping if you like (though purists like Nonna would serve them plain).

notes: Make your own aioli (garlic, mayonnaise, salt) or buy it, the rice and fish are the stars.
Ask the fishmonger for fillets that are thick and skin-on; the crispy skin is essential. Any firm white fish works.
The sofregit can be made ahead and refrigerated; reheat it gently before adding the rice.
Food safety: Cook fish until it is opaque and flakes easily (63°C in the thickest part), and prawns until pink and opaque all the way through.

steps.text: Heat the olive oil in a wide, shallow pan (a paella pan if you have one) over a medium heat. Add the finely chopped onion and cook, stirring often, until soft and golden, about 8 minutes. This is the sofregit, don't rush it, as the sweetness is the soul of the dish.
Add the grated tomato to the sofregit and cook, stirring, until the mixture is thick and darkened, about 5 minutes more. The tomato should lose its rawness and merge into the oil and onion.
Stir in the rice until well coated in the sofregit, about 1 minute. Pour in the warm seafood stock all at once, add the salt and saffron if using, and bring to a simmer.

Simmer, without stirring, for about 18 to 20 minutes, until the rice is tender and has absorbed almost all the stock. The top should look dry, with perhaps a few grains still glistening. Do not stir once the stock is added.

While the rice cooks, prepare the fish. Heat the olive oil in a large frying pan or on a grill plate over a medium-high heat until smoking slightly. Season the fish fillets with salt and pepper, then lay them skin-side down in the pan. Cook for 3 to 4 minutes until the skin is golden and crisp, then flip and cook for another 1 to 2 minutes until just cooked through.
Divide the rice among four shallow bowls or plates. Top each with a grilled fish fillet and a generous dollop of aioli. Serve immediately.

notes: Prep the vegetables the evening before and store in the fridge, makes baking day much easier.
Undhiyu keeps well and tastes even better the next day. Reheat gently in the oven or microwave.
If banana leaves aren't available, bake covered in parchment paper and foil; it won't have the same flavour but will still be delicious.

steps.text: Prep all vegetables: potatoes, sweet potato, eggplant, plantain, pumpkin and green beans. Thinly slice the onion. Have the chickpeas and peanuts ready.
Heat 3 tbsp oil in a heavy-bottomed pot or Dutch oven over medium heat. Add cumin seeds and let them crackle, about 1 minute. Add the sliced onion and cook, stirring, until golden, about 8 minutes.
Add asafoetida, ground coriander, turmeric and cayenne. Stir constantly for 1 minute until fragrant, being careful not to burn the spices.
Add all the prepared vegetables (potato, sweet potato, eggplant, plantain, pumpkin and green beans) and stir to coat with the spiced oil, about 2 minutes.
Add the drained chickpeas and roasted peanuts. Stir through.
Dissolve the jaggery in 60 ml warm water. Mix in the tamarind paste. Pour this over the vegetables and stir well to combine. Taste and add salt as needed.

Line a large baking dish or Dutch oven with banana leaves. Spoon the vegetable mixture into the centre. Fold the banana leaves over to cover, or add more leaves if needed to create a parcel. The leaves will char slightly but won't burn, and the vegetables should be tender when pierced with a knife.
Cover the baking dish tightly with foil. Bake at 180°C for 1 hour 15 minutes, until the vegetables are very tender and the flavours have melded into a rich, sweet-spicy-tangy mixture.
Unfold the banana leaves carefully (they will be hot), scatter with fresh coriander if you like, and serve warm with rotli, rice or as part of a thali.

notes: Make idli within a day or two of preparing your batter, the fresher it is, the fluffier the idli.
If your batter has separated, give it a gentle stir before using. A good batter ferments evenly and keeps in the fridge for up to five days.
No idli mould? Use a muffin tin or small bowls lined with cling wrap, they won't pop out as cleanly, but they'll steam just fine.

steps.text: Bring water to a boil in a large pot with an idli stand or steamer rack inside, until it is bubbling steadily and steam is rising. The water should come just below the rack.
While the water heats, check your batter. It should fall off a spoon in a thick stream, if it's too stiff, thin it with a little water. Taste and add salt if needed.
Oil the idli moulds well (the little metal cups that come with the stand). This matters: the idli pops out cleanly when they're properly greased.
Gently pour batter into each mould until three-quarters full. Don't overfill or they'll puff out of shape.
Carefully place the mould onto the steamer rack. Steam, covered, until a skewer poked into an idli comes out clean, about 8 minutes.
Let rest for 30 seconds, then slide a knife around each idli and turn the mould over onto a plate. They should fall out easily. Serve warm with sambar, chutney or warm oil.
Heat your cast-iron frying pan in the oven at 200°C for 10 minutes until very hot.
Whisk together the cornmeal, plain flour, caster sugar, baking powder and salt in a large bowl.
In another bowl, whisk the buttermilk, eggs and melted butter together until well combined.
Pour the wet mixture into the dry ingredients and stir until just combined, a few lumps are fine.
Carefully remove the hot frying pan from the oven and add a tablespoon of butter, swirling to coat the base and sides.
Pour the batter into the hot frying pan and return to the oven. Bake for 20–25 minutes, until golden brown and a skewer inserted in the centre comes out clean.
Let cool in the pan for 5 minutes before turning out or serving straight from the frying pan.

notes: Make it ahead: cool the sinigang completely, then store in the fridge for up to 3 days. Reheat gently on the stove. The flavours get better the next day, anak.
If you can't find tamarind paste, use 3 tbsp fresh lime juice instead, added at the end.
Food safety: Cook fresh pork to at least 70°C in the thickest part.

steps.text: Heat the oil in a large pot over medium-high heat. Brown the pork ribs on all sides, about 8 minutes. Remove and set aside.
In the same pot, fry the onion and garlic until fragrant, about 2 minutes.
Stir in the tamarind paste until well combined, then return the pork ribs to the pot.
Pour in the water and bring to a boil. Skim off any scum that rises to the surface. Reduce heat to low, cover, and simmer for 30 minutes until the pork is tender.
Add the potatoes and radishes. Simmer uncovered for 10 minutes until starting to soften.
Add the okra and leafy greens. Stir gently and cook for another 5 minutes until the greens are wilted and the okra is tender but still bright.
Season with salt and pepper to taste. Add the green chilli if using. Taste and adjust the tamarind and salt as needed, it should be sour, savoury and warm.
Ladle into bowls and serve hot with rice.

notes: Make ahead: Prep the chicken and onion earlier in the day, and cook the rice. The broth comes together in 10 minutes flat.
Chicken breast works too, but thigh stays juicier and cooks just as fast.

Food safety: Cook chicken and other poultry until the juices run clear and the thickest part reaches 75°C. Raw and lightly cooked foods aren't recommended for pregnant women, young children, older people or anyone with a weakened immune system.

steps.text: Bring the dashi, soy sauce and mirin to a gentle simmer in a large frying pan or shallow pan over medium heat, until small bubbles break the surface.
Add the chicken pieces and onion, and simmer for about 5 minutes until the chicken is just cooked through.
While the chicken cooks, lightly beat the eggs in a small bowl.
When the chicken is done, pour the beaten eggs slowly over the simmering broth in a thin stream, moving the pan gently so the eggs create soft curds. This should take about 1 minute.
Let the eggs set for another minute without stirring, they should be creamy and just cooked, not scrambled solid.
Divide the warm rice between two bowls and pour the broth, chicken and eggs over the top. Sprinkle with spring onion if using, and serve right away.

notes: Serve with steamed jasmine rice or on its own with a squeeze of lime.
If you can't find laksa paste, use 2 tbsp of any red curry paste as a swap, it won't be quite the same, but it'll still be good.
Makes good leftovers; reheat gently on the stove.
Food safety: Cook chicken and other poultry until the juices run clear and the thickest part reaches 75°C.

steps.text: Heat a large frying pan over medium heat. Add the laksa paste and fry, stirring, for about 2 minutes until fragrant.
Add the coconut milk and tamarind paste, stirring to combine. Bring to a gentle simmer until bubbling lightly and the sauce is smooth.
Add the chicken pieces and stir to coat in the sauce. Simmer for 15 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the chicken is cooked through.
Add the onion wedges and simmer for another 5 minutes until the onion is just tender but still holding its shape.
Taste and adjust seasoning with salt. Serve hot with a squeeze of lime and coriander if you like it.

notes: The soaking liquid is flavour, don't skip it.
Once you add stock, don't walk away. Risotto demands your attention for those 18 minutes.
Alba cooks would argue about the exact ratio. Make it how you like it.
Cook chicken until it reaches 75°C in the thickest part and the juices run clear.

steps.text: Soak the dried porcini in 200 ml of hot water for 10 minutes. Strain through a fine sieve, keeping the soaking liquid. Roughly chop the porcini.
Heat the stock in a separate pot until steaming, and keep it at a gentle simmer throughout cooking.
Heat the olive oil in a heavy-bottomed pot over medium heat. Add the diced onion and cook, stirring occasionally, until soft and translucent, about 5 minutes.
Add the rice to the onion and stir for 1 minute until lightly toasted. Pour in the white wine and stir until almost completely absorbed.

Add the porcini soaking liquid to the rice and stir until absorbed. Start adding the warm stock one ladle at a time, stirring gently, waiting for each ladle to be absorbed before adding the next. This takes about 18 minutes.
After about 16 minutes, taste the rice. It should be creamy but with a slight firmness at the centre of each grain. Stir in the chopped porcini.

When the rice is almost done and most of the stock is absorbed, remove from heat. Add the butter and parmesan, stirring gently until combined. The risotto should flow slightly on the plate, not stiff, not soup.
Season with salt and pepper. Serve immediately.

notes: This soup tastes even better the next day as the flavours deepen. Store in an airtight container in the fridge for up to 3 days; reheat gently.
If you can't find dried scallops, the soup is still good made with just shiitake mushrooms, use 10 or 12 instead.
Food safety: Cook fresh pork to at least 70°C in the thickest part. Cook fish until it is opaque and flakes easily (63°C in the thickest part), and prawns until pink and opaque all the way through.

steps.text: Bring a pot of water to a rolling boil. Add the pork ribs and blanch for 2 minutes. Drain and rinse the ribs under cold water until the water runs clear, scrubbing gently to remove impurities. This takes about a minute and makes the soup clean and bright.

In a large pot, add 2 litres of fresh water. Bring to a boil, then add the blanched pork ribs, dried shiitake mushrooms, dried scallops, smashed ginger, and half of the spring onion. Return to a boil, then lower the heat until the broth is at a gentle, rolling simmer with small bubbles.
Simmer uncovered for 60 minutes. The pork should be almost tender and the broth fragrant. Skim any foam that rises to the surface in the first 15 minutes.

Add the winter melon chunks. Bring back to a gentle simmer and cook for another 45 to 60 minutes, until the melon is very soft and translucent and the pork is completely tender. The broth should taste deep and savoury from the long cooking.
Taste and season with salt. Discard the ginger and the first batch of spring onion. Serve hot, garnished with the fresh spring onion.

notes: Makes great lunch packet food, it reheats well and tastes even better the next day.
Beef works just as well: use 600g diced beef steak and cook for 10 to 12 minutes until tender.
Store leftovers in an airtight container in the fridge for up to 3 days.
Food safety: Cook chicken and other poultry until the juices run clear and the thickest part reaches 75°C.

steps.text: Heat the oil in a large frying pan over medium-high heat. Add the mustard seeds and cook, stirring, until they start to pop, about 1 minute.
Add the onion and cook, stirring often, until soft and translucent, about 4 minutes.
Add the garlic, ginger and green chillies, and cook, stirring, for 1 minute until fragrant.
Stir in the cumin and turmeric, cook for another 30 seconds until fragrant.
Add the chicken pieces and cook, stirring frequently, until they're cooked through, no pink inside, about 8 to 10 minutes.
Pour in the vinegar and salt, and stir through. Taste and add more salt if needed. The dish should have a sharp, spicy edge.
Serve hot with rice, roti or hoppers, scattered with fresh coriander if you like.

notes: If you can't find fresh turmeric noodles, dried ones work fine, cook them a minute or two longer. Some shops sell them as bánh mì quang.
The broth is the hero here: don't skip the shallots and garlic, and don't be stingy with the fish sauce.
Prep the pork and prawns ahead of time, but make the dish fresh when you're ready to eat.
Food safety: Cook fresh pork to at least 70°C in the thickest part. Cook fish until it is opaque and flakes easily (63°C in the thickest part), and prawns until pink and opaque all the way through.
Use only the freshest sashimi-grade fish, ask your fishmonger if it's safe to eat raw.
Don't skip the draining step after the lime cure, or your oka will be too liquid.
Oka is best served straightaway, but you can make it up to 2 hours ahead and keep it cool.

The fish here is eaten raw or only cured in citrus. Buy sashimi-grade fish from a fishmonger, keep it cold and eat it the same day; skip it for anyone pregnant, very young, elderly or with low immunity.
Food safety: Raw and lightly cooked foods aren't recommended for pregnant women, young children, older people or anyone with a weakened immune system.
Make the patties up to 4 hours ahead and keep in the fridge; cook them just before serving.
The dipping sauce keeps in a jar in the fridge for a week, good for leftovers too.
Swap the herbs around depending on what's growing; mint and coriander are the core two, but thai basil and Vietnamese mint both work.
Food safety: Cook mince and sausages until no pink remains and the centre reaches 75°C.

steps.text: Make the dipping sauce first: whisk together fish sauce, sugar, lime juice, garlic, chilli if using, and warm water in a small bowl until the sugar dissolves. Taste and adjust the balance of salty, sour and sweet, it should be sharp and punchy. Set aside.

Put the pork mince in a bowl with garlic, fish sauce, sugar, salt and pepper. Mix gently with your hands until just combined, don't overwork it or the patties will be tough. Divide into 8 portions and shape each into a flat oval patty about 1.5 cm thick.

Heat a grill pan or barbecue hotplate over medium-high heat. Brush with oil, then cook the patties 3 to 4 minutes on each side, until cooked through (no pink inside) and charred at the edges. Transfer to a plate.
While the pork cooks, bring a pot of water to the boil and cook the rice vermicelli according to packet instructions until soft and tender. Drain and rinse with cold water to stop it cooking.
Arrange the lettuce, mint, coriander, thai basil if using, cucumber and noodles on a platter. Place the warm pork patties on top and scatter over the crushed peanuts.
Serve with the dipping sauce on the side, each person tears some herbs and lettuce, takes a bite of pork, and dips it all into the sauce.

notes: The pâté keeps in a sealed jar in the fridge for up to 4 days.
If you can find it, a layer of clarified butter poured over the top helps preserve it and keeps the surface from darkening.
A small glass of cold white wine or a squeeze of fresh lemon on the side is lovely.
Food safety:

steps.text: Bring a small pot of salted water to a gentle simmer. Add the cod livers and poach for 4–5 minutes, until they turn pale and opaque. Skim any foam from the surface. Drain well and let cool slightly.
In a mortar and pestle or small food processor, crush or pulse the warm cod livers with the softened butter until completely smooth and creamy, this should take 2–3 minutes.
Fold in the minced shallot, Dijon mustard and red wine vinegar, stirring until just combined. Taste and season with salt and pepper.
Press the pâté through a fine-mesh sieve into a serving bowl or small jar, pushing gently with the back of a spoon to create a silky texture. Alternatively, leave it chunky if you prefer.
Cover and chill for at least 30 minutes before serving. Serve on warm buttered toast or crackers.

notes: Make a big batch and freeze half. It keeps well and tastes even better reheated.
Goat meat works just as well, some say better. If using goat, cook for a bit longer, maybe 2 hours.
Food safety: Steaks and roasting cuts of beef or lamb can be served pink: about 60°C in the centre is medium-rare, 70°C is well done.

steps.text: Heat the oil in a large pot over medium-high heat. Add the meat and brown on all sides, about 8 minutes. Remove and set aside.
In the same pot, add the onion halves, whole chillies, crushed garlic and ginger. Stir for 2 minutes until fragrant.
Add the tomato paste, cayenne and black pepper. Stir well for 1 minute to coat the meat.
Return the meat to the pot. Add the crushed stock cubes and water. Bring to a boil, then reduce to a simmer until the broth is fragrant and the meat is tender.
Cover and cook for 1 to 1.5 hours, until the meat is very tender and the broth is rich and deeply flavoured. Stir occasionally.
Remove the onion halves and whole chillies (or leave them in if you like more heat). Taste and season with salt.
Serve hot in bowls, with a piece of meat and plenty of the spiced broth.

notes: Serve with roti, steamed rice or just with flatbread to soak up the sauce.
This curry is best eaten the day you make it, but keeps in the fridge for 2 days. Reheat gently so the fish doesn't toughen.
Food safety:

steps.text: Heat the oil in a heavy pot over medium heat. Add the sliced onion and cook, stirring occasionally, until soft and golden, about 8 minutes.
Add the garlic and ginger, and stir until fragrant, about 2 minutes.
Add the turmeric, fenugreek seeds and cumin seeds, stirring constantly for 1 minute to bloom the spices.
Pour in the coconut milk and water, and stir well to combine. Bring to a gentle simmer until the sauce is steaming and lightly bubbling at the edges.
Add the fish pieces and salt. Simmer gently, uncovered, for 12–15 minutes until the fish is cooked through and flakes easily with a fork. Don't stir aggressively or the fish will break apart.
Taste and adjust the salt. Add lime juice to brighten the flavour. Serve hot with roti or rice, scattered with fresh coriander if you like.

notes: Food safety: Cook fish until it is opaque and flakes easily (63°C in the thickest part), and prawns until pink and opaque all the way through.

steps.text: Pat the fish dry and season both sides generously with salt and pepper.

Heat the oil in a large frying pan over medium-high heat. Once shimmering, place the fish skin-side down and cook without moving for 4–5 minutes, until the skin is crispy and golden. Flip gently and cook for a further 2–3 minutes until just cooked through. Transfer to a warm plate.
Return the pan to medium heat and add the butter. Let it melt, then keep cooking, swirling often, until it turns golden and smells nutty, about 2–3 minutes. Watch it, it can burn quickly.
Add the capers to the butter and cook for 30 seconds, until they sizzle, split open and the butter smells nutty and turns golden brown. Remove from heat and stir in the lemon juice.
Pour the burnt butter and capers over the fish. Scatter with parsley if you like, and serve straight away.

notes: Injera keeps for a few days wrapped in a clean cloth at room temperature, or refrigerated for up to a week. Reheat gently in a covered pan.
The fermentation time is essential, don't rush it. The sour flavour and spongy texture both come from the three days of fermentation.
For the best results, use a proper injera pan (a shallow, wide non-stick pan) or a large non-stick crepe pan. A regular frying pan works but the edges can be harder to achieve.

steps.text: Mix the teff flour with about 375 ml of water and salt in a large bowl, stirring well to combine. The batter should be thick but pourable, similar to pancake batter. Add more water a little at a time if needed.

Cover the bowl loosely with a clean cloth and leave at room temperature for 3 days. Stir the batter once or twice a day. You'll see bubbles form and smell a pleasant sourness develop, this is the fermentation happening.
On the third day, stir the batter well. It should be slightly thinner and bubbly. If it seems too thick, add a little warm water and stir until it reaches the consistency of a thin pancake batter.
Heat a large non-stick frying pan or injera pan (or crepe pan) over medium-high heat. You want it very hot but not smoking. Don't oil the pan.
Once hot, pour about 150 ml of batter into the centre of the pan and immediately tilt and rotate the pan so the batter spreads out evenly to the edges, just like making a large, thin crêpe.

Cook for 2 to 3 minutes. The top will bubble and steam holes will form. You're looking for the bread to be cooked through but still pale, it shouldn't brown. The edges will lift slightly when it's ready.

Slide the injera onto a large plate once the surface is covered in small holes and the edges are just lifting and set. The spongy side (top) will have absorbed the steam and created the holes that make it perfect for scooping. Repeat with the remaining batter.
Stack the finished injera on a plate to keep warm. Serve immediately with your favourite stews and dishes.

notes: If you don't have a gas hob, skip the nori toasting, the rolls will still taste great untoasted.
Make ahead: assemble and slice the rolls up to 2 hours before serving; keep wrapped in cling film in the fridge.
The dough can be made ahead and refrigerated overnight; let it come to room temperature before stretching.
If your roti doesn't stretch thin enough, let it rest for a minute and try again, don't force it or it'll tear.
Dal curry keeps in the fridge for up to 3 days and reheats gently over low heat.

steps.text: Make the dough: mix flour and salt in a large bowl. Slowly add warm water while stirring, then add 2 tbsp oil. Mix until shaggy, then knead for 8–10 minutes by hand until smooth and elastic. Cover with damp cloth and rest for 20 minutes.

Meanwhile, make the dal curry: heat oil in a pan, fry onion until golden, about 5 minutes. Add garlic and ginger, cook for 1 minute. Add turmeric, cumin and chilli powder, cook for 30 seconds until fragrant.

Rinse lentils and add to the pan with coconut milk and 200 ml water. Bring to simmer and cook, stirring occasionally, until lentils break down and curry thickens, about 15–20 minutes. Season with salt to taste.

Divide dough into 4 equal balls. Lightly oil a bench top. Take one ball and press flat, then stretch it out slowly with your hands, working from the edge, until thin enough to almost see through, about 30 cm across. Don't worry if it tears.
Fold the stretched dough into a square or triangle shape, tucking in the edges to create layers. Flatten gently with your palms until it's about 1 cm thick.

Heat a non-stick pan or griddle over medium-high heat with a little oil. Cook each roti for 2–3 minutes on each side, pressing gently with a spatula, until golden and puffed with crispy edges. Transfer to a plate and cover with a clean cloth to keep warm.
Serve roti warm, torn into pieces, alongside the hot dal curry for dipping.

notes: If you don't have chilli oil, melt a knob of butter in a pan with a pinch of pul biber or dried chilli flakes.
The yoghurt can be mixed with garlic up to 30 minutes ahead; keep it at room temperature.
Food safety: Raw and lightly cooked foods aren't recommended for pregnant women, young children, older people or anyone with a weakened immune system.

steps.text: Mix the yoghurt with the chopped garlic and a pinch of salt. Divide between two shallow bowls and set aside.
Fill a saucepan with water, add a splash of white vinegar, and bring to a gentle simmer until tiny bubbles rise from the base, but the water is not at a rolling boil.

Crack an egg into a small cup, then slide it into the simmering water. Repeat with the remaining eggs, spacing them out. Poach for about 3 minutes, until the whites are just set but the yolks are still soft.
Using a slotted spoon, lift each egg out of the water and place on top of the yoghurt in the bowls.
Warm the chilli oil gently in a small pan, just until fragrant, don't let it smoke. Drizzle over the eggs and yoghurt.
Sprinkle the sumac and pul biber over the top. Serve straight away while everything is still warm.

notes: Make the sauce up to a day ahead and reheat gently.
You can roast and peel the chillies an hour before you fry them; keep them in a covered container at room temperature.
Fresh mozzarella is the closest you'll find to Oaxaca at Coles; if you can get to a Latin American grocer in Marrickville, grab the real thing.
Food safety: Raw and lightly cooked foods aren't recommended for pregnant women, young children, older people or anyone with a weakened immune system.

steps.text: Make the sauce first: put the tinned tomatoes, onion and garlic in a pot. Bring to a simmer and cook for 15 minutes until the tomato has broken down and the onion is soft. Blend until smooth (or blitz with a hand blender). Season with salt. Set aside.

Roast the poblanos directly over a gas flame, turning often with tongs, until the skin is blackened all over, about 5 minutes. If you don't have gas, put them under a hot grill. Place in a plastic bag for 5 minutes to steam, the skin will come off easier.
Peel off the blackened skin under cold running water, gently rubbing with your fingers. Make a slit down one side and carefully remove the seeds and white membrane, keeping the pepper whole.
Insert a baton of mozzarella into each pepper. Be gentle, they tear easily. Lay on a plate and let rest.
Beat the eggs in a bowl until pale. Spread the flour on a plate. Heat about 5 cm of oil in a deep frying pan to 170°C.
Working one at a time, coat each pepper in flour, shaking off excess, then dip in beaten egg to coat completely. Carefully slide into the hot oil.
Fry for 2 to 3 minutes each side until golden brown, turning gently. You want the outside crispy and the cheese melting inside. Drain on paper towel.
Pour the tomato sauce into a serving dish. Place the fried chillies on top, or serve the sauce on the side. Eat while the cheese is still hot.

notes: The salad is best eaten immediately while the papaya is still crisp. Don't make it ahead.
Adjust the chilli to your heat level, start with 1 or 2 birds eyes if you're not used to heat, then add more.
A proper pestle and mortar is key here; don't use a food processor, which will break down the vegetables too much.

steps.text: Pound the chillies and garlic in a mortar until bruised and fragrant, about 1 minute.
Add the long beans and tomatoes, gently bruise them, about 30 seconds, don't crush them to mush.
Add the papaya and gently pound and toss everything together, crushing and mixing, about 2 minutes. The papaya should start to release juice.
Add the lime juice, fish sauce and palm sugar. Toss everything well, tasting as you go.
Transfer to a plate, top with crushed peanuts, and serve right away while it's still crisp.

notes: Serve with steamed white or jasmine rice to soak up the broth.
You can swap the white fish for any firm white fish you have – barramundi is classic, but flathead and snapper work just as well.
Food safety:

steps.text: Bring the water and coconut milk to a gentle simmer in a large pot or deep pan over medium heat, until small bubbles form around the edge and the liquid is steaming.
Add the ginger slices and turmeric, stirring well. Let it bubble gently for 3 minutes until fragrant.
Add the fish pieces and the white parts of the spring onion. Return to a simmer and cook for 8–10 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the fish is cooked through and flakes easily.
Stir in the fish sauce and taste. Add salt if needed – go easy, as the fish sauce brings plenty of salt already.
Add the green parts of the spring onion and cook for 1 minute more until just wilted.
Ladle into bowls and serve hot with steamed white rice to soak up the silky broth.
Pat the drained chickpeas dry with a clean tea towel. This removes excess moisture so they'll bind better and fry crisper.

Add the chickpeas, onion, garlic, parsley, coriander, spring onions, green chilli, cumin, ground coriander and cayenne to a food processor. Pulse until the mixture is combined but still coarse, not smooth like a paste. It should hold together when squeezed but still have some texture.
Transfer to a bowl, stir through the flour, and season with salt and pepper. Refrigerate for at least 2 hours. Cold mixture holds together better when you fry.

Pour about 8 cm of neutral oil into a deep heavy-based pan and heat to 170°C. If you don't have a thermometer, drop a small piece of bread in, it should sizzle gently and turn golden in about 30 seconds.
Wet your hands lightly to stop the mixture sticking. Shape the mixture into 20 balls about the size of a walnut, then gently flatten each one slightly. Work quickly so they stay cold.

Carefully lower the falafel into the hot oil in small batches, don't crowd the pan or the temperature will drop and they'll absorb oil instead of crisping. Fry for 3–4 minutes until deep golden all over, turning halfway. They should be golden outside and cooked through inside.
Drain on paper towels and serve warm in flatbread with tahini sauce, fresh tomatoes and coriander. Eat them straightaway while they're still crisp.

notes: If you can't find fresh lemongrass or galangal, use 1 tbsp lemongrass paste and ½ tsp ground galangal instead.
This works just as well with any firm white fish cut into chunks, cook for 2–3 minutes until opaque.
Food safety:
This feeds a crowd and tastes even better the next day. Cool and refrigerate; reheat gently in a low oven.
No camp oven? Works just as well in a covered Dutch oven in the oven at home.
Food safety: Braised beef and lamb cook well past 75°C on the way to tender, so they are safe once soft.

steps.text: Combine wattleseed, bush tomato, native pepper, salt and black pepper in a small bowl. Rub all over the brisket, working it into the meat, and let sit for 10 minutes.
Heat oil in a heavy camp oven or large, heavy-bottomed oven-safe pot over medium-high heat. Sear the brisket on both sides until well browned, about 4 minutes each side. Remove and set aside.
Add onion and garlic to the pot and cook, stirring, until soft, about 3 minutes. Pour in stock and red wine, scraping up the browned bits from the bottom.
Return the brisket to the pot, fat-side up. Add bay leaves and thyme. Season with salt and pepper. Bring to a simmer until small bubbles break the surface of the liquid steadily.
Cover tightly and transfer to a 140°C oven (or set camp oven on low coals). Cook for 5 to 6 hours, turning the brisket halfway through, until the meat is so tender it falls apart with a fork.
Remove from the oven and let rest for 15 minutes. Skim any excess fat from the liquid. Slice the brisket or pull it apart, and serve with the pan juices.

notes: Make ahead: marinate the meat for up to 4 hours in the fridge, and caramelise the onions an hour before cooking.
The dum pukht (sealed steaming) is essential, resist the urge to open the lid. This is where the magic happens.
Some cooks add saffron soaked in warm milk to the rice before the final layer. If you have it, scatter 1 tsp saffron threads soaked in 100 ml warm milk over the meat layer.
Food safety: Braised beef and lamb cook well past 75°C on the way to tender, so they are safe once soft.
Food safety: Cook mince and sausages until no pink remains and the centre reaches 75°C.
The stock is the soul of this soup. If you don't have time to make your own, use a good-quality shop-bought beef stock, but warm it through gently, never let it boil hard.
Some cooks add a small handful of minced beef cooked separately; cooking it in the pot is simpler, and either way works.
Food safety: Braised beef and lamb cook well past 75°C on the way to tender, so they are safe once soft.

steps.text: Bring a pot of water to a rolling boil, until large bubbles break the surface constantly, and add the salt.
Add the edamame and return to a boil, then cook until the pods are bright green and the beans are tender.
Cook for 5 minutes if fresh, 4 minutes if frozen, until bright green and tender.
Drain in a colander and cool slightly.
Transfer to a bowl and serve. Squeeze the beans out of the pods into your mouth as you eat.

notes: Make it a day ahead and reheat gently at 160°C for 20 minutes, the flavours marry beautifully overnight.
Short on time? Buy good passata instead of tinned tomatoes and skip the simmering step.
If you can't find fresh mozzarella, use half the quantity of low-moisture mozzarella and mix it with the parmesan.
For a vegetarian version, use a vegetarian hard cheese (made without animal rennet).

steps.text: Arrange eggplant slices on a clean tea towel or paper towels. Sprinkle both sides generously with salt and let sit for 15 minutes to draw out moisture. Pat dry thoroughly.

While the eggplant rests, heat the tomato sauce: warm 2 tbsp of the oil in a large pan over medium heat. Add minced garlic and cook for 30 seconds until fragrant. Add tinned tomatoes, breaking them up with a wooden spoon. Tear in most of the basil leaves (reserve a few for garnish). Simmer for 10 minutes, stirring occasionally. Season with salt and pepper. Set aside.

Heat the remaining oil in a large frying pan over medium-high heat. Once hot, fry eggplant slices in batches for 3–4 minutes per side until golden brown and soft. Transfer to paper towels to drain. Don't crowd the pan; let them cook in a single layer.
Preheat the oven to 180°C.

Spread a thin layer of tomato sauce over the base of a 23 × 33 cm baking dish. Arrange a layer of fried eggplant slices over the sauce, overlapping slightly. Top with a layer of fresh mozzarella, then a sprinkle of grated parmesan. Repeat the layers, sauce, eggplant, mozzarella, parmesan, until everything is used, ending with a good handful of parmesan on top.
Bake uncovered for 30–35 minutes until the top is golden and bubbling at the edges. Let rest for 5 minutes before serving. Tear over the reserved fresh basil.
Heat the oil in a large frying pan over medium-high heat. Add the sliced onion and cook for 2–3 minutes, stirring, until just softened.

Add the chopped squash blossoms and a pinch of salt. Cook for 3–4 minutes, stirring gently, until the flowers have wilted and released their moisture. The mixture should be tender but not mushy. Taste and adjust salt.
Warm the corn tortillas in a dry frying pan or directly over a gas flame for 15 seconds each, or wrap them in a damp tea towel to keep them soft.
Divide the squash blossom filling between the tortillas, placing it on one half of each. Top the filling with pieces of cheese, then fold the tortilla in half.

In a clean frying pan, heat a little oil over medium-high heat. Fry the quesadillas for 1–2 minutes per side until they are warmed through and the cheese begins to soften. Don't cook them so long the tortilla becomes crisp, they should stay tender.
Serve immediately with salsa verde and a squeeze of fresh lime.

notes: Make it ahead: fry the rice earlier in the day and reheat gently, or serve at room temperature. Both sambals keep 2 days in the fridge.
Stretch it: add more veg sides like pickled papaya, blanched long beans or leftover roasted vegetables. Boiled egg, leftover chicken, or fried tofu work just as well as tempeh.
Food safety: Cool any leftover rice quickly and refrigerate it within an hour; reheat it until steaming hot.

steps.text: Make sambal matah: toss the sliced shallots and chillies with lime juice and salt, then pour over the hot oil and set aside to infuse.
Make sambal terasi: pound the chillies, shrimp paste, garlic and salt into a rough paste in a mortar, then stir through lime juice. (Or blend if you prefer it smoother.)
Heat the oil in a large pan over medium-high heat. Add the minced garlic and cook for 30 seconds until fragrant, then add the cooled rice, breaking up any lumps as it fries, about 5 minutes.
Stir through the spring onions, season with salt and white pepper to taste, and remove from heat.
Form the fried rice into small mounds on a large serving platter, each person gets 2 or 3 little portions to build on.

Arrange the tempeh, cucumber and tomato around the rice, and put both sambals in small bowls alongside. Everyone builds their own plate, taking a mound of rice and topping it with sambal, tempeh and veg as they like.

notes: Stockfish must be soaked in cold water for at least 4 hours (or overnight) before use, then flaked or shredded. Ask for it at West African or Asian grocers.
Make this soup in a big batch on Sunday and refrigerate for up to 3 days. Reheat gently and add a splash of water if it's thickened too much.
The okra will release plenty of slime, that's what makes the soup silky and satisfying. Stir it well as it cooks.
Food safety: Cook fish until it is opaque and flakes easily (63°C in the thickest part), and prawns until pink and opaque all the way through.

steps.text: Heat the palm oil in a large pot over medium heat. Add the chopped onion and cook, stirring, until soft, about 3 minutes.
Add the minced garlic and ginger, stir for 1 minute until fragrant.
Stir in the tomato paste and cook for 2 minutes, breaking it down into the oil.
Add the shredded stockfish and stir to coat. Cook for 3 minutes.
Pour in the chicken stock and bring to a gentle simmer. Cook for 15 minutes, stirring occasionally.
Add the sliced okra and stir well, don't worry if it looks very slimy at first. Simmer for 10 minutes.
Add the prawns and ground crayfish if using. Simmer for another 8–10 minutes until the prawns are pink and cooked through.
Taste and season with salt and black pepper. The soup should be thick and slippery. Serve hot over fufu.

notes: You can prepare the breaded chicken parcels up to 4 hours ahead and refrigerate them before frying. This helps them stay together and cook evenly.
If the oil is too hot, the coating will brown too quickly before the chicken cooks through. If it's not hot enough, the chicken will absorb oil and become greasy rather than crisp.
Serve with boiled potatoes and a simple salad of beetroot and dill, if you like.
Food safety:

steps.text: Mix the softened butter with minced garlic, fresh dill, salt and a pinch of black pepper. Divide into 4 portions and shape each into a small block. Freeze for at least 15 minutes until firm.

Place each chicken breast between two sheets of plastic wrap. Using a meat mallet or rolling pin, pound gently but firmly until the breast is about 5 mm thick. Work from the centre outwards, being careful not to tear the meat.

Lay one flattened chicken breast on a clean surface. Place a butter portion in the centre. Fold the long sides over the butter, then fold in the short sides to seal, creating a neat parcel. The seam should be on the bottom.

Place the flour on one plate, beaten eggs in a shallow bowl, and breadcrumbs on another plate. Coat each chicken parcel lightly in flour, shaking off excess. Dip in beaten egg to coat completely, then roll in breadcrumbs until fully covered. Place on a plate, seam-side down.
Heat the oil in a large, heavy-based frying pan over medium-high heat until a breadcrumb sizzles immediately when dropped in (about 160°C).

Carefully place the chicken parcels seam-side up into the hot oil. Fry for 5 to 6 minutes until the breadcrumb coating is deep golden brown, then gently turn and fry the other side for another 4 to 5 minutes until crisp and the internal temperature reaches 75°C.
Remove with a slotted spoon and drain on paper towels. Let rest for 2 minutes before serving. The butter inside will be hot, warn your family to cut carefully so they don't get splashed.

notes: Stinky tofu (chou doufu) is the star here, its pungent, funky smell is what makes it special. Find it in the refrigerated section of Asian grocers, often near the fresh tofu.
The tofu needs to be truly crispy outside to contrast with the QQ creamy interior. Don't skip the cornflour coating or lower the oil temperature.
Pickled mustard greens (xue cai) cut through the richness beautifully, swap for pickled daikon if you prefer something milder.

steps.text: Toss the stinky tofu cubes gently with cornflour and salt until coated.
Heat about 2 cm of neutral oil in a shallow pan or wok to 180°C. Test with a wooden chopstick, it should bubble gently around it.
Working in two batches, carefully slide the tofu into the hot oil. Fry for 4–5 minutes, turning once, until the outside is golden and crispy and the edges are bubbling. Drain on paper towels.
While the tofu fries, stir together the chilli sauce, soy sauce, sugar and 1 tbsp water in a small bowl.
Serve the hot tofu with pickled mustard greens on the side, the chilli sauce for dipping, and spring onion scattered over. Eat while it's still crackling.

notes: Make the sambal paste in advance (up to 2 days ahead) and store in an airtight container in the fridge. Bring it to room temperature before rubbing it on the chicken.
For less heat, use 1 or 2 chillies instead of 3. For more punch, add a bird's eye chilli or two.
Leftovers keep in an airtight container in the fridge for up to 3 days and are just as good cold the next day.
Food safety:

steps.text: Make the sambal paste: Combine the shallots, garlic, chillies, candlenuts, tamarind paste and salt in a food processor. Pulse until you have a coarse, chunky paste, not smooth. Heat 2 tbsp neutral oil in a pan over medium heat, add the paste and fry, stirring often, for about 5 minutes until it darkens and smells fragrant. Let it cool slightly.

Pat the chicken thighs dry with paper towel. Rub them all over with the cooled sambal paste, turmeric and coriander, working it into the skin and under it where you can. Ideally sit the chicken in a bowl for 30 minutes to an hour, but even 10 minutes helps.
Heat about 300 ml neutral oil in a large, heavy-based pan or wok over medium-high heat. Test the heat with a small piece of shallot, it should sizzle immediately.

Working in batches so you don't overcrowd the pan, carefully place the chicken skin-side down into the hot oil. Fry for 6–7 minutes until the skin is deep golden and crisps up, shaking the pan occasionally so it colours evenly.

Flip each piece and fry the other side for another 6–7 minutes until golden. The chicken should be cooked through, cut into the thickest thigh near the bone and check there's no pink; if unsure, the inside should reach 75°C.
Transfer the cooked chicken to a plate lined with paper towel to drain. Taste one piece and season with a pinch more salt if needed. Serve hot.
Get your braai hot, you want the coals glowing and ready.
Tear off a large piece of foil and lay the snoek in the middle. Season inside and out with salt and pepper.
Stuff the cavity with half the garlic slices and half the lemon slices. Top with a knob of butter.

Scatter the remaining garlic and lemon over the top, then dot with the last of the butter. Wrap the foil loosely around the fish, sealing it well so the steam stays inside, and bake until the fish is opaque and flakes easily with a fork.
Place the parcel on the hot coals and cook for about 10 to 12 minutes, until the flesh is opaque and flaking away from the bones.
Carefully unwrap the foil, watch the steam, and check that the fish is opaque and flakes easily. Slide the fish onto a plate. Spoon the buttery juices from the foil over the top.

notes: Make this a day ahead if you like, it keeps well in the fridge for up to 3 days.
Lucía sometimes stirs in a splash of water to loosen it on the day if it's thickened overnight.
Serve with small glasses of ice water on the side, or pour into shallow bowls if you're feeling elegant.

steps.text: Place the tomatoes, capsicum, cucumber and garlic in a large bowl. Pour over the olive oil and sherry vinegar, and add a pinch of salt. Let sit for 10 minutes to release the juices.

In batches, blend the vegetables and oil until completely smooth, this is a sieve-smooth gazpacho, not a chunky one. Pass the blended mixture through a fine sieve into a clean bowl, pressing gently to extract all the liquid. Discard the pulp.
Stir in the ice water to cool and lighten the soup. Taste and adjust the salt and vinegar to your liking.
Cover and refrigerate for at least 2 hours, or until well chilled. Serve ice cold in small glasses or shallow bowls.

notes: Base genep keeps in the fridge for up to 5 days, or freeze in ice-cube trays for up to 3 months.
If you don't have fresh turmeric, use 1 tsp ground turmeric instead.
A mortar and pestle gives the best flavour and texture, but you can use a food processor if needed, pulse until smooth, then stir through the lime and salt by hand.
Use day-old or cooled cooked rice, freshly cooked rice will clump and steam instead of fry.
Shrimp paste is pungent raw but mellows when cooked with oil and the other ingredients. Start with 1 tbsp and adjust to taste.
Double this easily if you're cooking for two, but it's designed for one burner and one wok.
Food safety: Cook chicken and other poultry until the juices run clear and the thickest part reaches 75°C.
Food safety: Cook fish until it is opaque and flakes easily (63°C in the thickest part), and prawns until pink and opaque all the way through.

steps.text: Preheat your camp oven with coals underneath and on top, or preheat a conventional oven to 200°C.
In a large bowl, mix together the flour, baking powder, wattleseed and salt.
Add the cubed butter and rub it in with your fingertips until the mixture resembles fine breadcrumbs.
Add the warm water gradually, stirring with a knife until the dough just comes together. Don't overwork it, damper should be rough and rustic.
Turn the dough out onto a lightly floured surface and gently shape it into a round loaf about 20 cm across. Make a shallow cross on the top with a knife.
Place the damper on a piece of baking paper or directly on a lightly oiled cast-iron trivet in your camp oven (or on a baking tray for conventional oven).
Bake for 40–45 minutes until the top is golden and it sounds hollow when tapped on the base. In a camp oven, rotate the coals if needed to ensure even cooking.
Cool on a wire rack for a few minutes, then tear into pieces and serve warm with butter.

notes: Cook the rice the night before and store in the fridge; it keeps for 3 days and is great eaten cold.
Press the tofu for 15 minutes before cutting to get it crispy, wrap it in a clean towel with a weight on top.
Swap the mango for peaches or papaya if that's what's at the farmers' market.
Make the stew up to 2 days ahead; the flavours deepen overnight. Reheat gently before serving.
Don't skip browning the kidney, it anchors the stew. If you can't find beef kidney, use lamb kidney (200 g) or omit it and add 100 g more beans instead.
Dried limes are essential to the flavour; they're sold in Middle Eastern grocers and most good supermarkets.

Food safety: Steaks and roasting cuts of beef or lamb can be served pink: about 60°C in the centre is medium-rare, 70°C is well done. If using dried kidney beans, soak them, then boil them hard for at least 10 minutes before simmering, to destroy a natural toxin.
Use oil you actually like the taste of, the simplicity means quality matters. Peanut oil or a fruity olive oil both work.
Don't prep the choy sum too early; it wilts quickly. Cut and dress it just before cooking.
If your stove doesn't run hot enough to get good wok hei, finish the pan under a very hot grill for 30 seconds instead.

steps.text: Get everything ready, the greens washed and cut, garlic bruised and sitting on the bench. High heat and speed matter here.
Heat your wok on high until it just begins to smoke lightly, about 2 minutes. Add the oil and swirl to coat the wok surface.
Add the bruised garlic and stir constantly for 20 seconds until fragrant. You want the oil infused but the garlic not burnt.

Immediately add all the choy sum. Toss and stir briskly, keeping the heat high, for 2 to 3 minutes until the stems are tender and the leaves have some char at the edges. The greens should still be bright.
Season with salt to taste. Serve immediately while the oil is still hot and the choy sum is at its best.

notes: The salmon can be cured up to 5 days ahead; keep it wrapped in the fridge. Slice only what you need and use the rest within a day or two.
The mustard sauce keeps refrigerated for up to 3 days.
Use the best salmon you can find, it's almost raw, so freshness matters.

The fish here is eaten raw or only cured in citrus. Buy sashimi-grade fish from a fishmonger, keep it cold and eat it the same day; skip it for anyone pregnant, very young, elderly or with low immunity.

Food safety: The seafood here is served raw or cured, so buy sashimi-grade, keep it cold and eat it the day it is made; for anyone who should avoid raw fish, cook it until opaque. Raw and lightly cooked foods aren't recommended for pregnant women, young children, older people or anyone with a weakened immune system.
If you can't find fresh pāua, tinned pāua from a specialist kai moana supplier works well, just drain and pound before battering.
Keep finished fritters warm in a low oven (120°C) while you fry the rest.
Food safety: Raw and lightly cooked foods aren't recommended for pregnant women, young children, older people or anyone with a weakened immune system.

steps.text: Pound each pāua gently but firmly with a meat mallet on both sides until soft and just starting to flatten. Don't overdo it or you'll tear them. Pat dry with paper towels.
Whisk together the flour, baking powder, salt and pepper in a large bowl. In another bowl, whisk the egg with the milk until combined.
Pour the wet ingredients into the dry and stir gently until just combined, the batter should be a little lumpy, not smooth.
Heat about 2 cm of neutral oil in a large frying pan over medium-high heat until shimmering. Test with a drop of batter; it should sizzle and float.
Dip each pāua into the batter, coating both sides, then carefully place into the hot oil. Fry in batches of 2 or 3 so you don't crowd the pan, about 2 minutes each side until golden and crispy.
Drain on paper towels and serve hot with a squeeze of fresh lemon.

notes: Make ahead: prepare the musubi the morning before and keep wrapped in the fridge. Bring to room temperature before eating, or warm gently in the microwave.
Swap the sweet soy sauce for tamari or regular soy sauce if that's what you've got, the musubi will taste less sweet but still good.
Any leftover seasoned rice can be used to make onigiri or fried rice.
Food safety: Cool any leftover rice quickly and refrigerate it within an hour; reheat it until steaming hot.
Use veal or beef. Veal is more tender, but a thin beef cutlet works just as well.
Don't skip the meat mallet. The escalopes must be thin so they cook through before the breadcrumb coating burns.
Food safety: Steaks and roasting cuts of beef or lamb can be served pink: about 60°C in the centre is medium-rare, 70°C is well done.

steps.text: Make the chimichurri first: whisk together the olive oil and red wine vinegar, then stir in the parsley, oregano, garlic, chilli flakes, salt and pepper. Set aside.
Place each veal escalope between two sheets of plastic wrap and pound with a meat mallet or rolling pin until very thin, about 3 mm. Season both sides with salt and pepper.

Set up three shallow bowls: one with flour, one with beaten eggs, and one with breadcrumbs. Coat each escalope in flour, shaking off excess, then dip in egg, then press firmly into the breadcrumbs on both sides.
Heat about 1 cm of neutral oil in a large frying pan over medium-high heat until it shimmers. Test with a small piece of bread, it should sizzle and brown quickly.
Carefully lay the breaded veal into the hot oil and fry for 2–3 minutes until golden brown. Turn and fry the other side for another 2–3 minutes until crispy and golden. Do not overcrowd the pan.
Transfer to a plate lined with paper towel to drain. Serve hot with lemon wedges and chimichurri on the side, with optional fresh parsley garnish.

notes: The yolk should be soft when you bite in, if you prefer it cooked through, fry for an extra minute, but you'll lose some of the magic!
If the pastry is splitting, brush the edges with a paste of flour and water to seal them better.
Food safety: Raw and lightly cooked foods aren't recommended for pregnant women, young children, older people or anyone with a weakened immune system.

steps.text: Set up a work station with one sheet of filo pastry in front of you, and have a small bowl of water nearby for sealing. In a small bowl, mix the drained tuna with the harissa, coriander and capers. Taste it and adjust the harissa and salt to your liking.
Take the first filo sheet and brush it lightly with oil on both sides. Fold it in half to create a rough square.

Spoon about 1 tbsp of the tuna mixture into the centre of the folded pastry, leaving a margin around the edges. Make a small well in the tuna mixture, then crack an egg directly into it. Season with a pinch of salt and pepper.

Fold the pastry over the filling to create a triangle or envelope, sealing the edges by pressing firmly or brushing them with a little water. The egg should be mostly contained but might leak slightly during cooking, this is normal.
Heat about 3 cm of oil in a deep frying pan to 180°C (or until a small piece of bread browns in about 30 seconds). Carefully place the first brik into the hot oil, seam-side down.

Fry for 2–3 minutes, turning once halfway, until the pastry is golden and crispy on both sides. The egg inside should still have a soft yolk. Use a slotted spoon to remove it and drain on paper towels.
Repeat with the remaining briks, making sure the oil returns to temperature between batches.
Serve hot, on their own or with a squeeze of lemon and extra harissa on the side!

notes: Shorshe ilish is traditionally made during spring when hilsa is in season (March–May). If hilsa is unavailable, use fresh pomfret or mackerel, both have the oily texture this dish demands.
Prepare the mustard paste fresh; it loses its pungency if made too far ahead. The dish can be made a few hours in advance and gently reheated.

steps.text: Soak the mustard seeds in a little water for 10 minutes, then grind to a coarse paste with the green chillies, turmeric and salt. The paste should be lumpy and pungent, not smooth.
Heat the mustard oil in a wide, shallow pan over medium-high heat until it just smokes, about 2 minutes. This is essential, the burnt edge of the oil gives shorshe ilish its character.
Gently lay the fish fillets skin-side up in the hot oil. Cook for 2–3 minutes without moving them, until the flesh begins to turn opaque at the edges.
Spread the mustard paste over the fish, then add 150 ml water around (not over) it. The sauce should be loose and gravy-like.

Bring to a simmer, then reduce heat to low. Cook, uncovered and barely disturbing the fish, for 15–18 minutes, until the flesh is cooked through and flakes easily when tested at its thickest point. The sauce should reduce and thicken slightly.
Taste and adjust salt. Stir in the jaggery if using, a hint of sweetness balances the mustard's heat. Serve hot, with rice to soak up the sauce.

notes: Rendang improves overnight as the flavours marry. Make it a day ahead and gently reheat, or store in the fridge for up to 4 days.
Use a heavy-bottomed pot so the heat stays even and the sauce doesn't catch at the bottom.
Food safety: Braised beef and lamb cook well past 75°C on the way to tender, so they are safe once soft.

steps.text: Blend the garlic, ginger, red chillies, shallots and macadamias with 60 ml of the coconut milk until you have a smooth, thick paste. This is your spice foundation, don't rush it.
Heat the oil in a large, heavy-bottomed pot or Dutch oven over medium heat. Add the lemongrass and bruise it gently with a wooden spoon to release its oils, about 1 minute.
Add the spice paste and cook, stirring constantly, until it darkens and the raw smell fades, about 8–10 minutes. The paste should start to break apart and release its fragrance.
Add the beef chunks and stir well to coat in the paste. Cook for about 5 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the beef is sealed on the outside.
Pour in the remaining coconut milk. Stir well, then bring to a gentle simmer, until small bubbles appear at the edges. Do not boil. Reduce the heat to low.

Simmer, uncovered, for about 60–70 minutes, stirring every 15 minutes or so. The coconut milk will gradually reduce and the sauce will thicken and darken. By the end, the beef should be very tender and the sauce should be thick and cling to the meat, not swim in liquid. This is where patience matters, watch that the heat stays gentle so the coconut doesn't split.
Taste and season with salt. If the rendang feels too sharp, stir in the palm sugar. Remove the lemongrass stalks.
The rendang is ready when the sauce is nearly absorbed, glossy and deep reddish-brown, and the beef is so tender it breaks easily with a spoon. Serve warm.

notes: These are best served warm or at room temperature, not hot, the flavours settle beautifully as they cool.
You can make them a few hours ahead and reheat gently in a 150°C oven for 15 minutes.
If your tomatoes are not very ripe, add a tbsp of tomato paste to the rice mixture for more depth.

steps.text: Cut the top off each tomato and set aside. Using a spoon, scoop out the insides, leaving about 1 cm of flesh around the walls. Chop the scooped flesh and set aside. Cut the capsicums in half and remove the seeds.
Heat 2 tbsp of the olive oil in a large frying pan over medium heat. Cook the onion until soft, about 5 minutes. Add the garlic and cook for another minute, stirring.
Add the rice and stir for 2 minutes to toast it lightly. Add the chopped tomato flesh, parsley, mint, oregano, and a pinch of salt and pepper. Stir well and remove from heat. Let cool slightly.

Arrange the tomato shells and capsicum halves in a large baking dish, cut-side up. Divide the rice mixture evenly among them, pressing gently and mounding slightly, they'll settle as they cook until the rice is tender and the tops are lightly golden.
Drizzle the remaining 2 tbsp olive oil over everything. Pour the water into the dish around (not over) the vegetables. Replace the tomato tops. Season with salt and pepper.

Roast, uncovered, at 180°C for about 60 minutes, until the tomatoes and capsicums are very soft and the edges are slightly charred. The rice will have absorbed most of the liquid. Serve warm or at room temperature.

notes: This keeps well in an airtight container in the fridge for up to 5 days, making it perfect for bento prep.
If you can't find burdock, use parsnip cut into thin matchsticks; it cooks a little faster but has a similar sweetness.
Hijiki expands as it soaks, so don't skip that step, the texture will be much better.

steps.text: Chop the tomatoes, cucumber and red onion into roughly the same size pieces. Put them in a big bowl.
Add the olive oil, lemon juice and oregano. Toss everything together and season with salt and pepper.
Let it sit for 2 minutes, until the salt has drawn out a little juice and the vegetables are glossy, so the flavours come together.
Scatter the feta on top and toss through gently. Serve straight away.
Heat the sesame oil in a large wok or wide frying pan over medium-high heat.

Add the zucchini and salt. Stir-fry, tossing gently and frequently, until the zucchini is tender but still holds its shape and the edges are lightly caramelised, about 6–8 minutes. The zucchini will release a little moisture; let it cook off.
Remove from the heat and allow to cool for a minute. Add the perilla leaves and toss gently to combine.
Transfer to a serving bowl, scatter with the sesame seeds and black pepper, and serve at room temperature or slightly warm.
Dice the tomatoes into small, even pieces, about the size of a pea. If they release a lot of juice, drain them slightly.
Dice the white onion into small pieces the same size as the tomato.
Chop the fresh coriander roughly, then go over it once more with the knife so it's fine.
Combine the tomato, onion and coriander in a bowl.
Squeeze the lime juice over, add a pinch of salt, and stir gently until the tomato is glossy and lightly coated in juice. Taste and adjust salt and lime.
Serve right away, or cover and keep in the fridge for up to an hour.

notes: Make the broth ahead and reheat gently; it keeps for 3 days in the fridge. Cook the noodles fresh just before serving.
No fresh crab? Use a good tinned crab in brine (drain well), or substitute more crab paste with a little extra stock to thin it.
The fried shallots are worth finding at any Vietnamese or Asian grocer, they're the difference between good and the stall version.
Cook chicken until it reaches 75°C in the thickest part and the juices run clear.
Food safety: Cook fish until it is opaque and flakes easily (63°C in the thickest part), and prawns until pink and opaque all the way through.
Marinate the chicken overnight for best flavour, it's worth the patience.
Use bone-in, skin-on chicken; it stays juicier and develops that crackling skin Yogyakarta style.
Serve at room temperature with steamed rice and sambal if you like heat.
Food safety:
Snapper is the go-to, firm, sweet, cooks quickly. Sub any fresh white fish fillet.
Make it vegetarian: swap the fish for 250 g firm tofu, cut into thick slices, pan-seared until golden.
Food safety:
Cook chicken until it reaches 75°C in the thickest part and the juices run clear.
Fresh molokhia is best and usually the cheapest; dried molokhia works too, use half the weight and crush it into a powder before adding. Frozen molokhia is also fine.
If you can't find molokhia, spinach is the closest substitute, though it's leafier and less slimy. Don't overcook spinach or it falls apart.
The stew thickens as it cools; add a splash more stock when reheating if needed.

steps.text: Bring the vegetable stock to a boil in a large pot, until it bubbles steadily.
Add the chopped molokhia leaves and stir to combine. Simmer for 5 minutes until the leaves start to break down.
While the molokhia simmers, heat a tablespoon of oil in a small pan over medium heat. Add the chopped garlic and fry gently, stirring often, until golden and fragrant, about 3 minutes.
Crush the fried garlic with the salt using the back of a spoon or a mortar and pestle until it forms a paste.
Stir the garlic paste and ground coriander into the molokhia. Simmer for a further 3 to 5 minutes until the stew is thick and cohesive.
Serve the molokhia over a bed of steamed rice, with lemon wedges on the side for squeezing.

Rinse the yellow split peas under cold water, then tip into a large pot with the water and quartered brown onion. Bring to a boil, then reduce the heat and simmer gently, uncovered, for about 50 minutes, stirring often, until the peas have broken down completely into a thick purée.
When the peas are very soft and falling apart, remove from the heat and discard the onion pieces. Season generously with salt.
Whisk in the olive oil, a little at a time, beating to incorporate air and make the purée smooth and pale. This will take 3–4 minutes of steady whisking.
Stir in the lemon juice, then taste and adjust the seasoning, you want salt, brightness and richness in balance.
Divide among four bowls and top each with a handful of raw red onion slices and a crack of black pepper. Serve warm or at room temperature.

notes: If you can't find ready-made tarhana paste, you can order it online. Turkish delis often stock it.
Tarhana keeps for months in an airtight jar, so it's worth having on hand.
A dollop of yoghurt stirred in at the end is traditional, use about 1 tbsp per bowl.
Cook chicken until it reaches 75°C in the thickest part and the juices run clear.

steps.text: If using a whole coconut, pierce the eyes and drain the liquid. Crack open the shell and peel away the brown skin with a vegetable peeler. Grate the white flesh on a fine grater or microplane until you have about 400 g of fine, fluffy coconut.
Put the grated coconut into a bowl and add the lime juice, chopped chillies, pounded dried fish, and red onion.
Mix gently but thoroughly until every grain of coconut is coated and the flavours are even.
Taste and adjust the seasoning with salt. The sambol should be bright, sharp, and hot, not timid.
Serve immediately alongside hot rice and curry.

notes: Make the filling and dough ahead: the filling keeps for 2 days in the fridge, and the dough keeps for up to 4 hours. You can freeze uncooked pierogi on a tray, then boil them straight from frozen (add 1 extra minute to the boiling time).
A potato ricer or food mill makes a smoother filling if you don't like lumps, though a rustic texture is traditional too.
Food safety: Raw and lightly cooked foods aren't recommended for pregnant women, young children, older people or anyone with a weakened immune system.

steps.text: Make the dough: mix flour and salt in a bowl. In another bowl, whisk the egg, then stir in the sour cream. Pour the wet mixture into the flour and mix until you have a soft, slightly sticky dough. Knead for 5 minutes until smooth and elastic. Cover and rest for 30 minutes.

Meanwhile, make the filling: boil the potato pieces in salted water until very tender, about 12 minutes. Drain well and mash roughly, you want some small lumps. Fry the chopped onion in 2 tbsp butter over medium heat until soft and golden, about 5 minutes. Stir the onion and butter into the potato, then fold in the cheese. Season to taste with salt and pepper. Let cool.

Make the caramelized onions for serving: slice the 2 onions thinly. Melt 3 tbsp butter in a wide pan over medium heat and cook the onions, stirring often, until they're golden and soft, about 15 minutes. Set aside.

Roll the pierogi: flour your work surface lightly. Roll the dough out to about 2 mm thick. Using a 7 cm round cutter or a glass, cut out circles. Place a heaped teaspoon of filling on each circle, fold in half, then press the edges to seal, fold the corner of the half-moon up and over itself to make a small curved seal (this is the traditional shape). Oil your hands if the dough sticks.

Bring a large pot of salted water to a boil. Working in batches, drop the pierogi in. They'll sink at first, then float to the surface when they're nearly done, about 2 minutes. Boil for another 30 seconds after they float, then lift out with a slotted spoon.
Serve the pierogi warm with the caramelized onions spooned over the top and a dollop of sour cream. Scatter with fresh dill if you like.

notes: The curry can be made a day ahead and reheated gently. The sambals are best made an hour or two before serving so the flavours meld.
Use leftover roast chicken or vegetables instead of making the curry, a generous spoonful stirred through the rice works just as well.
The rice can also be cooked in a rice cooker: fry the onion, garlic and ginger in a pot, add turmeric and rice to coat, then transfer to the rice cooker with the stock and bay leaves.
Cook mince and sausages until they reach 75°C in the centre, with no pink left.
Food safety:
Make this a day ahead: the pralines soften beautifully overnight and the flavours deepen.
Pink pralines are a Lyon specialty and worth hunting down in good delis or online. They're crunchy, delicately flavoured hazelnut pralines and not like anything else.
If your oven runs hot, tent the tart loosely with foil if it's browning too quickly.
Food safety: The eggs are cooked until just set. For pregnant women, young children, older people or anyone with a weakened immune system, cook them until firm all the way through.

steps.text: Make the pastry: rub the cold butter into the flour with your fingertips until it looks like breadcrumbs, then stir in the caster sugar and salt. Beat the egg yolk with the cold water and mix into the flour until just combined. Form a disc, wrap in cling film and refrigerate for at least 30 minutes.

Preheat the oven to 200°C. Roll out the pastry between two sheets of baking paper to about 3 mm thick. Press into a 24 cm tart tin, trim the edges and prick the base. Blind bake with baking paper and beans for 12 minutes, then remove the paper and beans and bake for another 5 minutes until just set. Set aside to cool slightly.
Roughly crush about three-quarters of the pink pralines with the back of a spoon, you want some texture, not a smooth paste. Stir the softened butter through the crushed pralines.
Whisk the cream, milk, egg yolks and vanilla together until smooth. Fold in the praline mixture, then pour into the cooled pastry shell. Scatter the remaining whole pralines over the top.

Bake at 180°C for about 10 minutes, until the filling is just set but still trembling slightly in the centre. The tart will continue to set as it cools. Chill for at least 4 hours, or overnight, before serving.

notes: The whole point is freshness and gentleness. Don't rush the poaching, low heat keeps the fish tender. If your fillets are very thick, give them an extra minute.
Brown butter can be made ahead and kept warm; reheat gently before serving.
Food safety:

steps.text: Pour the stock or water into a wide, shallow pan and add the bay leaf. Bring to a gentle simmer over medium heat, until the surface is barely trembling with tiny bubbles and not boiling.
Pat the fish fillets dry with paper towel and season lightly with salt on both sides.

Slide the fish into the simmering stock. The liquid should barely cover them. Poach gently, the surface should barely tremble, for about 8 minutes, until the fish is cooked through and flakes easily when tested with a fork.
Carefully lift the fish onto warm plates using a slotted spatula, leaving the poaching liquid behind.
Melt the butter in a small pan over medium heat, swirling occasionally, until it turns a light golden brown and smells nutty, about 3 minutes. Watch it carefully so it doesn't burn.

Drizzle the brown butter, which should smell nutty and be golden brown, over each fillet, which should be opaque and flake easily. Scatter the chives over the top, and finish with a grind of black pepper. Serve at once.

notes: The dough keeps well: store finished pancakes in an airtight container for 2 days, then reheat briefly in a dry frying pan. You can also freeze uncooked rested discs for up to a month, then cook straight from frozen (add 2 minutes to the cooking time).
Hydration is key here, 75% feels sticky at first, but it's what gives you those delicate, shattering layers. Don't add extra flour.

steps.text: Mix the boiling water into the flour and salt with a wooden spoon or chopsticks until shaggy. Let cool for 5 minutes, then knead by hand until smooth and soft, about 8 minutes. The dough will be slightly sticky, this is right. Cover with a damp cloth and rest for 20 minutes.
Divide the dough into 4 equal pieces. Roll each piece into a ball, brush all over with a little oil, and rest for 10 minutes covered.

On an oiled work surface, roll one ball into a thin rectangle about 30 cm × 20 cm. Brush generously with oil, scatter a quarter of the chopped spring onion evenly over the surface, then tightly roll up from one long edge into a log. Coil the log into a spiral, tucking the end underneath. Press gently to flatten slightly into a disc about 1 cm thick. Repeat with the remaining dough balls, spring onion and oil. Let rest for 5 minutes.
Roll each disc into a round about 20 cm across, being gentle so the layers stay distinct. If the dough springs back, let it rest for a minute and try again.

Heat 1½ tbsp oil in a large non-stick frying pan over medium heat. Once shimmering, place one pancake in and cook for 2–3 minutes until the underside is golden and crispy. Flip and cook the other side for 1–2 minutes until speckled and cooked through.
Transfer to a plate and immediately sprinkle with a pinch of coarse sea salt. Repeat with the remaining pancakes, adding a little more oil to the pan as needed. Serve warm, torn into pieces.

notes: Keep in the fridge for up to 3 days and serve cold, or reheat gently in a 180°C oven.
No chilli in the house? Use a pinch of dried oregano instead, or just the onions. The frittata doesn't need much.
Food safety: Raw and lightly cooked foods aren't recommended for pregnant women, young children, older people or anyone with a weakened immune system.
Make it ahead: cook it the day before, cool quickly, and refrigerate in an airtight container for up to 3 days. Reheat gently in the pot with a splash of water.
This is Jamaican rice and peas, which uses kidney beans, not the peas you might find elsewhere in the Caribbean.

steps.text: Pour the coconut milk into a large measuring jug and add water to make 600 ml total. Stir well to combine.
Heat the oil in a heavy-bottomed pot over medium heat. Add the onion and cook, stirring, until softened and fragrant, about 3 minutes.
Add the garlic and cook, stirring, for 1 minute more.
Add the rice, stirring to coat in the oil, about 1 minute.
Pour in the coconut milk mixture and stock, then add the kidney beans, thyme, salt and pepper. Stir well and bring to a boil until the liquid is bubbling steadily.
Once boiling, reduce the heat to low, cover with a tight-fitting lid, and cook for 18 to 20 minutes, until the rice is tender and the liquid is absorbed. Do not lift the lid during cooking.
Remove from the heat and let it rest, covered, for 2 minutes. Fluff with a fork, discard the thyme sprig if using fresh, and scatter with spring onion if you like.

notes: Use good-quality fresh tuna; frozen won't give you the same result.
Don't stir too much once the tuna is in, you want to keep the chunks intact.
Food safety: Cook fish until it is opaque and flakes easily (63°C in the thickest part), and prawns until pink and opaque all the way through.
If you can't find millet, substitute with 150 g of pearl barley or extra rice, though the texture won't be quite the same.
Make it the night before and reheat gently with a splash of water, the flavour deepens overnight.
The best toppings are fried plantain, avocado slices, grated hard-boiled egg, and a spoonful of hot shito (pepper) sauce on the side.
The horseradish cream can be made up to 2 hours ahead and kept in the fridge.
Use the best smoked mackerel you can get, local fishmonger quality makes all the difference.
Make it the day before and refrigerate, it actually improves. Just add 10 minutes to the baking time if cooking from cold.
