Lamb neck fillet works just as well as shoulder and gives you more flavour for the gravy.
Don't skip the second blast at high heat, that's what gets the potatoes crispy.
Food safety:

steps.text: Heat oven to 160°C. Layer half the potatoes in the bottom of a deep baking dish or casserole (about 2 litre capacity), then half the onions.
Add all the lamb pieces, then layer the remaining onions and remaining potatoes on top, seasoning each layer with salt, pepper and thyme as you go.
Warm the chicken stock and pour it over everything, it should come about three-quarters of the way up the dish. Dot the top with small pieces of butter.
Cover tightly with foil and bake for 2 hours at 160°C, until the lamb is completely tender.
Increase oven to 200°C, remove the foil, and bake uncovered for a further 15 minutes until the potato tops are golden and crispy.
Rest for 5 minutes before serving. The gravy should come from the lamb and stock, you don't need to make it separately.

notes: Serve with torn bread to soak up the sauce.
Make the sauce ahead and reheat gently before poaching the eggs.
Food safety: Raw and lightly cooked foods aren't recommended for pregnant women, young children, older people or anyone with a weakened immune system.
Make this salad just before eating, if it sits too long, the vegetables release water and it becomes watery.
The dice should be fine and even. This isn't just cutting vegetables small; it's about texture, so every piece sits together in the bowl.

steps.text: Dice the tomatoes into small, even pieces about the size of a pea, working over a bowl to catch the juice.
Dice the cucumber to the same size as the tomato.
Finely chop the parsley, removing the coarse stems and using mostly the leaves.
Combine the tomato, cucumber and parsley in a bowl.
Pour the lemon juice and olive oil over the vegetables and toss gently but thoroughly so everything is well coated.
Taste and add salt until it's right, not too much, just enough to bring out the flavour of the vegetables.
Serve straight away with warm bread to eat it with.

notes: Thieboudienne can be made a day ahead: cook the fish and vegetables up to step 5, cool and refrigerate, then finish the rice and reheat gently before serving.
If you can't find a whole fish, use thick fish steaks (about 200g each) and add them after the rice has cooked for 15 minutes, so they don't break up.
The caramelized onion base is everything, don't rush it. The darker and deeper the onions, the better the dish.
Food safety: Cook fish until it is opaque and flakes easily (63°C in the thickest part), and prawns until pink and opaque all the way through.
The chicken liver must not be overcooked or it becomes tough. Add it back to the pot at the very end.
Fresh egg noodles cook much faster than dried; if using dried noodles, add them earlier and cook for 8–10 minutes.
The cornflour slurry must be stirred in slowly to avoid lumps.
Food safety: Cook chicken and other poultry until the juices run clear and the thickest part reaches 75°C.
Beef ribs (short ribs or beef back ribs) cook beautifully the same way, just allow an extra 2–3 minutes per side.
No grill? A heavy cast-iron pan on the stove over high heat works. You won't get the same char, but the flavour will be there.
Best eaten straight off the heat with your flatmates and cold beers.
Food safety:

steps.text: Heat your grill or barbecue to hot. If using charcoal, wait until the coals are white and glowing; if gas, get it smoking.
Pat the beef dry with paper towel until the surface is no longer wet. This helps it char, not steam.
Rub the meat lightly with oil, then season generously with salt on both sides.
Lay the meat on the grill in a single layer. Don't move it for the first 4 minutes, you want a good char.
Flip and cook the other side for another 4 minutes. The meat should have a dark crust but still be pink inside (about 55°C on a meat thermometer).
Transfer to a warm plate. Squeeze lime over the hot meat, it'll sizzle and the juice will run into all the crevices.
Let it rest for 2 minutes, then serve with extra lime wedges and salt on the side for dipping.

notes: Use a rotisserie chicken from Coles if you don't have cooked chicken on hand, shred the meat, skip the skin.
Salsa verde comes in jars in most supermarkets (Coles has it). If you can't find it, blend canned green tomatoes (tomatillos) with a jalapeño, coriander, and lime juice.
Make ahead: assemble the dish, cover with foil, and refrigerate up to 24 hours. Bake for an extra 5 minutes if cooking from cold.
Cook chicken until it reaches 75°C in the thickest part and the juices run clear.
Make the filling and dough a day ahead; chill separately. Roll and fold the morning of, then chill on the tray.
Freeze uncooked tortellini on a tray, then transfer to a freezer bag. Cook from frozen, adding 1–2 minutes to the simmer time.
The filling should taste bold, it seasons the broth. Don't be shy with salt, pepper, and nutmeg.
Cook chicken until it reaches 75°C in the thickest part and the juices run clear.
Food safety:

steps.text: Make the pasta: mound flour on a bench, crack eggs into centre, add a pinch of salt. Work with a fork until shaggy, then knead by hand for 8–10 minutes until smooth and elastic. Wrap and rest 30 minutes.

Make the filling: fry pork mince in a pan over medium heat, breaking it up, until it loses its colour, about 5 minutes. Cool completely, then mix with ham, parmesan, breadcrumbs, egg yolk, nutmeg, salt and pepper. Taste and adjust.

Roll the pasta: divide dough into 4 pieces. Working with one at a time (keep others covered), roll very thin on a lightly floured surface, thin enough to read through. Using a 5 cm cutter or glass, cut circles.

Fill and fold: place ½ tsp filling slightly off-centre on each circle. Fold in half to make a half-moon, press edges firmly. Bring the two points of the half-moon together to seal into a ring. Place on a tray lined with baking paper, well spaced. Repeat until done.
Chill the tortellini on the tray, uncovered, for at least 30 minutes (or up to 4 hours before cooking).

Bring stock to a steady simmer in a large pot. Carefully drop in tortellini, a few at a time so the broth stays moving. They'll sink, then float to the surface; simmer for 2–3 minutes after they float.
Serve in bowls with hot broth, grated parmesan, a crack of black pepper, and parsley if you like.

notes: Beef tongue keeps well raw for 2 days in the fridge, wrapped. Ask your butcher to slice it thin on the deli slicer, or freeze for an hour and slice yourself with a sharp knife.
Cooked tongue is best eaten fresh, but any leftovers are good cold the next day.
Food safety: Steaks and roasting cuts of beef or lamb can be served pink: about 60°C in the centre is medium-rare, 70°C is well done.
If you can't find fresh tamarind paste, use 1½ tbsp tamarind concentrate or 2 tbsp lime juice for a lighter sour note.
The herbs are not optional, they're what makes it sing. Vietnamese mint (laksa leaf) is traditional, but use whatever fresh herbs you have.
Food safety:
Make the jalebi syrup and batter the day before if you like, this takes the stress out of frying day. Keep both in airtight containers at room temperature.
The garlic chutney keeps in the fridge for up to 3 days.
Fafda is best eaten warm and fresh, but jalebi will keep in the syrup for up to 2 days.

steps.text: Make the jalebi syrup first: In a heavy-bottomed saucepan, combine the caster sugar and 300 ml water. Bring to a boil, stirring until the sugar dissolves completely. Add the lemon juice and crushed cardamom pods. If using saffron, crumble it into the syrup. Simmer for 10 minutes until the syrup thickens slightly and coats the back of a spoon. Set aside to cool completely.

Make the jalebi batter: In a bowl, whisk together the plain flour and bicarbonate of soda. Add the yoghurt and water, stirring until you have a smooth, lump-free batter with a consistency like double cream, thin enough to flow through a piping bag, but not watery. If using saffron, crumble it into the batter. Stir in the 2 tbsp of neutral oil. Set aside for 15 minutes to rest.
Make the garlic chutney: Blend all the ingredients together in a food processor or with a mortar and pestle until you reach a smooth paste. Transfer to a small bowl and set aside.

Make the fafda batter: In a large bowl, whisk together the gram flour, yoghurt, salt, turmeric and cumin. Add the chopped green chilli. Gradually add the 200 ml water, stirring until you have a thick, smooth batter, it should be slightly thicker than the jalebi batter, dropping slowly from a spoon. Gently fold in the carrot, peas and red onion. Let the batter rest for 10 minutes.

Heat the 1 litre of neutral oil in a heavy-bottomed, deep saucepan or wok to 170°C. You can check the temperature with a thermometer; if you don't have one, a small piece of batter should sizzle gently and brown in about 60 seconds.

Fry the jalebi: Transfer the jalebi batter to a piping bag fitted with a thin nozzle (about 5 mm). Carefully squeeze the batter into the hot oil in spiral shapes, starting from the centre and spiralling outward, making each jalebi about 5 cm across. Fry 3–4 at a time so they don't touch. Fry for about 90 seconds until deep golden and crisp, then turn gently and fry the other side for another 30–45 seconds. Remove with a slotted spoon and immediately place in the cool jalebi syrup. Repeat until all the batter is used. Set the jalebi aside in the syrup.

Fry the fafda: Once the oil returns to 170°C, carefully lower a fafda mould (or use a kitchen spoon or ladle) into the oil if you have one. Alternatively, use your hands or two spoons to shape the batter into loose, irregular nests about 10 cm across, don't make them perfectly compact; fafda should be airy and crispy. Fry 2–3 at a time for 3–4 minutes, turning halfway, until golden and crispy all over. The edges should be lacy and crackly. Remove with a slotted spoon and drain on paper towel.
Serve the fafda warm with a jalebi on the side, a spoonful of garlic chutney, and a small bowl of the syrup for dipping.

notes: Make the wors up to 2 days ahead and store in the fridge. They freeze beautifully too.
If you don't have natural casings, make pattie wors instead: shape the mixture into thick patties and braai or pan-fry them.
Pap reheats well, if it thickens too much overnight, loosen it with a splash of water or milk on the stove.
Food safety:
Make it a day ahead: flavour deepens overnight. Reheat gently on the stove with a splash of water if needed.
For deeper colour and flavour, fry the paste longer in step 2, dark brown is better than light.
Serve with steamed white rice or fragrant jasmine rice to soak up the sauce.
Food safety: Cook chicken and other poultry until the juices run clear and the thickest part reaches 75°C.

steps.text: Blend the shallots, garlic, ginger, galangal and dried chillies with 100 ml water until smooth. This is your rendang paste.
Heat the oil in a large, heavy-based pot over medium heat. Add the paste and caraway seeds. Fry, stirring often, until fragrant and the oil begins to separate from the paste, about 8 minutes.
Add the chicken pieces and stir to coat well in the paste. Cook for 5 minutes, stirring, until the chicken is sealed.
Pour in the coconut milk and stir. Add the turmeric, lime leaves and a pinch of salt. Bring to a gentle simmer until the sauce is bubbling lightly and fragrant.
Reduce heat to low. Simmer uncovered for 60 minutes, stirring every 10 minutes or so. The sauce will gradually reduce and thicken, and the oil will begin to separate again, this is what you want.
Keep simmering until the sauce is thick, glossy and coats the chicken, and the chicken is very tender. Taste and adjust the salt. Serve with rice.

notes: Use the freshest white fish and seafood you can find, suquet is a stew that lets them shine.
The sofregit is the soul of this dish. Those 20 minutes of slow cooking transform the onions into something deep and essential.
Serve with aioli or toum on the side if you like, a dollop in each bowl is very Catalan.
Food safety:

steps.text: Heat the olive oil in a large, heavy-bottomed pot or cazuela over a low-medium heat. Add the sliced onions and cook, stirring often, for 15 to 20 minutes until very soft and golden. This is the sofregit, don't rush it. The onions should be almost jammy. Add the garlic and cook for another 2 minutes until fragrant.
Stir in the crushed tomatoes and paprika. Cook gently for 5 minutes, letting the tomato meld with the sofregit base.
Add the potatoes and fish stock. Bring to a simmer and cook for 12 to 15 minutes until the potatoes are almost tender.

Add the white fish chunks and mussels. Simmer gently for 4 minutes, then add the prawns. Cook for another 3 to 4 minutes until the fish is just opaque and cooked through, the mussels have opened, and the prawns are pink.
Discard any mussels that haven't opened. Taste and season with salt and black pepper.
Ladle into bowls and scatter with fresh parsley. Serve with crusty bread to soak up the broth.

notes: Make niter kibbeh at home: melt 200g butter over low heat, add 1 tsp fenugreek seeds, ½ tsp cardamom pods, 2 cloves, 1 bay leaf and a pinch of ground turmeric. Let it infuse for 10 minutes, then strain through muslin into a jar and refrigerate.
Doro wat keeps well: store in the fridge for up to 3 days and reheat gently with a splash of water if needed.
For a thinner sauce, add more water and simmer a few minutes longer. Selam likes her stew thick enough to sit on the injera without running.

Food safety: Cook chicken and other poultry until the juices run clear and the thickest part reaches 75°C. Raw and lightly cooked foods aren't recommended for pregnant women, young children, older people or anyone with a weakened immune system.
Make these a day ahead and refrigerate, they taste better when the flavours have settled. Bring to room temperature before serving.
If you can't find Aleppo pepper, use a mix of smoked paprika and a pinch of chilli flakes.
Milkfish can be bony: eat slowly and you'll find most of the small bones soften in the vinegar. If you can't find it, use any firm white fish about the same size, barramundi or snapper work well.
Make ahead: braise to completion, cool in the liquid, and refrigerate for up to 3 days. Reheat gently over low heat, covered.
Very fresh sardines are essential here. If you can't find them, use fresh anchovies (alici) instead.
The pasta water is crucial, it helps emulsify the oil and coat the spaghetti properly.
Food safety:

steps.text: Heat the oven to 200°C, then arrange the fish fillets, skin side down, in a baking dish large enough to hold them in a single layer. Season with salt and pepper.

Scatter the sliced brown onion over the fish. Pour the coconut cream and water around the fish, then squeeze the juice from the lime halves over the top. Season again lightly with salt and pepper. Cook until the fish is opaque and flakes easily and the onion is soft.
Bake, uncovered, for 25–30 minutes, until the fish is cooked through and flakes easily when tested with a fork.
Scatter the chopped spring onion over the top and serve hot with the coconut broth spooned over. Serve with steamed rice and pickled onions on the side.

notes: Swap the carrot for peas, corn, or any cooked veg you have left over.
If you've got leftover cooked chicken, use 400 g and add it after the garlic and ginger, just heat through before the soy mixture.
Food safety: Cook chicken and other poultry until the juices run clear and the thickest part reaches 75°C. Cook mince and sausages until no pink remains and the centre reaches 75°C.
This recipe uses cooked chicken for safe home cooking. Traditional lawar is made with raw poultry only when the cook has direct knowledge of the animal's health and handling.
Make base genep fresh if you can: blend together 4 shallots, 3 garlic cloves, 1 tbsp ginger, 1 tsp galangal, 1 tsp ground turmeric, 2–3 red chillies and 1 tbsp coconut oil.
Lawar is best served the same day it's made, on banana leaf if you have it.
Cook chicken until it reaches 75°C in the thickest part and the juices run clear.
This gulai keeps well in the fridge for up to 3 days and tastes even better the next day as the spices settle.
Freeze it in portions, it thaws and reheats beautifully.
Use 2 dried chillies for mild heat, 4 for proper burn; it depends on the family eating it that night.

steps.text: Soak the dried chillies in hot water for 5 minutes until soft, then drain.
Grind the soaked chillies, shallot, garlic, ginger, turmeric and cumin seeds to a paste using a mortar and pestle or spice grinder, adding a little water if needed.
Heat the oil in a large pot or wok over medium heat. Fry the paste for 2 to 3 minutes, stirring constantly, until fragrant and darkened slightly.
Add the cassava chunks and stir to coat with the paste, about 2 minutes.
Pour in the coconut milk and water. Bring to a simmer, then reduce heat to medium-low until the sauce is just bubbling at the edges.

Cook, uncovered, for 20 to 25 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the cassava is completely tender and the sauce has thickened slightly. The cassava should break apart easily when tested with a fork.
Add the fish sauce and taste. Adjust salt and heat to your preference, remembering the chillies will have released their full flavour by now.
Simmer for another minute, until the sauce is thick and glossy and the cassava is tender, then serve hot with steamed rice.

notes: Make this a day ahead, it reheats beautifully and tastes even better the next day.
Serve with egg noodles, boiled potatoes, or just good bread for soaking up the gravy.
Food safety:

steps.text: Heat the oven to 160°C. Pat the brisket dry with paper towels and season generously on both sides with salt and pepper.

Heat the oil in a large heavy-based pot or Dutch oven over medium-high heat. Working in batches if needed, brown the brisket on all sides until deep golden, about 3 minutes per side. Set the meat aside.
Add the sliced onions to the pot and cook, stirring, until they start to soften and caramelize, about 5 minutes. They don't need to be fully cooked, they'll finish in the oven.
Pour in the beef stock, scraping up any browned bits from the bottom of the pot. Return the brisket to the pot, nestling it into the onions. Add the bay leaves.
Cover the pot with a lid and transfer to the oven. Braise for about 3 hours, until the brisket is fork-tender and the meat shreds easily.
Remove from the oven and let the brisket rest in the braising liquid for 10 minutes. Slice against the grain and serve with the soft onions and braising liquid spooned over the top.

notes: Serve with rice, cornbread, or just a spoon and good company.
Tastes even better the next day, the flavours deepen as it sits.

steps.text: Heat your cast iron over medium-high heat. Brown the andouille slices, 3–4 minutes per side, until they've got a nice colour. Transfer to a plate.
Add the oil to the same pan. Sauté the onion until it's soft and golden, about 5 minutes. Stir in the garlic and cook for 1 minute until fragrant.
Add the okra and cook, stirring occasionally, for about 8 minutes. Don't fuss with it too much, you want it to brown slightly.
Pour in the crushed tomatoes and their juice, then add the corn and chicken stock. Bring to a simmer until the stew is bubbling gently and starting to thicken.
Return the sausage to the pan. Reduce heat to medium-low and simmer, uncovered, for 15–20 minutes, stirring gently now and then, until the okra is tender and the flavours have married.
Taste and season with salt and pepper. Serve warm.

notes: Rohan likes his pelau hot; remove the green chillies before serving if your household prefers it milder.
Leftover pelau keeps in the fridge for 3 days and reheats beautifully on the stove with a splash of water.
You can swap the chicken for beef chuck or lamb shoulder for a different flavour, both work beautifully and need the full cooking time.
Food safety:

steps.text: Heat the oil in a large, heavy-bottomed pot over medium heat. Sprinkle the caster sugar evenly across the base and let it sit without stirring for 2 to 3 minutes. Once it starts to brown at the edges, stir constantly until it's a deep golden brown, almost black, this is the burnt sugar that gives pelau its dark gravy, about 5 to 6 minutes total. It'll smell slightly burnt; that's right.

Working quickly, add the chicken pieces to the burnt sugar, stirring constantly to coat them. They'll sizzle and stick a little, that's fine. Cook, stirring, for 3 to 4 minutes until the chicken is sealed on the outside.
Add the sliced onions and stir well, scraping up any stuck bits from the bottom of the pot. Cook for 5 to 6 minutes until the onions soften and start to caramelise.
Stir in the garlic, ginger and green chillies, and cook for 1 minute until fragrant. Add the ground cumin and ground coriander, stir, and cook for another minute.
Add the tomato paste and stir through, coating everything for about 1 minute. Pour in the coconut milk and chicken stock, stirring to loosen any stuck bits. Add the thyme sprigs.
Bring to a boil, then reduce the heat to low. Cover and simmer for 15 to 20 minutes until the chicken is cooked through (75°C inside) and the liquid is starting to reduce.

Stir in the rice and pigeon peas, mixing well so the rice is submerged. Season with salt and black pepper to taste. Cover and simmer over low heat for 20 to 25 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the rice is tender and has absorbed most of the liquid. If it looks dry but the rice isn't quite cooked, add a little more stock or water.
Remove from heat, let it rest, covered, for 5 minutes. Fluff with a fork, sprinkle with fresh coriander, and serve with lime wedges on the side.
Heat the mustard oil in a large pan over medium-high heat until it smokes lightly and settles, this takes about 1 minute. This is important; the oil must announce itself.
Add the nigella seeds and let them crackle for a few seconds until fragrant.
Add the potatoes and stir to coat in oil. Cook for 3–4 minutes until they begin to colour at the edges.
Sprinkle in the turmeric and stir well.
Add the green chilli and cook, stirring occasionally, for 8–10 minutes until the potatoes are three-quarters cooked and lightly golden.
Mix the poppy seed paste with 2 tbsp water to loosen it slightly. Add to the pan and stir to coat the potatoes evenly. If it seems dry, add another tablespoon of water.
Cook, stirring gently now and then, for 5–7 minutes until the potatoes are tender and the paste is no longer raw. The dish should be almost dry, with the potatoes well coated in the dark paste.
Taste and adjust salt. Serve warm, scattered with fresh coriander if you wish.

notes: This stew reheats beautifully and tastes even better the next day. Keep in the fridge for up to 3 days.
Serve with crusty bread for soaking up the broth, or with plain white rice.
Food safety: Braised beef and lamb cook well past 75°C on the way to tender, so they are safe once soft.

steps.text: Heat the oil in a large pot over medium-high heat. Working in batches, brown the lamb on all sides, about 8 minutes total. Set aside.
Add the diced onion to the pot and cook, stirring, until soft and golden, about 5 minutes.
Return the lamb to the pot and stir in the cumin. Cook for 1 minute until fragrant.
Add the tinned tomatoes, breaking them up with the back of a spoon, then pour in the stock and add the lentils. Stir well and bring to a simmer until the liquid is bubbling gently.
Reduce the heat to low, cover partially, and simmer for 50 minutes, stirring occasionally. The lentils should be very soft and starting to break down, and the lamb should be tender.
Season with salt and pepper to taste. If the stew is too thin, simmer uncovered for a few more minutes until it is thick and the lentils are soft. Serve hot.

notes: Make ahead: Gumbo tastes even better the next day. Cool completely, refrigerate for up to 3 days, and reheat gently on the stove.
The roux is the foundation, keep the heat medium and stir constantly. A dark roux (not burnt) gives the gumbo its signature flavour and colour.
Food safety: Cook chicken and other poultry until the juices run clear and the thickest part reaches 75°C.

steps.text: Melt butter in a large heavy-bottomed pot over medium heat. Add flour and stir constantly, scraping the bottom, until the roux turns deep chocolate brown, about 25–30 minutes. Don't rush it, burnt roux tastes bitter, so keep the heat medium and stay patient.
Add the diced onion, celery and capsicum to the roux. Stir and cook until the vegetables begin to soften, about 5 minutes, scraping up any browned bits from the bottom.
Stir in the garlic and cook for 1 minute until fragrant.
Add the andouille sausage and cook, stirring, for 3–4 minutes until it releases its oil and the edges colour.
Add the chicken thighs and turn to coat in the roux. Cook for 2–3 minutes, then pour in the chicken stock. Add the bay leaves and thyme.
Bring to a gentle boil, then reduce heat to low. Simmer, partially covered, for 1 hour, stirring occasionally. The chicken should be very tender and the broth rich and dark.
Remove from heat. Pull the chicken thighs from the pot, let cool slightly, shred the meat from the bones and return it to the pot. Discard the bay leaves.
Taste and season with salt and black pepper.
Serve over cooked white rice in wide bowls with a spoon and fork for the broth and meat.

notes: Make ahead: cook the chicken and prepare the ají paste the day before. Reheat gently before serving.
Use leftover roast or poached chicken to save time on a weeknight.
Fresh ají amarillo peppers are best, but bottled paste (found in Latin American shops) works perfectly well.

Food safety: Cook chicken and other poultry until the juices run clear and the thickest part reaches 75°C. Raw and lightly cooked foods aren't recommended for pregnant women, young children, older people or anyone with a weakened immune system.
Make ahead: assemble the pastilla up to 2 hours before baking and refrigerate, covered with cling film. Brush with melted butter just before baking.
The eggs must stay soft and creamy, don't cook them through. They'll cook gently in the oven.
Filo dries out quickly. Keep sheets under a damp tea towel until you use them.

Food safety: Cook chicken and other poultry until the juices run clear and the thickest part reaches 75°C. Raw and lightly cooked foods aren't recommended for pregnant women, young children, older people or anyone with a weakened immune system.

steps.text: Place the chicken breast, quartered onion, ginger, turmeric, cinnamon, salt and pepper in a large pot. Cover with water and bring to a simmer. Cook for 20 minutes until the chicken is cooked through. Remove the chicken, let it cool slightly, then shred the meat finely, discarding the skin. Chop the coriander and parsley and set aside.
Toast the almonds in a dry frying pan over medium heat for 2 minutes until fragrant. Add 2 tbsp oil, the cinnamon, sugar and salt. Cook, stirring, for 1 minute, then transfer to a plate to cool.
In a small non-stick frying pan, lightly beat the eggs with salt and pepper. Melt 30 g butter and scramble the eggs gently until soft and creamy, about 3 minutes. Transfer to a plate.
Preheat the oven to 180°C. In a bowl, gently toss the shredded chicken with the herbs.
Lay a sheet of filo on a clean work surface and brush lightly with melted butter. Layer a second sheet on top and brush again. This is your base, it will be half the pastilla.
Spread half the scrambled eggs in a rough rectangle on the lower half of the filo stack, leaving a 5 cm border. Top with half the chicken mixture, then half the almonds.
Fold the sides of the filo inward, then roll up tightly from the bottom, creating a tight cylinder. Place seam-side down on a baking tray and brush the top with melted butter.
Repeat steps 5 to 7 with the remaining filo, eggs, chicken and almonds to make a second pastilla.
Bake for 25 to 30 minutes until the pastilla is deep golden brown and crisp.
Let rest for 2 minutes, then transfer to a serving plate. Dust generously with icing sugar and cinnamon at the table. Serve hot.

notes: This salsa keeps for up to a week in an airtight container in the fridge.
Don't rush the toasting, low heat brings out the deep, complex flavours that make this salsa special.

steps.text: Heat a heavy frying pan or comal over medium-low heat. Place the dried chillies in the pan and toast them, turning every 20 seconds, until fragrant and darkened but not blackened, about 4 to 5 minutes total. They should smell rich and earthy, almost like chocolate.
Remove the stems and most of the seeds from the cooled chillies, shaking out what comes loose. Leave a few seeds for heat.
In the same dry pan, toast the garlic cloves, turning occasionally, until lightly charred and soft, about 3 minutes.

Using a molcajete (lava rock mortar and pestle), grind the toasted chillies, garlic, and salt together in slow, circular motions. Work the pestle in a grinding motion until you reach a coarse paste, this takes patience, but the friction releases the true flavour. Stop when you reach your preferred texture; some like it smooth, some leave it rough.
Taste and add more salt if needed. If the salsa is too thick, stir in a few drops of water.

notes: Make ahead: cook dried beans the day before, or use quality tinned beans. Refried beans reheat beautifully on the stove with a splash of water.
The texture depends on mashing technique and cook time, not the fat. If they seem too thick after cooling, warm and stir in a little hot water.
Serve with warm tortillas, as part of breakfast, or alongside grilled vegetables.

steps.text: Heat the oil in a heavy-bottomed pan over medium heat. Add the diced onion and cook, stirring occasionally, until soft and translucent, about 5 minutes.
Add the minced garlic and cook for 1 minute, stirring, until fragrant.
Add the drained beans to the pan, stirring to coat them in the oil and aromatics.

Mash the beans with the back of a wooden spoon or a potato masher as they warm, breaking down the cell walls gradually. This is the key, you're not trying to purée them all at once, but rather let the starch and pressure do the work over time.

Continue cooking and mashing over medium-low heat for about 8–10 minutes, adding splashes of water (or bean cooking liquid if you have it) as needed to reach a creamy, spreadable consistency. The beans should hold together but not be stiff.
Taste and season with salt and cumin if using. The beans are ready when they're smooth, glossy, and slightly darker in colour from the slow breakdown of their starches.

notes: The filling can be made up to 4 hours ahead and kept in the fridge. Assemble the popiah just before serving so the skin stays soft.
Popiah are best eaten fresh, but you can wrap them tightly in plastic wrap and refrigerate for up to 2 hours. Don't freeze, the skin will crack when thawed.

Food safety: Cook mince and sausages until no pink remains and the centre reaches 75°C. Cook fish until it is opaque and flakes easily (63°C in the thickest part), and prawns until pink and opaque all the way through.

steps.text: Blanch the turnip matchsticks in boiling salted water for 1 minute, then drain well and squeeze dry with a clean cloth. Set aside.
Heat the oil in a wok or large pan over high heat. Add the garlic and cook for 30 seconds until fragrant.
Add the pork mince and fry, breaking it up as it cooks, for 2 minutes until cooked through.
Stir in the chopped prawn and cook for 1 minute until just cooked and still tender.
Add the blanched turnip, oyster sauce, soy sauce and salt. Toss everything together for 1 minute, then remove from heat and let cool to room temperature.
While the filling cools, make the sauce: stir together the hoisin, sweet chilli sauce, lime juice, sesame oil and minced garlic. Set aside.
Lay one popiah skin flat on a clean surface. Spread a thin line of the filling across the middle, don't overfill. Top with a small handful of fresh coriander and a few pieces of spring onion.
Fold the two sides of the skin over the filling, then roll tightly from the bottom up, tucking in the sides as you go. Place seam-side down on a plate.
Repeat with the remaining skins and filling.
Arrange the popiah on a serving plate, sprinkle with crispy fried shallots, and serve with the sauce on the side for dipping.

notes: Make ahead: shape and refrigerate the patties up to 4 hours before frying.
Serve with a simple green salad or steamed beets, Hamburg style.
Food safety: Cook fish until it is opaque and flakes easily (63°C in the thickest part), and prawns until pink and opaque all the way through.

steps.text: Bring a pot of salted water to the boil. Cut the potato into chunks and cook until just tender, about 12 minutes. Drain and let cool slightly.
Meanwhile, check the fish for any fine bones and discard. Finely chop the onion.
Grate the cooled potato into a large bowl. Finely chop or pulse the fish in a food processor until roughly textured but not a paste, then add to the potato.
Add the onion, egg, breadcrumbs, mustard, salt and white pepper. Mix gently with your hands until just combined, don't overwork it.
Shape the mixture into 8 patties about 7 cm across and 1.5 cm thick. Rest for 5 minutes if time allows.

Heat a thin layer of oil in a large frying pan over medium heat. When hot, fry the patties in two batches, about 3–4 minutes each side, until golden and cooked through. Don't move them around; let them develop a good crust.
Serve warm with a dollop of Dijon mustard on the side or a squeeze of lemon.

notes: Make these up to 4 hours ahead and reheat wrapped in foil in a 180°C oven for 10 minutes.
The dough will keep in the fridge, covered, for up to 2 days. Bring to room temperature before rolling.
Cook pork until it reaches at least 70°C in the thickest part (75°C for mince and sausages).
Slice the pork thinly while it's cold, pop it in the freezer for 30 minutes first if it's hard to cut.
Pickled chilies are the soul of this dish. Look for them in a tin in the Asian aisle, not the fresh chilli section.
This reheats beautifully; store leftovers in the fridge and warm gently in a wok or pan with a splash of water.
Food safety: Cook fresh pork to at least 70°C in the thickest part.
The pickled vegetables keep for up to 5 days in the fridge, so you can make them ahead.
Press the tofu well, this is what makes it absorb flavour and fry up crisp. If you skip this step, you will have a sad bánh mì.
Leftover fried tofu keeps in an airtight container for 2 days and can be reheated gently in a low oven.

steps.text: Bring a large pot of salted water to the boil. Add the bean sprouts and cook for 4 minutes, they should be tender but still have a slight bite. Drain well and spread on a clean kitchen towel to cool completely.
Toast the sesame seeds in a small dry pan over medium heat, stirring often, for 2 minutes until fragrant. Transfer to a mortar and pestle and crush lightly, leaving some seeds whole.
In a large bowl, whisk together the soy sauce, sesame oil and ginger. Add the cooled sprouts and toss gently to coat. Taste and adjust salt if needed.
Sprinkle the toasted sesame over the top just before serving.

notes: The crust is everything. Don't rush it, you want deep gold, not pale. If it's not crackling by minute 25, turn heat up slightly.
Use day-old cooked chicken if you have it; rotisserie works perfectly. The yoghurt binds everything and keeps the rice from drying out.
Make ahead: prepare the rice and yoghurt mixture up to 4 hours in advance. Cook in the pan just before serving.
The batter must ferment 8 hours or overnight, start the day before.
If you don't have an appam pan, use a shallow non-stick frying pan with a lid; the pancakes will be less lacy but still delicious.
The stew can be made up to 2 days ahead and warmed through before serving.
Food safety: Cook chicken and other poultry until the juices run clear and the thickest part reaches 75°C.
Use the best beef you can find, this dish lives or dies by the meat. Ask your butcher for a thick-cut rib eye on the bone, minimum 4 cm.
A txuleta is not about technique. It's about respecting good meat and not mucking it about.
Food safety:

steps.text: Take the txuleta out of the fridge 30 minutes before cooking so it comes to room temperature.
Get your grill smoking hot, charcoal if you can, or a cast-iron griddle over high heat if you can't.
Pat the meat dry. Season both sides generously with salt when it hits the grill, which should be smoking hot so the meat sizzles on contact.
Grill for 5–6 minutes on the first side without moving it. You want a dark crust.
Flip once. Grill for another 4–5 minutes for medium-rare (around 52°C inside). A thick chop like this needs time; don't rush it.
Rest on a warm plate for 3–4 minutes. Crack pepper over the top and serve.

notes: Make it ahead: cook the rice the morning before and reheat gently with a splash of water in a covered pot. The flavours deepen overnight.
Serve alongside rendang, grilled chicken, or slow-cooked beef, whatever you have time for.

steps.text: Heat the oil in a large heavy-based pot over medium heat. Add the garlic and cook, stirring, until fragrant, about 1 minute.
Add the turmeric, cumin seeds, cloves, and cinnamon stick. Toast, stirring gently, for 2–3 minutes until the spices smell rich and the seeds start to pop.
Pour in the coconut milk and chicken stock, then add the lemongrass stalks. Stir well and bring to a gentle simmer until the liquid is steaming and lightly bubbling and the kitchen smells fragrant.
Add the rinsed rice and salt. Stir once to combine, then reduce the heat to low. Cover with a tight-fitting lid.
Cook without lifting the lid for 18–20 minutes, until the rice is tender and all the liquid has been absorbed.
Remove from the heat and let it rest, covered, for 5 minutes. Fluff gently with a fork, discard the lemongrass stalks and cinnamon stick, then scatter spring onions over the top if you like.

notes: The marinade also works on pork shoulder, beef or cauliflower. Cook times will vary.
If you don't have time to marinate overnight, 4 hours is the minimum, but the flavour won't be as deep.
Food safety:

steps.text: Blend the spring onions, Scotch bonnets, garlic, ginger, thyme, allspice, black pepper, salt, olive oil, soy sauce and lime juice in a food processor until you have a thick, textured paste. Taste it, it should make you sit up straight.

Rub the jerk paste all over the chicken, working it into the skin and under any flaps you can lift. Put the chicken in a bowl, cover, and refrigerate overnight (or at least 6 hours, though overnight is better).
Take the chicken out of the fridge 30 minutes before cooking so it comes to room temperature.
Heat a large cast-iron or heavy-based pan over medium-high heat until it's very hot, or preheat your grill to high. Lightly oil the pan or grill grates.
Working in batches if needed so you don't crowd the pan, place the chicken skin-side down. Don't move it for 6–8 minutes until the skin is charred and sticky. You want some blackened edges.

Turn the chicken and cook for another 8–10 minutes on the other side until cooked through (the thickest part of the thigh should reach 75°C inside, or the juices run clear when pierced with a knife). If the outside is colouring too fast, lower the heat slightly.
Rest the chicken for 5 minutes, then serve hot with rice and peas, or with a simple salad and lime wedges.
Rinse the rice and moong dal together under cold water until the water runs clear.
Heat the ghee in a large saucepan over a medium heat. Add the cumin seeds and dried red chilli, and let them crackle for about 30 seconds.
Add the asafoetida and stir for a few seconds until fragrant, then add the rinsed rice and dal, stirring to coat in the ghee for about 2 minutes.
Add the turmeric and salt, stir, then add the water and bring to a boil until the water is bubbling steadily.
Add the diced carrot and other vegetables, stir well, then reduce the heat to low, cover with a lid and cook for about 12–15 minutes, until the rice and dal are tender and the water is absorbed.
Stir through gently with a fork to fluff, taste and adjust the salt if needed. Serve hot.

notes: Fa'ausi keeps in the fridge for 2 days and reheats gently in a covered dish at 160°C for 15 minutes.
You can prep the parcels several hours ahead and refrigerate them before baking, add 10 minutes to the cooking time.

steps.text: Preheat oven to 180°C. Prepare banana leaves by briefly wiping with a damp cloth and cutting into 30 cm squares, you'll need about 6 pieces.
In a bowl, combine taro chunks, sliced onion, salt and white pepper. Divide the mixture among the banana leaf squares, spooning about 150 ml coconut cream over each portion.
Fold the banana leaves over the filling to make neat parcels, tucking the edges underneath. Place seam-side down on a large baking tray.
Bake for 45 to 50 minutes, until the taro is very tender when pierced with a fork and the coconut cream is bubbling gently at the edges.
Remove from oven and let rest for 5 minutes. Unwrap carefully, the steam inside is very hot, and serve straight from the banana leaf.

notes: Make it ahead: cool and refrigerate for up to 2 days, then reheat gently on the stove with a splash of water if the glaze has set. The flavours deepen overnight.
No mirin? Use 1 tbsp more caster sugar instead, though you'll lose a bit of the subtle sweetness.
Serve with steamed rice or over kimchi and rice for something richer.
Food safety:
Chimichurri lasts 3 days in an airtight jar in the fridge, though the parsley will darken slightly.
Make it fresh the day you need it if you can. Inés never makes it more than a few hours ahead.
Serve with grilled beef, chicken, or even crusty bread, it's not just for meat, though that's what Inés says it's for.

steps.text: Finely chop the parsley, not in a food processor, by hand with a sharp knife. This matters.
Mince the garlic very fine; Inés says you should be able to see each piece.
In a bowl, combine the parsley, garlic, and red wine vinegar. Let it sit for 2 minutes so the vinegar softens the parsley.
Slowly pour in the olive oil while stirring until the sauce is glossy and just slightly emulsified, so it stays bright and fresh, not heavy.
Taste and season with salt and black pepper. If you like, add the oregano and chilli flakes, but Inés says this is between you and your conscience.
Let it rest for at least 10 minutes before serving so the flavours marry. Serve at room temperature with grilled meat, bread, or anything that needs the taste of home.

notes: Make ahead: shape the rings, let them rise, then freeze for up to 3 weeks. Bake directly from frozen, adding 5 minutes to the bake time.
The molasses dip is key, it makes the sesame stick like glue. Don't skip it or use water alone.
If you can't find taro root, use potato or yam, either works well and cooks in about the same time.
This dish is even better the next day: cover and store in the fridge, then reheat gently in a 160°C oven for 15 minutes with a splash of water.
A tagine pot keeps the braise gentle and even, but a wide shallow pan works just as well.
This is equally good made a few hours ahead and gently reheated before serving.
Food safety:

steps.text: Heat the olive oil in a large tagine or heavy-based pan over medium heat. Add the onion and cook, stirring gently, until soft and translucent, about 5 minutes.
Add the garlic, ginger, turmeric and cinnamon. Stir for 1 minute until fragrant.
Pour in the stock and bring to a gentle simmer until the liquid is bubbling lightly. Add the preserved lemon and olives, and season lightly with salt and pepper.
Nestle the fish fillets into the liquid, skin-side up if they have skin. Simmer gently for 12–15 minutes, until the fish is cooked through and flakes easily when tested with a fork.
Taste and adjust seasoning. Scatter with fresh coriander if you like, and serve straight from the tagine with couscous or crusty bread.

notes: Use a good, spicy harissa here, it's not a garnish, it's the whole point.
Make sure the eggs go into a shallow pan so the yolks stay runny while the whites cook through.
Cook mince and sausages until they reach 75°C in the centre, with no pink left.
Food safety: Raw and lightly cooked foods aren't recommended for pregnant women, young children, older people or anyone with a weakened immune system.

steps.text: Cook the egg noodles in salted boiling water until tender, about 8 minutes. Drain well and set aside.

While the noodles cook, melt the butter in a large heavy-bottomed pan over medium heat. Add the sliced onions and cook, stirring often, until they're soft and deeply golden, about 12 minutes. This is where the flavour happens, don't rush it.
Add the sliced cabbage to the pan with the caramelized onions. Stir to coat with butter. Cook, stirring occasionally, until the cabbage is very soft and golden at the edges, about 8 minutes.
Tip the cooked noodles into the pan with the cabbage and onions. Toss everything together until well combined. Season with salt and pepper to taste.
Divide among bowls and top with crispy fried onions or fried shallots if you like the crunch, they're optional, but they add something special.

notes: Make ahead: cook the dashimaki tamago the night before, wrap in cling film and refrigerate. It's fine cold or at room temperature.
No tamagoyaki pan? A regular non-stick frying pan works, but you'll get a circular roll instead of rectangular slices.
If you can't find instant dashi, use 60 ml water mixed with a tiny pinch of salt and bonito flakes instead.
Food safety: The eggs are cooked until just set. For pregnant women, young children, older people or anyone with a weakened immune system, cook them until firm all the way through.
Swap the green beans for whatever green veg you have: broccolini, bok choy, snap peas or zucchini all work.
Use fresh prawns if you have them, they'll cook in about 2 minutes instead of 3–4.
Food safety: Cook fish until it is opaque and flakes easily (63°C in the thickest part), and prawns until pink and opaque all the way through.

steps.text: Heat 2 tbsp coconut milk in a large pan over medium-high heat. Stir in the curry paste and cook for 1 minute until fragrant.
Pour in the remaining coconut milk and stock, stirring to combine. Bring to a simmer until the curry is bubbling gently and fragrant.
Add the green beans and cook for 5 minutes until just tender.
Add the frozen prawns and cook, stirring occasionally, for 3–4 minutes until they're pink and cooked through.
Stir in the fish sauce, lime juice and sugar. Taste and adjust the seasoning, add more fish sauce or lime to taste.
Serve over steamed jasmine rice with fresh Thai basil or coriander if you have it.

notes: Cook and cool the rice ahead, leftover rice works best. You want it cold and separate so it fries properly.
If clams are very sandy, soak them in salted water for 30 minutes before cooking to help them expel grit.
Fried shallots can be made several hours ahead and stored in an airtight container.

Food safety: Cook fish until it is opaque and flakes easily (63°C in the thickest part), and prawns until pink and opaque all the way through. Throw away any mussels or clams whose shells stay closed after cooking. Cool any leftover rice quickly and refrigerate it within an hour; reheat it until steaming hot.
Make a double batch, it tastes better the next day when the flavours have settled. Keeps in the fridge for 3 days.
Don't have makrut lime leaves? A squeeze of fresh lime juice works, but the leaves are worth hunting for.
Use whatever vegetables are cheap at the market: zucchini, cabbage, or even frozen mixed vegetables all work.
Make ahead: form the kebabs up to 2 hours ahead and keep in the fridge covered.
Swap: lamb mince works beautifully here, use the same amount and follow the same method.
Food safety: Cook mince and sausages until no pink remains and the centre reaches 75°C.

steps.text: Put the mince in a bowl with the minced onion, garlic, ginger and green chilli. Add the cumin, coriander, garam masala and chilli powder. Crack in the egg, season with salt and pepper, and mix gently with your hands until just combined, don't overwork it or the kebabs will be tough.

Wet your hands with water and divide the mixture into 8 equal portions. Mould each portion around a metal skewer (or flat wooden skewer soaked in water), pressing gently to form a long, even kebab about 15 cm long.

Heat the oil in a large frying pan or griddle over medium-high heat until it's smoking. Working in batches if needed, lay the kebabs in the pan and cook without moving them for 2–3 minutes until darkly charred on the bottom.
Turn the kebabs and cook the other side for another 2–3 minutes until charred and cooked through. Transfer to a plate.
Serve hot with lime wedges and fresh coriander.

notes: This adobo keeps well in the fridge for 3 days. The flavour deepens overnight.
For a less rich version, use light coconut milk instead of full-fat.
Food safety: Cook chicken and other poultry until the juices run clear and the thickest part reaches 75°C.
Make it ahead: Toast the farofa in bulk and store it in an airtight container for up to 4 days. Warm it in a dry pan before serving.
Swap the sausage for bacon, chorizo, or diced leftover churrasco meat.
Serve with grilled meat, rice and beans, this is the trifecta of a proper churrasco plate.

Food safety: Cook mince and sausages until no pink remains and the centre reaches 75°C. Raw and lightly cooked foods aren't recommended for pregnant women, young children, older people or anyone with a weakened immune system.

steps.text: Heat a large frying pan over medium-high heat. Cook the diced linguiça until the fat renders and it's golden, about 5 minutes. Push to the side and add the diced onion, cooking until soft, about 3 minutes.
Add the minced garlic and cook, stirring, until fragrant, about 1 minute.
Push everything to the side of the pan. Crack the eggs into the empty space and scramble gently until just cooked through, then stir everything together, about 2 minutes.
Add the cassava flour in three stages, stirring well after each addition to avoid lumps. Let it toast between each addition, about 2 minutes per stage. It should be golden and smell nutty.
Stir through the spring onion and fresh coriander. Taste and season with salt and pepper. Serve warm, this is best eaten straight from the pan at a churrasco.

notes: Tarte tatin is best served warm or at room temperature on the day it is made, though it can be gently reheated. Once cooked, do not refrigerate, the pastry will lose its crispness.
The apples can be prepared an hour ahead; keep them in a bowl of lemon water to prevent browning, then pat dry before arranging in the pan.
If your pan handle is not ovenproof, wrap it in foil before the tart goes into the oven.

steps.text: Heat your oven to 200°C. Have a 25 cm ovenproof frying pan ready.

Sprinkle the caster sugar evenly over the base of the pan. Place over medium heat and watch as it begins to melt at the edges. Resist the urge to stir; instead, tilt the pan gently so the unmelted sugar slides into the liquid. When all the sugar has dissolved and turned a deep amber, about 8 minutes, remove from heat. It should smell like caramel, nutty and rich.
Working quickly, dot the 60 g butter over the caramel in small pieces. Stir in the vanilla extract.

Arrange the apple halves cut-side up in concentric circles, starting at the outside and working towards the centre. They will fit snugly and overlap slightly. The apples will release their juice and seem to fill the pan; this is normal.
Return the pan to medium heat and cook, without stirring, for 15 minutes. The apples will soften and the caramel will darken further. Tilt the pan occasionally to ensure even cooking.
Roll out the puff pastry to a circle slightly larger than the pan. Lay it over the apples, tucking the edges down inside the pan. If the handle is not ovenproof, wrap it in foil.
Bake for 20 to 25 minutes, until the pastry is golden and puffed. The edges will brown before the centre, this is fine.

Remove from the oven and let rest for 5 minutes. Place a serving plate over the pan, then quickly and confidently invert the tart onto the plate. If any apples stick, gently replace them. Serve warm or at room temperature.

notes: Make the ragù the day before and reheat gently. It improves overnight.
If you can't find pork shoulder, beef chuck works just as well.
Cook pork until it reaches at least 70°C in the thickest part (75°C for mince and sausages).
Food safety:

steps.text: Heat the oil in a large, heavy-bottomed pot over medium-high heat. Working in batches, brown the pork on all sides, don't crowd the pan. Set aside, about 10 minutes total.
Lower the heat to medium. Add the carrot, celery and onion to the same pot and cook, stirring, until soft and golden, about 12 minutes. This is your soffritto; don't skip it.
Return the pork to the pot. Pour in the wine and let it bubble away, scraping up the brown bits, about 2 minutes. Add the tomatoes, stock and bay leaves. Stir.
Bring to a gentle simmer. Partially cover and cook for 3 hours, stirring occasionally. The ragù is done when the meat falls apart and the sauce is thick and dark. Season with salt and pepper.
Twenty minutes before serving, bring a large pot of salted water to a boil. Cook the pappardelle until al dente, about 3 minutes for fresh pasta. Reserve a cup of pasta water.
Drain the pappardelle and add directly to the ragù. Toss, adding pasta water a splash at a time until the sauce coats the ribbon. Serve with grated Parmesan.

notes: Food safety: Cook chicken and other poultry until the juices run clear and the thickest part reaches 75°C.

steps.text: Bring a large pot of water to the boil. Add the egg noodles and cook for 2 minutes until just softened but still a little firm, they'll cook a bit more in the pan. Drain well in a colander.
Heat 1 tbsp of the neutral oil in a large wok or frying pan over high heat. Add the chicken and cook, stirring, for 4 to 5 minutes until cooked through. Transfer to a plate.

Add the remaining oil to the pan. Add the garlic and cook, stirring, for 30 seconds until fragrant. Add the spring onions and choy sum, and stir-fry for 2 minutes until the choy sum is tender and bright.

Return the chicken to the pan. Add the cooked noodles, soy sauce, oyster sauce and sesame oil. Toss everything together, stirring gently but constantly, for 2 minutes until heated through and well mixed. Taste and adjust the seasoning with salt and white pepper.
Divide between bowls and top with fried shallots if you like.

notes: This is best eaten fresh, the moment it comes off the stove, the broccoli stays crispest that way.
If you don't like chilli heat, leave it out or just use half a slice. It's your table.

steps.text: Heat a large frying pan over high heat without any oil. Add the broccoli and toss it around for 5–6 minutes, stirring often, until the florets are brown and crispy on the edges and tender inside. Tip onto a plate.
In the same frying pan, warm the olive oil over low-to-medium heat. Add the sliced garlic and chilli, stirring gently for 1–2 minutes until fragrant but not brown. The oil will flavour as it warms.
While the oil and garlic warm, bring a pot of salted water to a boil and cook the pasta until just al dente, about 10–12 minutes.
Drain the pasta, reserving a cup of the cooking water. Add the hot pasta to the frying pan with the garlic oil, tossing gently to coat. Add the crispy broccoli back in and toss again.
If it looks dry, splash in a splash of the pasta water to loosen it, you want it silky, not oily. Taste and add more salt and chilli if you like. Serve straightaway.

notes: If you don't have tamarind paste, use ½ tsp tamarind concentrate or a squeeze of lemon juice, adjust to taste.
Rasam keeps well in the fridge for 2–3 days. Reheat gently on the stove; make the tempering fresh each time for maximum crackle.
Make a double batch on Sunday: divide into two jars and it lasts the week. The flavour deepens after day two.
Serve cold or at room temperature with white rice and other banchan.
Food safety: Cook fish until it is opaque and flakes easily (63°C in the thickest part), and prawns until pink and opaque all the way through.

steps.text: Blanch the calamari in boiling water for 1 minute, then drain and set aside, this stops it toughening when you stir-fry it.
Heat the sesame oil in a large pan or wok over medium-high heat. Add the garlic and fry, stirring, for about 30 seconds until fragrant.
Add the gochugaru and stir for another 30 seconds to bloom the spice. Pour in the soy sauce and sugar.
Add the calamari and the white parts of the spring onion. Stir-fry for 2–3 minutes until everything is coated and heated through. Don't overcook or the squid will be rubbery.
Remove from heat. Fold through the green parts of the spring onion and sprinkle with sesame seeds.
Let it cool to room temperature, then transfer to a clean jar. It keeps covered in the fridge for 5 days.

notes: Make this a day ahead and reheat gently; the flavours deepen overnight. Serve with mashed potato, crusty bread or steamed greens.
A dry Tasmanian apple cider works best, but you can use any dry cider. If you only have sweet cider on hand, reduce the honey.
Leftovers keep in the fridge for up to 4 days and freeze well for a month.
Food safety: Cook fresh pork to at least 70°C in the thickest part.

steps.text: Heat the oven to 160°C. Pat the pork dry and season generously with salt and pepper.

Heat the oil in a large heavy-bottomed pot or Dutch oven over medium-high heat. Working in batches, brown the pork for 2–3 minutes on each side, then set aside on a plate. Don't crowd the pan, you're looking for a good golden colour, not steam.

In the same pot, cook the onions and garlic until the onions soften and just begin to colour, about 5 minutes. Pour in the cider, scraping up the browned bits at the bottom, and let it bubble for a minute.
Return the pork to the pot, add the stock, thyme and bay leaves. Bring to a simmer, then cover and transfer to the oven for 2 hours, stirring occasionally.
Add the apples and stir through. Return to the oven, uncovered, for another 30 minutes, until the pork is very tender and the apples have softened into the sauce.
Taste and adjust the seasoning. If you like, stir through the honey for a little sweetness. Serve with crusty bread or mashed potato.

notes: If you can't find shishitos, long green chillies work fine, just halve them lengthways so they cook through faster.
Make the dressing ahead of time if you like, but toss the peppers while they're still hot so they soak up the flavours.
Make ahead: Prepare the batter up to 4 hours before steaming and keep chilled. Assemble and steam when ready.
Banana leaves: If you have fresh or frozen banana leaves, wrap each portion in a leaf before steaming for that authentic texture.
This uses raw or lightly cooked egg. Use fresh, clean, uncracked eggs (pasteurised if you can get them), keep it cold, and skip it for anyone pregnant, very young, elderly or with low immunity.
Food safety: Raw and lightly cooked foods aren't recommended for pregnant women, young children, older people or anyone with a weakened immune system.

steps.text: Boil the 2 eggs for 8 minutes until just hard-boiled, then peel and set aside.

In a blender, combine the drained black-eyed peas, red onion, red chillies, garlic, raw egg, oil, ginger, salt and pepper. Blend until completely smooth, 2–3 minutes; the batter should be light and silky.
Lightly oil four small ramekins (about 200 ml each) or line four coffee cups with plastic wrap.
Divide one-third of the batter among the ramekins. Place a hard-boiled egg in the centre of each, then top with the remaining batter until each ramekin is three-quarters full.
Pour water into a large pot to a depth of 3 cm. Place a trivet or heat-proof saucer in the bottom. Bring to a boil until the water is bubbling steadily and steam is rising.

Carefully place the ramekins on the trivet. Cover the pot with a lid and steam over medium heat for 40 minutes, until the moi moi is set and springs back when lightly touched. Refill the water if it falls below the level of the trivet.
Remove from the pot and let rest for 5 minutes. Run a knife around the edge of each ramekin and turn out onto a plate (if using ramekins) or unwrap carefully. Serve warm with bread or rice.

notes: Make the filling up to 3 hours ahead and reheat gently before using. It's best warm but not piping hot when you wrap it.
Use waxy potato if floury is hard to find, it'll be a bit stickier but still work fine.

steps.text: Boil the potato in salted water until tender, about 15 minutes. Drain well.
While the potato cooks, heat the oil in a large pan over medium heat. Add the cumin seeds and let them crackle for 30 seconds until fragrant.
Add the diced onion and cook, stirring, until soft and golden, about 5 minutes.
Add the chopped green chillies and cook for another minute, until fragrant and the chillies have softened slightly.
Tip the hot potato into the pan and mash gently with the back of a wooden spoon, breaking it into floury pieces rather than a smooth paste. The potato should be chunky and still slightly warm.
Mix in the salt and pepper to taste. Set aside to cool slightly before using to fill roti.

notes: You can prep the octopus the day before: boil it, cool, cut it, and store it in the fridge. Grill it fresh on the day.
Charring the lemon is crucial, don't skip it. The bitterness and colour make the dish.
If you can't find whole fresh octopus, use frozen. Thaw it overnight in the fridge first.
Food safety: Cook fish until it is opaque and flakes easily (63°C in the thickest part), and prawns until pink and opaque all the way through.

steps.text: Fill a large pot with water and bring to a boil. Add the octopus, onion and bay leaves. Simmer gently for 45–60 minutes, until the octopus is tender, a fork should pierce it easily. Drain and let cool slightly.
Cut the octopus in half lengthwise, then cut each half into 4 or 5 pieces. Pat dry with paper towel.
Heat your grill to high until very hot and smoking lightly. Brush the octopus pieces with a little olive oil and season with salt and pepper.
Grill the octopus for 3–4 minutes each side until charred and crispy on the outside. Transfer to a plate.
Place the lemon halves cut-side down on the grill and char for 2–3 minutes until dark and caramelised.
Arrange the octopus on a serving platter. Drizzle generously with olive oil, scatter with oregano, squeeze the charred lemon juice over everything and season with more salt and pepper. Serve warm.

notes: Use sashimi-grade or very fresh crab meat if available; tinned crab in brine works too.
White pepper, not black, keeps the soup's refined appearance, no dark specks.
Don't let the broth boil hard when pouring the egg white, or it will scramble into lumps instead of forming ribbons.
Cook chicken until it reaches 75°C in the thickest part and the juices run clear.
Food safety: Cook fish until it is opaque and flakes easily (63°C in the thickest part), and prawns until pink and opaque all the way through.
Make the remoulade up to 3 days ahead and keep it in the fridge.
Use really good-quality roast beef sliced thin from the deli counter, it makes all the difference.
Assemble the smørrebrød just before serving so the bread stays crisp and the onions don't soften too much.
Food safety: Steaks and roasting cuts of beef or lamb can be served pink: about 60°C in the centre is medium-rare, 70°C is well done.

steps.text: Make the remoulade: whisk together mayonnaise, Dijon mustard and wholegrain mustard until smooth. Fold in the capers and pickled gherkin. Add lemon juice and season with salt and pepper. Taste and adjust the mustard or lemon if needed.
Lightly butter each slice of bread, spreading it all the way to the edges.
Lay the roast beef slices on top of the butter in a slightly overlapping layer, until the bread is fully covered and the beef is soft and draped.
Spoon remoulade generously over the beef.
Top with pickled cucumber slices and a handful of crispy fried onions.
Garnish with a small sprig of fresh parsley and serve immediately.

notes: The 'tarik' (pull) is what creates the signature smooth texture and foam. At home, a careful pour from height into the glass works; the mamak masters pour between two vessels for even more drama.
Use a strong black tea, English Breakfast or Assam works perfectly. The tea needs to be robust enough to stand up to the milk.
Drink it straight away while hot and foamy; it's not the same when it cools down.

steps.text: Boil the water in a kettle or small saucepan until it reaches a rolling boil with large bubbles.
Place the black tea leaves in a small pot or teapot. Pour the boiling water over the leaves and let steep for 2–3 minutes until the tea is very strong and dark.
Strain the tea into a large jug, leaving behind the leaves (or remove the tea bags).
Pour the condensed milk and evaporated milk into two glasses or cups.
Carefully pour the hot tea into each glass over the milk, stirring well to combine. If you're feeling brave, pour the tea from a height to create the signature foam and mix.
Taste and add a pinch of salt if you like. Serve hot, and drink while the foam is still there.

notes: The pork can marinate for up to 24 hours, the longer, the better the flavour.
If you can't find achiote paste, use the annatto seed swap, or swap in 1 tbsp smoked paprika plus ½ tsp ground turmeric for a different but still delicious flavour.
Leftover cooked pork keeps in the fridge for 3 days and makes a great burrito filling.
Food safety: Cook fresh pork to at least 70°C in the thickest part.

Nopales prep: Remove the spines carefully with a sharp knife or peeler, then trim the base. If you can't find fresh nopales, jarred or tinned ones work, just drain and rinse before use, and reduce simmering time to 5–8 minutes.
This soup keeps well in the fridge for 3 days and can be frozen for up to a month.

steps.text: Heat olive oil in a large pot over medium heat. Add the quartered onion and crushed garlic, cooking gently until softened and fragrant, about 4 minutes.
Add the diced nopales to the pot, stirring to coat in the oil. Cook for 3–4 minutes; the nopales will release a slight mucilage, which is normal and helps thicken the broth.
Pour in the tinned tomatoes and vegetable stock, breaking up the tomatoes gently. Bring to a simmer until the soup is bubbling gently.
Simmer, uncovered, for 15–18 minutes until the nopales are tender and the broth has developed flavour. Taste and season with salt and black pepper.
Ladle into bowls. Serve hot, scattered with fresh coriander and a lime wedge on the side.

notes: Make these just before serving, they're best eaten warm straight off the tawa.
Pair with sarson da saag, a dollop of yoghurt and sliced onion.

steps.text: Mix the cornmeal, green chilli and salt in a large bowl.
Pour in the warm water slowly, stirring with your fingers until you have a soft, sticky dough that just comes together. It should feel wetter than wheat dough, don't try to knead it smooth.
Heat a cast iron tawa or non-stick frying pan over medium-high heat until a drop of water sizzles and disappears in a second.
Wet your hands with water. Take a golf-ball-sized piece of dough and flatten it between your palms into a rough circle about 5 mm thick. It won't be perfect and it doesn't need to be.
Carefully lay it on the hot tawa and cook for 1 to 2 minutes, until the bottom is pale golden and starting to blister. It will look fragile but it's not.
Flip gently and cook the other side for another 1 to 2 minutes until golden and speckled brown. The roti will stay soft and slightly crumbly.
Transfer to a plate and dot with a tiny bit of ghee or butter. Serve hot, while they're still warm enough to tear easily.

notes: Make it a day ahead; the flavour deepens as it sits.
Use sterilised jars, run them through the dishwasher on a hot cycle or boil them for 10 minutes.
Serve as a side to mezze, with fresh bread, or alongside grilled vegetables and legumes.
Serve with steamed white rice, taro or fresh soda bread to soak up the coconut broth.
You can use any firm white fish: barramundi, snapper, flathead or basa all work well.
Food safety:

steps.text: Heat the oil in a large pan over medium heat. Add the onion and cook, stirring, until soft and golden, about 5 minutes.
Add the garlic and stir for 1 minute until fragrant.
Pour in the coconut milk and crushed tomatoes. Stir to combine and bring to a gentle simmer until the sauce is bubbling lightly.
Add the silverbeet stems and cook for 3 minutes. Then add the silverbeet leaves and stir through.
Gently add the fish chunks to the pan, stirring carefully to distribute them evenly. Simmer for 10 to 12 minutes, until the fish is cooked through and flakes easily.
Season with salt and black pepper to taste. Serve hot with rice or taro.

notes: Make ahead: soak the rice overnight, then steam and serve fresh.
Keep the rice warm: wrapped in a damp cloth in the bamboo basket for up to an hour.
No sticky-rice basket? A covered bamboo steamer or any covered pot works fine, just keep it warm and wrapped.
The meringue base can be made up to 2 days ahead and kept in an airtight container.
Quandongs are tart stone fruit sourced locally in Central Australia; if unavailable outside the region, use fresh or lightly stewed stone fruit like peaches, nectarines or apricots.
Assemble just before serving so the meringue stays crisp.
Food safety: Raw and lightly cooked foods aren't recommended for pregnant women, young children, older people or anyone with a weakened immune system.
Make ahead: boil potatoes the night before and keep in the fridge. The sauce also keeps for 2 days. Warm gently and serve at room temperature.

If you can't find ají amarillo paste, look for it in the Latin or South American aisle of your supermarket, or online. It's worth seeking out, it has a distinctive mild heat and fruity flavour unique to Peruvian cooking.

steps.text: Place the sliced daikon in a large bowl. Add 1 tbsp salt and toss gently but thoroughly until every slice is coated. Set a timer: salt the radish for exactly 20 minutes, this is crucial. The radish should release its water and become pliable but still crisp.

While the radish salts, prepare the brine: dissolve 2 tbsp salt in 1 litre of cold water in a separate bowl. Stir in the fish sauce and sugar until dissolved. Taste and adjust the salt if needed, it should taste pleasantly salty, like a good broth.
After 20 minutes, gently rinse the radish under cold running water, pressing softly to remove excess salt and liquid. Drain well in a colander for 2 minutes.
Transfer the drained radish to a clean container or bowl. Add the gochugaru, garlic, ginger and spring onions, tossing gently to combine.
Pour the cold brine over the vegetables until they are just covered. Press a piece of plastic wrap or a small plate onto the surface to keep everything submerged.

Cover and refrigerate for at least 2 hours before serving. The nabak kimchi will taste good cold from the fridge and will keep for up to 2 weeks. The flavour deepens as it ferments; after 3–4 days in the fridge, it develops a gentle fizz and tang.
Pour the dashi into a small pot. Add soy sauce and mirin, and bring to a simmer over medium heat until small bubbles form at the edge and the mixture is fragrant. Keep it warm.
Cut the chilled tofu into 4 cubes, patting them dry very gently with paper towel, moisture is the enemy of crispness.
Put cornflour in a shallow dish and season lightly with salt. Coat each tofu cube gently on all sides.
Heat a thin layer of neutral oil in a small frying pan over medium-high heat until it shimmers. It should be hot but not smoking.
Carefully place the tofu cubes in the oil and cook for 3 to 4 minutes, turning once, until the outside is golden and crisp all over.
Divide the hot dashi between two bowls. Gently place two tofu cubes into each bowl.
Top with spring onion and ginger, and serve at once, while the dashi steams and the tofu still has its gentle warmth.
Heat the oil in a heavy-bottomed pot over medium heat. Add the rice and stir constantly until it turns pale golden and smells toasted, about 3 minutes.
Add the onion halves and bay leaf, then pour in the chicken stock. Stir once, then bring to a boil until the stock is bubbling steadily.
Once boiling, reduce the heat to low, cover with a tight-fitting lid, and cook without lifting the lid for 15 minutes, until the rice is tender and the liquid is absorbed.
Remove from the heat and let it rest, covered, for 2 minutes. Remove the onion halves and bay leaf, fluff the rice with a fork, season with salt to taste, and serve.

notes: Make it a day ahead. The flavour only gets better sitting in the fridge overnight.
Serve with crusty bread, mash, or over rice to soak up the gravy.
Food safety: Braised beef and lamb cook well past 75°C on the way to tender, so they are safe once soft.
Make ahead: Assemble the lumpia up to 4 hours ahead and refrigerate on a tray before frying. Fry just before serving.
Oil temperature is key, too cool and they'll be greasy; too hot and they'll burn. Use a thermometer or the wrapper test.
Serve with sweet chilli sauce, vinegar, or a quick dipping sauce made from soy sauce and a squeeze of lemon.

Food safety: Cook mince and sausages until no pink remains and the centre reaches 75°C. Cook fish until it is opaque and flakes easily (63°C in the thickest part), and prawns until pink and opaque all the way through.
Make ahead: marinate the chicken up to 4 hours. Fry it just before serving so it stays crispy.
The numbing heat comes from Sichuan peppercorn, the burn from dried chilies. Neither are mistakes, they're the point.
Serve with plain steamed rice or congee to cool your mouth between bites.
Food safety: Cook chicken and other poultry until the juices run clear and the thickest part reaches 75°C.
Shiro keeps for 3 days in the fridge. Reheat gently with a splash of water or stock, stirring often.
Shiro is a classic Ethiopian fasting dish: vegan, filling and humble.
Serve over jasmine rice. One batch feeds one person with rice.
Make ahead: the curry keeps in the fridge for 3 days and reheats gently on the stove.
Swap peanut butter for ground peanuts (2 tbsp) stirred in at the end if you prefer texture.
Food safety:

steps.text: Heat oil in a wok or wide pan over medium-high heat until shimmering, about 1 minute.
Add curry paste and cook, stirring, for 1 minute until fragrant.
Add chicken and stir-fry until the edges turn opaque, about 3 minutes.
Pour in coconut milk and bring to a simmer, stirring gently, until the sauce is bubbling lightly and thickens slightly.
Add peanut butter, fish sauce and palm sugar. Stir until peanut butter dissolves, about 2 minutes.
Tear in the makrut lime leaf and simmer for 5 minutes until chicken is cooked through (75°C inside) and sauce is thick and glossy.
Taste and adjust fish sauce or palm sugar to balance salty and sweet.
Serve in a bowl with jasmine rice, topped with fresh Thai basil and chilli if using.

notes: Food safety: Cook chicken and other poultry until the juices run clear and the thickest part reaches 75°C.

steps.text: Heat the oil in a large pot over medium heat. Add the turmeric and crushed garlic, stirring for 30 seconds until fragrant and the oil turns golden yellow.
Pour in the stock and coconut milk, stirring to combine. Bring to a simmer over medium-high heat until the broth is bubbling gently and steaming.
Add the fish sauce and stir. Add the chicken slices and simmer gently for 8–10 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the chicken is cooked through.
While the chicken cooks, bring a large pot of water to the boil. Add the noodles and cook according to packet directions until just tender. Drain well.
Divide the noodles between two bowls. Ladle the hot broth and chicken over the top.
Scatter the spring onions over each bowl. Serve with a lime wedge and fresh coriander on the side if you like. Squeeze the lime in before eating.

notes: Make it ahead: the curry tastes better the next day. Store in the fridge for up to 3 days, or freeze for a month.
Use whatever mushrooms you have, cremini, button, portobello all work. Firmer varieties hold their shape better in the long simmer.

steps.text: Heat the oil in a large pot or deep pan over medium heat. Add the curry paste and cook, stirring, for 2 minutes until fragrant.
Add the ginger and garlic, cook for another minute until fragrant, then pour in the coconut milk and stir well to combine.
Add the mushrooms and stir to coat with the curry mixture. Cook for 5 minutes until they start to soften.
Pour in the vegetable stock, tamarind paste and palm sugar. Stir until the sugar and tamarind dissolve, about 2 minutes.

Bring to a gentle simmer and cook uncovered for 25–30 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the mushrooms are very tender and the curry has reduced and darkened. The sauce should coat the back of a spoon.
Taste and adjust salt and sourness if needed. Serve hot with jasmine rice.

notes: Make them ahead: assemble the rolls, refrigerate up to 4 hours, then bake as directed.
The eggplants need to lose their water first – salt them well and don't rush this step.
For a vegetarian version, use a vegetarian hard cheese (made without animal rennet).
Make ahead: marinate the chicken overnight in the fridge for deeper flavour and better texture.
Leftovers: keeps in an airtight container in the fridge for 3 days; serve cold in bento or reheat gently.
Oil temperature matters: use a thermometer if you have one; too cool and it will be oily, too hot and the outside burns before the inside cooks.
Food safety:

steps.text: Combine soy sauce, mirin, garlic, ginger and sesame oil in a bowl. Add the chicken pieces and toss to coat well. Cover and marinate in the fridge for at least 2 hours, preferably overnight.
When ready to cook, remove the chicken from the marinade and place on paper towel. Pat dry thoroughly, this is important for crispiness. Reserve the marinade.
Mix potato starch and plain flour together on a plate. Season the chicken pieces lightly with salt and white pepper, then coat each piece in the starch mixture, shaking off any excess.
Heat neutral oil in a deep-sided pan or wok to 170°C. Working in batches so the pan isn't crowded, carefully lower the chicken into the oil.
Fry for 8 to 10 minutes, turning halfway through, until the coating is golden and the thickest pieces are cooked through (75°C inside). Transfer to a paper towel to drain.
Serve hot with lemon wedges and fresh coriander if you like. Any leftovers keep well cold in a bento box for the next day.

notes: Make the filling up to a day ahead; store in the fridge. Assemble sambuusas up to 2 hours before frying.
If filo dries out as you work, cover the sheets with a damp tea towel.
Freeze uncooked sambuusas on a tray, then transfer to a container. Fry from frozen, adding a minute or two to the cooking time.
Food safety: Cook mince and sausages until no pink remains and the centre reaches 75°C.
Biscuits are best served warm from the oven. Leftovers can be split and toasted the next day.
For extra tender biscuits, chill the dough for 15 minutes before cutting and baking.
Make sure your butter and buttermilk are cold, this is what gives the biscuits their flaky layers.

steps.text: Preheat oven to 200°C. Place a 25 cm cast-iron frying pan in the oven to heat.
