Whisk together flour, baking powder and salt in a large bowl. Add the cold butter cubes and use your fingertips to rub the mixture until it resembles coarse breadcrumbs with some pea-sized pieces of butter remaining.
Make a well in the centre and pour in the cold buttermilk. Using a fork, gently mix until a shaggy dough just comes together, don't overwork it or the biscuits will be tough.
Turn the dough out onto a lightly floured bench and gently pat it into a 2 cm thick round. Using a 7 cm biscuit cutter dipped in flour, cut out biscuits, pressing straight down without twisting.
Carefully remove the hot frying pan from the oven and brush lightly with melted butter. Arrange biscuits in the pan, they should just touch each other.
Brush the tops with a little more melted butter. Bake for 12–15 minutes, until golden brown on top and cooked through.
Let cool in the pan for 2 minutes, then turn out onto a wire rack. Serve warm.

notes: Use day-old or chilled rice, fresh hot rice gets mushy. If you only have hot rice, spread it on a plate to cool first.
Toast the Sichuan peppercorns in a dry pan for 1 minute before grinding for deeper flavour.
Leftovers keep in the fridge for 2 days and reheat well in a hot pan.
Food safety: Cook mince and sausages until no pink remains and the centre reaches 75°C.
Maklouba keeps well in the fridge for up to 3 days. Reheat gently in a low oven wrapped in foil, or flash it in a hot pan to recrisp the bottom layer.
Use a non-stick or well-seasoned pot, this makes the flip much less stressful.
The spice blend is forgiving. If you don't have cardamom, add a pinch more cumin. If you don't have cinnamon, leave it out entirely.

steps.text: Fry the eggplant slices in batches in hot oil until golden on both sides, about 4 minutes. Transfer to a plate lined with paper towel. This step is crucial, the eggplant will soften in the steam, so frying it first keeps its shape and flavour.

In the same oil, fry the potato matchsticks in batches until just starting to turn golden, about 3 minutes. You want them still a bit firm because they'll cook further in the rice. Transfer to the paper towel plate.
Fry the cauliflower florets until lightly golden, about 3 minutes. Set aside. You should have about 3 tablespoons of oil left in the pot; if not, add a little more.
In the same pot, cook the sliced onions over medium heat, stirring, until soft and golden, about 8 minutes. Add the garlic and cook for 1 minute more until fragrant.

Stir in the cumin, coriander, cardamom and cinnamon, cooking for 1 minute. You'll smell the spices bloom, this is when their flavour becomes most alive. Add the rice and stir to coat it in the spiced oil, cooking for 2 minutes.

Layer the rice mixture back into the pot in this order: half the rice on the bottom, then the eggplant, potato and cauliflower mixed together, then the remaining rice on top. Press down gently to compact the layers. Pour the warm stock over carefully.

Bring to a boil, then reduce heat to low. Cover with foil, then place the lid on top, the foil traps steam, which cooks the rice evenly. Cook for 20 minutes until the rice is tender and the stock is absorbed. Listen: when the liquid stops bubbling, you're done.

Let it rest, covered, for 5 minutes. Run a thin knife around the edges of the pot to loosen it. Place a large platter over the pot, and in one confident motion, flip the pot onto the platter. Lift the pot away slowly. You should see a golden crust on top.
Serve warm with generous dollops of Greek yoghurt and fresh parsley if you like. Eat it while the crust is still crispy.

notes: Fesenjan tastes better the next day. Make it ahead and reheat gently.
If you can't find pomegranate molasses, use equal parts pomegranate juice and lemon juice reduced in a pan until syrupy, or use a mix of pomegranate juice and balsamic vinegar.
Serve with tahdig, rice cooked until the bottom catches and caramelizes in a thin, crispy layer.
Food safety: Cook chicken and other poultry until the juices run clear and the thickest part reaches 75°C.

steps.text: Heat the oil in a large, heavy pot over medium-high heat. Season the chicken generously with salt and pepper. Working in batches, brown the chicken skin-side down for 5 minutes, then turn and brown the other side for 3 minutes. Set aside.
In the same pot, add the onion halves and cook, stirring occasionally, until they soften and colour, about 8 minutes. Add the tomato paste and cook for 1 minute, stirring.
Stir in the walnuts, cinnamon and turmeric. Cook for 2 minutes until fragrant.

Pour in the pomegranate juice and pomegranate molasses, scraping up any brown bits from the bottom of the pot. Return the chicken to the pot, skin-side up. Bring to a simmer until the sauce is bubbling gently and starting to thicken.

Cover and cook on low heat for 50–60 minutes, until the chicken is tender and cooked through and the sauce has deepened in colour and thickened slightly. Taste and adjust the salt, pepper, and balance of sweet and sour as needed.
Remove the onion halves. Serve over rice, with fresh coriander if you like it.

notes: Food safety: Cook fish until it is opaque and flakes easily (63°C in the thickest part), and prawns until pink and opaque all the way through.

steps.text: Heat the oil in a large heavy-bottomed pot over medium heat. Add the flour and stir constantly for 8 to 10 minutes, until the roux is deep golden brown, this is the foundation of everything. Don't rush it; if it starts to burn, pull it off the heat for a moment.
Add the onion, capsicum, and celery to the roux. Stir well and cook for about 5 minutes, until the vegetables soften and release their flavour. This is the holy trinity, cher.
Push the vegetables to the side, add the sausage, and let it sear for 2 to 3 minutes. Stir in the garlic, cayenne, paprika, thyme, and oregano, cooking for 1 more minute until fragrant.

Pour in the crushed tomatoes and chicken stock. Scrape the bottom of the pot to loosen any browned bits. Bring to a gentle boil until bubbling, then reduce the heat to medium-low. Stir in the rice, making sure it's covered by liquid.
Simmer, stirring occasionally, for about 20 minutes, until the rice is nearly tender and most of the liquid is absorbed.
Gently fold in the prawns, crab, and oysters (if using). Cook for 3 to 4 minutes, until the prawns are pink and cooked through and the oysters have just firmed up.
Season to taste with salt and pepper. Serve hot, scattered with fresh parsley if you like.

notes: Make sure your dosa batter is at room temperature; cold batter won't spread and cook evenly.
If your batter is too thick, add a splash of water, it should be pourable but thicker than a dosa batter.
Uttapam keeps for a day in an airtight container and reheats well in a toaster or griddle.

steps.text: Heat a non-stick griddle or heavy-bottomed pan over medium heat and lightly oil it.
Pour 1/4 cup of batter onto the griddle and gently spread into a thick round, about 8 cm across. Don't thin it out like a dosa, keep it thick and spongy.
Let it cook, undisturbed, for about 2 minutes until the bottom is golden and set.
Sprinkle a small handful of chopped onion, tomato, green chilli and coriander (if using) over the top. Press gently into the batter.
Flip carefully and cook the other side for another 2 minutes until golden. If the top toppings aren't cooked enough, cover the pan with a lid for 30 seconds.
Transfer to a plate and repeat with the remaining batter and toppings.
Serve hot with sambar, rasam or fresh coconut chutney.

notes: Soak wooden skewers in water for 30 minutes before threading if using them instead of metal ones.
Make the suya spice ahead and store in an airtight container for up to two weeks.
Food safety:

steps.text: Thread the beef cubes onto skewers, packing them tightly together. Rub with oil, salt, black pepper and ground ginger.

Pulse the roasted peanuts in a food processor until they're finely ground but still have some texture, not a smooth butter. Tip into a shallow bowl and stir through the cayenne, paprika, ground ginger, salt, black pepper and garlic.

Heat a griddle, grill or large frying pan over high heat until very hot. Working in batches, sear the skewers for 3 to 4 minutes, turning to cook all sides until the beef is deeply browned and cooked through (the meat should reach 75°C inside).
Immediately after cooking, while still hot, roll each skewer in the suya spice mixture until generously coated on all sides.
Serve hot, straight away.

notes: A potjie needs at least 45 minutes on low, steady heat. If your braai is too hot, move the pot to the edge and add less frequent wood.
You can prep all the veg at home and bring it in containers to the braai for faster assembly.
Leftover potjiekos reheats beautifully the next day.
Food safety: Braised beef and lamb cook well past 75°C on the way to tender, so they are safe once soft.

steps.text: Place a 7-litre cast iron potjie (or large heavy-based pot) over medium coals on the braai. Heat the oil until shimmering, then add the beef in batches. Brown on all sides, about 8 minutes per batch, then remove and set aside.
Reduce the heat to low coals (move the pot away from the hottest part of the braai). Add the onion to the pot and cook, stirring, for 3 minutes until slightly softened.
Add the browned beef back to the pot, then layer in the carrots and potatoes. Sprinkle with garlic and thyme, then season with salt and pepper.

Pour the beef stock over everything. Cover with the lid and let it cook on low heat for about 1 hour, until the potatoes and beef are almost tender. Resist lifting the lid too often, you want to keep the heat in.
Add the cabbage wedges, nestling them into the liquid. Replace the lid and cook for another 20 minutes until the cabbage is tender and the beef is cooked through.
Taste and adjust the seasoning. Serve straight from the pot, family-style, with crusty bread to soak up the liquid.

notes: Make the macaroni salad ahead: it's even better the next day.
If you can't find mirin, use 2 tbsp honey instead.
Leftover chicken keeps for three days in the fridge; reheat gently with a splash of water.
Food safety:

steps.text: Cook the macaroni according to packet directions until al dente, then drain and rinse under cold water. In a bowl, mix the mayonnaise, rice vinegar, sugar, carrot, and onion. Toss the cooled pasta through. Season to taste with salt and pepper. Chill while you cook the chicken.
In a small bowl, whisk together the soy sauce, brown sugar, mirin, garlic, and ginger. Set aside.

Heat the oil in a large frying pan over medium-high heat. Season the chicken thighs with salt and pepper on both sides. Place skin-side down in the pan and cook for 6–7 minutes until the skin is golden and crispy.
Turn the thighs skin-side up and cook for another 4–5 minutes until cooked through (internal temperature 75°C). Pour off most of the fat from the pan, leaving about 1 tbsp.

Pour the teriyaki sauce over the chicken. Mix the cornflour with the water until smooth, add to the pan, and stir gently. Simmer for 2–3 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the sauce thickens and coats the chicken.
Divide the rice between four plates, making two scoops per plate. Top with the glazed chicken thighs and any sauce. Serve the macaroni salad on the side and garnish with spring onion if you like.

notes: Perkedel is best served warm. You can make the fritters ahead and reheat them in a moderate oven (180°C) for 8 minutes.
Let the boiled potato cool completely, warm potato breaks down when you fry it and won't stay soft inside.
Serve with sambal or sweet soy sauce for dipping.
Food safety: Raw and lightly cooked foods aren't recommended for pregnant women, young children, older people or anyone with a weakened immune system.
This keeps in the fridge for 3 days and tastes better the next day as the flavours deepen. Serve it cold as banchan or gently reheat.
You can use any dried chillies you have, guajillo or ancho work well too, though the flavour will shift. Stay with long varieties if you can; they soften into beautiful strands.
Lugaw keeps in the fridge for 2 days; reheat gently with a little extra stock to loosen it.
Add crispy fried garlic and egg just before serving so the garlic stays crunchy.
Cook chicken until it reaches 75°C in the thickest part and the juices run clear.

steps.text: Bring the chicken stock to a boil in a large pot until bubbling steadily. Add the rice and salt, stir well, and return to a boil.
Reduce heat to low, cover partly, and simmer, stirring often, for 40 minutes. The rice should break down and the porridge should be creamy and thick.
While the lugaw cooks, boil the eggs in a separate pot for 10 minutes until hard-boiled. Cool, shell, and halve them.
Heat the neutral oil in a small frying pan over medium-high heat. Add the sliced garlic and fry, stirring, until golden and crispy, about 3 minutes. Drain on paper towel.
Divide the lugaw among serving bowls. Top each with a halved egg, crispy fried garlic, and spring onion if using. Serve warm.

notes: Make ahead: prepare the parcel up to 4 hours before roasting.
The cooking liquid makes a silky pan sauce, don't skip it. Serve with horta (simply boiled greens) or crusty bread to mop it up.
Leftovers shred beautifully and work in pies or as a filling for spanakopita.
Food safety:

steps.text: Pat the lamb dry and season generously inside and out with salt and pepper.
Tear off a sheet of baking paper about 1 m long. Place the lamb in the centre and scatter the onion, garlic, tomatoes, feta and oregano around and over it.
Drizzle with olive oil, then fold the paper up and over the lamb, folding and creasing the edges to seal it completely, the parcel should be airtight.
Place the parcel on a large roasting tray and roast at 160°C for 4 to 5 hours. The lamb is done when a fork slides through the meat like butter.
Carefully open the paper (steam will billow out). Transfer the lamb to a serving platter and let it rest for 10 minutes while you pour the cooking liquid into a small saucepan.
Skim the fat from the surface of the liquid and warm it gently over medium heat. Season with salt, pepper and lemon juice to taste, then pour over the lamb and serve.

notes: The coconut bread keeps wrapped for two days. Taro and pisupo are best made the day of, but can be reheated gently.
Scale up easily for bigger gatherings: add another tin of pisupo and kg of taro for every five extra people.
Let everyone build their own plate, the mains are flexible, and plenty of fruit rounds it out for those with lighter appetites.
Food safety: Raw and lightly cooked foods aren't recommended for pregnant women, young children, older people or anyone with a weakened immune system.

steps.text: Start the taro: bring a large pot of salted water to the boil. Add taro chunks and simmer for 25–30 minutes until tender and cooked through. Drain well and place in a serving bowl. Keep warm.

While the taro cooks, heat oil in a large frying pan over medium heat. Add onions and cook, stirring, until soft and golden, about 8 minutes. Add corned beef, breaking it up with a wooden spoon, and stir-fry for 5–8 minutes until warmed through. Season with salt and pepper. Transfer to a serving platter.

Make the coconut bread: preheat oven to 180°C. Sift flour, baking powder and salt into a large bowl. In another bowl, whisk together sugar, coconut milk, desiccated coconut, eggs, oil and vanilla. Pour wet ingredients into dry ingredients and stir until just combined, don't overmix.

Divide batter between two greased 20 cm loaf tins and bake for 35–40 minutes until a skewer inserted in the centre comes out clean. Cool in tins for 5 minutes, then turn out onto a wire rack. Slice and arrange on a platter.
Arrange all fruit on platters, keeping different types separate so people can choose.
Set the table with pisupo, taro, coconut bread and fruit platters. Serve family-style, with everyone helping themselves.

notes: Make the sausages up to a day ahead and refrigerate on a tray before grilling.
Pork sausage casings are in the meat section at good butchers and some larger supermarkets. Soak them in water for 30 minutes before filling so they're easier to work with.
Food safety: Cook mince and sausages until no pink remains and the centre reaches 75°C.

steps.text: Mix the pork mince with coriander, garlic chives, spring onion, chilli, fish sauce, ground cumin and ground coriander in a bowl until just combined.

Fit a sausage casing onto a sausage stuffer or piping bag fitted with a large plain nozzle. Pipe the filling into the casing, pushing gently so it's loosely packed until the sausage is plump but not tight, which stops it bursting on the grill. Tie the end.
Heat your barbecue or grill plate to medium-high until hot and sizzling when a little oil hits it, and oil the grates.

Coil the sausage onto the hot grill. Cook for 12 minutes, turning every couple of minutes to colour all sides evenly. The casing should be dark brown and crackling, and the meat cooked through when you press it.
Transfer to a plate and let it rest for a minute. Serve with sticky rice, lime wedges and fresh coriander and chilli on the side.
Bring a large pot of salted water to a boil. Add the greens in batches if needed, stirring so they wilt evenly.
Simmer until the greens are completely tender, about 10–15 minutes. The water should taste like the sea.
Drain in a colander, gently pressing out excess water with the back of a spoon, don't squeeze them dry.
Divide the warm greens among plates. Drizzle each serving generously with olive oil, then squeeze lemon juice over the top. Season with salt to taste and serve warm or at room temperature.

notes: Make it the day before, it thickens as it sits and tastes even better reheated. Add a splash of stock when you warm it up.
Use any crusty bread: sourdough, ciabatta, or even that discounted loaf from the Central Market.
Make the kebab mixture up to 2 hours ahead and chill until ready to cook.
If you don't have metal skewers, use wooden ones soaked in cold water for 30 minutes.
A cast iron pan works brilliantly for the high heat and even browning.
Food safety: Cook mince and sausages until no pink remains and the centre reaches 75°C.
Make the sambal paste up to a day ahead and store in a jar in the fridge, it keeps well and the flavours deepen.
For extra richness, use coconut oil instead of neutral oil for the sambal.
If you prefer it milder, use fewer dried chillies or remove more seeds; if you like serious heat, add an extra fresh chilli.
Haleem improves overnight: make it the day before, cool and store in the fridge, then gently reheat and add fresh crispy onions and ginger before serving.
If using a slow cooker, use the same ingredients and cook on low for 8 hours, stirring halfway through. The texture will be slightly looser, add a little less stock if using this method.
For a leaner dish, use lamb shoulder or goat instead of beef; cooking time stays the same.
Food safety: Braised beef and lamb cook well past 75°C on the way to tender, so they are safe once soft.

steps.text: Heat 3 tbsp ghee in a large heavy-based pot over medium heat. Working in batches, brown the beef on all sides, 8–10 minutes total. Set aside.
In the same pot, add the diced onion and cook, stirring, until soft and golden, about 5 minutes. Add the garlic and ginger, cook for 1 minute until fragrant.
Add cumin, coriander, garam masala, turmeric and cayenne. Stir constantly for 1 minute to bloom the spices.
Return the beef to the pot. Add the crushed tomatoes and stir well. Cook for 2 minutes.

Add the brown lentils, split chickpeas, stock and salt. Stir to combine. Bring to a boil, then reduce heat to low, cover with a lid slightly ajar, and simmer gently for 2½ to 3 hours, stirring occasionally to prevent sticking. The meat should fall apart, the lentils dissolve, and the mixture thicken into a porridge-like consistency. If it's too thick, add more water; if too thin, simmer uncovered toward the end.
Taste and adjust salt and spice. The haleem should be creamy and almost paste-like, with no visible lentil pieces, break up any remaining chunks with a wooden spoon.

About 15 minutes before serving, prepare the garnish. Heat 2 tbsp ghee in a small pan over medium heat. Add the sliced onion and cook, stirring often, until deep golden and crispy, about 8–10 minutes. Add the ginger matchsticks and cook for 1 minute.

Spoon the haleem into bowls, top generously with the crispy onions and ginger, scatter with fresh coriander if using, and serve with lemon wedges on the side. Pour any remaining ghee and pan juices over the top.

notes: Make ahead: shape the stuffed breads the night before, cover and refrigerate, then bring to room temperature and bake the next morning.
Swap the feta for any cheap cheese on sale, white cheddar or halloumi both work well.
Leftover bread keeps wrapped in foil for 2 days and reheats beautifully in a dry pan.
Use beef or chicken stock depending on what you have, both work just as well.
If you have fresh Vietnamese herbs like Thai basil or Vietnamese mint, use those instead of or alongside the coriander and dill.
Food safety: Cook mince and sausages until no pink remains and the centre reaches 75°C.

steps.text: Heat the oil in a large pot over medium-high heat. Add the beef mince, breaking it up as it cooks, until no longer pink, about 4 minutes. Drain any excess fat if needed.
Add the onion and garlic, stirring until fragrant, about 1 minute.
Add the tomato chunks and stir to combine, cooking for 2 minutes.
Pour in the stock and bring to a simmer until the broth is bubbling gently. Add the fish sauce and sugar, stirring to combine.
Simmer for about 10 minutes, until the tomato is soft and the broth is flavourful. Taste and adjust seasoning with salt and white pepper as needed.
Ladle into bowls and serve hot, topped with fresh coriander and dill if using.

notes: The romesco keeps for three days, covered, in the fridge. Make it ahead if you like.
If you can't find calcots, any large spring onion works, the charring is what matters.

steps.text: Char the red capsicums directly over a gas flame or under a hot grill, turning often, until the skin is blackened all over, about 10 minutes. Place in a plastic bag for 5 minutes to steam, then peel away the charred skin. Discard the seeds.
While the capsicums cool slightly, toast the bread in a dry pan over medium heat until golden, about 2 minutes each side. Tear into pieces.
In a mortar or food processor, pound or blitz the hazelnuts with the garlic and toasted bread until you have a rough paste.
Add the peeled capsicums and pound or pulse until you have a chunky sauce. Stir in the vinegar and olive oil. Taste and add salt. The romesco should be thick but spoonable.
Trim the calcots, leaving the white and pale green parts. Rinse well.

Heat a grill pan or cast-iron frying pan over high heat. Brush the calcots lightly with olive oil and place on the hot pan in a single layer. Char, turning occasionally, until the outside is blackened and the inside is tender, about 12–15 minutes. Work in batches if needed.
Transfer the charred calcots to a serving plate. Sprinkle lightly with salt. Serve warm with the romesco sauce for dipping.

notes: Caponata is best made a day or two ahead, the flavours deepen and marry together. Store in an airtight container in the fridge for up to a week.
Serve it at room temperature or cold, as a side dish, on bruschetta, or alongside grilled fish. Some families add a handful of pine nuts, try a small handful if you like.

steps.text: Heat 2 tbsp of the olive oil in a large frying pan over medium-high heat. Working in batches so the eggplant isn't crowded, cook until golden on all sides, about 3–4 minutes per batch. Transfer to a plate as you go. Add the remaining oil if needed.
In the same pan, reduce the heat to medium and cook the onion, stirring, until soft and golden, about 5 minutes. Add the garlic and cook for another minute, until fragrant.
Stir in the tomato paste and cook for 1 minute. Pour in the crushed tomatoes, vinegar and sugar. Bring to a gentle simmer.

Return the eggplant to the pan along with the olives and capers. Stir well. Simmer, uncovered, for 20–25 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the eggplant is very tender and the sauce has thickened and darkened slightly. The flavours should be balanced, sweet, sour and savoury all at once.
Taste and adjust the salt, pepper, vinegar or sugar as needed. Serve at room temperature or cold, scattered with fresh parsley if you like.

notes: Make sure to use waxy potatoes, floury ones will fall apart. Unpeeled skin holds them together better.
Serve warm or at room temperature, but not cold. The flavours are best when the potatoes are still warm enough to absorb the dressing.
This keeps for a few days, covered, in the fridge. Warm gently before serving again.
Store in an airtight tin for up to three days; the custard will firm up further and the flavour will deepen.
If you don't have baking beans, use dried rice or lentils. Make sure the pastry is fully blind-baked or it will be soggy.
For a neater slice, chill the tart for at least 2 hours before serving.
Food safety: The eggs are cooked until just set. For pregnant women, young children, older people or anyone with a weakened immune system, cook them until firm all the way through.

steps.text: Make the pastry: rub the cold butter into the flour and salt until it resembles fine breadcrumbs. Mix the egg yolk with the caster sugar and cold water, then stir into the flour mixture until just combined. Knead gently to bring the dough together, wrap in plastic and refrigerate for 20 minutes.

Preheat the oven to 180°C. Roll out the pastry between two sheets of baking paper to fit a 23 cm loose-bottomed tart tin. Press it gently into the tin and prick the base with a fork. Line with baking paper and fill with baking beans, then bake blind for 12 minutes. Remove the beans and paper, and bake for another 3 minutes until pale golden.
While the pastry bakes, warm the milk with the cinnamon stick over medium heat until steaming, then remove from the heat and let it infuse for 5 minutes. Remove the cinnamon stick and cool slightly.

Whisk the eggs with the sugar until pale and thick, about 3 minutes. Sift the cornflour, flour and salt together, then fold into the eggs. Slowly pour in the warm milk, stirring constantly to avoid lumps. Stir in the vanilla extract.

Strain the custard through a fine sieve into the warm pastry case, pushing gently through any remaining lumps. Bake for 20 to 25 minutes, until the custard is just set but still trembling slightly in the centre, it will set as it cools.
Remove from the oven and let the tart cool completely in the tin. Dust generously with ground cinnamon just before serving.

notes: Make it a day ahead and reheat gently, the flavours deepen. Just prepare the tempering fresh before serving.
If your pumpkin is watery, simmer a little longer to reduce the liquid to a proper sauce.
Erisseri freezes well for up to a month; thaw and reheat on the stove.

steps.text: Toast the coriander seeds, cumin seeds, cloves, cardamom pod and dried red chillies in a dry pan over medium heat, shaking constantly, until fragrant (about 2 minutes). Tip into a bowl and let cool slightly, then grind to a fine powder. Stir in the jaggery.
Heat 1 tbsp of the coconut oil in a heavy-bottomed pot over medium heat. Add the pumpkin and green beans, and fry, stirring gently, for 5 minutes until they start to soften at the edges.
Sprinkle over the ground spice mixture and turmeric, stir well, and cook for another 2 minutes to let the spices coat everything.

Pour in the coconut milk and add enough water so the vegetables are just covered. Bring to a gentle simmer and cook, uncovered, for 20–25 minutes until the pumpkin is completely tender and breaks easily with a spoon, and the beans are soft. Stir occasionally and watch the liquid, it should reduce to a creamy sauce that coats the vegetables.
Taste and adjust salt. The curry should taste warm and mellow, with no raw spice edges.

Just before serving, heat the remaining coconut oil in a small pan over medium-high heat. When it shimmers, add the mustard seeds and a few curry leaves. Let them crackle and pop for about 30 seconds until the seeds finish jumping and the leaves darken slightly. Pour this tempering (tadka) over the curry and stir through. Serve hot with rice.

notes: If you can't find dried oyster mushrooms, use 100 g dried shiitake instead, or a mix of any dried Chinese mushrooms you have on hand.
The chicken must be cooked through (75°C at the thickest part); check with an instant-read thermometer if unsure.
Food safety:

steps.text: Soak the dried shiitake and oyster mushrooms in 250 ml hot water for 10 minutes until softened. Drain, reserving 125 ml of the soaking liquid. Trim the shiitake stems and halve both types of mushrooms.

Pat the chicken breasts dry and place them on a shallow steaming plate that fits in your wok or steamer. Scatter the mushrooms around and under the chicken. Tuck the ginger slices and spring onion pieces beneath and around the chicken.
In a small bowl, whisk the soy sauce, sesame oil, neutral oil, and reserved mushroom liquid. Pour evenly over the chicken and mushrooms. Season lightly with salt, the soy is already salty.

Fill your wok or steamer base with water so it comes to about 5 cm deep. Bring to a rolling boil over high heat until the water is bubbling vigorously and steam is billowing. Place the steaming plate inside on a stand or trivet, making sure the plate doesn't touch the water.
Cover and steam for 12 minutes on high heat. The chicken is done when a skewer inserted into the thickest part meets no resistance, and the juices run clear.

Carefully remove the plate using tongs or oven mitts, the steam is hot, once the chicken is cooked through with no pink and the mushrooms are tender. Serve hot in the steaming dish, spooning the aromatic broth over the chicken and mushrooms. Pour any remaining broth into a small bowl to drizzle over rice.

notes: If you can find pandan extract, use a tsp in one portion instead of food colouring for authentic flavour. Gula melaka (coconut sugar) can replace caster sugar for a deeper flavour.
Each layer must set properly before the next, don't rush this. If you pour the next layer onto a runny layer, the colours will muddy.
Food safety: Raw and lightly cooked foods aren't recommended for pregnant women, young children, older people or anyone with a weakened immune system.

steps.text: Preheat the oven to 180°C. Line an 8 × 8 inch square tin with baking paper, letting it hang over the sides.

Mix desiccated coconut, coconut milk, caster sugar, plain flour, baking powder, salt and eggs in a bowl until smooth. Divide the mixture into 3 or 4 portions and add a few drops of food colouring to each portion (or leave some plain for white layers), stirring well. Keep each colour in a separate bowl.
Pour the first colour into the prepared tin and spread evenly to fill the bottom. Bake for 8 to 10 minutes until just set but still soft, it should not be completely firm.
Pour the second colour slowly over the first layer and bake again for 8 to 10 minutes until set.
Repeat with the remaining colours, baking each layer for 8 to 10 minutes, until all layers are done.
Remove from the oven and let cool completely in the tin on a wire rack, about 30 minutes. The cake should be cool before you try to remove it.
Once cool, use the baking paper to lift the cake out of the tin. Cut into small squares with a sharp, lightly oiled knife.
Store in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 3 days.

notes: Charcoal or hardwood fire makes a big difference to the flavour. If using a gas barbecue, crank it high and let it preheat for 10 minutes.
Don't move the meat around, let it sit and develop that dark, caramelised crust. That's where the flavour is.
Serve with black beans (feijão), white rice, and farofa, as it's served in Brazil.
Food safety:

steps.text: Build your fire in a churrasco grill or barbecue, using charcoal or wood. Let it burn down to glowing coals, you want high, consistent heat, not flames. This should take about 15 to 20 minutes.
Pat the beef, pork and chicken completely dry with paper towels. This helps them get a proper crust.

Oil your grill grates well to stop sticking, then place them about 10 cm above the coals, once the coals are glowing red and covered in a light grey ash, with no flames, and the grates are smoking hot.

Season the beef and pork generously with coarse rock salt on both sides just before they hit the grill. Place them directly on the hot grates and cook without moving them for 4 to 5 minutes, until a dark crust forms. Flip, salt the other side, and cook for another 4 to 5 minutes. The meat should be hot inside (use a meat thermometer: 63°C for medium-rare beef, 70°C for pork).

Season the chicken thighs with rock salt and place skin-side down on the grill. Cook for 6 to 7 minutes until the skin is golden and crispy, then flip. Cook for another 6 to 7 minutes until cooked through (75°C inside).
Rest all the meat on a warm plate for 5 minutes before serving. Drizzle with any pan juices, and serve hot with your favourite side, beans, rice, or farofa all work bem (well).
Heat the oil in a large pot over medium-high heat. Add the onion and cook, stirring, until soft and translucent, about 4 minutes.
Stir in the garlic and cook for 30 seconds until fragrant, then add the tomatoes. Simmer for 5 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the tomatoes break down.
Add the kidney beans, corn, potato and water. Bring to a simmer, then reduce heat to medium and cook until the potato is tender when pierced with a knife and the liquid has thickened slightly.
Cook, stirring occasionally, until the potato is tender, about 12 minutes. The mixture should be thick and saucy.
Season with salt and pepper to taste. Serve hot, scattered with fresh coriander if you like.

notes: Make a day ahead: braise the oxtail, cool completely, then refrigerate overnight. The fat will set on top and you can lift it off easily. Reheat gently on the stove before serving, the flavour only improves.
Serve with creamy mash, crusty bread or buttered rice to soak up every drop of gravy.
Food safety:
Use any leftover roasted or braised meat, beef, pork, lamb or even chicken all work well. Cold roast is traditional.
Stovies keep well; reheat gently with a splash of stock if needed, or it makes a good cold lunch the next day.

steps.text: Heat the oil or dripping in a large heavy pot over a medium heat. Add the sliced onions and cook, stirring often, until soft and golden, about 8 minutes.
Layer half the potato slices on top of the onions. Scatter the meat over the potatoes, then top with the remaining potatoes.

Pour the stock over everything. Sprinkle with thyme, salt and pepper. Bring to a simmer, then reduce the heat to low and cover with a lid, cooking until the potatoes are tender and starting to break down into the stock.
Cook gently for 30 to 35 minutes, until the potatoes are tender and have broken down slightly and the liquid has reduced to a thick, creamy sauce. Stir gently a couple of times during cooking.
Taste and adjust the seasoning. Serve warm, straight from the pot if you're not bothered with washing extra dishes.

notes: The escovitch tastes even better made an hour or two ahead and served at room temperature.
Any firm white fish works, ask the fishmonger what's fresh that day.
Food safety:
The ras keeps in the fridge for up to 2 days covered. Make the puri just before serving so it's hot and crisp.
Use the ripest, sweetest mangoes you can find, Alphonso, Kesar or another fragrant variety work best.
If you don't have Greek yoghurt, use thick plain yoghurt or even mascarpone for a richer version.

steps.text: Cut the mangoes into chunks and blend smooth in a food processor or blender. Pass through a fine sieve if you prefer it completely smooth; otherwise leave it rustic, both are good. You want about 500 ml of pulp. If your mangoes are very fibrous, sieve it.
Whisk the Greek yoghurt, caster sugar, cardamom powder and salt together in a large bowl until the sugar dissolves completely.
Add the mango pulp to the yoghurt mixture and fold together gently until just combined. Taste and add the lemon juice if the mangoes are very sweet. Chill the ras while you make the puri.

To make the puri dough: mix the flour and salt in a bowl. Make a well in the centre, add the oil and warm water, and mix with your fingers until a soft, slightly sticky dough forms. Knead lightly for 2 minutes until smooth.
Let the dough rest for 10 minutes covered with a damp cloth. Divide into 8 equal pieces and roll each into a ball.

On a lightly oiled surface, roll each ball into a thin disc, about 10 cm across. Heat 3 cm of neutral oil in a wide, deep pan to 190°C (a piece of dough should float and puff immediately). Carefully slide one puri into the hot oil and press it down gently with the back of a slotted spoon, it should puff up within seconds. Flip and cook the other side until golden, about 1 minute total. Drain on paper towel. Repeat with the remaining dough.
Serve the chilled ras in bowls or small glasses, with the hot puri on the side for dipping or tearing into pieces and stirring through.

notes: Sorrel is best in spring and early summer. Grow it in a pot if you can, it comes back year after year.
The soup is best eaten the day it's made. Don't add the egg until just before serving, it doesn't keep well.
If you can't find sorrel, use spinach with a squeeze of lemon juice, though the flavour will be milder and less tart.
Food safety: Raw and lightly cooked foods aren't recommended for pregnant women, young children, older people or anyone with a weakened immune system.

steps.text: Heat the oil in a large pot over medium heat. Add the diced onion and cook, stirring occasionally, until soft and pale golden, about 5 minutes.
Add the potato and stock, and bring to a simmer. Cook, uncovered, for about 12 minutes, until the potato is tender.
Add the sorrel and stir through. Cook for 2–3 minutes, just until the sorrel wilts and softens.

In a small bowl, whisk the eggs together. Remove the pot from the heat and slowly pour the eggs into the hot (but no longer boiling) soup while stirring gently with a fork, this will create soft ribbons of cooked egg.
Taste and season with salt and pepper. Stir through most of the fresh dill.
Ladle into bowls and top with a spoonful of Greek yoghurt if you like, and a final sprinkle of fresh dill.

notes: Ndolé has a pleasantly bitter taste, if you can't find it at an African grocer, spinach works but tastes gentler
Make this up to the point of adding the fish, cool quickly, and refrigerate for up to two days. Reheat gently and add fresh fish just before serving
Food safety: Cook fish until it is opaque and flakes easily (63°C in the thickest part), and prawns until pink and opaque all the way through.
You can prepare the onion, garlic and ginger up to 2 hours ahead. Store in small bowls, covered.
Frozen prawns work well; thaw them completely and pat dry before cooking so they don't release water into the curry.
Food safety:

steps.text: Heat the mustard oil in a heavy-bottomed pan over medium-high heat. Once it's hot and fragrant, add the sliced onion and cook, stirring often, until golden and just beginning to crisp at the edges, about 6 minutes.
Add the minced garlic and grated ginger to the pan and stir constantly for about 1 minute until fragrant. Be careful not to let it burn.

Add the slit green chillies to the pan and cook for another minute, then add the ground turmeric and cumin. Stir well to coat the onions and release the spice aromas, about 30 seconds, until fragrant.
Pour in the coconut cream and stir to combine. Bring the mixture to a gentle simmer and let it bubble softly for 3 to 4 minutes, allowing the flavours to meld.

Slide the prawns into the simmering coconut curry and stir gently. Cook for 4 to 5 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the prawns turn pink and opaque throughout. Do not overcook or they will toughen.
Taste and adjust the salt to your liking. If you prefer a thinner sauce, add a splash of warm water. Serve hot with steamed rice, garnished with fresh coriander if you like.

notes: Make it ahead: prepare in the morning, cover and refrigerate, then roast in the evening, just add 30 minutes to the cooking time.
Kai Māori: serve with boiled corn, pumpkin, or kūmara if you want it more like a proper boil-up.
Leftovers shred and freeze well for kai later in the week.
Food safety:

steps.text: Heat oven to 160°C. Pat the lamb shoulder dry and season well all over with salt and pepper.
Heat oil in a large roasting pan over medium-high heat. Sear the lamb on all sides until golden brown, about 10 minutes total. Remove and set aside.
In the same pan, toss the potatoes, carrots, pumpkin, onions and garlic together. Season with salt and pepper.
Place the lamb back on top of the vegetables. Scatter rosemary over everything and pour water around the base.

Cover the pan tightly with foil, then place a roasting pan lid or another baking tray on top to seal it well, this traps the steam like an earth oven would. Press the foil around the rim until the seal is tight and no steam escapes.
Roast low and slow for 5 hours, until the lamb is fall-apart tender and the vegetables are soft and caramelised.
Carefully remove the foil (watch the steam), then pull the meat from the bone. It is ready when it is tender and falls away easily. Serve everything together with the cooking liquid spooned over.

notes: Samgyetang is traditionally eaten on Chobok, the hottest days of summer, to restore energy. Dong-hyun says it keeps for two days in the fridge, reheat gently before serving.
If you can find Korean red ginseng (홍삼), substitute 3 or 4 pieces for the fresh ginseng; they are denser and more assertive.
Use a chicken under 1 kg (a young bird); older birds take too long and become stringy.
Food safety:

steps.text: Bring the water to a boil in a large pot until it is at a steady rolling boil. Add the salt.

Meanwhile, combine the glutinous rice, date halves, crushed garlic, and salt in a small bowl. Stuff the chicken cavity loosely with this mixture, do not pack it tight, as the rice will expand. Secure the opening with a cocktail pick if needed.

Gently lower the whole chicken into the boiling salted water. Return to a boil, then reduce the heat to a bare simmer, with only a few small bubbles breaking the surface. Skim the surface once, at the beginning, until the scum is cleared.

Add the ginseng, whole red dates, garlic cloves, ginger, and mushrooms to the broth around the chicken. Cover the pot and simmer gently for 1 hour and 45 minutes, until the chicken is very tender and cooked through (the thigh should reach 75°C inside). Do not stir, and add no more salt, the flavour is in the restraint.
Add the spring onion whites in the last 5 minutes.

Remove the chicken carefully with tongs and transfer to a serving bowl or to individual bowls. Ladle the hot broth over it. Serve the ginseng, dates, garlic, mushrooms, and ginger alongside in the bowl, for each person to enjoy.
Make the dipping sauce: whisk together soy sauce, rice vinegar, sesame oil, gochugaru if using, and garlic. Set aside.
Make the batter: whisk flour, salt, water and egg together until smooth. Fold in the grated zucchini, carrot and spring onion, don't overmix.
Heat 2 tbsp oil in a large frying pan over medium-high heat until it shimmers.
Working in batches, pour the batter into the pan in rough 10 cm pancakes (they don't need to be perfect). Fry for 3 to 4 minutes until the edges are golden and crispy.
Flip and fry for a further 2 minutes until golden on the second side and cooked through.
Drain on paper towel and serve hot with dipping sauce.

notes: Make the braise up to 2 days ahead and refrigerate; it actually tastes better the next day. Assemble the gratin and bake just before serving.
The reserved braising liquid is good in soups or risotto.
Any leftover gratin can be reheated gently in a 160°C oven, covered, until warm through.
Food safety:

steps.text: Heat the oil in a heavy-bottomed pot or casserole over medium-high heat. Season the oxtail pieces with salt and pepper, then brown them in batches, about 3 minutes per side. Don't crowd the pot. Set the meat aside.
In the same pot, sauté the onions, carrots and celery until lightly golden, about 8 minutes. Add the garlic, stir, then add the tomato paste and cook for 2 minutes, stirring constantly.

Pour in the red wine, scraping up any brown bits from the bottom of the pot. Add the beef stock, bay leaves and thyme. Return the oxtail to the pot and bring to a simmer. Cover and braise in a 160°C oven for 3 hours, until the meat is very tender and falls easily from the bone.

Remove the pot from the oven and let cool slightly. Strain the braising liquid through a fine sieve, pressing gently on the vegetables to extract all the liquid. Pick the meat from the bones, discarding the bone and any fat. You should have about 400–500 g of shredded meat and about 600 ml of braising liquid.

Make the béchamel: melt the butter in a saucepan over medium heat. Whisk in the flour and cook for 2 minutes, stirring constantly, don't let it brown. Gradually whisk in the warm milk, whisking constantly to avoid lumps. Cook, stirring often, until the sauce is thick and smooth, about 8 minutes. Season with salt, white pepper and nutmeg.
Combine the shredded oxtail meat with 300 ml of the braising liquid (reserve the rest for another use). Gently fold in the béchamel sauce until just combined.

Transfer the mixture to a gratin dish. Scatter the Gruyère evenly over the top. Bake at 200°C until the gratin is bubbling around the edges and the cheese is golden brown, about 30–40 minutes. Let rest for 5 minutes before serving.

notes: Bitso-bitso means 'this and that' in Kapampangan, here, a mix of offal. You can add pork kidney (about 150 g, trimmed and halved) if you like.
The adobo keeps well in the fridge for up to 3 days. The flavour deepens overnight.
Fresh offal is essential. Ask your butcher for the freshest pork liver and heart available.
Make it a day ahead: cool, cover, and refrigerate. Reheat gently on the stove, adding a splash of water if it's too thick.
Use bone-in lamb shoulder if you can find it, the bones add flavour.
Food safety: Braised beef and lamb cook well past 75°C on the way to tender, so they are safe once soft.
You can prep the parcels a few hours ahead, cover them with a damp cloth, and steam them just before serving.
If you can't find banana leaves, use parchment paper, it won't look as pretty but tastes the same.
Make sure your rice is cooled first, this stops it from becoming mushy. Leftover rice from yesterday works perfectly.
If you don't have tinned tomatoes, use 150 g of fresh tomato, chopped, or 2 tbsp tomato paste mixed with 2 tbsp water.

Food safety: Raw and lightly cooked foods aren't recommended for pregnant women, young children, older people or anyone with a weakened immune system. Cool any leftover rice quickly and refrigerate it within an hour; reheat it until steaming hot.
You can cook the pork up to a day ahead and refrigerate it, this actually makes slicing cleaner. Reheat gently in the wok before adding the bean paste.
The doubanjiang (or doubanjiang with chilli if you prefer a little more warmth) is your backbone here; don't skip it or use substitutes. It's what makes this dish sing.
Serve with plain steamed rice to balance the rich, umami sauce.
Food safety: Cook fresh pork to at least 70°C in the thickest part.

steps.text: Cut the pork belly into thin slices, about 3 mm thick (easier if the pork is slightly cold). Simmer the pork in a pot of water for 20 minutes until just cooked through, then drain and set aside on a plate.
Heat 1 tbsp neutral oil in a wok or large frying pan over medium heat. Add the spring onion whites, garlic and ginger, stirring for about 1 minute until fragrant.
Add the doubanjiang and stir constantly for 2 minutes, breaking it up as it heats, until the paste darkens slightly and releases its aroma.
Add the cooked pork slices and toss gently but thoroughly, coating each piece in the bean paste, for about 3 minutes.
Add the capsicums, soy sauce, sugar and a pinch of salt. Cook, stirring often, for 8 to 10 minutes until the peppers are tender and the sauce is glossy and clingy.
Add the spring onion greens, drizzle with sesame oil, toss once and taste, adjust salt if needed. Serve hot with steamed rice.

notes: Make sure you don't lift the lid while the rice is cooking, opening it lets the steam out and stops the rice cooking evenly.
This keeps in the fridge for up to three days. Reheat gently in a rice cooker or microwave with a splash of water.
You can stir in sautéed mushrooms or crispy bacon to the eggs before baking if you like.
The æggeost is best served warm, but it's also nice cold for lunch the next day.
Food safety: Raw and lightly cooked foods aren't recommended for pregnant women, young children, older people or anyone with a weakened immune system.
Kibbeh can be shaped up to 4 hours ahead and refrigerated, but don't freeze before frying, the texture gets grainy.
If the mixture is too sticky to work with, add a little more bulgur; if it's too dry, add cold water a teaspoon at a time.
The filling must be completely cool before you stuff, or it will start cooking the shell from inside.
Food safety: Cook mince and sausages until no pink remains and the centre reaches 75°C.

steps.text: Make the filling first: heat the olive oil in a large pan over medium-high heat. Add the chopped onion and cook until soft and golden, about 4 minutes. Add the mince, breaking it up as it cooks, and stir for 5–6 minutes until cooked through. Add the pine nuts, cinnamon and cloves, season with salt and pepper, and stir for another minute. Set aside to cool completely.

Meanwhile, rinse the bulgur under cold water until the water runs clear, then drain well. In a bowl, combine the bulgur, 500 g mince, chopped onion, allspice and cinnamon. Season with salt and pepper. Add cold water a little at a time, mixing with your hands, until the mixture holds together like a dough, you want it moist but not wet. Cover and rest for 10 minutes.

Wet your hands with cold water. Take a handful of the bulgur mixture (about the size of a golf ball) and shape it into an oval. Push your thumb into the centre to make a cavity, then gently hollow it out, rotating it in your palm, until the walls are thin. Fill with about 1 tbsp of the cooled filling, then pinch and seal the opening, gently smoothing the seam. Shape into an oval or pointed torpedo. Repeat with the remaining mixture.

Heat the oil to 160°C in a deep heavy-based pot or wok (use a thermometer to check). Fry the kibbeh in batches, without crowding the pan, for 4–5 minutes, turning halfway, until golden brown and crispy all over. Do not let the oil get too hot or they'll brown before cooking through. Remove with a slotted spoon and drain on paper towel.
Serve the kibbeh warm with Greek yoghurt and lemon wedges on the side.

notes: The marinade can be prepared up to 24 hours ahead; overnight is ideal for full flavour.
The peanut sauce can be made earlier in the day and reheated gently before serving.
Food safety:
Bamia freezes beautifully. Cool completely, then freeze for up to 3 months. Reheat gently on the stove with a splash of water.
This is even better the next day as the flavours deepen. Make it ahead and warm through before serving.
Some Iraqi cooks add a touch of pomegranate molasses at the end instead of lemon juice, try it both ways and see what you prefer.
Food safety: Braised beef and lamb cook well past 75°C on the way to tender, so they are safe once soft.
Food safety: Cook chicken and other poultry until the juices run clear and the thickest part reaches 75°C.
Freeze in ice-cube trays for perfect portion control. One or two cubes is usually enough for a child's serve, three to four for an adult.
Make a double or triple batch and freeze for up to three months. No thawing needed, drop cubes straight into pasta water or a hot pan.
Swap the gravy powder for 1 tsp dried oregano and a splash of Worcestershire sauce if you prefer.
Cook mince and sausages until they reach 75°C in the centre, with no pink left.
Food safety:

steps.text: Heat the oil in a large frying pan over medium-high heat. Add the onion and cook, stirring, until soft, about 3 minutes.
Add the garlic and cook for 30 seconds until fragrant.
Add the beef mince and break it up as it cooks, stirring often, until browned through, about 5 minutes.
Stir in the carrot and tomato paste, cooking for 1 minute.
Add the crushed tomatoes and gravy powder, stir well to combine, and bring to a simmer, cooking until the sauce has thickened and turned glossy.
Cook, stirring occasionally, for 8 to 10 minutes until the sauce thickens slightly and the carrot is tender. Season with salt and pepper to taste.
Cool completely, then freeze in ice-cube trays. Once frozen, pop the cubes into a freezer bag and label with the date. Thaw and reheat on the stove or stir straight into hot pasta water.

notes: This is a dish about technique, not ingredients. The emulsion of cheese and starch from the pasta water is everything. If your sauce breaks, start again with a little cold water.
Use whole peppercorns and crack them yourself just before cooking, pre-ground pepper will be too fine.
For a vegetarian version, use a vegetarian hard cheese (made without animal rennet).

steps.text: Bring a large pot of salted water to a rolling boil, until large bubbles break across the whole surface. The water should taste like the sea.
Toast the cracked pepper in a large, dry frying pan over medium heat for 1 minute, stirring, until fragrant. Add 100 ml of pasta water and bring to a gentle simmer.
Cook the spaghetti until al dente, about 9–10 minutes. Reserve 200 ml of pasta water before draining.

Add the drained spaghetti to the pan with the pepper water. Remove from heat. Working quickly, add half the grated cheese, tossing constantly with two wooden spoons. Add pasta water a splash at a time, tossing all the while, until the sauce comes together and clings to the pasta. It should be creamy but have no cream in it.
Divide between two bowls. Finish with the remaining cheese and a crack of fresh pepper.

notes: Zaalouk keeps well in the fridge for up to 3 days; serve warm or at room temperature.
You can roast the eggplants directly over a gas flame for a more charred, smoky flavour if you prefer, use tongs and turn carefully.
This is traditionally served as part of a mezze spread alongside olives, preserved lemons and bread.

steps.text: Preheat your oven to 200°C. Prick each eggplant several times with a fork, then place on a baking tray. Roast for 35–40 minutes, turning halfway, until the skin is blackened and the flesh is very soft.
While the eggplants roast, warm 2 tbsp olive oil in a large pan over medium heat. Add the chopped garlic and cook gently for 1 minute until fragrant, don't let it brown.
Add the chopped tomatoes to the pan, season with salt and pepper, and simmer for 8–10 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the tomatoes begin to break down and release their juices.

When the eggplants are soft and charred, remove them from the oven and let cool for a few minutes. Peel away the skin and chop the flesh into small pieces, don't worry about getting it perfect; some texture is good.
Add the eggplant to the tomato pan and stir gently to combine. Cook for 2 minutes to warm through, then taste and adjust the seasoning.

Stir in most of the fresh coriander, reserving some to scatter over the top. Transfer to a serving dish and drizzle with a little extra olive oil. Scatter the remaining coriander over the top and serve warm or at room temperature with bread.

notes: Store in an airtight container for up to 5 days. They stay crispy at room temperature.
Don't skip the honey, it's traditional and brings everything together. Just a light coating is enough.
If you want to make these ahead, you can prepare the dough and filling the day before and assemble and fry them on the day.

steps.text: Make the filling first: melt the 60 g butter in a saucepan over low heat. Add the dates and stir constantly, breaking them down with the back of a wooden spoon, until they form a smooth paste, about 5 minutes. Stir in the orange blossom water and salt, then set aside to cool.

For the dough: put the semolina, baking powder and salt in a bowl. Add the softened butter pieces and rub together with your fingertips until the mixture looks like breadcrumbs. Add the orange blossom water and warm water, a little at a time, mixing gently until the dough comes together, it should feel soft and slightly moist but not sticky. Knead lightly for 1 minute.

Lightly oil your work surface. Take a piece of dough about the size of a walnut and flatten it into a disc about 5 mm thick. Place a teaspoon of date paste in the centre, fold the dough in half over the filling, then pinch the edges firmly to seal. You can press it gently with the tines of a fork to make ridges if you like. Repeat with the remaining dough and filling, you should make about 12 cookies.

Heat the neutral oil in a deep saucepan to 180°C (a piece of dough should sizzle immediately and turn golden in about 30 seconds). Working in batches so you don't crowd the pan, fry the makroudh until they're deep golden brown all over, about 2–3 minutes, turning halfway through. Use a slotted spoon to transfer them to a paper-towel-lined plate.
While they're still warm, brush or drizzle the warmed honey lightly over each makroudh. Let them cool for a few minutes on the paper towels, they'll crisp up as they cool.

notes: Chimichurri can be made up to 2 hours ahead and kept at room temperature.
Asado de tira is best cooked over charcoal or hardwood fire. If using a gas grill, preheat to high heat and cook for the same time, checking for tenderness.
Internal temperature for medium is 65°C. For a softer, more melting texture, cook to 68°C.
Food safety:
Make it ahead: this keeps in the fridge for up to 5 days, or freeze it for a month.
No blender? Mash it with a fork or stick blender in the pan.
If you can't get red chillies, use jalapeños, or even a pinch of chilli powder, it's still salsa.

steps.text: Heat a large frying pan or comal (or frying pan if that's what you have) over medium-high heat. Work in batches if needed: char the tomatoes, turning occasionally, until soft and blackened in spots, about 5 minutes. Set aside.
In the same pan, char the red chillies and garlic cloves until soft and blistered, about 3 minutes. Add to the tomatoes.
Add the onion to the pan and cook until soft and lightly coloured, about 3 minutes.
Transfer the tomatoes, chillies, garlic and onion to a blender. Blend until smooth or to your preferred texture, some people like it chunky.
Return the salsa to the pan and simmer over medium heat for 5 minutes, stirring occasionally, until it's thick and the flavours have come together.
Season with salt to taste. Serve warm or at room temperature with tacos, quesadillas or whatever you're cooking.

notes: Make this a day ahead, the flavours deepen overnight and the beef becomes even more tender. Reheat gently on the stove with a splash of water if the sauce is too thick.
If you prefer a hotter rendang, add extra red chillies to the paste, or finely chop a bird's eye chilli to stir in at the end.
Serve with steamed jasmine rice and a cool cucumber sambal to cut through the richness.
Food safety: Braised beef and lamb cook well past 75°C on the way to tender, so they are safe once soft.
Prep everything before you start cooking, there's no time once the wok is hot.
If you can't find king prawns, use medium prawns (just reduce the cooking time by 30 seconds).
Food safety: Cook fish until it is opaque and flakes easily (63°C in the thickest part), and prawns until pink and opaque all the way through.
This curry tastes even better the next day. Cool and store in the fridge for up to 3 days, or freeze for up to a month.
Dilan brings this to work in a thermos flask for night shifts, it keeps beautifully and reheats gently.

steps.text: Heat oil in a large pot over medium heat. Add onion and cook, stirring, until soft and golden, about 5 minutes.
Add garlic and ginger, stir well, and cook for 1 minute until fragrant.
Add curry powder and turmeric, stir to coat the onions, and cook for 30 seconds, until fragrant.
Add eggplant cubes and stir to coat in the spice mixture. Cook for 2 minutes.
Pour in coconut milk and water. Add the green chillies and season with salt.
Bring to a simmer, then reduce heat to low. Cover and cook for 15 to 18 minutes, until the eggplant is tender and the curry has thickened slightly.
Taste and adjust salt if needed. Serve hot with rice.

notes: Keeps in the fridge for 3 days, or freeze for up to 3 months. Reheat gently on the stove.
If you can't find dried bush tomato at your local grocer, look for it at farmers markets or Aboriginal-owned food suppliers.
Food safety: Braised beef and lamb cook well past 75°C on the way to tender, so they are safe once soft.
Serves well alongside shrimp, sausage or collard greens.
Can be made a day ahead and reheated gently on the stove with a splash of stock.

steps.text: Heat a cast iron frying pan over medium heat. Cook the bacon until crispy, about 5 minutes, then transfer to a plate, leaving the fat in the pan.
Add the onion to the bacon fat and cook, stirring often, until soft and starting to caramelize, about 8 minutes.
Stir in the rice and cook for 1 minute, coating it in the fat.
Add the crushed tomatoes, stock, salt, pepper and cayenne (if using). Stir well, then bring to a gentle simmer until small bubbles break the surface.
Cover and cook for 20 minutes without lifting the lid, until the rice is tender and has absorbed the liquid.
Remove from heat, stir in the cooked bacon, and let it rest for 2 minutes before serving.

notes: The broth can be made up to 3 days ahead and stored in the fridge, or frozen for up to 3 months. Matzo balls can be cooked and frozen separately for up to 1 month.
For a lighter broth, use chicken breasts instead of bones; reduce cooking time to 45 minutes. For richer broth, add extra chicken fat (schmaltz) when serving.
The soda water is key to light, fluffy matzo balls, don't skip it. And cold hands matter more than you'd think; it keeps the batter from getting tough.
Cook chicken until it reaches 75°C in the thickest part and the juices run clear.
Food safety:

steps.text: Make the broth: place chicken bones in a large pot, cover with 3 litres of cold water, and bring to a boil. Skim off any grey foam that rises to the surface, about 2 minutes.

Add the onions, carrots, celery, parsnip (if using), parsley and bay leaf. Reduce heat to low and simmer gently, uncovered, for 1½ to 2 hours. The broth should be clear and golden. Season with salt and pepper to taste.

While the broth simmers, make the matzo balls: beat the eggs with oil and soda water until combined. Stir in the matzo meal, salt, white pepper and ginger (if using) until just mixed, the batter will be thick and slightly chunky. Cover and refrigerate for 30 minutes.

Bring a large pot of salted water to a boil until it is at a steady rolling boil (use a separate pot so it doesn't interfere with your broth simmering). With cold, wet hands, gently roll the matzo batter into balls about 4 cm in diameter. Place them on a wet plate as you go.

Carefully drop the matzo balls into the boiling water one at a time. They will sink, then float to the surface after a few minutes. Once they float, simmer them gently for 30 minutes, do not let them boil hard or they'll become tough.

Strain the broth through a fine sieve, discarding the vegetables and bones. Return to a clean pot and gently reheat. Carefully transfer the matzo balls to serving bowls and ladle the golden broth over them. Serve hot.

notes: Make ahead: cook the barbacoa the day before, then shred and reheat gently in the braising liquid. Keeps in the fridge for up to 3 days.
Serve on warm flour tortillas with diced onion, fresh coriander and lime wedges.
This is a weekend cook: take your time and let the low heat do the work.
Food safety:

steps.text: Heat the oven to 120°C. Toast the dried guajillo and chipotle chillies in a dry pan for 2 minutes until fragrant, then transfer to a bowl and cover with hot water. Let sit for 15 minutes until soft.

Drain the rehydrated chillies, then blitz them in a blender with garlic, cumin, oregano, cloves, beef stock, vinegar and salt until smooth. Strain through a sieve if you want a silky paste; for rustic texture, leave it coarse.
Pat the brisket dry. Rub all over with the chilli paste until well coated. Wrap tightly in agave or banana leaves and then in foil, sealing the edges.
Place the wrapped brisket in a heavy-based pot or Dutch oven. Cover and braise in the oven for 7 to 8 hours, until the meat shreds easily with a fork.
Remove from the oven and let rest for 15 minutes. Unwrap carefully, watch out for steam, and shred the beef using two forks, pulling it apart along the grain.
Strain the braising liquid into a jug. Skim any fat from the surface and season with salt to taste. Toss the shredded beef with a few tbsp of the braising liquid to keep it moist.

notes: Make it ahead and reheat gently with a splash of milk, it keeps for 3 days in the fridge.
If you can't find broken rice, crush short-grain white rice coarsely with your hands or a rolling pin before cooking.
Food safety: Cook chicken and other poultry until the juices run clear and the thickest part reaches 75°C.
Serve with white rice, collard greens or a simple slaw to cool the heat.
The frying pan must be smoking hot, don't skip this step or you won't get that proper blackened crust.
Swap catfish for any firm white fish fillet.
Food safety:

steps.text: Mix paprika, cayenne, cumin, onion powder, garlic powder, thyme, oregano, black pepper and salt in a shallow dish.
Pat the catfish fillets dry with paper towels. Coat both sides generously with the spice mixture, pressing it on so it sticks.
Heat the oil in a cast-iron frying pan over high heat until it's smoking and a drop of water beads and rolls across the surface, about 2 minutes.
Add the butter and swirl it through the hot oil. When it's foaming and just starting to brown, lay the catfish fillets in the frying pan, they should sizzle hard.
Sear without moving them for 3 to 4 minutes, until the crust is dark brown and charred. Flip carefully.
Sear the other side for another 2 to 3 minutes, until the fish is cooked through and flakes easily with a fork. Serve hot.

notes: Kopytka can be made ahead: shape and boil them, then store in the fridge for up to 2 days. Toss with the mushrooms and onions to warm through.
The dough should stay slightly loose, too much flour and the kopytka become heavy. If it's very sticky, dust with a little more flour, but resist the urge to knead.
Food safety: Raw and lightly cooked foods aren't recommended for pregnant women, young children, older people or anyone with a weakened immune system.

steps.text: Boil the potato in salted water until tender, about 12 minutes. Drain well and pass through a ricer while still hot into a large bowl.
Add the flour, egg, and salt to the potato. Mix gently with your hands until just combined, it should feel a little soft and slightly sticky, not smooth. Don't overwork it.

Bring a large pot of salted water to a boil. Dust the work surface lightly with flour. Break off a piece of dough about the size of a walnut, roll it roughly into a stick about 5 cm long, and press gently with your thumb to make a small indent (this is the little hoof). Drop each kopytka into the boiling water as you shape them. They will sink, then float to the surface; cook for 2–3 minutes after they float. Drain and spread on a tray to cool.

While the kopytka cook, heat the oil in a large pan over medium-high heat. Add the mushrooms and fry, stirring often, until they are golden and any liquid has evaporated, about 8 minutes. Transfer to a plate.

Lower the heat to medium and add the onions to the same pan. Cook, stirring now and then, until they are soft and deeply golden, about 12 minutes. Add the garlic and thyme, if using, and cook for another minute.
Return the mushrooms to the pan with the onions. Add the drained kopytka and toss gently until everything is warm and coated. Season with salt and black pepper. Serve hot.

notes: Fresh masa is best, but masa harina (corn flour) works well too: use about 125 g mixed with a little warm water to a smooth paste.
Oaxacan chocolate is grainy and textured, sold as tablets, seek it in Latin or Mexican markets, or use good dark chocolate with a tiny pinch of ground almond added.
A molinillo whisk creates the traditional frothy top, but a regular whisk does the job.

steps.text: If using dried noodles, cook in boiling salted water until just tender, drain well and spread on a tray to cool. Fresh noodles can be used as they are.
Heat the oil in a large wok or wide frying pan over high heat. When shimmering, add the sliced garlic and ginger. Stir-fry for about 1 minute until fragrant but not brown.
Add the water spinach and toss constantly for 2–3 minutes until it begins to wilt but the stems still have a gentle firmness.
Add the cooled noodles to the wok, breaking them apart gently with chopsticks or tongs as you toss. Stir-fry for 2–3 minutes until heated through.
Pour the soy sauce and rice vinegar over the noodles and toss well for another minute, letting the flavours coat everything evenly.
Taste and season with salt and black pepper. If you like heat, sprinkle with dried chilli flakes.
Serve at once, while the noodles are still warm and the spinach stems hold their slight crispness.

notes: Make it a day ahead if you like, the flavours deepen overnight. Reheat gently on the stove.
The scotch bonnet stays whole while cooking so you control the heat. Leave it out if you prefer a gentler dish.
If you don't have a pudding basin, a 1.5-litre heatproof bowl wrapped in foil will work, though you may need to adjust the steaming time slightly.
Leftovers can be reheated gently in the steamer for 30 minutes, or covered in foil in a 150°C oven for about 45 minutes.
Food safety: Braised beef and lamb cook well past 75°C on the way to tender, so they are safe once soft.

steps.text: Heat the oil in a large pan over medium-high heat. Season the beef with salt and pepper. Brown the meat in batches, about 3 minutes per batch, until well coloured on all sides. Set aside.
In the same pan, cook the onion until soft, about 5 minutes. Add the garlic and tomato paste, stir well, and cook for 2 minutes more.

Return the beef to the pan. Pour in the ale and stock, scraping the bottom of the pan. Add the bay leaves and thyme. Bring to a simmer, then remove from heat and leave to cool completely, at least 1 hour. The filling needs to be cold before you add it to the pastry.

While the filling cools, make the suet crust. Mix the flour and salt in a large bowl. Add the suet and stir until it's distributed evenly. Add the cold water a little at a time, stirring with a knife until a soft, slightly sticky dough forms. Knead gently until just combined; don't overwork it.

Lightly flour a work surface. Roll out two-thirds of the dough into a circle about 40 cm across and 5 mm thick. It should be large enough to line a 1.5-litre pudding basin with some hanging over the edge.
Use this large circle to line the pudding basin, leaving the excess hanging over the rim.

Strain the cooled filling, reserving the liquid. Discard the bay leaves and thyme. Spoon the beef and onions into the lined basin, then pour in enough of the reserved liquid to come halfway up the filling (about 200 ml). Save the rest for serving.
Roll out the remaining dough into a circle about 25 cm across, 5 mm thick. Lay this on top of the filling. Fold the overhanging pastry inward over the lid, pressing down to seal.
Cover the pudding with a pleated piece of baking paper (the pleat allows for expansion), then a pleated piece of foil. Tie both down with string under the lip of the basin.

Place the pudding basin in a large pot and add enough boiling water to come halfway up the sides of the basin. Cover the pot with a lid. Steam for 3 hours, checking every 45 minutes and topping up the water if needed, it should stay at the same level.
Carefully remove the pudding from the pot. Let it rest for 10 minutes. Warm the reserved liquid in a small pan.
Turn the pudding out onto a warm plate or serving bowl. Serve with the warmed gravy poured over the top, and mashed potato on the side.

notes: Make the dough the day before if it suits you, cold dough ferments gently overnight. Shape and prove the next morning.
If you grind whole cardamom pods yourself, use about 1½ tsp of pods; they're more fragrant than pre-ground.
Semlor are best eaten the day they're made. Store in an airtight container for up to a day, but the bun will soften.
Food safety: Raw and lightly cooked foods aren't recommended for pregnant women, young children, older people or anyone with a weakened immune system.
If you can't find khoya, reduce 500 ml milk slowly in a heavy pan until it becomes a thick paste (about 30 minutes), then use that instead, it will give you more authentic flavour and texture.
For a softer sandesh (Arnab's preference), use only 50 g khoya and don't chill for as long; for a firmer set (his wife's way), add an extra 25 g khoya.
Regional variations: try adding a few strands of saffron, a tablespoon of mango pulp, or a teaspoon of rose water instead of cardamom, the arguments are endless and that's rather the point.

steps.text: Bring the milk to a rolling boil in a heavy-bottomed pan over high heat, until it foams up and rises towards the rim. Once it reaches a full boil, remove from the heat.

Add the yoghurt slowly, stirring gently. The milk will curdle immediately. Let it sit for 2 minutes, then pour through a fine sieve lined with muslin cloth, collecting the whey in a bowl beneath. Let it drain for 5 minutes.
Gather the corners of the muslin and hang it to drain for 30 minutes until the paneer is quite dry but still soft.

Turn the paneer into a bowl and crumble it finely with your fingertips. Add the khoya, sugar, cardamom seeds (discarding the husks), and salt. Mix gently but thoroughly until the mixture just holds together.
Divide the mixture into 12 portions and shape each into a small smooth ball or oval with damp hands. You can press each into a small mould if you have one, then tap it out onto a plate.
Chill for at least 15 minutes before serving. Store in an airtight container in the fridge for up to 3 days.

notes: Sole is the classic choice, but halibut, plaice or any firm white fish works. You can also cook fillets, they'll need only 1–2 minutes per side.
The brown butter is everything. Don't skip it or rush it; the aroma tells you when it's ready.

steps.text: Pat the sole dry with paper towels. Season inside and out with salt and pepper.
Spread the flour on a shallow plate. Lightly coat both sides of each fish, shaking off the excess.
Heat the oil in a large frying pan over medium-high heat until shimmering.
Lay the sole in the pan and cook, without moving, for 2–3 minutes until the skin is golden and crisp. Flip and cook the other side for 2–3 minutes until cooked through.
Transfer the fish to a warm plate. Reduce the heat to medium, add the butter to the same pan, and let it melt and brown, swirling gently, for 1–2 minutes until it smells nutty and turns golden.
Pour the brown butter over the fish, squeeze lemon juice over the top (it will sizzle briefly), scatter with parsley if using, and serve at once while the butter is still hot and nutty.

notes: For extra richness, some cooks stir in a spoonful of crème fraîche or Greek yoghurt just before serving.
Make this ahead and reheat gently, the flavour deepens overnight.
Kalua pork keeps well in the fridge for 4 days, and freezes for up to 3 months. Reheat gently with a splash of water.
Serve with rice, cabbage slaw and gravy for a real plate lunch, or use it for musubi.
The longer you cook it, the more tender it gets, even 8 or 9 hours won't hurt.
Food safety: Cook fresh pork to at least 70°C in the thickest part.
Make the gochujang butter ahead and keep it in a pot in the fridge; it'll come together faster in the morning.
Use leftover rice from the night before, or make a quick batch while you wait for the egg to fry.

Food safety: Raw and lightly cooked foods aren't recommended for pregnant women, young children, older people or anyone with a weakened immune system. Cool any leftover rice quickly and refrigerate it within an hour; reheat it until steaming hot.
This pudding can be made a few hours ahead and gently reheated, or served at room temperature.
Use good-quality rose water, it should smell fragrant but not perfumy. Add it slowly and taste as you go.

steps.text: Bring the water to a boil in a large saucepan. Add the sago slowly, stirring constantly to prevent lumps from forming. Cook, stirring often, until the sago is translucent and tender, about 12 minutes.
Add the milk, caster sugar, cinnamon stick and crushed cardamom pods. Stir well and bring to a gentle simmer until the sugar has dissolved and the milk is fragrant.
Cook, stirring occasionally, until the pudding thickens slightly and the sago pearls are completely soft, about 5 minutes. The mixture should be creamy but not stiff.
Remove from the heat and stir through the rose water. Taste and add a pinch of salt to balance the sweetness. Discard the cinnamon stick.
Divide among bowls while still warm and dust lightly with ground cinnamon. Serve warm or at room temperature.

notes: Make the sofregit ahead: cook the onions and tomatoes up to an hour before, then reheat gently before adding the rice.
Fresh squid ink from the fishmonger can replace the sachets, ask for 2 sachets' worth (about 4 g). It will be fresher and give a rounder flavour.
Arròs negre reheats poorly, so cook it fresh and serve at once, still warm from the pan.
Food safety:

steps.text: In your rice pan or large shallow casserole over medium heat, warm the olive oil. Add the chopped onions and cook very slowly, stirring often, until completely soft and lightly golden, this is the sofregit, and it should take 12 to 15 minutes. Do not rush it; this is where the flavour lives.
Add the tinned tomatoes to the sofregit and stir well. Cook for another 5 to 8 minutes, until the sauce thickens slightly and the raw tomato taste disappears. Season with salt and pepper.
Stir in the garlic and chilli (if using), and cook for 1 minute until fragrant.
Add the rice and stir constantly for 2 minutes, coating each grain with the sofregit and oil.

Dissolve the squid ink sachets in the warm stock until the stock is jet black, then pour the stock gradually into the rice, stirring occasionally. Bring to a simmer until bubbles break across the surface.
Cook the rice uncovered at a gentle simmer for about 15 to 18 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the rice is almost tender and the liquid has been mostly absorbed.

Scatter the squid rings and mussels across the top of the rice. Do not stir them in. Continue cooking for 5 to 7 minutes, until the squid is just cooked through, the mussel shells have opened (discard any that don't), and the rice is tender with a slight bite.
