The bottom should form a thin, crispy layer (called socarrat).
Remove from heat, cover loosely with foil, and rest for 3 minutes. Scatter fresh parsley over the top and serve at the table in the pan.

notes: Make it a day ahead and reheat gently, the flavours deepen overnight.
If you can't find fresh palm nuts, use tinned palm cream (about 800 ml), though fresh is far superior. Skip the pounding and straining; just heat the tinned cream gently and follow from step 3.
Stockfish is essential, dried, smoked whole fish. Don't substitute with stock cubes or powder, you'll lose the soul of the soup.
Food safety: Cook fish until it is opaque and flakes easily (63°C in the thickest part), and prawns until pink and opaque all the way through.

steps.text: Pound the palm nuts in a large bowl with 2 litres of hot water (not boiling), working in batches. Press through a fine sieve or colander lined with muslin cloth, squeezing gently to extract all the cream. Reserve this golden liquid and discard the fibre.

In a large pot, bring 1 litre of water to the boil. Add the stockfish, one halved onion, and a pinch of salt. Simmer for 20 minutes, then remove the stockfish and set aside to cool. Strain the cooking liquid and reserve it (discard the onion).
Once the stockfish is cool enough to handle, remove the meat from the bones and break into chunks. Discard the bones.
Pour the palm nut cream into the pot over medium heat. Stir constantly for 3–4 minutes until it thickens slightly and the oil begins to separate on top, this is how you know it's ready.

Add the reserved stockfish cooking liquid, the stockfish meat, dried crayfish, remaining halved onion, and the scotch bonnet chillies if using. Stir well and simmer gently for 20 minutes, stirring occasionally to prevent sticking.
Stir in the ground crayfish, salt, and black pepper. Taste and adjust seasoning. Simmer for another 10 minutes, then remove from heat. Remove the onion halves and whole chillies before serving.
Serve hot with boiled white rice, gari, or fufu.

notes: Make ahead: Cook the rice and prepare the chikuwa mixture up to 4 hours ahead. Reheat gently and pour over fresh rice.
Chikuwa keeps in the fridge for up to a week, so this is perfect for bento prep.
Food safety: Raw and lightly cooked foods aren't recommended for pregnant women, young children, older people or anyone with a weakened immune system.

steps.text: Combine dashi, soy sauce, mirin and sugar in a small saucepan or shallow pan. Bring to a simmer over medium heat until the sugar has dissolved and small bubbles appear at the edges.
Add the sliced chikuwa and simmer for 2 minutes until heated through.
Lightly beat the eggs in a bowl. Pour into the simmering broth in a thin stream, stirring gently until the egg is just set but still soft, about 1 minute.
Divide the cooked rice between two bowls. Spoon the chikuwa, egg and sauce over the top. Garnish with spring onion if using, and serve hot.

notes: The batter can be made the night before and stored in the fridge, it actually develops better flavour overnight.
Wonton wrappers crisp up quickly, so fry them just before you start making the crepes.
A non-stick or well-seasoned crepe pan is essential. The pan must be hot enough that the batter sets instantly, or you'll struggle to spread it.

steps.text: Mix plain flour and salt in a bowl. Slowly add water, stirring until smooth. Let the batter rest for 10 minutes.
While the batter rests, break the wonton wrappers into rough pieces and fry in a small pan with a little oil until crispy and golden, about 2 minutes. Set aside.
Heat a large non-stick pan or crepe pan over high heat. It should be very hot, test with a drop of water; it should sizzle and evaporate immediately.
Pour 120 ml of batter into the centre of the pan and immediately tilt and rotate the pan so the batter spreads into a thin, even circle about 20 cm across. Work quickly.
Let the batter cook for about 30 seconds until the bottom is set and starts to turn light golden. Crack an egg onto one half of the crepe, then use a spatula to break the yolk and spread it evenly.
Scatter half the chopped spring onion and half the crispy wonton pieces over the egg. Fold the other half of the crepe over to enclose the filling, pressing gently.
Cook for another 30 seconds until the egg is set, then slide onto a plate. Serve immediately with sweet chilli sauce and soy sauce for dipping.
Repeat with the remaining batter, egg, spring onion and wonton to make a second jianbing.
Heat the oil in a large pot over medium heat. Add the onion and cook, stirring, until soft and golden, about 5 minutes.
Add the garlic and ginger, and cook for 1 minute until fragrant.
Stir in the cumin, coriander and turmeric, and cook for 1 minute to release the spices.
Add the eggplant chunks and stir to coat in the spice mixture. Cook for 5 minutes, stirring occasionally.
Pour in the coconut milk and bring to a simmer until gentle bubbles appear and the sauce is slightly thickened. Add the chopped chillies and stir well.
Reduce heat to low and simmer gently, uncovered, for 20 minutes until the eggplant is very tender. Stir occasionally.
Taste and add salt as needed. Serve hot, scattered with fresh coriander if you like.

notes: Make the rice cakes up to 2 hours ahead and keep them at room temperature, covered with a damp cloth. Assemble and fold just before serving so they stay pliable.
If you can't find banana leaves, plastic wrap works fine, or serve the bánh nậm on a plate with lettuce underneath instead.

Food safety: Cook mince and sausages until no pink remains and the centre reaches 75°C. Cook fish until it is opaque and flakes easily (63°C in the thickest part), and prawns until pink and opaque all the way through.
Serve warm or at room temperature with crusty bread for scooping.
Keeps in the fridge for up to 3 days and tastes even better the next day.
The notebook's version with dried tomatoes works too, reduce the roasting time to about 45 minutes if using them.
Halloumi must be proper Cyprus halloumi, soft halloumi will melt and won't squeak. Find it at the deli counter or with the international cheeses.
Eat it straight from the pan while it's still hot and squeaky. Once it cools, it toughens up.
This works as an appetiser before a big feed, or as a quick snack with cold beer on a Saturday arvo.

steps.text: Heat a shallow pan over medium-high heat. Pour in enough oil so it's about 5 mm deep, then get it really hot, it should shimmer and just start to smoke.
Dust the halloumi slices lightly in flour on both sides, shaking off any excess.
When the oil's smoking, carefully lay the halloumi slices into the pan. You should hear them sizzle immediately. Don't move them.
Cook for about 2 minutes until the underside is deep golden. Flip and cook the other side for another 2 minutes until it's the same colour. It should squeak when you bite into it.
Transfer to a plate, season with salt, and serve straight away with lemon wedges on the side. Squeeze lemon over each piece and eat it hot.

notes: Make ahead: Shape the kebabs up to 4 hours ahead, cover and refrigerate until ready to fry.
For extra flavour, add 1 tbsp of tamarind paste to the mixture before shaping.
These freeze well raw: freeze shaped kebabs on a tray, then transfer to a container. Fry from frozen, allowing an extra 2 to 3 minutes per side.

Food safety: Cook mince and sausages until no pink remains and the centre reaches 75°C. Raw and lightly cooked foods aren't recommended for pregnant women, young children, older people or anyone with a weakened immune system.
The oysters must be eaten as soon as they come out of the oven, while the butter is still foaming.
If shucking oysters yourself, chill them in the freezer for 15 minutes first, they open more easily.
You can make the herb butter a few hours ahead and chill it, then scoop it on to the oysters just before baking.
Press the tofu overnight or for at least 2 hours before cooking so it fries crispy and stays that way. You can make the filling components ahead and assemble the rolls right before serving.
Swap the herbs for whatever's fresh, Thai basil works beautifully, or try rocket for something peppery.
Don't overcrowd the pan, if you're cooking for more than 4, cook in two batches so the squid fries rather than steams.
Squid cooks fast: longer than 3–4 minutes and it toughens. In and out.
Serve with crusty bread to mop up the pan juices.
Food safety:

steps.text: Score the squid tubes in a fine crosshatch, cutting about halfway through the flesh. Pat dry with paper towel and cut into bite-sized pieces (about 4 cm square).
Place a large frying pan or wok over high heat until it's smoking hot, about 2 minutes.
Add the olive oil, then immediately add the squid pieces, chilli and garlic. Stir constantly for about 2 minutes, the squid will curl and become opaque.
Season with salt and pepper to taste, then squeeze lemon juice over and toss through.
Serve immediately, scattered with fresh parsley if you like, with extra lemon wedges on the side.

notes: Make the pasta and filling up to 2 hours ahead; keep the cut agnolotti on a tray in the fridge, uncovered, until you cook them.
If your filling is too wet, the agnolotti will split. If the ricotta is very creamy, drain it in a sieve lined with kitchen paper for 10 minutes first.
For a vegetarian version, use a vegetarian hard cheese (made without animal rennet).

steps.text: Make the pasta dough: tip flour into a mound on a work surface, make a well in the centre, crack in eggs, add oil and a pinch of salt. Work with a fork until shaggy, then knead for 8 minutes until smooth. Wrap and rest 20 minutes.
While the dough rests, make the filling: mix ricotta, spinach, parmesan, egg yolk and garlic. Season generously with salt, pepper and nutmeg, taste it, it should be well-seasoned.
Dust your work surface. Roll the dough to the thickness of a coin (about 1 mm). Using a 7 cm round cutter, stamp out circles.

Place a small spoonful of filling (about ½ tsp) on one half of each circle. Fold in half, press the edges to seal, then fold the corners up and press them together to make a purse shape. Place on a floured tray as you go.
Bring a large pot of salted water to a boil. Melt the butter in a separate pan over medium heat until it turns golden and smells nutty, 5 minutes. Add the sage leaves.

Drop the agnolotti into the boiling water. They'll sink, then bob to the surface after 2–3 minutes. Cook for another 2 minutes, then remove with a slotted spoon and add to the brown butter. Toss gently.
Divide among bowls. Add a pinch of salt and grate parmesan over the top.

notes: Use fresh egg noodles from the fridge section if you can, they won't clump. No fresh? Cooked noodles work fine; just break them up as you add them.
The paste can be made 30 minutes ahead and kept in a bowl.
Push for medium heat, you want the paste to fry properly but the noodles not to burn on the bottom.
Food safety: Cook fish until it is opaque and flakes easily (63°C in the thickest part), and prawns until pink and opaque all the way through.
Best served warm with crusty bread to soak up the sauce.
Keeps well in the fridge for 3 days. Reheat gently on the stove, adding a splash of water if it's too thick.
The toasted rice powder is the heart of this dish, make it fresh each time you cook. It won't keep.
Naam tok is best eaten warm, but it's fine at room temperature too. Leftovers don't hold up overnight.
Food safety:

steps.text: Toast the jasmine rice in a dry frying pan over medium heat, shaking often, until it turns golden and smells nutty, about 3–4 minutes. Let it cool, then pound it in a mortar until it's crumbly with some fine powder, not flour-fine, but grainy.

Pat the chicken dry and brush lightly with oil. Heat a chargrill or barbecue to high, then grill the chicken, turning once, until cooked through (75°C inside), about 8–10 minutes. Let it rest for 2 minutes, then slice into bite-sized pieces.
Whisk the lime juice, fish sauce and sugar together in a small bowl until the sugar dissolves.
Put the warm chicken in a large bowl with the dressing and toss well. Add the toasted rice powder, green chilli, coriander, mint and spring onions, and toss again.
Taste and add salt or a squeeze more lime juice if you need it. Serve warm or at room temperature.
Make the vinegar dip: combine vinegar, garlic, chilli and a pinch of salt in a small bowl. Let it sit for 5 minutes so the flavours come together.

Pat the grouper dry inside and out. Make three shallow scores across each side of the fish – this helps it cook through and caramelises the skin. Brush lightly with oil and season generously with salt and pepper, inside the cavity and on both sides.
Heat a large char-grill or grill plate to high until very hot and smoking lightly. Oil the grates well.

Place the grouper on the grill and cook without moving it for 8–10 minutes, until the skin is charred and crisp and releases easily from the grate. Flip carefully and cook the other side for 8–10 minutes, until the flesh near the backbone is opaque and cooked through (check by inserting a knife at the thickest point).
Transfer to a warm plate, squeeze lime over it and serve at the table with the vinegar dip on the side for each person to help themselves.

notes: Mash or mashed potato on the side soaks up the gravy beautifully.
Use a good butcher's sausage, it makes all the difference.
Food safety: Cook mince and sausages until no pink remains and the centre reaches 75°C.

steps.text: Heat oil in a large heavy pan or cast-iron frying pan over medium-high heat. Brown the sausages all over until golden, about 8 minutes. Set aside.

In the same pan, add the sliced onions and reduce heat to medium-low. Cook, stirring occasionally, until the onions are soft and deep golden brown, about 20 minutes. Be patient, this is where the flavour comes from.
Stir in the tomato paste and cook for 1 minute, then add the beef stock and worcestershire sauce. Return the sausages to the pan.
Simmer gently for 15 minutes until the sausages are cooked through and the gravy has thickened slightly. Season with salt and pepper to taste.
Serve the snags on a plate with the onion gravy spooned over.

notes: Store in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 3 days, or refrigerate for up to a week.
This cake is best made a day ahead, the flavour deepens and the texture becomes even better.
Don't skip squeezing out the moisture from the cassava; it makes all the difference to how the cake sets.

steps.text: Preheat the oven to 180°C. Line a 20 cm × 30 cm baking tin with baking paper.
Squeeze the grated cassava firmly over a bowl to remove excess moisture, this is important for the right texture. Transfer to a large bowl.
Add the coconut milk, caster sugar, vanilla extract and salt. Stir well until the sugar is dissolved and everything is combined.
Pour into the prepared tin, spreading evenly.
Bake for 45–50 minutes, until the top is golden and a skewer inserted into the centre comes out clean.
Cool in the tin for 10 minutes, then turn out onto a wire rack to cool completely. Cut into squares to serve.

notes: Barramundi is best when fresh and cooked simply. If you can't find barramundi, use any firm white fish fillet like snapper or bream.
Serve with steamed jasmine rice and a quick salad of cucumber and lime to cut through the richness.
Food safety: Cook fish until it is opaque and flakes easily (63°C in the thickest part), and prawns until pink and opaque all the way through.
Use bone-in chicken thighs if you can find them, they add more flavour to the broth as everything cooks.
This keeps well in the fridge for up to 3 days and reheats gently on the stove with a splash of water.
Cook mince and sausages until they reach 75°C in the centre, with no pink left.
Food safety:
Make ahead: prepare the dashi dressing the night before and keep chilled.
The spinach must be cooled completely before dressing, or the dashi will warm and lose its clean taste.
Serve in shallow bowls if you have them, obanzai looks best on good ceramics.

steps.text: Bring a large pot of salted water to a boil. Cook the spinach, stirring gently, until tender and wilted, about 2 minutes. Drain in a colander.
Gather the spinach into a ball and gently squeeze out excess water with your hands. Do this carefully, the leaves should stay tender. Set aside to cool.
Combine the dashi, soy sauce and mirin in a bowl. Chill in the refrigerator until cold.
Once the spinach has cooled, cut it into 4 cm lengths and arrange in a serving bowl or on a plate.
Pour the cold dashi dressing over the spinach just before serving, or let each person pour their own at the table. Top with bonito flakes.
Serve immediately, chilled.

Make the paste: whisk glutinous rice flour, water and sugar in a saucepan. Bring to a simmer over medium heat, stirring constantly, until thickened and translucent, about 3 minutes. Remove from heat and stir in the garlic, ginger, gochugaru and fish sauce. Set aside to cool slightly.
Prepare the gat: cut the stems into 5 cm lengths. Leave the leaves whole or tear into 10 cm pieces if very large. Rinse well under cold water.

Salt the gat: layer the stems and leaves in a large bowl, sprinkling 2 tbsp of salt evenly as you go. Let sit for 15 minutes, then massage gently with your hands, turning the leaves over to coat all sides. The gat will soften and release liquid, this is correct. Drain off most of the liquid.

Season: add the cooled paste to the salted gat along with the spring onions and sesame seeds. Using clean hands, toss and massage everything together for 2 minutes so every leaf is coated. Taste a small piece: it should taste pleasantly salty now, but not salty enough to eat as is, the flavour will develop as it ferments.

Pack: transfer the gat kimchi into a clean glass jar, pressing down so the vegetables are submerged under their own liquid. Leave a 5 cm gap at the top. If there isn't enough liquid to cover, sprinkle the remaining 1 tbsp salt over the top and leave for 10 minutes to release more brine.

Ferment: seal the jar loosely (not airtight) and leave at cool room temperature or in the cold part of your kitchen for 3 days. After day 1, open the lid to let gas escape. By day 3, it will have a gentle fizz and a deep, funky flavour. Taste it, when it suits you, seal it tightly and refrigerate. It will keep for up to 3 weeks.
Make the marinade: whisk together pomegranate molasses, tamarind paste, oil, garlic, cumin, coriander, Aleppo pepper and salt in a small bowl.
Prepare the fish: lay each fish on a cutting board and, using a sharp knife, cut down the spine from head to tail. Gently press the fish open so it lies flat like a butterfly, skin side down.
Rub the marinade all over the fish, inside and out, making sure to coat the flesh well. Let sit for 10 minutes.
Heat oil in a large heavy-based pan or cast iron frying pan over medium-high heat until shimmering. Carefully lay the fish skin side up in the pan.

Cook for 6–7 minutes without moving, until the skin is golden and crispy. Gently flip and cook the other side for another 6–7 minutes until the flesh is opaque and cooked through (the flesh should flake easily when pressed with a fork).
Serve hot with lemon wedges and fresh parsley scattered over.

notes: Shave the burdock on a mandoline or with a vegetable peeler to keep the pieces thin and cook evenly.
You can make this with chicken thigh or thinly sliced pork instead of beef, same cooking time.
Food safety: Steaks and roasting cuts of beef or lamb can be served pink: about 60°C in the centre is medium-rare, 70°C is well done.

steps.text: Bring a large pot of salted water to a boil. Add potatoes and cook until completely tender, about 15 minutes. Drain well in a colander.

While potatoes cook, heat 2 tbsp oil in a large frying pan over medium-high heat. Add onions and cook, stirring occasionally, until they're golden and crispy, about 12 minutes. Season with salt and transfer to a paper towel.

Mash warm potatoes with butter and milk until creamy but still with a little texture. Fold in most of the crispy onions and all the dill, reserving some onions for the top. Season generously with salt and pepper.
Transfer to a serving bowl and top with reserved crispy onions. Eat immediately.

notes: Buy the pipis the day you cook and keep them on ice. Tap any open shells, they should close; if they don't, discard them.
You can make this with mussels or littleneck clams if you can't find pipis.
Food safety:
Pisua is a great make-ahead dish, prepare it and refrigerate for up to a day, then bake when needed (add 10 minutes to cooking time).
Leftovers keep in the fridge for 3 days and are even better reheated gently in a warm oven.
This is even better made a day ahead. Cool, refrigerate overnight, then gently reheat. The flavours deepen and the fat is easy to lift off the cold surface.
Serve with crusty bread to soak up the sauce, and a simple green salad or steamed greens on the side.
Food safety: Braised beef and lamb cook well past 75°C on the way to tender, so they are safe once soft.
Use day-old rice for the best texture, fresh rice tends to clump when fried.
The corned beef tin is already cooked, so you're just heating and browning it for flavour.
Swap the fried egg for a sunny-side up or poached egg if you like, but that runny yolk over everything is the proper way to do it.

Food safety: Raw and lightly cooked foods aren't recommended for pregnant women, young children, older people or anyone with a weakened immune system. Cool any leftover rice quickly and refrigerate it within an hour; reheat it until steaming hot.

The chicken can be cooked and shredded up to 1 day ahead; reheat gently in a low oven before plating. The chili oil keeps in a clean glass jar in the fridge for up to 2 weeks, use it on tofu, greens, or noodles.

Doubanjiang is spicy fermented bean paste from Sichuan; if you can't find it, skip this step rather than substituting, as it's essential to the flavour. Without it, this becomes a different (still good, but different) dish.
The numbing comes from the Sichuan peppercorns, not heat. If you prefer less mala, reduce them to 2 tablespoons.
Food safety:

steps.text: Bring the 6 cups water to a boil in a large pot. Add the spring onion pieces, ginger slices, smashed garlic and salt. Simmer for 2 minutes to infuse the broth.

Add the chicken pieces to the simmering broth and return to a gentle boil. Skim any scum that rises. Reduce heat to a low simmer and poach until the chicken is cooked through (check the thickest pieces reach 75°C inside), about 15 minutes. Remove the chicken to a plate and let cool slightly, then shred or cut into bite-sized pieces. Discard the poaching liquid.

While the chicken cooks, make the chili oil. Heat the neutral oil in a small pan over medium heat. When it shimmers, add the Sichuan peppercorns and dried chillies. Toast, stirring gently, for 2–3 minutes until fragrant and the oil is a deep amber, do not let it smoke or burn.

Remove the pan from heat. Add the doubanjiang, sliced garlic, sliced ginger, star anise and cinnamon stick. Stir well and let it infuse for 1 minute off the heat. The residual heat will open the flavours without charring them. Taste and add salt to balance.
Arrange the shredded chicken on a serving plate. Pour the warm chili oil (including the aromatics and spices) over the chicken.
Scatter with fresh coriander, chives, sliced spring onion and black sesame seeds if using. Serve warm or at room temperature with steamed rice.

notes: If you don't have a proper cendol maker, use a fine sieve or even a ladle with small holes; the noodles don't need to be perfect, just thin.
Everything must be ice-cold before serving, chill the glasses if you want to be proper about it.

steps.text: Make the syrup first: In a small saucepan, combine the palm sugar and 200 ml water. Stir over medium heat until the sugar dissolves completely, about 5 minutes. You should have a thick, smooth golden syrup. Remove from the heat and let it cool to room temperature.

Make the cendol batter: In a bowl, mix the rice flour, 200 ml water, salt and the pandan leaves together, stirring until smooth and lump-free. The batter should be thin, like condensed milk in consistency. Remove the pandan leaves and set the batter aside.

Bring a large pot of water to the boil (about 2 litres). Place the cendol maker (a special mould with holes, or use a sieve with small holes) over the boiling water. Working in batches, pour the batter slowly through the mould so the thin noodles drop straight into the boiling water. They will sink at first, then float to the surface in about 1 minute, that is when they are cooked.
Remove the cooked cendol with a slotted spoon and place them immediately into a bowl of ice-cold water to stop the cooking. Drain well and set aside. Repeat with the remaining batter.
In a small saucepan, warm the coconut milk gently over low heat until steaming, do not let it boil. Add a pinch of salt and stir. Let it cool to room temperature.

To serve, divide the cendol noodles among four glasses or bowls, pour a little of the palm sugar syrup over them (about 50 ml per serving), then pour the cooled coconut milk on top (about 100 ml per serving). Fill each glass with ice and serve immediately, ice-cold.

notes: The sambal can be made up to 2 hours ahead; keep it at room temperature so the flavours stay fresh and sharp.
Any firm white fish works here. Adjust cooking time by a minute or two depending on thickness.
Food safety: Raw and lightly cooked foods aren't recommended for pregnant women, young children, older people or anyone with a weakened immune system.
This banchan keeps for up to three days refrigerated. It's equally good cold, straight from the bowl.
The quality of your sesame oil matters here, use a good toasted variety for the full nutty flavour.
The broken rice should have a slight bite, don't overcook it. If you can't find it, use jasmine rice but reduce the cooking time to 10 minutes.
Make the fish sauce caramel up to a day ahead and store in a jar; reheat gently before serving.
Pickled daikon and carrot (cà chua cà rốt) from the supermarket are traditional but optional, they add a salty, vinegary edge.

Food safety: Cook fresh pork to at least 70°C in the thickest part. Raw and lightly cooked foods aren't recommended for pregnant women, young children, older people or anyone with a weakened immune system.
Make the toasted rice powder ahead and keep it in a jar, it will keep for weeks and makes larb het much quicker on the day.
Larb het is best served at room temperature or warm. It doesn't keep well, so make it just before you want to eat.
The kanji keeps in the fridge for up to 10 days, and the vada soften into it beautifully.
If you don't have a wet grinder, a good blender works fine, just be patient and add water slowly so the batter stays light.

steps.text: Make the kanji first. Heat the mustard oil in a pan until it just smokes, then remove from heat. When it has cooled to warm, add the mustard seeds, fenugreek seeds, and dried chillies. Let them crackle for a few seconds, then stir in the asafoetida. In a jar, combine the carrot sticks with salt, then pour the hot oil and spices over them. Add the citric acid, stir well, and set aside to cool completely.
Drain the urad dal and grind it to a thick, smooth paste using a wet grinder or food processor, adding just a splash of water if needed, the batter should be light and fluffy, not wet.
Transfer the batter to a bowl. Fold in the rice flour, green chilli, cumin seeds, and salt, mixing gently to keep the batter airy.
Heat the oil for frying in a large, heavy pan to 180°C (a small piece of batter should sizzle and rise to the top immediately).

Wet your fingers and shape small balls of batter about the size of a walnut, then gently slide them into the hot oil. Fry in batches until golden and crisp all over, being careful not to crowd the pan.
Fry for 4 to 5 minutes, stirring gently and turning the vada so they brown evenly. They should be golden and crispy. Remove with a slotted spoon and drain on paper towel.
Once the vada have cooled to room temperature, add them to the kanji jar and mix gently so each one is coated with the pickle. Cover and leave for at least 4 hours, or overnight, before serving.

notes: This is traditionally made in a heavy pot called a dizi. An enamelled cast iron or stainless steel pot works just as well.
Some cooks add dried limes (loomi) or a pinch of saffron for extra depth. This version keeps it simple.
The broth keeps well for 3 days in the fridge, and tastes even better the next day.
Food safety: Braised beef and lamb cook well past 75°C on the way to tender, so they are safe once soft.

steps.text: Heat the oil in a large heavy pot over medium-high heat. Brown the beef chunks on all sides, about 8 minutes total. Don't rush this step.
Add the onions and turmeric, stirring, until fragrant, about 2 minutes.
Pour in the water and bring to a boil. Skim any foam from the surface until the liquid looks clear. Add the black pepper and a pinch of salt.
Reduce to a low simmer, cover, and cook for 45 minutes.
Add the potatoes and chickpeas, and simmer, covered, for another 45 minutes until the meat is very tender and the broth is rich and deep in colour.
Taste and adjust the salt. You should have a clear, flavourful broth and very soft solids.
To serve, ladle the broth into bowls as the first course. Pour the remaining broth over the meat and vegetables.

Pound the cooked meat and potatoes with a wooden spoon or potato masher directly in the pot until roughly crushed. Pile onto toasted bread, drizzle with a little broth, and serve as the second course. Garnish with fresh herbs if you have them.

notes: Cook from leftover rotisserie chicken or use tinned tuna (drained) for a different angle.
The gravy thickens as it cools slightly, aim for thick but pourable at the stove.
Scale up easily: double the stock and starch for two bowls, cook noodles separately.
Cook chicken until it reaches 75°C in the thickest part and the juices run clear.

steps.text: Bring a pot of salted water to a rolling boil. Cook the egg noodles until soft, about 3–4 minutes, stirring gently to prevent sticking. Drain and tip into a bowl.
In the same pot (no need to rinse), heat the oil over medium heat. Add the minced garlic and fry gently until fragrant and golden, about 1 minute, don't burn it.
Pour in the chicken stock and bring to a simmer until the sauce is bubbling gently. Add the soy sauce and sugar, then taste. Adjust salt and white pepper to your liking.

Stir the tapioca starch mixture to recombine it (it will have settled), then slowly pour it into the simmering stock while stirring constantly. Keep stirring for 1–2 minutes until the gravy thickens and turns glossy and translucent.
Add the shredded chicken and stir to heat through, about 1 minute. The gravy should be thick enough to coat the back of a spoon but still pour easily.
Place the soft noodles in a bowl and carefully pour the hot gravy over them. Top with fried garlic, fresh coriander if you have it, and pickled chilli if you like heat. Eat while it's hot.

notes: Clean the clams by scrubbing them under cold water and soaking in salted water for an hour if you have time; this helps them expel sand.
Make-ahead: prepare the dashi and have the clams cleaned and ready the night before. The soup itself takes just 15 minutes on the day.
If clams are very large, you can halve them after opening for easier eating.

Food safety: Cook fish until it is opaque and flakes easily (63°C in the thickest part), and prawns until pink and opaque all the way through. Throw away any mussels or clams whose shells stay closed after cooking.

steps.text: Bring the dashi to a gentle simmer in a pot until tiny bubbles rise at the edges.
Add the cleaned clams and a thin slice of ginger if using. Cover and simmer until the clams just begin to open, 3 to 4 minutes.
Scoop the clams into serving bowls as they open (don't wait for all of them; they open in stages).
Dissolve the white miso in a small bowl with a ladle of the hot broth until smooth, then pour it back into the pot. Stir gently, do not let the broth boil or the miso flavour will flatten.
Add the mirin to the pot and taste. Add a small pinch of salt if needed.
Pour the broth over the clams in each bowl, scatter the spring onion on top, and serve immediately.

notes: You can make the broth a day ahead; store it in the fridge and add the prawns just before serving.
Quesillo or fresh mozzarella works best here, it melts into silken clouds in the hot broth. Avoid hard cheeses.
If you can't find ají amarillo paste, substitute 2 tsp of ají amarillo powder mixed with a little water.
Food safety: Raw and lightly cooked foods aren't recommended for pregnant women, young children, older people or anyone with a weakened immune system.

steps.text: Heat oil in a large pot over medium heat. Add onion and cook, stirring, until soft and golden, about 5 minutes.
Stir in garlic and ají amarillo paste, cooking for 1 minute until fragrant.
Pour in stock and bring to a simmer. Add potato and capsicum, then stir in cumin. Cook for 12–15 minutes, until potato is just tender.
Season with salt and pepper. Add prawns and cook, stirring gently, until they turn opaque and firm, about 3–4 minutes. Do not overcook.
Remove from heat. Divide fresh cheese among serving bowls, then ladle the hot chupe over it, the cheese will soften and melt into the broth.
Top each bowl with two egg halves and garnish with coriander if you like. Serve immediately.

If you have a gas stove, char the tomatoes, chillies and garlic directly over the flame, turning with tongs, until blackened and soft all over, about 10–12 minutes. If you only have electric, use a grill pan or cast iron over high heat, turning often, until deeply charred. The darker the better.
Let cool for a minute, then peel away the charred skin from the tomatoes and discard. Peel the garlic cloves.
Pound the charred tomatoes, chillies and garlic in a mortar and pestle until you have a rough paste, it should be chunky, not smooth.
Stir in the lime juice and fish sauce. Taste and add salt if needed. The dip should be smoky, hot and sharp all at once.

notes: Make ahead: Shape the kebabs up to 4 hours ahead and refrigerate on a lined tray, covered.
For extra crunch, add 2 tbsp finely chopped pistachios or almonds to the mince.
Serve with naan or flatbread, sliced onions, lemon and a dollop of cooling yoghurt.
Food safety:

steps.text: In a large bowl, combine the lamb mince, pomegranate seeds, green chilli, onion, garlic, fresh coriander, mint and egg. Add the ground cumin, ground coriander, chilli powder, garam masala and salt. Mix gently with your hands until just combined, don't overwork it or the kebabs will be dense.
Divide the mixture into 8 equal portions. Wet your hands lightly and shape each portion into a thick oval, pressing gently but firmly so it holds together.
Heat a large frying pan or tawa over medium-high heat and add 2 tbsp oil. Once shimmering, carefully place 4 kebabs in the pan without crowding.

Cook for 5 to 6 minutes on the first side until golden brown and crispy, then flip carefully. Cook for another 3 to 4 minutes until the second side is golden and the meat is cooked through (the internal temperature should reach 75°C).
Transfer to a paper-towel-lined plate and cook the remaining 4 kebabs in the same way, adding a little more oil if needed, until each is deep golden brown and crisp at the edges.
Serve hot with lemon wedges, sliced onions and yoghurt on the side.

notes: Store in an airtight container for up to 5 days.
You can make this in a conventional oven at 180°C if you don't have a camp oven, bake for 18–20 minutes.
If you can't find wattleseed flour locally, use the same weight of plain flour instead, though you'll lose the earthy, distinctive flavour.
Make the filling ahead: it keeps in the fridge for up to 3 days. Warm it gently before stuffing.
If you don't have a tawa, use a flat non-stick frying pan or cast iron frying pan.
The dough can be made and left covered for up to 1 hour before rolling.
Use jarred vine leaves if fresh aren't available. Rinse off the brine and pat dry.
Any whole white fish works: bream, snapper, flathead. Aim for 350–450 g per fish.
The blackened leaves are not meant to be eaten. Unwrap carefully and discard.
Food safety:

steps.text: Light your charcoal and let it burn down to glowing coals. You want heat, not flame.
Pat the fish dry inside and out. Season the cavity with salt, pepper and a pinch of oregano. Stuff each fish with 2 lemon slices and 1 oregano sprig.

Lay 6 vine leaves on a work surface, overlapping them to form a base. Place a fish on top, then fold the leaves up and around it, tucking and overlapping to seal it completely. Do the same with the other fish.
Brush each parcel lightly with olive oil. Place on the grill grate over the coals and cook until the leaves are charred and the fish flakes easily and is opaque inside.

Cook for 10–12 minutes until the vine leaves are charred black on top. Flip the parcel carefully, then cook for another 8–10 minutes on the other side until the second side is charred and the fish is cooked through (the flesh should be opaque and flake easily at the thickest part).
Slide onto a plate and let rest for 2 minutes. Unwrap at the table. The leaves are burnt, but the fish inside is perfect, steamed in its own juices with lemon and herb.

notes: The dough can be made up to 4 hours ahead and kept covered at room temperature. If you're short on time, you can stretch the noodles thinner and cook them a little faster, just watch they don't break.
You can use beef mince instead of lamb; the cumin-to-meat ratio stays the same. Some cooks add a handful of fresh coriander or a drizzle of chilli oil to finish.
Food safety: Cook mince and sausages until no pink remains and the centre reaches 75°C.
Kokotxas are expensive and seasonal. Buy them very fresh from a good fishmonger, or ask them to order them in.
The sauce must never boil after the egg yolks are added, or it will scramble. Keep the heat low.
Don't skip the white pepper, it's gentler than black and won't speckle the delicate pale sauce.
Food safety:

steps.text: Put the kokotxas in a wide, shallow pan with the white wine and fish stock. Bring to a gentle simmer and poach for 3 to 4 minutes, until just cooked through, they should be opaque but still delicate. Carefully transfer the kokotxas to a warm plate with a slotted spoon, keeping the cooking liquid in the pan.
Heat the olive oil in another pan over low heat. Add the sliced garlic and cook gently, stirring, until it is just starting to soften and colour, about 2 minutes. Do not burn it.
Pour the cooking liquid (about 300 ml) into the pan with the garlic and oil, and bring to a simmer. Add the chopped parsley and cook for 1 minute.

In a small bowl, beat the egg yolks lightly. Remove the pan from the heat, let it cool for 30 seconds, then slowly pour in the egg yolks while whisking constantly, this makes the sauce silky and rich without scrambling the eggs. Taste and season with salt and white pepper.
Gently return the kokotxas to the pan and warm through for 30 seconds without letting the sauce boil, until the fish is just opaque and the sauce is glossy.
Divide among four bowls, pour the salsa verde over and around the kokotxas, and serve with crusty bread to soak up every drop.

notes: If you can't find fideuà noodles, break thin spaghetti or vermicelli into short pieces before toasting.
The socarrat is crucial, that dark, crackling crust at the bottom. Listen for it; don't walk away during those last 30 seconds.
Make the aioli ahead if you like; it keeps in the fridge for a day.
Food safety: Raw and lightly cooked foods aren't recommended for pregnant women, young children, older people or anyone with a weakened immune system.

steps.text: Make the aioli first: in a mortar or small bowl, pound the garlic with a pinch of salt until smooth. Add the egg yolk and stir well. Add the oil a drop at a time, whisking constantly, until it begins to emulsify. Once thickened, add the oil in a thin stream, whisking continuously. Finish with lemon juice and salt. Set aside.

Heat the oil in a paella pan or large shallow frying pan (about 30 cm) over medium heat. Add the noodles and toast, stirring often, until they turn golden and fragrant, about 3 to 4 minutes. Remove and set aside.

In the same pan, heat a little more oil if needed and soften the onion, garlic and capsicum over medium heat, stirring often, until soft and translucent, about 8 minutes. This sofregit should be slow and gentle, don't rush it.
Add the tomato and cook for 2 minutes, stirring.

Return the toasted noodles to the pan and stir to coat. Pour in the warm stock and the saffron with its soaking water. Bring to a simmer and cook without stirring for about 10 minutes, until most of the liquid has been absorbed and the noodles are tender.

Scatter the prawns and squid over the top, season with salt and pepper, and continue cooking for about 5 minutes, stirring gently, until the prawns are cooked through (opaque and firm) and the squid is tender.
Increase the heat to medium-high for the last minute to create the socarrat, listen for a gentle crackling sound from the bottom. Don't burn it; you want a dark, crispy crust, not black.
Remove from heat. Scatter with fresh parsley and serve straight from the pan with the aioli on the side.

notes: Make it no more than an hour or two before serving, the cucumbers release water over time and the salad becomes watery.
If using English cucumbers (continental), use 2 large ones and skip peeling if you prefer, the skin is thin and tender.
Holds well in a low oven (150°C) for 30 minutes if dinner runs late.
Use waxy potatoes like Kipfler or baby potatoes, they hold their shape. Don't use floury potatoes.
If your anchovies are very salty, rinse and pat them dry first.

steps.text: Heat the oven to 200°C. Butter a 2-litre baking dish.

Layer half the potatoes into the dish, then half the onion and half the anchovies. Season lightly with salt and pepper (go easy on the salt, the anchovies are already salty). Repeat with the remaining potatoes, onion, and anchovies.

Whisk the cream and milk together, then pour over the potato layers. Stir gently to distribute the anchovies and onions, but don't mash the potatoes. Scatter the remaining butter in small pieces on top. If you want a crust, sprinkle the panko over the butter.
Bake for 45–50 minutes, until the potatoes are tender and the top is golden. If the top browns too fast, cover loosely with foil and uncover for the last 10 minutes to crisp up.
Let it rest for 5 minutes, then serve warm straight from the dish.

Heat the oil in a large frying pan over medium-high heat. Season the trout inside and out with salt and pepper. When the oil shimmers, lay the trout in the pan and cook for 6–7 minutes without moving them, until the skin is golden and crisp.
Carefully turn the trout and cook for another 4–5 minutes on the other side, until the flesh is just cooked through and flakes gently at the thickest part near the backbone. Transfer to a warm plate.

Reduce the heat to medium. Add the butter to the same pan and let it melt, swirling often. After 2–3 minutes, the butter will begin to foam. Keep swirling until the milk solids turn golden and the butter smells nutty, about 1–2 minutes more.

Add the hazelnuts to the brown butter and stir gently for 30 seconds, until the hazelnuts are golden and fragrant. Pour the hazelnut brown butter over the trout. Serve with lemon wedges and parsley scattered over, if using.

notes: The fish cake is essential, it's what makes this feel authentic. Find it at Asian grocers or substitute firm tofu if needed.
Make the gravy up to 4 hours ahead and reheat gently before serving; the flavours deepen. Boil the eggs separately to avoid overcooking.
Cook chicken until it reaches 75°C in the thickest part and the juices run clear.
Food safety: Raw and lightly cooked foods aren't recommended for pregnant women, young children, older people or anyone with a weakened immune system.

steps.text: Bring a small pot of water to the boil and gently lower in the eggs. Boil for 7 minutes for firm but slightly runny yolks, or 10 minutes for hard-boiled. Cool in cold water, then peel and halve.
Heat the oil in a large pot over medium heat. Fry the shallots until golden and crispy, about 5 minutes, then add the garlic and cook for 30 seconds until fragrant.
Add the laksa paste and fry, stirring, for 1 minute. Add the tamarind paste and stir through, then pour in the coconut milk and stock, stirring to combine.
Add the palm sugar and turmeric, then bring to a gentle simmer. Cook for 8 to 10 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the gravy thickens slightly. Taste and season with salt and pepper.
While the gravy simmers, bring a separate pot of salted water to the boil and cook the egg noodles according to packet directions. Drain and set aside.
In the last minute of simmering the gravy, add the fish cake slices and bean sprouts, stirring gently.
Divide the noodles between two bowls. Pour the gravy over each bowl, then top with the egg halves, spring onions, fried shallots and fresh chilli if you like. Serve with a lime wedge on the side.
Squeeze the lime over just before eating, it lifts the whole thing.
Preheat the oven to 160°C. Line a 20 cm square baking tin with baking paper.
Rub the cold butter into the flour and salt with your fingertips until the mixture resembles fine breadcrumbs. Don't overwork it.
Stir in the caster sugar until just combined. The dough will be crumbly and hold together only loosely.
Press the dough evenly into the prepared tin, using the back of a spoon or your fingers. It should be about 1 cm thick.
Bake for 20–25 minutes, until pale golden and just firm to the touch. It will still feel slightly soft in the middle, that's correct.
Remove from the oven and let cool in the tin for 5 minutes, then cut into fingers or squares while still warm. Leave to cool completely on the tin before lifting out.

notes: Serve with rice and peas, or white rice and a green salad.
The Scotch bonnet stays whole so you can fish it out, leave it in if you like heat, or use a milder green chilli instead.
Food safety:

steps.text: Pat the chicken dry. Heat the oil in a large heavy-bottomed pot over medium-high heat. Working in batches, brown the chicken pieces, turning them until deeply caramelised all over, about 8–10 minutes per batch. Remove to a plate.
Reduce the heat to medium. Add the onion and garlic to the pot, and cook, stirring, until soft and fragrant, about 3 minutes.
Stir in the tomato paste, allspice, black pepper and salt. Cook for 1 minute, then pour in the stock and add the sugar.

Return the chicken to the pot. Add the whole Scotch bonnet and thyme. Bring to a simmer, then reduce the heat to low, cover with a lid, and cook for 30 minutes, turning the chicken halfway through. The chicken should be cooked through (the thickest part reaching 75°C inside).
Taste the broth and add more salt if needed. Remove the whole Scotch bonnet before serving, it will have infused the stew with flavour without overwhelming it.

notes: Rice cakes keep in the freezer. No need to thaw, just separate and add straight to the boiling stock.
Swap the carrots for whatever's in the crisper: daikon, mushrooms, bok choy, even spinach all work.
Make the dough the night before and refrigerate, it gives better flavour and texture.
The chole can be made up to 2 days ahead; reheat gently before serving.
Don't skip frying the bhatures to order; they're best eaten warm and puffy straight from the oil.
Mafé tastes better the next day as the flavours deepen. Make it ahead and reheat gently.
You can swap the pumpkin for sweet potato or potato, and the eggplant for green beans or okra.
Serve with plain white rice, or with fried plantain on the side for the kids.
Food safety: Braised beef and lamb cook well past 75°C on the way to tender, so they are safe once soft.
Make the pavlova base up to 2 days ahead and store in an airtight container. Assemble just before serving so the ice cream melts into the warm berries.
If you can't get hokey pokey ice cream, vanilla works fine, drizzle with toffee or caramel sauce for that honeycomb sweetness.
Food safety: Raw and lightly cooked foods aren't recommended for pregnant women, young children, older people or anyone with a weakened immune system.
Make the rice ahead: cook it the morning of, cool it completely before mixing with the mince so the meatballs hold their shape.
Freeze unbaked meatballs on a tray, then transfer to a container. Cook from frozen, adding a few extra minutes to the simmering time.
This broth is just as good the next day, it tastes even better as the flavours settle overnight.
Food safety: Cook mince and sausages until no pink remains and the centre reaches 75°C.

steps.text: In a bowl, combine the lamb mince, cooled rice, half the diced onion, half the garlic, cumin, coriander, and a pinch of salt and pepper. Mix gently until just combined, don't overwork it. Form into 12 meatballs, about the size of walnuts.
Heat the oil in a large pot over medium heat. Working in batches, brown the meatballs on all sides, about 8 minutes total. Transfer to a plate.
In the same pot, add the remaining onion and garlic. Cook, stirring, until softened and fragrant, about 3 minutes. Stir in the tomato paste and cook for 1 minute.
Add the crushed tomatoes and stock. Bring to a gentle simmer until bubbling, stirring to scrape up any browned bits from the bottom of the pot.
Return the meatballs to the pot, nestling them into the broth. Reduce heat to low, cover, and simmer for 25 minutes, until the meatballs are cooked through and the broth has thickened slightly.
Taste and adjust seasoning with salt and pepper. Serve hot in bowls with the broth, garnished with fresh coriander if you like.

notes: If you can't find fernbrake (gosari), use the same amount of fresh spinach added at the very end, or skip it entirely.
Make ahead: simmer the beef with the stock up to step 5, then cool and refrigerate. Reheat gently and add the vegetables fresh when serving.
Use a good beef stock, homemade or from the butcher makes a real difference. Store-bought is fine, but taste it first as some are very salty.
Food safety: Braised beef and lamb cook well past 75°C on the way to tender, so they are safe once soft.

steps.text: Place the sliced beef in a large bowl and sprinkle with 1½ tsp salt. Toss to coat evenly. Let it sit for exactly 10 minutes, this draws out the juices and seasons the meat deeply.
Add the soy sauce, gochugaru, minced garlic and sesame oil to the beef. Mix well and let sit for another 2 minutes.
Heat a large pot or Korean stew pot (galbijjim or ttukbaegi) over medium-high heat. Add the beef mixture and stir-fry for 2 minutes until the meat begins to brown and release its juices.
Pour in the stock and bring to a boil, about 5 minutes. Skim any foam that rises to the surface.
Add the carrot and fernbrake (if using), and simmer for 8 minutes until the carrot is just tender.

Add the bean sprouts and green onion, and simmer for 2 more minutes, until the sprouts are wilted but still crisp. Taste and adjust with the extra ½ tsp salt if needed, it should taste savoury and bold.
Divide into bowls and top each with sesame seeds. Serve hot with steamed rice.

Wash the beetroot well, leave the skins on, and place in a large pot of cold water. Bring to a boil, then reduce heat and simmer for 25–30 minutes, until tender when pierced with a fork but still firm, this takes longer than you might think, but it matters because the inside cooks gently and stays sweet.
While the beetroot cooks, toast the sesame seeds in a dry frying pan over medium heat, stirring constantly, for 2–3 minutes until golden and fragrant. Tip onto a plate to cool.
Toast the walnuts in the same pan, stirring, for about 2 minutes. Set aside to cool.
When the beetroot is tender, drain well and let it cool enough to handle, about 5 minutes. Rub off the skins under cold running water, they'll slip off easily, then cut into chunks about 2 cm across.
In a small bowl, whisk together the pomegranate molasses, olive oil, lemon juice, minced garlic, salt and pepper.
Place the warm beetroot in a serving bowl, pour the dressing over it, and toss gently. Let it sit for 5 minutes so the flavours meld.
Just before serving, scatter the toasted sesame seeds and walnuts over the top, and garnish with fresh parsley if you like. The seeds stay crisp this way, you understand why when you taste them.

notes: Make the paste up to a day ahead and store in the fridge, covered. It also freezes well.
Any firm white fish works: barramundi, snapper, flathead or jewfish. Whole is best for flavour and drama, but you can use 800 g of thick fillets instead.
Don't have makrut lime leaves? Use a squeeze of fresh lime juice in the curry instead.
Food safety:

steps.text: Make the curry paste: toast the coriander and cumin seeds in a dry frying pan over medium heat until fragrant, about 2 minutes, then grind in a mortar or spice grinder. Pound the red chillies, ground spices, garlic, shrimp paste, fish sauce and palm sugar together in a mortar until a rough paste forms. Add the neutral oil and stir to combine.
Heat 2 tbsp neutral oil in a large saucepan or wok over medium-high heat. Add the curry paste and cook, stirring, until fragrant and darkened slightly, about 3 minutes.
Pour in the coconut milk and fish stock, stirring to combine. Bring to a gentle simmer until small bubbles break the surface and the curry is lightly thickened.
Carefully lay the whole fish into the simmering curry. The liquid should come partway up the sides of the fish. Tear in the makrut lime leaves and add the fish sauce and palm sugar.

Simmer gently for 15–20 minutes, spooning the curry occasionally over the top of the fish, until the fish is cooked through (the flesh should flake easily and be opaque at the thickest point near the backbone).
Taste and adjust the seasoning with fish sauce, palm sugar or lime juice as needed. Scatter fresh Thai basil and sliced chillies over the top and serve with jasmine rice.

notes: If you can't get rabbit, this works just as well with chicken thighs, they're tougher and hold up to long cooking like rabbit does.
Make it a day ahead; the flavours deepen overnight and it reheats beautifully.
Camp oven tip: bed the pot in hot coals and place coals on the lid for even heat, aim for about 150°C equivalent.

steps.text: Heat the oil in a camp oven or heavy-based pot over medium-high heat. Season the rabbit pieces with salt and pepper. Brown them in batches, about 3 minutes per side, then set aside.
Add the onions to the pot and cook, stirring, until softened and starting to colour, about 5 minutes. Add the garlic and cook for another minute.
Return the rabbit to the pot. Pour in the red wine, scraping the bottom to lift any browned bits. Let it bubble for a minute, then add the stock, bay leaf and thyme.
Bring to a simmer, then cover and cook low and slow, either in a camp oven over coals, a slow cooker on low for 3 hours, or a covered pot in a 150°C oven for 2 hours.
After 1½ hours, add the carrots, potatoes and parsnip. Stir well and return to the heat.
Continue cooking until the rabbit is tender and falling from the bone, the veg is soft, and the sauce is rich and glossy, about another hour. Taste and season with salt and pepper.
Serve hot, straight from the pot.

notes: Marinate overnight for best flavour, but 2 hours works in a pinch.
No grill? Use a hot cast-iron pan or oven grill, watch it so the skin chars without burning.
Serve with vinegar dipping sauce (sukang with garlic) if you've got it.
Food safety:

steps.text: Make the marinade: warm the oil in a small bowl and cook the minced garlic for 1 minute until fragrant. Stir in the turmeric, lime juice and fish sauce. Season with salt and pepper to taste.
Pat the chicken dry with paper towels. Place in a large bowl and pour the marinade over, turning to coat well. Cover and marinate for at least 2 hours, or overnight if you have time.

Heat a grill or grill pan to medium-high heat until hot and sizzling when a drop of water hits it. Lightly oil the grates or pan. Remove the chicken from the marinade (reserve it), shaking off excess.

Grill the chicken skin-side down for 6–8 minutes until golden and charred. Turn and cook the other side for another 6–8 minutes, turning occasionally and basting with reserved marinade. The chicken is done when cooked through (75°C inside) and the skin is charred and smoky.
Rest the chicken for 3–4 minutes, then transfer to a plate. Squeeze fresh calamansi over if you like, and scatter spring onion on top. Serve hot with rice.

notes: Make ahead: prepare the fish paste up to 4 hours ahead and keep it covered in the fridge. Assemble and steam just before eating.
Can use barramundi, snapper or any firm white fish. Some cooks add egg white to make the paste lighter.
If you can't find banana leaves, use parchment paper parcels and omit the skewer, tie with kitchen string instead.
Food safety: Cook fish until it is opaque and flakes easily (63°C in the thickest part), and prawns until pink and opaque all the way through.

steps.text: Pound or mince the fish fillet until very fine and sticky, about 3 minutes by hand or 1 minute in a food processor. Work it until it becomes almost a smooth paste.

Mix the tamarind paste with 2 tbsp water. In a bowl, combine the fish paste with the diluted tamarind, coconut milk, palm sugar, garlic, ginger, chillies, spring onions, fish sauce and salt. Mix well with a fork or your hands until the paste is even and aromatic. Taste and adjust salt or tamarind to your liking.
Soften the banana leaves by holding them over a gas flame for a few seconds on each side, or dip them briefly in hot water, until they are pliable. Pat dry.

Lay one banana leaf square on a clean surface. Spoon about 2 tbsp of the fish paste into the centre. Fold the leaf into a triangle or rectangle parcel, then lay it seam-side down on your work surface. Skewer it with a wooden stick through both layers to keep it sealed. Repeat with the remaining leaves and paste, making 8 parcels.

Bring water to a boil in a steamer or a pot with a bamboo steamer basket until steam is rising steadily. Arrange the otak-otak parcels seam-side down in a single layer in the basket, or on a steamer rack standing upright if you prefer (they hold the shape better that way).

Steam for 12 to 15 minutes over boiling water. The otak-otak is ready when the filling is firm and cooked through, the edges should feel set when you press gently, and the banana leaf may brown slightly at the tips.
Remove from the steamer and let cool slightly before serving. Serve warm or at room temperature with rice or as a snack on their own.

notes: Make it vegetarian by leaving out the prawns and cooking the bottle gourd a few minutes longer until very tender.
Can be made ahead and reheated gently; add the prawns fresh when you reheat so they don't toughen.
Food safety:
Fufu is best eaten fresh and hot. If you need to hold it, cover it loosely with foil to keep it warm but not sweating.
You can make fufu ahead and reheat it gently in the microwave with a splash of water, but the texture won't be quite as pillowy.
Green (unripe) plantains are essential, yellow or ripe ones will make it sweet.

steps.text: Put the plantain and cassava in a large pot. Cover with cold water and add the salt. Bring to a boil, then reduce the heat and simmer for 20–25 minutes, until both are very soft and you can easily pierce them with a fork.
Drain well in a colander, then return to the pot (or transfer to a food processor in batches if using one). Mash or process until smooth and uniform, it should be pale, creamy and hold together.

If mashing by hand, use a wooden spoon or potato masher and work in one direction, folding the mixture over itself, until it becomes pillowy. If using a food processor, pulse until you reach a smooth, slightly sticky paste.
Serve hot in a mound on a plate, with your favourite soup or stew on the side for dipping.

notes: Ask your fishmonger to scale and gut the flathead for you if you'd prefer. If you can't find flathead, this works beautifully with any other firm white fish of similar size, snapper, bream or barramundi all take to the same gentle treatment.
Serve with something simple: crushed new potatoes, a green salad, or just good bread to soak up the juices.
Food safety:
Make the caramelised onions a day ahead and refrigerate; reheat gently with the finished soup.
Freeze the soup (without parsley garnish) for up to three months. Thaw overnight in the fridge and reheat slowly on the stove.
Kanpyo keeps for months in a cool cupboard. Opened packages store best in an airtight container.
This dish is equally good served cold the next day. The flavour deepens as it sits.
If you can't find kanpyo, this method works beautifully with other dried vegetables, lotus root or burdock, both softened first.

steps.text: Soak the kanpyo in warm water for 5 minutes until pliable. Drain and rinse gently under cold water, rubbing between your fingers to remove any dust. Cut into 8 cm lengths.
Bring a pot of water to a boil. Add the kanpyo and simmer for 15 to 20 minutes, stirring gently now and then, until the strips are very tender and pale. Drain well.
While the kanpyo cooks, bring the dashi to a simmer in another pot until small bubbles rise at the edges. Add the mirin, soy sauce and a pinch of salt. Taste and adjust.
When the kanpyo is cool enough to handle, gather 4 to 5 strips together and tie loosely in a bundle using another strip of kanpyo, or a softened kombu strip. Make 6 to 8 bundles.
Gently place the bundles into the simmering dashi. Simmer for 10 to 15 minutes, turning once halfway through, until the broth is absorbed and the kanpyo is glossy and tender.
Transfer to a serving dish, spooning any remaining broth over the top. Serve warm or at room temperature.

notes: You can shape these on the skewers several hours ahead and grill just before serving.
Palm sugar gives the traditional caramel edge, but brown sugar works if you can't find it.
The paste is the soul of sate lilit, pounding it by hand rather than processing keeps the texture alive.
Food safety: Cook mince and sausages until no pink remains and the centre reaches 75°C.

steps.text: Pound the garlic, shallot, galangal, turmeric and chilli to a fine paste in a mortar and pestle. Add the salt.
In a bowl, combine the pork mince, spice paste, coconut cream and palm sugar. Mix gently with your hands until just combined.

If using lemongrass, trim each stalk to about 15 cm, keeping the white base. Wet your hands and mould about 2 tbsp of meat around the lower part of each stalk, pressing firmly so it sticks. If using skewers, press the meat firmly onto the skewer in a long shape, leaving 5 cm at the bottom clear.
Heat a grill pan or barbecue to medium-high until hot enough to sizzle when the skewers touch it.
Grill the sate lilit for 12–15 minutes, turning every 3 minutes, until the outside is deeply charred and the meat is cooked through (the juices should run clear).
Let rest for 2 minutes before serving warm with sambal and jasmine rice.

notes: Dirty rice keeps well in the fridge for 3 days and reheats gently with a splash of stock if needed.
Can't find andouille? Any spicy smoked sausage will work, but andouille's got that Cajun soul.
Food safety: Cook chicken and other poultry until the juices run clear and the thickest part reaches 75°C.

steps.text: Heat the oil in a large heavy-bottomed pot over medium-high heat. Brown the sausage until the edges caramelize, about 5 minutes. Remove and set aside.
In the same pot, brown the chicken liver in batches until cooked through (no pink inside), about 4 minutes. Remove and set aside.
Lower the heat to medium. Add the onion, capsicum, and celery, that's your holy trinity, and cook, stirring often, until soft and starting to colour, about 8 minutes.
Stir in the garlic and tomato paste, cooking for 1 minute until fragrant.
Add the rice, stirring constantly to coat in the oil, for 2 minutes.
Pour in the stock, add the cayenne, and bring to a simmer until bubbling. Return the liver and sausage to the pot, stir, and cover.
Cook over low heat until the rice is tender and the liquid is absorbed, about 18 minutes. Don't lift the lid.
Season with salt and black pepper to taste. Scatter the spring onions over the top before serving.

notes: Make a double batch and freeze half in a container; they'll keep for a month and reheat beautifully on the stove.
If you can't find lard, use neutral oil or a little butter, though lard gives them the best flavour.
Serve alongside arepas, white rice, or grilled meat.
Cook pork until it reaches at least 70°C in the thickest part (75°C for mince and sausages).
Make it ahead: Laabda tastes even better the next day. Cool, cover, and refrigerate for up to 3 days, then reheat gently on the stove.
Scale it up: This recipe doubles easily for big family gatherings. Use a larger pot and add 30 minutes to the braising time.
Food safety: Braised beef and lamb cook well past 75°C on the way to tender, so they are safe once soft.

steps.text: Heat the ghee in a large heavy-bottomed pot over medium-high heat. Working in batches, brown the beef on all sides, about 3 minutes per side. Transfer to a plate.
Add the sliced onions to the pot and cook, stirring often, until deep golden and caramelized, about 20 minutes. This takes patience, let them colour properly for the sweetness.
Add the minced garlic and cook for 1 minute until fragrant.
Stir in the cardamom, cinnamon, cloves, turmeric, salt and pepper. Cook for 1 minute.
Add the tomato paste and stir to coat the onions, cooking for 2 minutes.

Return the beef to the pot along with the water and bay leaves. Bring to a simmer, then reduce heat to low, cover, and braise for 2½ to 3 hours, stirring occasionally. The meat is ready when it's very tender and breaks apart easily, and the sauce is rich and thickened.
Taste and adjust seasoning. Serve hot with rice or flatbread.

Char the poblanos directly over a gas flame or under a hot grill, turning with tongs, until the skin is blackened all over, about 8 minutes. Place them in a plastic bag, seal it, and let them steam for 5 minutes.
Peel off the blackened skin under cool running water. Remove the stem and seeds, then chop the poblano flesh into bite-sized pieces.
Heat the oil in a large frying pan over medium heat. Add the onion and cook, stirring, until softened, about 4 minutes. Add the garlic and cook for 1 minute more.
Reduce the heat to low. Add the Oaxaca cheese and cheddar in handfuls, stirring constantly until melted and smooth, about 5 minutes. The cheese should be creamy and flowing.
Fold in the roasted poblano pieces. Taste and season with salt and pepper.
Transfer to a warm serving dish and serve immediately with hot tortilla chips on the side.

notes: Olluco releases starch as it cooks, which naturally thickens the sauce. Don't rush it, the longer you simmer, the creamier it becomes.
Make it ahead: this dish tastes even better the next day. Reheat gently over low heat with a splash of milk or water.

steps.text: Heat the oil in a large pot over medium heat. Add the onion and cook, stirring, until soft and golden, about 5 minutes.
Add the garlic and ají amarillo paste, stirring constantly to combine, about 1 minute. The mixture should be fragrant and bright yellow.
Add the olluco, cumin, salt and pepper. Stir to coat the tubers in the ají mixture, about 2 minutes.
Pour in just enough water to barely cover the olluco, about 300 ml. Bring to a simmer, then reduce heat to medium-low and cover, cooking until the olluco is tender when pierced with a knife.
Cook for 20 minutes, until the olluco is very tender and the liquid has reduced slightly. Stir occasionally to prevent sticking.
Pour in the milk and gently stir. Add the crumbled queso fresco and fold in carefully until it begins to melt into the sauce, about 3 minutes.
Taste and adjust salt and pepper. The sauce should be creamy and the tubers very soft. Serve hot, scattered with coriander if you like.

notes: Use fresh wide rice noodles (from the chilled aisle) for the best texture, they're done the moment they're hot.
The heat matters: your wok needs to be smoking hot when the garlic goes in. This keeps the chicken from stewing.
Add the basil right at the end so it stays bright and fragrant.
Food safety: Cook chicken and other poultry until the juices run clear and the thickest part reaches 75°C.
Tripe is sold cleaned in most butchers, ask them to confirm it's ready to cook. If you find it tough after 30 minutes, keep simmering until it breaks down easily with a fork.
This keeps well in the fridge for 2 days and tastes better reheated the next day.
The chillies can be charred and peeled up to 4 hours ahead; keep them in a covered container in the fridge until you're ready to stuff them.
If you can't find Oaxaca cheese, fresh mozzarella (torn into chunks) or even grated Oaxaca from a package will work, the key is using cheese that melts easily.
The tomato sauce can be made ahead and reheated gently just before serving.
Labskaus is best made with cooked corned beef from a deli or tin. If using homemade, cook it until very tender, then cool before dicing.
Use waxy potatoes like kipfler or baby potatoes; they hold their shape better than floury varieties.
Add a fried egg on top if you'd like the traditional presentation, Anna's Oma always did.

steps.text: Heat the oil in a large pot over medium heat. Add the onion and cook, stirring occasionally, until softened and just beginning to colour, about 5 minutes.
Add the diced potato and corned beef. Stir to combine and cook for 2 minutes, letting the beef warm through.
Pour in the stock and add the bay leaf. Bring to a simmer, then cook uncovered for 12 to 15 minutes, until the potato is tender.
Stir in the chopped herring and the herring brine. Cook for another 2 minutes to warm through and let the flavours meld.
Taste and adjust seasoning with salt and pepper, remember the herring and brine are already salty.
Serve hot in bowls, with dark bread on the side.

notes: Make the batter up to 2 hours ahead and keep it in the fridge. Shape and fry just before serving.
Don't skip drying the chickpeas, it's what gets them crispy. If they're wet, they'll steam instead.

steps.text: Pat the drained chickpeas completely dry with paper towels; this helps them crisp. Mash them roughly in a bowl with a fork, you want some texture, not a smooth paste.
Stir through the onion, garlic, parsley, mint, ground coriander, salt and pepper. Add the flour and water and mix until the mixture holds together when squeezed. Let it rest for 5 minutes.
With damp hands, shape into 12 flat patties about 6 cm across and 1.5 cm thick. Place on a plate.
Heat 60 ml of olive oil in a large heavy-based frying pan over medium-high heat until it shimmers. Working in batches, carefully place 4 fritters into the oil.
Fry for 3 to 4 minutes until deep golden and crispy on the first side, then flip and fry for another 3 minutes until the second side is also crispy. Drain on paper towels.
Repeat with the remaining fritters, adding more oil to the pan as needed.
Serve warm with lemon wedges and extra salt. They're best eaten straight away, while they still crackle.

notes: Make it ahead: braise fully, cool, then refrigerate for up to 2 days. Reheat gently over low heat with a splash of stock.
Swap green olives for kalamata if you prefer, it's richer but still very Tunisian.
Food safety:
Food safety:
Mac salad can be made a few hours ahead and chilled, the flavours improve as it sits.
For a real plate lunch vibe, use a compartment plate. Any firm white rice works; short-grain Japanese-style rice is traditional, but long-grain is just as good.
Prawns cook fast, so watch them carefully. Raw prawns are best, but you can swap in cooked prawns, just heat them through for 1–2 minutes instead.

Food safety: Cook fish until it is opaque and flakes easily (63°C in the thickest part), and prawns until pink and opaque all the way through. Cool any leftover rice quickly and refrigerate it within an hour; reheat it until steaming hot.
Swap the root veg: swede, beetroot or sweet potato all work. Just keep pieces roughly the same size so they cook evenly.
Use bone-in thighs if that's what's in your trolley, just add 5 minutes to the braise time.
Leftovers are even stickier and better the next day. Reheat gently on the stove with a splash of water.
Food safety:
This dish tastes even better the next day. Refrigerate in an airtight container for up to three days, or freeze for a month.
Food safety: Braised beef and lamb cook well past 75°C on the way to tender, so they are safe once soft.

The fermentation time depends on your kitchen temperature: warmer rooms will ferment faster (3 days), cooler ones may take 5 days. Taste the batter after day 3, it should be pleasantly sour, not sharp.
Injera freezes well for up to a month. Layer cooked injera between greaseproof paper, wrap tightly, and thaw at room temperature before serving.
Make injera a day or two before you plan to serve it. It stays soft and slightly chewy when wrapped loosely in a clean cloth.

steps.text: Mix teff flour, water and salt in a large bowl. Stir until you have a smooth, thin batter with no lumps, thinner than pancake batter, about the consistency of single cream. Cover loosely with a clean cloth.

Let the batter ferment at room temperature for 3 to 5 days. It will develop a slightly sour smell and small bubbles will rise to the surface. Stir it down gently each day. You'll know it's ready when it smells pleasantly sour and tastes a little tangy.
After fermentation, stir the batter well. It should still be thin and pourable. If it's too thick, add a little warm water, a tablespoon at a time.
Heat a large non-stick frying pan or crepe pan (about 30 cm across) over medium-high heat. Don't oil it, injera cooks on a dry surface.

Once the pan is hot, pour about 120 ml of batter into the centre. Quickly tilt and swirl the pan so the batter spreads into a thin, even circle that covers the whole base. Work fast, injera sets quickly.

Cook for about 1 to 2 minutes without flipping. The top will start to look spongy and develop small holes. The bottom should be light golden and slightly chewy, not crispy. When the steam stops rising, it's done.
Slide the injera onto a plate. Repeat with the remaining batter.
Stack the finished injera loosely on a plate or cloth to keep them warm and slightly soft.

notes: Make the cashew cream up to 2 days ahead and keep in the fridge; assemble with herbs and walnuts just before serving.
If you don't have raw cashews, use store-bought cashew butter (about 150 g) and skip the soaking step. You'll need a bit less water, start with 60 ml.
Traditionally made with yoghurt; this version is just as creamy, and Layla's family has eaten it both ways for years.
Keeps in the fridge for three days. Reheat gently in a pot over low heat, or microwave in a covered bowl.
Make it a day ahead: the flavour deepens overnight.
Freeze the cooled braised ribs in the sauce for up to three months.
Food safety: Steaks and roasting cuts of beef or lamb can be served pink: about 60°C in the centre is medium-rare, 70°C is well done.

steps.text: Blanch the short ribs: bring a large pot of water to the boil, add the ribs and boil for 3 minutes. Drain and rinse the ribs under cold running water, scrubbing gently to remove any scum. Pat dry.
Heat a heavy-based braising pot or large Dutch oven over medium-high heat. Add 1 tbsp of the sesame oil. Working in batches, brown the ribs on all sides, about 10 minutes total. Transfer to a plate.
Return the pot to medium heat and add the remaining sesame oil. Add the garlic and ginger, stirring for 30 seconds until fragrant.

Return the ribs to the pot. Add the soy sauce, water, honey, spring onions, drained shiitake mushrooms (reserving the soaking liquid) and jujubes. Pour in 100 ml of the mushroom soaking liquid. Bring to a boil, then reduce heat to low, cover, and simmer gently for 1.5 to 2 hours, until the ribs are completely tender and the meat pulls easily from the bone.
Remove the pot from the heat. Discard the spring onions, garlic and ginger pieces (or leave them in if you prefer). Taste and season with salt if needed, the soy sauce will likely be salty enough.
Serve the short ribs hot in shallow bowls with the braising liquid spooned over. Scatter with toasted sesame seeds. Serve with steamed white rice and kimchi on the side.

notes: Kuah lkor is gentler than laksa, if you like more heat, add a sliced green chilli or two to the paste.
The tamarind paste keeps the broth light and stops it feeling too rich; don't skip it.
Food safety: Cook chicken and other poultry until the juices run clear and the thickest part reaches 75°C.

steps.text: Toast the sesame seeds in a heavy-bottomed pan over medium heat, stirring constantly, until fragrant and lightly golden, about 5 minutes. Tip onto a plate.

Pour the honey into the same pan over medium heat. Warm, swirling gently, until it turns a deep amber, about 8 minutes. Don't stir it, just let it happen. You'll know it's ready when it smells toasted and a drop in cold water snaps cleanly.
Remove from heat. Working fast, add the vanilla and salt, then tip in the toasted sesame seeds. Stir hard until everything is coated.
Pour onto a baking tray lined with baking paper, spreading it thin and even with an oiled spatula. Work quickly, it sets fast.
Cool completely at room temperature, about 2 hours. Break into pieces with your hands. That's it, mate.

notes: Fresh fish cakes are best if you can find them at an Asian grocer. Canned work fine too, just drain them well.
The shrimp paste makes this dish. It's pungent and funky on its own, but dissolves into the broth and gives it depth.
If you can't find fresh Vietnamese mint, use extra Thai basil or regular mint, it won't be the same, but it still works.

steps.text: In a small bowl, mash the shrimp paste with a fork until it breaks down. Add 2 tbsp of hot water and stir well until it dissolves into a pungent liquid; set aside.
Heat 1 tbsp oil in a large pot over medium heat. Add the minced garlic and sliced chillies, stirring constantly until fragrant, about 1 minute.
Add the shrimp paste liquid to the pot and stir for another minute, until fragrant, letting the flavour bloom. Pour in the stock and bring to a simmer until bubbling gently.
Add the fish sauce and caster sugar, stirring to dissolve. Taste and adjust, it should be salty, pungent, and slightly sweet. This is Huế food; don't be timid.
Gently slide the fish cake slices into the simmering broth and cook for 5 to 8 minutes until they're heated through and tender.
While the broth cooks, divide the cooked rice vermicelli between four bowls.
Ladle the hot broth and fish cakes over the noodles. Top with fresh Vietnamese mint, coriander, and spring onion. Serve with lime wedges and extra chillies on the side for those who want more heat.

notes: Serve with white rice and farofa (toasted cassava flour) on the side to soak up the sauce.
Any firm white fish works, barramundi, snapper, ling or flathead are all good choices. Avoid delicate fish like flake.
Make ahead: prep the vegetables and fish the day before; cook just before serving so the fish stays tender.
Food safety:
