steps.text: Heat the dendê oil in a large, heavy-bottomed pot over medium-high heat. Add the onion and capsicum, stirring occasionally, until softened and the onion is starting to caramelize, about 8 minutes.
Add the garlic and chilli, stirring constantly for 1 minute until fragrant.
Stir in the tomato paste and cook for 1 minute to deepen the flavour.
Pour in the coconut milk and fish stock, stirring to combine. Bring to a gentle simmer until small bubbles break the surface, then reduce the heat to medium-low.

Carefully add the fish chunks to the pot, season with salt and pepper, and simmer gently for 12 to 15 minutes, until the fish is just cooked through and flakes easily. Do not stir vigorously; gently turn the fish once halfway through.
Taste and adjust seasoning if needed. Serve hot, scattered with fresh coriander and lime wedges on the side.

notes: This freezes brilliantly, make a double batch and freeze the cooled stir-fry in containers for a quick weeknight reheat. Thaw overnight in the fridge and warm in a pan over medium heat.
Use any frozen mixed veg (broccoli, carrot, capsicum, snap peas all work), or what's on special.
Food safety: Cook chicken and other poultry until the juices run clear and the thickest part reaches 75°C.

steps.text: Heat 1 tbsp oil in a large wok or frying pan over high heat. Add the chicken strips and cook, stirring often, until cooked through (no pink inside), about 5 minutes. Transfer to a plate.
Add the remaining oil to the pan. Add the frozen mixed vegetables and stir-fry for 2 minutes until starting to soften.
Pour in the stir-fry sauce and honey, stirring to combine. Return the chicken to the pan and toss everything together until well coated and hot, about 1 minute.
Divide rice or noodles between bowls, top with the stir-fry while the chicken is glossy and cooked through, and garnish with spring onion and sesame seeds if using.

notes: Cime di rapa can be hard to find outside Italian delis, but gai lan (Chinese broccoli) works just as well, it's the same plant, just called by a different name.
Serve with a generous pour of your best olive oil and crusty bread to wipe the bowl.

steps.text: Bring a large pot of salted water to the boil. Add the orecchiette and cook until al dente, about 12 minutes.

While the pasta cooks, heat the olive oil in a large frying pan over medium heat. Add the garlic and chilli, and cook gently for 2–3 minutes, stirring often, until the garlic just turns golden, don't let it burn.

Add the cime di rapa to the pan with a splash of water (about 100 ml) and a pinch of salt. Increase the heat to medium-high and cook, stirring occasionally, until the greens are tender, about 8 minutes.
Reserve 200 ml of the pasta cooking water, then drain the pasta. Add it to the pan with the cime di rapa.
Toss well, adding pasta water a little at a time, until everything is coated in a loose, silky sauce. The starch in the water helps emulsify the oil. Taste and adjust the salt and pepper.
Serve hot, with a scatter of flaky salt if you like, and more chilli on the side for anyone who wants it.

notes: Food safety:

steps.text: Heat the oil in a large shallow pan over medium-high heat. Season the fish pieces with salt and pepper on both sides.
Fry the fish for 2 minutes each side until lightly golden, then remove to a plate.
In the same pan, sauté the garlic until fragrant, about 1 minute. Add the sliced onion and cook, stirring, until soft and translucent, about 4 minutes.
Pour in the soy sauce and vinegar, stirring to combine. Bring to a gentle simmer until small bubbles appear and the sharp vinegar smell has softened.

Return the fish to the pan, nestling the pieces among the onions. Simmer gently for 5–7 minutes, spooning the sauce over the fish occasionally, until the fish is cooked through and flakes easily when tested with a fork.
Taste and adjust the salt if needed. Serve hot with the braising liquid and onions spooned over the fish, alongside steamed white rice.

notes: Siraegi keeps well in the fridge for 3 days and can be served hot, warm or at room temperature.
If you can't find dried radish greens, look for them in Asian markets labelled as 'siraegi' or 'siraegi', they're worth seeking out.
This works best on a gas burner where you can crank the heat. The wok needs to be hot enough that the curry paste caramelises rather than steams.
If you don't have Thai basil, regular basil works, or just serve it plain with rice.
Scale up easily: use 400g chicken for two plates, but keep cooking time about the same, high heat, 8–10 minutes total.
Food safety:

steps.text: Heat your wok or heavy frying pan over high heat until it's smoking hot, about 2 minutes.
Pour in the oil and swirl it around. It should shimmer immediately.
Add the garlic and chillies. Stir for 15 seconds until fragrant.
Add the chicken pieces, breaking them up with your spatula. Let them sit for 30 seconds without moving, you want them to catch colour.
Stir and cook for 2 minutes until the chicken is mostly cooked through and the edges are starting to char.
Add the curry paste, fish sauce and palm sugar. Toss everything together for another 2 minutes. You're looking for the paste to caramelise into the chicken and the whole thing to smell fierce.
Taste and adjust the salt and heat if you need to. The chicken should be cooked through (75°C inside), with charred, sticky edges.
Serve straight onto a plate with jasmine rice and fresh Thai basil if you have it.

notes: For a fully vegan dish, use soy sauce instead of fish sauce and check that your curry paste and coconut milk are vegan-certified.
You can prep all the vegetables ahead of time. Layer them in the pot just before cooking.
Leftovers keep well for 2 days in the fridge. Reheat gently on the stove with a splash of water.

steps.text: Heat the oil in a clay pot (or heavy-bottomed pot) over medium heat. Add the curry paste and sliced garlic, stirring gently until fragrant, about 2 minutes.
Pour in the coconut milk, vegetable stock, fish sauce and palm sugar. Stir well and let it come to a gentle simmer until bubbling lightly and the palm sugar has melted.
Layer the noodles evenly over the curry sauce. Don't stir, just press them down gently so they're submerged.
Layer the potato slices over the noodles, then add the mushrooms, capsicum and bok choy in separate layers on top. Pour any remaining sauce over everything.
Cover the pot and simmer gently for 20 to 25 minutes, until the potatoes are tender and the noodles have absorbed the sauce. Peek at it after 15 minutes, it should smell deeply fragrant.
Gently stir everything together just before serving. Taste and adjust the seasoning. Serve hot, topped with fresh Thai basil and coriander if you have them.

notes: Saltfish needs to be soaked overnight to remove excess salt. If you're short on time, use 400 g fresh white fish fillet instead, add it to the stew in the last 5 minutes of cooking.
Green fig is unripe plantain, boiled until tender. Look for it in Caribbean or Latin markets, or swap for potato or sweet potato.
The stew tastes better the next day. Keep it in the fridge for up to 3 days and reheat gently on the stove.
The batter can be made several hours ahead and chilled.
The apple compote keeps in the fridge for up to 3 days and can be gently reheated.
Food safety: Raw and lightly cooked foods aren't recommended for pregnant women, young children, older people or anyone with a weakened immune system.
The balance of tamarind to palm sugar is personal. Start with equal parts and adjust to taste, some prefer it more sour, others more rounded.
Make the vegetable stock a day ahead if you can; let it chill overnight so any sediment sinks to the bottom, and the broth will be clearer.

steps.text: Bring the vegetable stock to a gentle simmer in a large pot. Stir in the tamarind paste and palm sugar until dissolved, about 2 minutes. Taste and adjust the balance of sour and sweet, it should brighten your tongue but not overwhelm it.
Add the pumpkin slices and simmer for 5 minutes until they are just tender but still hold their shape.
Add the mushrooms and tofu cubes. Simmer gently for 8 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the mushrooms are soft and the tofu has absorbed some of the broth's flavour.
Add the tomato wedges and season with salt and black pepper. Simmer for 2 more minutes until the tomatoes are softened, the tomatoes should be warm but still hold their shape.
Remove from heat and stir through most of the fresh dill and coriander, reserving some for serving. Taste once more and adjust the seasoning if needed.
Ladle into bowls and garnish with the remaining herbs and red chilli slices if using. Serve at once, while the broth is still steaming.

notes: Tepsi galay is best served warm from the dish. If you don't have an ovenproof dish, brown the meat in a frying pan and transfer to a large baking dish before adding the other ingredients.
The okra really does need to go in at the end, if you add it earlier it will break down and make the sauce slimy. Don't stir once the okra is in.
Food safety:
Make it fresh each time, sambal matah is best eaten within an hour of pounding, while the shallots still have bite.
Adjust the heat by using fewer chillies, or add a splash more lime juice if you prefer it sharper than hot.

steps.text: Combine the sliced shallots, chopped bird's eye chillies and sliced garlic in a mortar or bowl.

Using a pestle or the back of a spoon, gently pound to release the oils and aromas, about 1 to 2 minutes, until the ingredients are bruised, glistening and beginning to break down. You want them bruised, not completely crushed.
Stir in the lime juice, neutral oil and salt. Taste and adjust salt or lime to your liking, it should be sharp, hot and bright.
Leave to sit for a few minutes before serving so the flavours marry, then stir through fresh coriander if you like. Serve at room temperature with rice, grilled fish or sate.

Line a fine sieve with cheesecloth or a clean tea towel. Pour the yoghurt into it, add the salt, and stir gently to combine. Tie the corners of the cloth together and hang it over a bowl (or suspend it in the fridge) to drain overnight, or for at least 12 hours, until the whey has stopped dripping. You want all the whey to drip away; the longer it strains, the thicker and more cheese-like the labaneh becomes.

Once drained, the labaneh will be thick and creamy. Scrape it into a bowl and stir it smooth. You can serve it at this point, or for a richer texture and more authentic presentation, roll it into balls about the size of walnuts. Chill them for at least 1 hour so they hold their shape.

Just before serving, arrange the balls on a plate or in a shallow dish. Sprinkle the za'atar evenly over the top, then drizzle generously with olive oil. The za'atar will stick to the oil and stay bright. Serve immediately with warm flatbread or pita for dipping, the bread is how you eat labaneh, never with a spoon alone.
Rinse the sushi rice under cold water until the water runs almost clear. Cook in 360 ml water in a rice cooker or pot, about 15 minutes for a cooker or 20 minutes on the stove with the lid on.

While the rice cooks, bring the dashi, soy sauce, caster sugar, mirin and sake to a gentle simmer. Carefully open each tofu pouch along the folded edge with your fingernail or a small knife, then slide them into the liquid. Poach for 8 to 10 minutes until they absorb the broth and soften, turning halfway. Set aside to cool until you can handle them, about 5 minutes.

As the rice finishes, whisk the rice vinegar, salt and caster sugar together. Turn the hot rice into a shallow bowl and gently fold in the vinegar mixture, using a wooden spatula to cool it as you fold. This takes about 5 minutes. Let it rest while you prepare the filling.
Dice the carrot, daikon and mushroom very finely, about the size of a sesame seed. If you like, blanch them in boiling water for 1 minute, then drain well. This keeps them crisp.
Fold the diced vegetables, pickled ginger if using, sesame seeds, salt and white pepper gently through the cooled rice.

Gently squeeze the tofu pockets to remove any excess broth. Hold one open and, using a small spoon, carefully fill each pocket with a modest amount of rice mixture, it should be gentle and not packed tight. The pocket should be full enough to hold its shape but not bursting.
Arrange the filled pockets, seam-side up, on a plate. Serve at room temperature.

notes: Cassava fries are best eaten fresh and hot. If making ahead, reheat them in a 180°C oven for 5 minutes to restore crispness.
Don't skip soaking the cassava, it removes starch and makes the fries crispier.
Serve with crusty bread to soak up the sauce, or over rice or mash.
Makes great leftovers. Cool and store in the fridge for up to 3 days.
Works just as well in a camp oven at low heat, about 3 hours if the coals are right.
Make this a day ahead if you like, the flavour deepens overnight. Reheat gently on the stove or in a 160°C oven until warmed through.
Native pepper is available from good delis and spice shops, but if you can't find it, use a grind of black pepper instead.
Food safety:

steps.text: Preheat the oven to 160°C. Pat the beef cheeks dry with paper towel, then season with salt and pepper.
Heat the oil in a large heavy-bottomed pot or casserole dish over medium-high heat. Brown the beef cheeks in batches, 3 to 4 minutes each side, until golden. Transfer to a plate.
Add the onions to the pot and cook until just coloured, about 4 minutes. Add the carrots and parsnips and stir for 2 minutes.

Return the beef cheeks to the pot. Pour in the tinned tomatoes and beef stock, and add the bay leaves and thyme. The liquid should mostly cover the beef. Bring to a simmer until gentle bubbles break the surface.
Cover and transfer to the oven. Cook for 3 hours, turning the beef cheeks halfway through, until they are very tender and the meat shreds easily with a fork.

Remove from the oven. Stir through the ground native pepper. Taste and adjust seasoning with salt and pepper. Divide among bowls, spoon the gravy and vegetables over, and finish with a light grind of native pepper.
Serve with mashed potato or crusty bread.

notes: Flaki tastes even better the next day. Make it ahead and reheat gently before serving.
Tripe should be cleaned already when you buy it, but if you have any doubt, rinse it well under cold water and rub gently with salt.
Some Kraków cooks add a little strong mustard or horseradish at the end. It's optional.
This keeps well in the fridge for 2 days and reheats gently, add a splash of milk if it's thickened too much.
Traditionally you'd use the poaching liquid, as this recipe does.

steps.text: Put the smoked haddock in a large saucepan with the milk and bay leaves. Bring gently to a simmer and cook for 8 minutes until the fish is just cooked through. Lift the fish out onto a plate, discard the skin and any bones, and break the flesh into flakes. Keep the milk in the pan.
In a separate pan, melt the butter and cook the chopped onion gently, stirring occasionally, until soft and pale, about 5 minutes.
Add the diced potatoes to the buttered onion and stir to coat. Pour in the reserved milk with the bay leaves, bring to a simmer and cook for about 12 minutes until the potatoes are tender.
Return the flaked haddock to the pan, add the cream and stir gently. Heat through for 2–3 minutes without boiling.
Season with salt and pepper to taste, go easy on the salt as the smoked fish is already quite salty. Serve hot, scattered with fresh parsley if you like.

notes: Make ahead: This actually tastes better the next day. Cool quickly, store in the fridge for up to 3 days, or freeze for up to 2 months. Add a splash of water when you reheat.
Brown lentils hold their shape better than red; French lentils work too. Skip the fancy stuff, everyday brown lentils from the market are perfect.
Best made the day before and reheated, the flavours deepen overnight.
Serve with Swedish mustard, rye bread, and a shot of aquavit if you're so inclined.
Food safety: Cook fresh pork to at least 70°C in the thickest part.

steps.text: Rinse the split peas in cold water and drain. Place the pork, water, and bay leaf in a large pot and bring to a boil until a grey foam rises to the surface. Skim off any foam from the surface.
Add the split peas, onions, carrots, and celery. Stir in the peppercorns and salt.
Reduce the heat to low and simmer, partially covered, for about 2 hours, stirring occasionally. The peas should break down into the broth and the pork should be very tender.
Taste and adjust seasoning with salt as needed. Serve hot in bowls with rye bread and Swedish mustard on the side.

notes: Keep this in an airtight container in the fridge for up to 4 days, it reheats gently and actually improves as the flavours settle. Make it in bulk and freeze portions.
If you prefer less sweetness, use just 1 tbsp golden syrup, or substitute a splash of apple juice instead.
Halwa keeps in an airtight container for 3–4 days. You can reheat it gently in a pan with a splash of water if it dries out.
The toasting of the semolina is important, it takes time but the flavour change is worth it. Don't rush it.

steps.text: Heat the ghee in a large, heavy-based saucepan over medium heat. Add the semolina and stir constantly, breaking up any lumps. Toast for 8–10 minutes, stirring often, until the semolina is golden and smells nutty.
Add the crushed cardamom pods and salt, stirring for 30 seconds to release the flavour.
Carefully pour in the water, it will bubble, and stir constantly to combine. The mixture will be thick and pasty.
Add the caster sugar and stir until it dissolves completely into the semolina mixture, about 2 minutes.
Remove from the heat and fold through most of the almonds and raisins, reserving some for the top.
Spoon the halwa into a serving dish and smooth the surface. Scatter the remaining almonds and raisins over the top.
Let it cool to warm, then serve. It sets as it cools but stays soft inside.

notes: Make this ahead: gumbo tastes even better the next day. Reheat gently on the stove, and stir in the filé powder just before serving.
Food safety: Cook chicken and other poultry until the juices run clear and the thickest part reaches 75°C.

steps.text: Heat the oil in a large, heavy-bottomed pot over medium heat. Add the flour slowly, stirring constantly with a wooden spoon. Keep stirring, don't walk away, until the roux is deep chocolate brown, about 30 to 40 minutes. It'll go from light tan to darker shades; when it smells nutty and toasted, you're close.
Add the onion, celery and capsicum to the roux. Stir well and cook, stirring often, until the vegetables are soft and golden, about 8 minutes.
Add the chicken and sausage. Stir to coat with roux, and cook for 5 minutes.
Pour in the stock slowly, stirring constantly until smooth to break up any lumps. Add the bay leaf, thyme and cayenne. Bring to a simmer, then reduce heat to low.
Simmer gently, uncovered, for about 40 minutes, until the chicken is cooked through and the flavours have melded. Skim any fat from the surface if you like.
Taste and season with salt and pepper. Remove from heat and stir in the filé powder until smooth. Don't boil after adding filé, or it gets stringy.
Serve in bowls over white rice, scattered with spring onion if you like.

notes: Tastes even better the next day. Reheat gently on the stove.
Traditional Colombian comfort food: serve with white rice and avocado on the side.
Food safety:
Make a bigger batch of ful and store it in the fridge for 3 days; reheat gently with a splash of water.
Use tinned or cooked dried fava beans, the tinned kind saves time and money if you're cooking on a weeknight.
Food safety: Raw and lightly cooked foods aren't recommended for pregnant women, young children, older people or anyone with a weakened immune system.

steps.text: Soak the pine nuts in warm water for 15 minutes, then drain well.

In a bowl, combine the drained pine nuts, shiitake, carrot, potato, and spring onion whites. Stir in the minced ginger, sesame oil, soy sauce, rice vinegar and a pinch of salt until everything is evenly coated.
Prepare a steamer by bringing water to a simmer in a pot until steam is rising steadily. Transfer the pine nut mixture to a heatproof bowl or steaming plate that fits in your steamer.
Steam over simmering water for 20 to 25 minutes, until the potato is tender and the pine nuts have softened but still hold their shape.
Remove from the steamer and let cool to room temperature. Scatter the spring onion greens and toasted sesame seeds over the top.
Serve at room temperature in small bowls.

notes: Make sure to press the tofu well, this is key to getting it crispy. Soft tofu won't work; stick with extra-firm.
You can prep the tofu cutlets and coat them hours ahead, then fry just before serving.
Food safety: Raw and lightly cooked foods aren't recommended for pregnant women, young children, older people or anyone with a weakened immune system.

steps.text: Press the tofu between kitchen towels or in a tofu press for at least 15 minutes to remove excess moisture.
Slice the pressed tofu block in half lengthways, then slice each half in half again to create two thick, flat cutlets. Pat dry with paper towels.
Set up three shallow bowls: one with plain flour, one with beaten egg, and one with panko breadcrumbs.
Season the tofu cutlets lightly with salt and pepper on both sides.
Coat each cutlet in flour, shaking off excess, then dip in egg, then press firmly into panko until completely coated on both sides.
Heat about 1 cm of neutral oil in a large frying pan over medium-high heat until shimmering.

Once the oil is hot, carefully place the tofu cutlets in the pan and fry for 3–4 minutes per side, until the panko is golden brown and crispy. Don't move them around too much, let them sit so they get a good crust.
Transfer to a plate lined with paper towels to drain any excess oil.
Drizzle tonkatsu sauce generously over the top of each cutlet and serve immediately with pickled cabbage and steamed white rice on the side.

notes: Make the rolls up to 3 hours ahead and keep them covered with a damp cloth at room temperature. Steam just before serving.
If you don't have a non-stick crêpe pan, use a small non-stick frying pan and work quickly, the batter sets fast.

Bánh cuốn freezes well before steaming: place rolls on a tray lined with baking paper, freeze until firm, then pack in an airtight container for up to 1 month. Steam straight from frozen, adding 2 to 3 minutes to the cooking time.
Food safety: Cook mince and sausages until no pink remains and the centre reaches 75°C.
Escabeche is even better the day after you make it, the fish stays moist and the flavours marry beautifully. Cover and keep in the fridge for up to 3 days.
If you can't find barramundi or flathead, any firm white fish works well. Avoid delicate fish like basa.
This is a dish built for sharing. Take it out of the fridge 20 minutes before serving to let the oil loosen up a bit.
Food safety: Cook fish until it is opaque and flakes easily (63°C in the thickest part), and prawns until pink and opaque all the way through.
Andouillettes are sold fresh at good butchers and some French delis. If you can't find them, they're not worth substituting, save this recipe for when you do.
The success of the dish depends on getting the sausage skin crispy in the pan. Don't crowd them, and don't fidget with them while they cook.
Serve with mustard-roasted potatoes or a simple green salad to cut through the richness.
Cook chicken until it reaches 75°C in the thickest part and the juices run clear.
Food safety:
Make the ragù on Sunday to let the flavours deepen overnight. You'll have leftovers, which freeze well.
If you don't have fresh mozzarella, use fior di latte or even a cube of cold butter instead.
Arancini can be coated and refrigerated for up to 12 hours before frying. This actually helps them hold their shape better.
Cook mince and sausages until they reach 75°C in the centre, with no pink left.
Food safety: Raw and lightly cooked foods aren't recommended for pregnant women, young children, older people or anyone with a weakened immune system.

steps.text: Make the ragù: heat oil in a heavy-based pot, add diced onion and cook gently until soft, about 5 minutes. Add beef and pork mince, stirring to break it up, until browned, about 8 minutes. Pour in wine and let it bubble away for 2 minutes. Add crushed tomatoes, season with salt and pepper, then lower heat and simmer gently, uncovered, for at least 30 minutes (longer is better). The ragù should be thick and the flavours rich. Let cool completely.

Make the risotto: bring stock to a gentle simmer in a separate pot and keep it there. In a heavy-based pan, melt butter over medium heat, add diced onion and cook until soft and golden, about 5 minutes. Add rice and stir constantly for 1 minute until the grains are coated and lightly toasted. Pour in wine and stir until absorbed.

Add stock one ladleful at a time, stirring often, letting each addition absorb before adding the next. After about 18 minutes, the rice should be creamy and just tender. Stir in parmesan and season with salt and pepper. Spread the risotto on a large tray to cool to room temperature, about 20 minutes.

Once risotto is cool, mix in 200 g (about half) of the ragù and all the thawed peas. Wet your hands and shape the mixture into 12 balls, each about the size of a golf ball. Make an indent in the centre of each ball with your thumb, press in a cube of mozzarella and a generous pinch of the remaining ragù, then seal the opening and reshape into a smooth ball. This takes patience but it's what keeps the filling hidden inside.

Set up three shallow bowls: one with beaten eggs, one with panko breadcrumbs, and one empty. Roll each arancino ball in egg, then roll in breadcrumbs until well coated. Place on a tray and chill for at least 30 minutes (or up to 12 hours) so the coating sets firmly.

Heat oil in a deep, heavy-based pot or deep-fryer to 170°C. If you don't have a thermometer, test with a wooden spoon handle: it should sizzle gently at the edge of the oil. Fry arancini in batches of 3–4, turning occasionally, for 3–4 minutes until golden brown all over. Don't crowd the pan. Remove with a slotted spoon and drain on paper towel.
Serve warm, while the mozzarella inside is still soft and the outside is crispy. Arancini are best eaten fresh but are still good at room temperature.
Drain and pat the salt cod dry. Cut into 4 thick pieces, about 150 g each.

Heat 100 ml olive oil in a wide, shallow earthenware dish (cazuela) or heavy-based pan over very low heat. Add the sliced garlic and red chilli (if using). Cook gently, stirring, until the garlic is fragrant and just beginning to soften, about 2 minutes. Don't let it brown.

Lay the salt cod pieces skin-side up in the warm oil. The oil should just barely cover them, add a little more if needed. Keep the heat very low and poach gently, uncovered, for 5–7 minutes. The cod will begin to flake at the edges and turn opaque.

Now the critical part: remove the pan from the heat and let it cool for 1 minute. Using a wooden spoon or your wrist in a smooth, circular motion, begin tilting and rotating the pan while gently stirring the cod in the oil. The gelatine from the fish will start to emulsify the oil into a creamy sauce.

Return the pan to very low heat and continue this tilting and stirring motion. Gradually add the remaining 100 ml olive oil in a thin stream while rotating and tilting, as if you were making a sauce. The emulsion builds slowly, this is the pil-pil. Keep going for 8–10 minutes until the sauce is pale, silky and creamy.
Taste and season with salt if needed. Serve in the pan, spooning the creamy pil-pil sauce over the cod. Scatter with fresh parsley if you like.

notes: Baklava keeps in an airtight container for up to 5 days. The pastry stays crisp and the flavours deepen.
Use room-temperature syrup on hot baklava, not the other way around, this is what makes it properly absorb.
Pistachios are traditional, but walnuts or almonds work if that's what you have. Just chop them fine.

steps.text: Make the syrup first: combine water, sugar, cinnamon stick, cloves and lemon slice in a saucepan. Bring to a boil, then reduce heat and simmer for 10 minutes. Remove from heat, stir in honey, and set aside to cool to room temperature.
Preheat oven to 175°C. Mix pistachios with caster sugar and ground cinnamon in a bowl.
Brush a 33 x 23 cm baking dish generously with melted butter. Lay down one yufka sheet and brush with butter. Repeat until you have 6 layers, this is your base.
Spread a thin, even layer of pistachio mixture over the top sheet. Layer 2 more yufka sheets on top, brushing each with butter.
Repeat the pistachio layer and 2 more yufka sheets. Keep going until you've used most of your pistachios, finishing with at least 6 yufka sheets on top, each brushed with butter.
Using a sharp knife, cut the baklava into diamond or triangular pieces all the way through to the base, about 20 pieces total. Pour any remaining melted butter over the top.
Bake for 35 to 40 minutes, until golden brown and the edges are darker. You'll hear it starting to crisp as it cools.
Remove from oven and immediately pour the room-temperature syrup slowly and evenly over the hot baklava. It will sizzle and soak in. Let cool completely in the pan, at least 2 hours, before serving.

notes: Cook mince and sausages until they reach 75°C in the centre, with no pink left.
Food safety: Raw and lightly cooked foods aren't recommended for pregnant women, young children, older people or anyone with a weakened immune system.
The noodle cakes can be formed up to 2 hours ahead; stack them between sheets of baking paper and refrigerate. Grill straight from the fridge, adding 1–2 minutes per side.
If your grill pan is small, grill the components in batches and keep them warm on a plate in a low oven (120°C) while you finish cooking.
The pork belly will spit as the fat renders, keep the heat steady and watch closely after the 2-minute mark to avoid burning.
Food safety: Cook fresh pork to at least 70°C in the thickest part.

steps.text: Pour chicken stock into a saucepan and bring to a simmer. Add rice vermicelli and cook until just tender, about 3 minutes, stirring occasionally. The noodles will be soft and may break slightly, this is right. Drain in a fine sieve and spread on a tray to cool to room temperature, about 10 minutes.
While the noodles cool, make the dipping sauce: stir fish sauce, lime juice and sugar together in a small bowl until the sugar dissolves. Set aside.

Divide the cooled noodles into 8 equal portions. Take one portion and press it gently on an oiled piece of baking paper, forming a flat rectangle about 15 cm × 10 cm and roughly 1 cm thick. Do not press too hard or the cake will become dense. Repeat with the remaining noodle portions.
Heat a large grill pan or outdoor grill to medium-high heat until very hot and a drop of water sizzles on contact. Brush the grill grates lightly with oil.

Carefully transfer one noodle cake to the hot grill (start with the baking paper if using, then slide it away). Grill until the underside is golden and charred in patches, about 3–4 minutes. Flip carefully and grill the other side until golden and crispy, another 2–3 minutes. Transfer to a warm plate. Repeat with the remaining noodle cakes.

On the same grill or a separate pan at medium-high heat, grill the pork belly slices for 2–3 minutes per side until the fat has rendered and the edges are crisp and caramelised. The pork should be cooked through with no pink remaining. Transfer to a warm plate.
Grill the prawns over medium-high heat for 1–2 minutes per side until they are opaque throughout and have a light char. Transfer to a warm plate.

Arrange one noodle cake on each serving plate. Tear or arrange the grilled pork belly and prawns over the top. Garnish with fresh coriander if using and serve immediately with lime wedges and the fish sauce dipping sauce on the side.

notes: Make the fish sauce mayo and prepare the pickled daikon up to a day ahead; toast the baguette and cook the pork just before eating.
The pork can marinate for up to 2 hours in the fridge for deeper flavour, but 15 minutes is enough for a quick lunch.
If you can't find pickled daikon, use pickled mustard greens or a mix of pickled vegetables, the acid and brightness matter more than the exact vegetable.
Cook pork until it reaches at least 70°C in the thickest part (75°C for mince and sausages).
Food safety:

steps.text: Mix fish sauce, palm sugar, garlic, lemongrass and ground coriander in a bowl. Add the pork slices and toss to coat. Let sit for at least 15 minutes (or up to 2 hours in the fridge).
Combine mayonnaise, fish sauce and lime juice in a small bowl, stirring until smooth. Taste and adjust seasoning.

Heat a large frying pan or grill pan over high heat until it's smoking hot. Working in batches if needed, cook the pork until the edges are charred and caramelised, about 2–3 minutes per side. Don't move the pieces around, let them sit so they get a dark, crusty exterior. Set aside on a plate.
Lightly toast the baguette cut-side down in the same hot pan for about 1 minute, until golden and crispy.

Spread the fish sauce mayo on the cut side of each baguette. Layer the charred pork, then pickled daikon, fresh coriander and chilli. Season with salt and pepper. Serve immediately while the bread is still warm.

notes: Slice the beef when it's partially frozen (about 30 minutes in the freezer) for cleaner, thinner cuts.
This is best served immediately. The beef toughens if it sits in the wok too long, aim for 2 minutes total cooking time from wok to plate.
If you can't find fermented black beans (douchi), use 2 tbsp more oyster sauce and a pinch of extra salt, though it won't be quite the same dish.
Food safety: Steaks and roasting cuts of beef or lamb can be served pink: about 60°C in the centre is medium-rare, 70°C is well done.

steps.text: Slice the beef thinly against the grain and set aside. Rinse the black beans, drain well, and chop roughly. Slice the garlic and chilli.
Heat the wok over high heat until smoking, about 2 minutes. Add 1 tbsp oil, swirl to coat.
Working quickly, add half the beef and let it sit for 30 seconds without stirring, this helps it catch colour. Toss for 30 seconds, then transfer to a plate. Repeat with the remaining oil and beef.
Return the wok to high heat. Add the garlic and chilli, toss for 10 seconds until fragrant. Add the black beans, toss for another 10 seconds.
Return all the beef to the wok with the oyster sauce and sesame oil. Toss everything together for 30 seconds, until coated and heated through.
Serve immediately over steamed rice, scattered with spring onion.

notes: Make the broth a day ahead for deeper flavour; reheat gently and add the sausage and noodles to serve.
The blood sausage is traditional, but if you can't find it, add extra beef shin or pork instead.
Central Vietnamese bún bò is spicier than northern versions, add more chillies to your bowl to taste.
Food safety: Braised beef and lamb cook well past 75°C on the way to tender, so they are safe once soft.
Use only the freshest sashimi-grade fish. Ask your fishmonger for corvina or snapper that's been kept for raw preparation.
The ceviche is at its best eaten within 30 minutes of mixing, the acid continues to work and the texture gets softer the longer it sits.
Make the ají amarillo paste fresh if you can find the chillies; if using paste from a jar, start with 3 tbsp and adjust to taste.

The fish here is eaten raw or only cured in citrus. Buy sashimi-grade fish from a fishmonger, keep it cold and eat it the same day; skip it for anyone pregnant, very young, elderly or with low immunity.
Food safety: Raw and lightly cooked foods aren't recommended for pregnant women, young children, older people or anyone with a weakened immune system.

steps.text: Soak the sliced red onion in salt water (about 1 tsp salt per 250 ml water) while you prepare the fish. This takes the edge off the raw onion and cures it slightly, about 5 minutes.
Blend the ají amarillo with the garlic clove and 2 tbsp of the fresh lime juice until smooth. Pass through a fine sieve if you want a completely silky sauce.

Put the fish cubes in a glass or ceramic bowl. Add the ají amarillo paste, the remaining lime juice, and a pinch of salt. Stir gently to coat all the fish. Let sit for 10–15 minutes, the lime juice will turn the fish opaque and firm. Taste and adjust salt.
Drain the cured red onion and gently fold it into the ceviche just before serving, along with any juice from soaking.

Serve in chilled bowls with fresh coriander and toasted corn kernels scattered over the top. Eat while the ceviche is at its brightest, don't leave it sitting or the acid will keep breaking down the fish.

notes: The noodles need to be fresh and thick (kway teow), sold in the refrigerated section, they're usually stuck together in a slab. If you can only find thin dried rice noodles, use them, but fresh ones give you that lovely charred edge.
The heat and speed are everything here. Once you start cooking, don't stop stirring. A slow char koay teow is a sad char koay teow.
Cockles are traditional, use fresh ones from the fishmonger if you can find them, or tinned ones from the Asian aisle. If you really can't find them, use more prawns instead.
Food safety:

steps.text: Set a large wok over high heat until it's very hot, you'll feel the heat rise from it. Add 1 tbsp of the oil and swirl to coat.

Push the noodles into the wok. They'll clump at first, but keep them moving with your spatula, breaking them apart, until they're loosened and just beginning to brown at the edges, about 2 minutes. Push everything to the side of the wok.
Add the remaining oil to the empty side. Crack in the eggs and scramble them quickly with the back of your spatula until just set, then mix them through the noodles.

Push everything to the side again. Add the garlic to the empty spot and cook, stirring constantly, until fragrant, about 20 seconds. Then add the prawns and cockles, tossing them with the garlic for 1 minute until the prawns turn pink and opaque.
Add the soy sauce, dark soy sauce and oyster sauce, tossing everything together. The noodles will darken and smell wonderful, this takes about 1 minute.
Add the bean sprouts and spring onions, tossing for another 30 seconds. If using fresh chilli, toss that through now.
Taste and add more soy sauce if you need it. Divide between bowls and serve straight away, while it's still hot and the edges are a bit charred.

notes: Make this the day before and reheat gently on the stove; the flavours deepen overnight.
Whole green chillies stay mild if you don't break them open; remove them before serving if you prefer no heat.
Duck makes this special, but chicken thighs work if duck is hard to find. Reduce the cook time to 45 minutes.
Food safety: Cook chicken and other poultry until the juices run clear and the thickest part reaches 75°C.
Make ahead: Roll the dolma up to 1 day ahead and store in the fridge. Cook just before serving.
Room temperature: These are just as good served at room temperature the next day, making them perfect for packed lunches.
Cook mince and sausages until they reach 75°C in the centre, with no pink left.
Food safety:
Make ahead: prepare the dolma up to the end of step 3, then cover and refrigerate for up to 24 hours before cooking.
Swap the beef for lamb mince for a richer flavour, which some prefer.
Cook mince and sausages until they reach 75°C in the centre, with no pink left.
Food safety:
Make the hummus up to a day ahead; store it covered in the fridge and bring to room temperature before serving.
Toast your own pine nuts in a dry pan over medium heat for 2–3 minutes if you have time, it makes a real difference.
This is just as good made with tinned chickpeas as it would be with soaked dried ones.
You can prep the meat sauce ahead and reheat it just before assembling.
If you don't have a deep fryer, use a deep heavy-based pan with at least 8 cm of oil. Use a thermometer to check the temperature.
Some Cape Town versions add sliced cheese or a fried egg, feel free to customize.
Cook mince and sausages until they reach 75°C in the centre, with no pink left.
Food safety:
Holubtsi freeze beautifully. Cool them in their sauce, then freeze in an airtight container for up to three months. Reheat gently in a 160°C oven, covered, for about 30 minutes.
If you can't find buckwheat groats, use cooked white rice or pearl barley instead.
The dish tastes even better the next day, once the flavours have settled together.
Cook mince and sausages until they reach 75°C in the centre, with no pink left.
Food safety: Raw and lightly cooked foods aren't recommended for pregnant women, young children, older people or anyone with a weakened immune system.

steps.text: Bring a large pot of salted water to the boil. Carefully remove the core from the cabbage with a sharp knife, then place the whole cabbage in the boiling water. After 8–10 minutes, gently peel away the softened outer leaves and set aside on a clean kitchen towel. Repeat until you have about 12 large leaves; reserve any remaining cabbage, finely shredded.

While the cabbage cools, heat 1 tbsp oil in a frying pan over medium heat. Cook the onion until soft, about 5 minutes, then add the garlic and cook for 1 minute more. Remove from heat and let cool slightly. In a large bowl, combine the cooled onion and garlic with the beef mince, buckwheat, egg, salt and pepper. Mix gently until just combined, don't overwork it.

Lay a cabbage leaf on a clean surface. Place about 2 tbsp of the filling near the base of the leaf, fold the sides in, then roll away from you into a tight parcel. Repeat with the remaining leaves and filling.

Heat the remaining 1 tbsp oil in a large heavy-based pan over medium-high heat. Arrange the cabbage rolls seam-side down in a single layer (work in batches if needed). Cook for 2–3 minutes until golden on the base, then turn carefully and cook for another 2 minutes. Remove and set aside on a plate.

In the same pan, stir together the tomato paste and cook for 1 minute. Add the crushed tomatoes and beef stock, scraping up any brown bits from the base of the pan. Add the caraway seeds if using, and season with salt and pepper. Scatter the reserved shredded cabbage over the base of the pan.

Return the cabbage rolls to the pan, nestling them into the sauce, seam-side down. Bring to a gentle simmer, then reduce heat to low. Cover and braise for 60–70 minutes, until the rolls are tender and the sauce is rich and glossy. Serve warm with a generous dollop of sour cream.

notes: Ilish, hilsa fish, is prized for its soft, buttery flesh and its brief monsoon season. If hilsa is impossible to find, use another oily river fish such as Indian salmon or mackerel, though the dish will be subtly different.
The mustard oil is not negotiable. It is the backbone of this dish. Do not substitute.
Serve with steamed rice to catch every drop of the broth.

steps.text: Heat the mustard oil in a heavy-bottomed pan over medium heat until it just begins to smoke. This is essential: the pungency mellows into warmth.
Add the nigella seeds and let them crackle for a few seconds until fragrant, about 30 seconds.
Stir in the turmeric and cook for a few seconds, until fragrant, to release its colour and flavour into the oil.
Carefully arrange the fish pieces in the pan. They will sizzle. Let them sit undisturbed for 2 minutes on each side so the flesh firms gently.
Add the water and green chillies. Bring to a gentle simmer, until small bubbles break the surface. Add salt.

Cover and cook over low heat for about 15 minutes, until the fish is cooked through and flakes easily when tested, and the broth has begun to amalgamate with the oil and turmeric. Turn the thicker pieces halfway through.
Taste and adjust salt if needed. Serve hot, with rice. The broth is as important as the fish.

notes: Food safety: Cook chicken and other poultry until the juices run clear and the thickest part reaches 75°C.

steps.text: Heat the oil in a large pot or deep frying pan over medium-high heat. Add the chicken pieces, skin-side down, and cook for 3 to 4 minutes until the skin is golden. Flip and cook for another 2 to 3 minutes on the other side. Remove and set aside.
Add the onion, potato and carrot to the pot. Stir and cook for 3 to 4 minutes until the vegetables are lightly browned.
Return the chicken to the pot and add the water, bringing to a simmer. Cover and cook for 15 to 20 minutes until the potatoes are tender and the chicken is cooked through.

Break the curry roux into chunks and stir into the pot until dissolved. Simmer, uncovered, for 3 to 5 minutes, stirring often, until the sauce thickens slightly. Taste and add salt if needed. Serve over steamed rice.

notes: Sour cream or Greek yoghurt to serve is traditional.
The rolls can be assembled up to a day ahead, wrapped in plastic, and refrigerated. Bring to room temperature before adding the broth and baking.
Leftovers keep well for 3 days in the fridge and reheat gently in a low oven.
Cook mince and sausages until they reach 75°C in the centre, with no pink left.
Food safety: Raw and lightly cooked foods aren't recommended for pregnant women, young children, older people or anyone with a weakened immune system.
The khoresh tastes better the next day. Make it ahead and reheat gently before serving.
If you can't find fresh rhubarb, use frozen; no need to thaw. The stew will be slightly thinner and more sour.
The tahdig is forgiving. If it burns black, you've learned something for next time. If it doesn't form at all, the stew is still worth eating.
Food safety: Braised beef and lamb cook well past 75°C on the way to tender, so they are safe once soft.

steps.text: Heat 3 tbsp oil in a large heavy pot over medium-high heat. Working in batches, brown the lamb on all sides, about 8 minutes total. Set aside.
Add the onion to the same pot and cook, stirring, until soft and golden, about 8 minutes. Stir in the turmeric and cook for 1 minute until fragrant.
Return the lamb to the pot. Add the tomato paste and stir to coat. Pour in the stock, bring to a simmer, then reduce heat to low. Cover and cook for 45 minutes, stirring occasionally.

Add the rhubarb pieces and season with salt and pepper. Continue to simmer, covered, for another 30 minutes. The rhubarb should soften and break down slightly, and the lamb should be tender. The stew will taste sharp and rich. Taste and adjust seasoning.

While the stew cooks, prepare the rice. Rinse the basmati rice in a sieve under cold running water until the water runs clear. Bring 1 litre of salted water to a boil in a separate pot. Add the rice and stir gently. Boil for about 10 minutes, until the rice is just tender but still has a slight bite. Drain well.

Return the drained rice to the pot. Drizzle 2 tbsp of oil or melted butter over the rice and gently fold it in. Make a well in the centre of the rice. Mix the yoghurt (if using) with 1 tbsp oil and spread on the bottom of a small bowl or saucer to place in the well, this helps the tahdig form. Cover the pot tightly with foil, then place the lid on top.

Cook over medium heat for 8 to 10 minutes. You should hear a gentle sizzle and smell the toasted rice. This is the tahdig forming. Lower the heat to the lowest setting and cook for another 10 minutes.
To serve, spoon the rice onto a platter, breaking up the tahdig gently from the bottom of the pot and scattering it over the top. Pour the khoresh over and around the rice. Serve hot.

notes: Kina is best eaten fresh and raw, buy it the day you plan to cook it. Your fishmonger can crack it open for you.
Rēwena is a traditional Māori sourdough made with a rewena starter (potato ferment). If you can't find it, look for it at a good bakery or make your own.
This is kai moana at its finest, respect the kai and don't overthink it.

steps.text: Toast the rēwena bread until golden and crisp on both sides, about 3–4 minutes.
Divide the toasted bread between two plates.
Spoon the fresh kina roe evenly over each slice of toast, which should be golden and crisp.
Season lightly with salt.
Serve immediately with lemon wedges on the side to squeeze over.

notes: Make the honey syrup up to 2 hours ahead and reheat gently before serving.
Use a good white cheese, feta works, but halloumi won't melt as much. Some people use a mix.
Künefe is best eaten warm and straight away, when the pastry is still crispy.

steps.text: Make the honey syrup first so it's ready to pour hot. In a small saucepan, combine the honey, water, lemon juice and cinnamon stick. Bring to a simmer over medium heat until the syrup is bubbling and slightly thickened, then remove from the heat and let it cool slightly while you prepare the pastry.
Preheat the oven to 190°C. Gently separate the kataifi pastry strands, they'll come apart easily if you loosen them with your fingers.
Pour a thin layer of melted butter into a round baking dish about 20 cm across. Spread half the kataifi strands evenly over the base, pressing gently to form a layer. Drizzle with more butter.
Scatter the crumbled cheese and walnuts over the pastry, leaving a small border around the edges.
Layer the remaining kataifi strands on top, press down gently, and pour the rest of the melted butter evenly over everything. Bake for 20 to 25 minutes, until the pastry is deep golden and crispy.

Remove from the oven and immediately pour the hot honey syrup all over the künefe. It will sizzle and soak into the pastry. Scatter the pistachios on top if using, and serve right away with plenty of napkins.

notes: Leftover soup keeps for 3 days in the fridge. Reheat gently with a splash of water to loosen.
You can use any lentils you've got, red lentils will make it even creamier but break down faster, so check it at 20 minutes.
Cook chicken until it reaches 75°C in the thickest part and the juices run clear.
This mole keeps in the fridge for up to 5 days and freezes beautifully for up to 3 months. Make it ahead, it tastes better the next day.
Use the mole with poached chicken, or pour it over enchiladas, turkey or meatballs. A little mole goes a long way.
Cook chicken until it reaches 75°C in the thickest part and the juices run clear.

steps.text: Heat 2 tbsp oil in a large, heavy pot over medium heat. Toast the cinnamon stick, cloves and coriander seeds until fragrant, about 1 minute. Add the deseeded chillies, a few at a time, pressing them gently against the bottom of the pot for a few seconds until they release their aroma. Do not burn them. Remove to a bowl.
In the same pot, add 2 tbsp oil. Cook the garlic and onion over medium heat, stirring often, until soft and golden, about 8 minutes.
Meanwhile, soak the toasted chillies in 500 ml hot water for 10 minutes until very soft. Strain, reserving all the soaking liquid.
Add the soaked chillies, raisins, almonds, sesame seeds and torn tortilla to the pot with the garlic and onion. Stir to combine and cook for 3 minutes.

Working in batches, transfer the mixture to a blender with 250 ml of the reserved chilli soaking liquid. Blend until completely smooth. Pour through a fine sieve into a clean pot, pressing with the back of a spoon to extract all the mole.

Add the remaining reserved soaking liquid (about 250 ml) to the strained mole and stir to combine. Place over medium-low heat and simmer, stirring often, for 20 minutes. The mole should be thick but pourable.

Warm the chicken stock in a separate pot. Add 250 ml of the warm stock to the mole and stir well. Continue simmering, stirring often, for 15 minutes. Add the remaining stock, a little at a time, until you reach the consistency you want, it should coat the back of a spoon but flow slowly.

Reduce the heat to very low. Add the chocolate and the remaining 2 tbsp oil, stirring constantly until the chocolate is completely melted and incorporated. Taste and add salt as needed. Keep warm until you're ready to serve.
Serve the mole poured over cooked chicken, rice or with warm tortillas. Sprinkle with the extra sesame seeds.

notes: Keeps well in the fridge for 3 days, or freezes beautifully in portions for up to a month, perfect for reheating before a shift.
If you can't find fenugreek seeds, just use a touch more cumin instead.
Serve with rice, or tear up some bread to dip in.
Cook chicken until it reaches 75°C in the thickest part and the juices run clear.
Nihari is best made a day ahead: cool completely, refrigerate overnight, and reheat gently before serving. The flavour deepens and the fat layer keeps the meat moist.
For a thicker gravy, mix cornflour with a little water and stir in during the last 15 minutes of cooking.
If you prefer lamb, use lamb shoulder instead of beef and reduce cooking time to 90 minutes.
Food safety: Braised beef and lamb cook well past 75°C on the way to tender, so they are safe once soft.
If you can't find fresh okra, frozen okra works fine, add it straight to the curry without thawing, though it'll break down a bit more.

Japanese curry paste comes in tubes or blocks from Asian grocers and many supermarkets now. If you can't find it, use 2 tbsp curry powder mixed with 1 tbsp tomato paste and a little water to make a paste.
Food safety: Raw and lightly cooked foods aren't recommended for pregnant women, young children, older people or anyone with a weakened immune system.
The sauce is crucial to the QQ texture, it creates that custard centre while the high heat makes the edges crisp. Use tapioca starch if you can find it, it gives better texture than cornflour.
Have all ingredients ready before you start cooking; this is a fast dish once the pan is hot.
Serve immediately. The magic is eating it right away when the edges are still crackling.
This uses raw or lightly cooked egg. Use fresh, clean, uncracked eggs (pasteurised if you can get them), keep it cold, and skip it for anyone pregnant, very young, elderly or with low immunity.
Food safety: Raw and lightly cooked foods aren't recommended for pregnant women, young children, older people or anyone with a weakened immune system.

steps.text: Heat a non-stick or cast iron pan over high heat until very hot, about 2 minutes. The pan should be smoking slightly.
While the pan heats, whisk the eggs in a bowl until well beaten. In another bowl, mix the tapioca starch with the water.

Pour the oil into the hot pan, tilting to coat evenly. Working quickly, pour in the beaten eggs, letting them spread thin across the pan. Immediately scatter the oysters and spring onion over the egg.
Let the eggs set for 1 minute without stirring, until the bottom is golden and crispy. Pour the sauce mixture around and over the eggs.

Using a spatula, gently push the omelette toward the centre as the sauce cooks, letting uncooked egg run to the edges, about 2 minutes. You want the edges lacy and crispy while the centre stays creamy.

Once the eggs are mostly set but still slightly custard-like in the centre, fold the omelette in half (or leave it open) and slide onto a plate. Drizzle with a little extra sauce and serve immediately while the edges are still QQ.

notes: Make the brandade the day before if you like; keep it covered in the fridge and bring to room temperature before serving.
The peppers can sit stuffed for a few hours. This is actually better, the flavours marry.
Quality salt cod is essential. Buy from a Spanish deli if you can; ask the owner where they get it.

steps.text: Soak the salt cod in cold water for 36 hours, changing the water every 12 hours. Rinse well, then place in a pot of cold water and bring just to a gentle simmer. Cook until the flesh flakes easily, about 15 minutes. Drain and let cool slightly, then flake finely, removing any remaining bones or skin.
Meanwhile, peel the potatoes, cut into chunks, and cook in salted boiling water until very tender, about 15 minutes. Drain well and return to the pot.

Warm the olive oil gently in a small pan over low heat. Add the sliced garlic and cook slowly, stirring often, until it just begins to turn golden and sweet, about 5 minutes, do not let it brown. Pour the oil and garlic into the potatoes.

Mash the potatoes with the garlic oil until completely smooth. Add the flaked bacalao and fold in gently, being careful not to break the fish into a paste. Season carefully with salt and white pepper, remember the salt cod has residual salt.
If using tinned piquillo peppers, drain them well on paper towels. Carefully open each pepper and spoon the bacalao brandade into it, filling gently without tearing the pepper.
Arrange the stuffed peppers on a serving plate. Serve at room temperature, drizzled lightly with a little extra virgin olive oil and a sprinkle of fresh parsley if you like.
Fill a large steamer or a pot with a steamer basket with water and bring to the boil until it is bubbling and steam is rising steadily. Pat the fish dry inside and out.

Place the fish on a piece of baking paper on the steamer rack. If using a steamer basket, brush the basket lightly with oil first. Steam over boiling water until the fish is just cooked through and the flesh flakes easily, about 12–15 minutes depending on size.
While the fish steams, whisk together the fish sauce, lime juice and palm sugar in a small bowl until the sugar dissolves.
Transfer the steamed fish to a warm serving plate. Pour the dressing over the hot fish.
Top with the fried shallots and fresh chilli slices. Scatter with coriander and serve at once.

notes: Make the dough and filling the morning before and chill separately. Shape the dumplings while they're cold.
Boiled dumplings can be frozen uncooked on a tray, then transferred to a freezer bag, boil from frozen, adding a couple of minutes to the cooking time.
Cook mince and sausages until they reach 75°C in the centre, with no pink left.

steps.text: Make the dough: mix plain flour with salt in a bowl. Pour in boiling water, stirring with chopsticks until it comes together. Once cool enough to handle, knead on an oiled surface for 10 minutes until smooth. Cover and rest for 30 minutes.

Make the filling: combine pork mince, garlic chives, soy sauce, sesame oil, ginger and water in a bowl. Mix gently with chopsticks, don't overwork it or the filling gets tough. Chill until ready to use.
Divide the dough into 16 pieces. Roll each into a ball, then flatten with your palm. Using a rolling pin or your fingers, stretch each into a 10 cm circle, keeping the edges thinner than the centre.
Place 1 tbsp filling in the centre of each circle. Fold in half to make a half-moon, pinching the edges to seal. Then bring the two pointed ends together and press to seal, forming a purse shape.

Bring a large pot of salted water to a boil. Working in batches, gently drop dumplings in and stir so they don't stick. Once they float, simmer for 2–3 minutes more. Remove with a slotted spoon and drain well.

Heat 2 tbsp oil in a large frying pan over high heat. Arrange dumplings flat-side down and fry without moving for 3–4 minutes until golden and crisp. Pour in 120 ml water, cover, and steam for 2 minutes. Uncover, let the water evaporate, and fry for another minute until the base is crispy again.
Serve hot with soy sauce or chilli oil for dipping.

notes: The quenelle mixture can be made up to 4 hours ahead and kept chilled.
If you can't find Madeira, use a good dry sherry instead.
Don't rush the butter-whisking at the end, add it slowly off the heat to keep the sauce silky.
Cook chicken until it reaches 75°C in the thickest part and the juices run clear.

steps.text: Process the chicken liver, softened butter, cream, egg yolks, shallot, salt, pepper and nutmeg until smooth. Chill for at least 20 minutes.
Heat the stock in a wide shallow pan to a bare simmer, it should barely bubble. Bring the Madeira to a simmer in a separate small saucepan and add the tomato paste, stirring until it dissolves.

Using two warm, wet soup spoons (dip them in hot water and dry well), shape the liver mixture into rough ovals and gently slide them into the simmering stock. Work in batches of 4 or 5. Poach for 4 to 5 minutes, they should rise and feel just firm.
Remove the poached quenelles carefully with a slotted spoon to a warm plate. Strain the poaching liquid into a saucepan (discard the solids if any).
Add the Madeira mixture to the poaching liquid and simmer for 3 minutes. Whisk in the cornflour mixture and simmer gently, stirring, until the sauce thickens slightly, about 2 minutes.
Remove from heat. Whisk in the cold butter cubes one or two at a time until the sauce is glossy and silky. Taste and adjust the seasoning.
Gently reheat the quenelles in the sauce for 1 minute. Divide among warm bowls, spoon the sauce over and finish with a pinch of fleur de sel.

notes: Make ahead: sambar keeps well in the fridge for up to 3 days and tastes even better the next day as the flavours deepen. Reheat gently on the stove.
Vegetable swap: use whatever you have, pumpkin, beans, carrots and drumstick are all traditional. Avoid watery vegetables like tomato.
If you have a pressure cooker, this halves the time: toast the spices, cook the base (steps 2–3), then pressure cook for 5 minutes once steaming.

steps.text: Toast the cumin seeds, coriander seeds, black pepper and dried chillies in a dry pan over medium heat for 1 minute, shaking the pan, until fragrant. Set aside to cool, then grind to a powder with a mortar and pestle. Stir in the chilli powder.
Heat the oil in a large heavy-based pot over medium heat. Add the onion and garlic, and cook, stirring, until the onion is soft and golden, about 5 minutes.
Add the asafoetida and toasted spice powder, and stir for 30 seconds until fragrant.

Add the lentils, vegetables, tamarind paste, water and salt. Stir well, then bring to a simmer. Cook uncovered for 20 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the lentils have broken down and the vegetables are very tender.
Stir in the torn curry leaves and cook for another 2 minutes. Taste and adjust the salt and tamarind to your liking, the stew should be tangy and well-seasoned. Serve hot with steamed rice or dosa.

notes: Barramundi, snapper and bream all work beautifully. Avoid oily fish like mackerel here, the flavour's too strong for this delicate broth.
If green papaya is hard to find, use a green mango or even just leave it out. The soup is just as good with more greens instead.
Make the stock the day before if you want the broth to sit overnight in the fridge. Reheat gently before serving.

Make the stock infusion up to an hour ahead; the flavours only get better. Add the fish just before serving.
If you can't find fresh Thai basil, use regular basil, but add it at the last second so it doesn't wilt into the broth.
Barramundi is perfect here because it's sweet and holds its shape, but snapper, bream or any firm white fish works.
